en: The Preface and Examples for the Commentary on the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra state:
"In the past, when I read the text and commentary of the *Miaojing*, it was as if I were reading from memory;

yet, upon seeing that the various fascicles did not accord with the fundamental unity [of the work], I was struck by this discrepancy. Why is this so? It is because the structural conventions of commentaries and records in antiquity were not those of later generations."
This is comparable to the manner of those who later produced commentaries (*zhùjiě*), who intentionally carved out sections of the text to fit them into their notes;
and to those of antiquity who produced sub-commentaries (*shūjì*), who intentionally intended for the sutra and its commentary to circulate separately.
Indeed, ancient sub-commentaries were like a vast landscape painting on a single large scroll; suppose there were someone who cut it apart...
Having separated them, they are arranged in sequence; if their arrangement does not lose its order, then the purpose is not lost.
However, their momentum has already declined. If that momentum is obscured, then those who observe them may perhaps become confused.
This is because the commentaries of later generations are like small paintings on silk scrolls hung upon a wall; each scroll possesses its own distinct momentum.
When [the teachings] are exhausted, their contemplation becomes complete; thus, this is a convergence of the fundamental [teachings].
It is certainly not something of antiquity, yet the various sections such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Avataṃsaka* encompass the three [vehicles] and their volumes are vast.
If one converges [these teachings], there are few who would not find benefit for those of initial capacity. Now, this commentary on the present sutra encompasses only two [vehicles], yet...
The volumes are small; to assemble them would yield little benefit and much harm.
Thus, it was truly not something that could be undertaken through assembly, yet now they have been assembled. Why? Because there was no other way.
It appears that the original edition by Lin [Muxi] once borrowed a copy from the collection of an ancient monastery and had a scribe transcribe it for him.
Having transcribed it, I wished to have both the sutra and its commentary carved together, but the required funds were divided among various associations.
As for me, I am like one who stands by the side of a national character, looking at a painting before it has been completed;

I say that it would be better to have it carved as a single edition alone, for in this way one may truly grasp the intention of the author—is this not excellent? Yet those people merely responded with "yes, yes" and withdrew.
Thus one might say, "Alas! Alas! for in the end they refuse me. I say: "Sigh! If you will not hold a meeting, then you shall not have it engraved.
Yet, this is to take the magnificent treasure of his teaching and, having cast it aside into a chest, merely provide fodder for hungry bookworms.
This is indeed a pity; rather than not holding a meeting, it would be better to let it circulate in the world."
Who could have foreseen that such a combination would result in harm? This is what is meant by "that which could not be avoided.
Therefore, in our current assembly, we must strive not to fracture the meaning of the text, and none dare pursue mere branches or categories to divide and prune it.
I have heard it said that even when one constructs a wheel with a thousand wonders and a hundred designs, there still remains work yet undone; such is my own meager talent and flawed execution.
How rare are those who do not err! This is merely what is called "sweeping the path with a broom in anticipation of the dust.
It is almost as if a gentleman were to enter this field and furthermore investigate it, even drilling into its depths.
This sutra also uses the Huangbo edition from our country; its fourteen chapters are divided into three fascicles—designated as Upper, Middle, and Lower.
While the Upper Fascicle bears two titles presented side by side, the Middle and Lower Fascicles bear only the single title *The Sutra Spoken by Vimalakīrti*.
The current combined edition separates these into five fascicles; therefore, it follows the commentary accordingly.
Since this fascicle was compiled according to the commentary (*śāstra*), the titles "Fascicle One" and "Part One" have been removed from the beginning of the sutra,
and no further sutra titles are provided thereafter. Furthermore, where characters in the sutra text differ from those cited in the commentary,
these discrepancies are marked above the grid.
This is the name of the translator; it originally appeared at the beginning of each fascicle of the scripture.
Since the present edition no longer divides the fascicles according to the scripture, it has been placed here alone at the head of the volume.

The original commentary consisted of five fascicles. However, the *Koryo Chejonggyeongjang Chongnok* (Catalogue of the Tripitaka of the Heavenly Dharma Master of Koryo) states that there were twelve or six fascicles of Ji-zang’s *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-śāstra*.

It is likely that the number of fascicles was altered for this reason. As for the version in six fascicles, it appears to have been compiled by combining the topical outlines (*kōdai*) into a single scroll.
Furthermore, there is a record stating: "I once read an old edition of this teaching from our own country..."

As for the *Zhanglu*, it contains details that were not fully elaborated upon in the Master’s two commentaries—the extensive and the abridged—and while the titles of the original versions were not uniform—some calling it a "Commentary" (*shu*), some a "Meaning-Commentary" (*yishu*), and others an "Abridged Commentary" (*lieshu*)—we have now preserved each according to its original form in its respective location.
As for its structural character, it ought properly to be titled the "Abridged Commentary. Indeed, such is this commentary.
It has gradually reached our land, occurring at a pivotal moment of a thousand years, and its carving in wood truly begins this very day.
Now, the title at the head of the main text is *The Sūtra Spoken by Vimalakīrti* (also titled *The Inconceivable Liberation*), and this is the first fascicle of the commentary (*śāstra*).
Regarding the title of the sūtra, the words "Fascicle One" (*juan shang*) have been removed; regarding the title of the commentary, the words "Vimalakīrti Sūtra" (*Weimo jing*) have been removed.
The character "之" (zhī) is used to form the title by combining [the scripture's name with the word "commentary"]. From the second fascicle onwards, the title of the commentary alone is cited;

thus, it no longer follows the scripture and is detached from its fascicles. Regarding the three names of the commentary, only the term "commentary" (shū) is employed as its heading, which is done to preserve the ancient tradition.
As for the titles of the chapters (pǐn), they remain as they were in the original version of the commentary, which circulated separately. Now...
Furthermore, because I weary of prolixity, I have merely demarcated the boundaries of the sections and have not further distinguished them by their respective practices.
Regarding the commentary on the scriptural text, I did not dare to compose it in the same style as the text itself, nor did I differentiate it by varying the size of the characters;
rather, the commentary is distinguished from the scriptural text by setting the characters of the commentary lower by one space.
In recent times, various masters of holy practice have compiled editions of the various sections, placing the topical outline (ke-mon) first, followed by the sutra text, and finally the commentaries;
consequently, errors and discrepancies have become numerous. Why is this so?

It is because in antiquity, when producing commentaries, one necessarily set forth the topical outline separately; thus, in their exegesis, they did not cite the outline within the commentary itself, but treated them as distinct entities.

The *zi-ke* (son-section) is also a derivative of the *zi-ke*, yet it stands alone; the *mu-ke* (mother-section) likewise follows the names of the registers (*dian-ke*), directly exhausting the meaning of the text.
All of these arise because the *ke-wen* (section-texts) have branched out separately.

Consequently, when later generations view the *ke-wen*, they treat them like discarded hair-bands (*bian-mao*), for the most part failing to preserve them. Alas! They do not even know that they exist.

For this reason, what was previously categorized as erroneous need not be further classified here. As for the preceding scriptures, I have arranged them according to my ability so that the text may be clearly organized.
Since I did not dare to analyze the scriptural text in minute detail, I have generally concluded the intermediate branches with the character "分" (fen).
This is intended to make them easy to see, as the scriptural text and its commentary are otherwise separated by great distance.
Regarding those sections that are difficult to correlate, headings are established at the top of the grid to facilitate easy interpretation.
The *Sū* (Commentary) is that which provides profound exegesis of the major chapters; circles are placed at the beginning of each chapter to indicate the start of its commentary.
Regarding the characters in this commentary, there may be those that are superfluous or redundant, and there may be those that have been omitted or lost;
yet, at present, no other excellent edition exists with which to collate them. If gentlemen of the world can obtain a superior copy, I pray they will undertake a comparative examination of it.
As for the original text of this commentary, its script is archaic and coarse, featuring many variant characters;
I judge it to be a copy of a manuscript from the Sui or Tang dynasties that has not been altered by later scholars.
Setting aside its status as a magnificent treasure within the Dharma, it is surely a rare marvel of the world. If there are scholars who delight in antiquity and behold it, how could they—?
I hope that these may still hold as much weight as the *yufan* jade of Lu.
Currently, regarding the characters in this text, scribes have altered them in five or six cases out of ten, making it impossible to restore them to their original form. Alas!
As for those remaining, I have marked them at the top of each column, noting: "So-and-so is identical," or "So-and-so is a variant form."
In these commentaries, there is a great deal of reliance on phonetic loans (jiǎjiè) for the sake of reading;

now, as I read them privately, I have marked these instances above the characters. However, the reason why these commentaries particularly abound in such loans for reading is somewhat suspicious and strange.
Why is this? It is said that there are two reasons for this. The first is: "As for the various sections that have circulated in the world, they are..."
Those who came after have frequently altered the text by carving it with errors or emending it through their own interpretations; my current commentary does not do so, for this reason.

Second, it is because those who were literate at that time wrote it down with a desire for antiquity and elegance, intending that readers should attain its meaning only through deep and contemplative study, rather than reading it carelessly and superficially, lest they fall into error.
One must exhaustively examine what the commentators have employed; yet, as for the characters in ancient commentaries (*zhāngshū*), they are frequently read using phonetic loans (*jiǎjiè*).
This is often the case. For instance, *xiāo* is used for *tiē*, *yǐng* for *qíng*, and *dé* for *dé* (this is so;

these three examples appear in the Tiantai *Fahua shu*). Furthermore, *xìng* is used for *xìng*, *yuān* for *quán*, and *dài* for *dé* (this is so; these three examples appear in the Cien *Weishi shu*).
Their categories are beyond counting; if this is the case for official memorials, it is surely no different for the sutras and śāstras—how could one then cease to apply one's mind to them?
Furthermore, among the old transcriptions, there are instances where "shi" (釋) was written as "chi" (尺), or "bian" (辨) as "bian" (弁), and so forth.
That people today deride such usage as vulgar corruption is perhaps due to a lack of discernment.

Is this not a book? It is the very basis by which people steal its reading. Is it not through awakening that one becomes profoundly enlightened, and thereby surveys the commentaries and exegeses of all sections?
Wherein lies anything other than this marvelous efficacy?

This is like Lu Xun’s binding of torches to attack a single camp first, thereby suddenly understanding the method for breaking Shu; how could there be anything else? I am merely [expressing] my own [insight].
How could a person of but a peck or a pint’s capacity, who has carelessly collated this text and arrogantly overstepped his bounds, truly find peace? How could he escape his transgressions?
How could he escape his transgressions?
Recorded by the śramaṇa Shi Dao-kong on the day of Gengzi in the second month of the year Wuyin of the Yuanlu period.

Commentary on the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra (also titled the Acintyavimokṣa Sūtra), Fascicle One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty by Imperial Decree.
Composed by Hu Jizang.
Chapter One: On the Buddha-lands.
Regarding Vimalakīrti, we revere his person; regarding the inconceivable liberation, we honor the Dharma.
Now, the ultimate resonance is wordless, yet the profound scriptures are spread far and wide; the Dharma-body has no form, yet it pervades all things.
Because resonance gives rise to form, there is nothing that is not spoken though no words are uttered, and nothing that is not manifested though no image exists.
Because there is nothing that is not spoken though no words are uttered, the great net of the Teaching is spread across the flow of birth and death;

because there is nothing that is not manifested though no image exists, he dwells as one with the wisdom of a child, playing within the five realms of existence. Therefore, this sutra presents both the person and the Dharma together, as does the Vimalakīrti.
As for "Ji" (詰), here it is called "Jingming" (淨名). Because pure virtue fills his inner being and the sound of joy pervades the world outside, he is thus named Jingming.
It is not merely that he subdues demons and resentment or restrains various non-Buddhists;
rather, five hundred śrāvakas confessed their own lack of eloquence and eight thousand bodhisattvas were unable to respond. At that time, those who spoke of the Dharma found themselves at a loss.
Because they contemplate liberation, they unify all practices by taking skillful wisdom as primary; because they plant the roots of virtue, they take the six perfections as their foundation;
because they rescue the ignorant, they take compassion as their foremost priority; and because they speak of the ultimate truth, they take non-duality as their discourse.

Thus, they can embrace the celestial bodies within their robes and grasp the great trichiliocosm with their hands; they borrow a seat from the King of Lamps and request a meal from the Buddha of Infinite Light.
The Fragrant Land is vast and boundless; it acts without acting and there is nothing it does not do. It knows not how it comes to be so, yet it is able to be so—this is the inconceivable liberation.
Furthermore, this sutra is the very marrow of the Mahāyāna and the lard for the *vaipulya* teachings.
Therefore, Master Sengrui sighed, saying: "Other [sutras] inspire the mind and enlighten the ignorant as this one does. Moreover, Sengzhao...

The Preface states: This is the most wondrous and sublime designation for that which exhausts the source and completes the transformations. His family was poor, and he constantly made his living by hiring out to copy books.
He regularly read the works of Laozi and Zhuangzi, often sighing with deep emotion: "How beautiful, how supremely beautiful!

Yet, while these allow the spirit to roam within the methods of profound principle, they do not yet reach the ultimate perfection. Later, upon seeing this scripture, he immediately received and upheld it with the highest reverence, saying: [text continues]
A close friend said, "I know the ultimate place of refuge. He then immediately left the household life and encountered Master Shi in Chang'an, where he received instruction;
he was ordained by Master Zhaor, and Master Rui awakened him—these all occurred because of this sutra. Therefore, the Great Sutra says: "Sentient beings have many spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra);
they do not belong to a single land, nor do they arise from a single condition or teaching; indeed, there are immeasurable virtues [in them]."
Although the gates of the teachings of infinite knowledge are indeed infinite, the true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) for sentient beings are the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
These Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are the spiritual friends of persons; the teachings spoken by these Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are the spiritual friends of the Dharma.
Therefore, spiritual friends do not transcend these two types—persons and the Dharma—and yet one encounters them.
Furthermore, spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) are not like the case of a single person meeting immeasurable people, or immeasurable people meeting a single person;
there are four permutations. The first permutation—where a single person meets immeasurable [friends]—is exemplified by Sudhana entering the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*):
beginning with his initial vision of Mañjuśrī and subsequently encountering Maitreya, he met one hundred and ten spiritual friends, and further encountered three thousand great [beings].

If each of the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), numbering as many as the atoms within a thousand-fold world system, were to each teach a single Dharma gate, there would then be as many Dharma gates as the atoms within a three-thousandfold great thousand-fold world system;

thus, one person encounters the immeasurable. As for the immeasurable persons encountering one, it is like immeasurable sentient beings encountering a single Buddha or a single Bodhisattva, and so forth.

The two phrases may be understood [as explained above] (and so forth). However, because Sudhana dwells within a pure land where many bodhisattvas preach the Dharma, he encounters numerous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

In contrast, in this defiled land of Sahā, only the Buddha and those such as Vimalakīrti and Śrīmālā preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings as spiritual friends. Here, we shall briefly address the remaining phrases for now.
Clarity and purity are called the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) for sentient beings;

Vimalakīrti is the person who serves as that spiritual friend, and the inconceivable liberation (*acintyavimokṣa*) is the Dharma that serves as that spiritual friend. Therefore, by encountering the person and receiving the Dharma, all may attain awakening to the Way.
However, since the textual versions of this sutra differ, we shall now establish a single, standardized arrangement that transcends the Northern and Southern traditions.
The past is distinct from the present; how so? From the beginning, the text is divided into three sections: the Introduction, the Main Body, and the Dissemination.

Specifically, the first four chapters constitute the Introduction, beginning from the "Questions of Mañjuśrī" and ending with the "Gandhavyūha. The next six chapters constitute the Main Body, beginning from the "Bodhisattvacaryā" chapter and continuing through the end of the sutra.
The remaining sections constitute the Dissemination. The reason for making this judgment is based on the "Indoor" [classification].

Because it occurs outside [the house], it is divided into these sections. Since this sutra is titled the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, that which takes place within Vimalakīrti’s chamber is considered the primary section;
what was previously taught outside the chamber serves as the introduction, and what is subsequently taught outside the chamber serves as the dissemination—this has been the traditional usage.
What I shall now clarify is that while the *Avataṃsaka* consists of seven locations and eight assemblies, this sutra contains two.
Regarding the statement that there are two locations within the four assemblies: the "two locations" refers to the Garden of Āmra (Āmrapālīvana) and the private quarters (vāsagṛha).
Regarding the "four assemblies," there are two for the Garden of Āmra and two for the private quarters. As for the two instances in the Garden of Āmra:

in the *Buddhakṣetraparivarta*, the fourfold assembly all gathered and the eight classes of beings assembled like clouds; the Buddha preached the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land and commanded his disciples and bodhisattvas to inquire about purity.

The "Illness" refers to the single assembly at the Āmrapālī Grove, from the "Bodhisattva Conduct" chapter onward, when Mañjuśrī, Vimalakīrti, and the great assembly of devas and nāgas went to the Buddha’s dwelling;
this is the second assembly at the Āmrapālī Grove. Regarding the two "Vihāras":
the first is the "Expedient Means" chapter, prior to the command to inquire after the illness, when Vimalakīrti manifested his illness as a householder.
Countless thousands of kings all went to inquire after his illness; Vimalakīrti, on account of his own physical ailment, preached the Dharma for them—this was the first assembly in the chamber.

Subsequently, the Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī to go [to inquire after his illness], and eight thousand bodhisattvas followed Mañjuśrī as they entered the chamber to inquire after his illness—this was another assembly. Now, regarding this...
These two locations refer to the two locations of the monastic and the lay, and the two locations of the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas;

they are the expedient means of the monastic and the lay, and the expedient means of the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas (and so forth). Question: Regarding the two assemblies at the Āmra grove, how do these two assemblies differ?

And regarding the two gatherings at the Vihāra, how do these two gatherings differ? Explanation: These two locations and two assemblies are both distinct. To speak of the difference between the two assemblies at the Āmra grove: [text continues].

The difference between the extensive and the abbreviated versions is as follows: the initial abbreviated version clarifies the dharma-gate of the causes and effects of the Pure Land for the sake of the original assembly alone;

the subsequent extensive version, however, clarifies the bodhisattva practices in detail for both the guest and the original assemblies. Furthermore, regarding the differences between the two assemblies at the Venerable’s quarters:
the first merely teaches two dharma-gates—first, the faults and afflictions of birth and death, and second, the merits of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.

That is to say, the latter assembly follows the two preceding assemblies by immediately urging, drawing forth, praising, and criticizing; it subsequently provides an extensive exposition on various dharmas, such as the inconceivable, and so forth.

Furthermore, the people differ from the first assembly: whereas the former consisted only of kings, elders, and hundreds of thousands of people—being exclusively laypeople and belonging solely to the manifest assembly—the latter assembly includes both monastics and laity, comprising both the hidden and the manifest congregations; therefore, there are four assemblies.

It is the same; although there are distinctions between the two locations and four assemblies, when condensed into three sections, they still constitute the Introduction, the Main Body, and the Circulation.
These three chapters differ from traditional interpretations. Traditionally, the distinction was made between the "inner" and "outer" [sections], but here it is not so.
Regarding these three chapters: from the beginning until the conclusion of the verses is the Introduction; from the section on Ratnakūṭa... [text continues].

Question: Having concluded the discussion on the causes and effects of the Pure Land, does the "Chapter on Dharma Offerings" properly belong to the main body of the text, while the "Chapter on Entrusting" constitutes the circulation?
Question: What fault is there in the traditional judgment that distinguishes between the "internal" and "external" sections, such that you would suddenly reject it?
Explanation: There is a great error. Why? If you take the first four chapters as the "external" introductory section, only then...
Where, then, is the "Expedient Means" chapter (*upāya-paṭala*) said to have been taught? It cannot be said that the "Expedient Means" chapter was taught outside the hall.
This "Expedient Means" chapter is for Mañjuśrī to speak to those who have come to inquire after the illness; how could it possibly have been taught outside the hall?

If it were taught inside the hall, it should have been designated as the formal discourse (*samyag-deśanā*); why then is it judged to be the introduction (*nidāna*)? Second, from the preceding section up to the "Dharma-offering" (*dharma-pūjā*).
The "Chapter on Cultivation" clarifies the contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) of the Bodhisattva; how could it possibly be considered a chapter for circulation? Why is this so?

The first four chapters clarify the practices for the Pure Land; the "Expedient Means" chapter破除 (destroys) the delusions of ordinary beings; the subsequent two chapters on the Disciples and the Bodhisattvas destroy the illnesses of the sages.
Since there are great and small illnesses among the sages, and this being the case, how can these be considered the Prologue? The latter part clarifies the conduct of the Bodhisattva.
How could the "Dharma-gate of Distinguishing the Exhaustible and the Inexhaustible" possibly be merely for the purpose of circulation?

Furthermore, regarding what you said—that the interior and exterior of the room constitute the introduction and the main body—this conceals the meaning while manifesting the facts. To "manifest the facts" means to judge by way of the room;
thus, it manifests the facts but does not adopt the meaning. To "divide the text" means to conceal the meaning; however, here we do take the meaning and divide the text.
If one merely attains the meaning and further attains the meaning of each individual phenomenon, both are simultaneously clarified;

since both are simultaneously lost [otherwise], one should not judge based on the distinction between "inside" and "outside" the room. Question: Who made this judgment regarding the division of "inside" and "outside"? Answer:

It is explained that while the *Mūlasarvāstivāda* is the fundamental *Vinaya*, the *Sarvāstivāda* was subsequently employed by Zhāngchí; therefore, it cannot be relied upon. Question: If that is so...
Question: For what reason did the Great Master employ this interpretation? Answer: The Master merely made this statement for a particular occasion;
how could it be intended as a permanent, fixed rule? Question: Upon what basis do you make this judgment? Answer:
This is a tradition handed down by the ancients, an old teaching from Guanzhong. Why is this so? As Master Sengzhao said: "This sutra begins with the Pure Land and concludes with..."
Although the phrasing of the "Dharma-offering" (dharmapūjā) differs, its inconceivable essence is one.

Since the first six matters are placed at the beginning as a brief introduction and the subsequent entrustment (*parindanā*) is at the end, we know that the first six matters constitute the introduction (*nidāna*), the final entrustment constitutes the dissemination (*pravartana*), and the intermediate "inconceivable" section constitutes the main body (*śarīra*).
Master Sengzhao personally consulted with Master Kumārajīva; after completing his commentary on this sutra, he sent it to Liu Yao via Tanung.
The Relics-Remnant (Yimin) said: "Though my words are not elegant, their meaning is grounded in a source. For this reason, this judgment may be relied upon.
Among the three types of prefaces, this is now the 'Introductory Preface' (*nidāna*). Within this chapter, it is subsequently divided into two:

first, the General Introduction (*sāmānyanidāna*); second, the Specific Introduction (*viśeṣanidāna*). The several meanings of the general and specific [prefaces] have already been explained as in the records of other sutras."
(Question: It has been stated that since this is an introductory exposition, it ought to be titled the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*).

Why, then, is it titled the "Chapter on the Buddha-land" (*Buddhakṣetra-parivarta*)? (Answer: The explanation is as follows: Chapters (*parivarta*) are titles assigned by later generations; what fixed rule is there for them?

Sometimes they are named according to what precedes, sometimes according to what follows, and sometimes according to the subject matter or the meaning. In this case, the name is derived from what follows, and the title is established according to its meaning. Therefore...
Regarding the "Chapter on the Buddha-land" (*Buddhakṣetraparivarta*): it further clarifies that this chapter primarily elucidates principles (*artha*) and only slightly elucidates matters (*vastu*).

As for "principles," they refer to the dharma-gate of the causes and effects of the Pure Land; because this chapter extensively elucidates these principles, it is titled "Chapter on the Buddha-land" based on what is predominant.

Question: Why is it not called the "Chapter on the Pure Land" (*Śuddhakṣetraparivarta*)? Explanation: The term "Buddha-land" (*buddhakṣetra*) is a general designation, whereas "Pure Land" (*śuddhakṣetra*) is a specific one.
The general term encompasses the particular, whereas the particular does not include the general; thus, it is named after the general and not designated by the particular.
To speak of the "Buddha-land" in its general sense, one simply says "Buddha-land," for whether pure or impure, all lands are none other than the Buddha-land.
If one speaks of the "Pure Land," one obtains only the pure and does not encompass the impure. For this reason, "Buddha-land" is the general term, while "Pure Land" is the particular.

Furthermore, it is named based on the manifest phenomena that obscure [the mind]; since among these obscurations there are Buddha-lands of the ten directions, some pure and some defiled, one can only refer to them as "Buddha-realms" (*buddhakṣetra*) without designating them specifically as "pure lands. Moreover, it is named based on the causes and conditions of the lands as taught by the Buddha to Ratnakūṭa;
herein, it clarifies that not only is purity explained, but defilement is also distinguished. Thus the text says: "One should..."
In which lands does one give rise to the roots of bodhisattvahood and thereby take up a buddha-field?
By means of which lands does one enter the wisdom of a Buddha and thereby take up a buddha-field? If it is thus, then one clarifies both pure and impure lands to benefit sentient beings:
if sentient beings should see purity, one manifests purity; if they should see impurity, one manifests impurity. This is precisely according to what is appropriate for sentient beings.
He immediately manifested the land; it was not that he responded exclusively to Ratnarāja by failing to manifest the earth and sand.
For this reason, it is merely titled "The Buddha-land" (*buddhakṣetra*) rather than "Pure Land" (*śuddhakṣetra*). Question: Why is this chapter called "The Chapter on the Buddha-land"?

Is it named after the manifestation of the land by the Tathāgata when Ratnākara previously offered his canopy? Or is it named after the Tathāgata’s subsequent clarification of the causes and conditions of the Pure Land?

Regarding the title *Yajie* (Ya-jie), it is explained that this chapter possesses these two meanings; because it elucidates these two matters, it is named after them, hence the title "Chapter on the Buddha-land.
Thus it is: "Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Āmra Grove in Vaiśālī."
That which is thus is the first part of the introductory sequence. Regarding these six matters, they have already been explained in detail elsewhere;
here, I shall explain them briefly. As for "thus" (*evam*), although there are many interpretations, they do not exceed the two criteria of "conjunction" and "separation.
To explain this according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma is entered through faith and realized through wisdom."
To be able to transcend such [states] is faith (*śraddhā*). Although there are these two expressions, they are collectively termed "faith.
That which is "thus" is faith; that which is "not thus" is non-faith. What dharma does faith believe in?
It believes in the dharma of inconceivable liberation (*acintya-vimokṣa*); this is faith in inconceivable liberation. The *Vasubandhu-sūtra* says: "That which is 'thus' is decisive."
This establishes the certainty that Ānanda transmitted the Buddha’s words exactly as they were. Regarding the term "is" (*shi*):
traditionally it has been said that the text and the principle are two distinct things; when they correspond, it is called "like" (*ru*), and when there is no discrepancy, it is called "is.

This clarifies that because Ānanda spoke in accordance with what the Buddha spoke, it is called "like" (*ru*); and because the principle of what Ānanda spoke does not differ from the Buddha’s principle, it is called "is" (*shi*).
Furthermore, Emperor Wu of Liang stated that such a text is what was spoken by the Buddha;
he also said that "thus" (evam) means that because it is exactly as spoken by the Buddha, it is therefore what was spoken by the Buddha—hence the term "evam" (thus).

Regarding "Thus have I heard," which clarifies the person who transmits the sutras: there are three types of "Thus have I heard. First, there is that which was actually heard, yet one says, "Thus have I heard.
Second, there is that which was not heard, yet one says, "Thus have I heard. Third, there is that which was both heard and not heard, yet one says, "Thus have I heard.

As for the case where it was heard and one says, "Thus have I heard," this refers to those such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, whose compilers attended the Buddha from beginning to end and received the teachings directly from him.
Because it is the literal meaning of the sound, one says "I have heard" even when one has not actually heard;

that is, when the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* describes the time of the Parinirvāṇa, Ānanda was not present at the assembly and was confused by Māra, yet even though he did not hear the preaching of the *Nirvāṇa*, the sūtra nonetheless begins with "Thus have I heard.
This is precisely what it means to say "I have heard" despite not having heard it at that time.

Regarding the phrase "I have heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*): it refers to those who have both heard and not heard. Those who say "I have heard" are precisely those who were previously in the Āmrapālī Grove personally attending the Tathāgata;

thus, they have indeed heard. Furthermore, before he was commanded to inquire after the illness, there were kings, elders, and countless thousands of people who inquired after his illness and he preached the Dharma for them, yet Ānanda did not hear this. Next, there was Mañjuśrī with eight thousand bodhisattvas.
Five hundred śrāvakas, along with the eight classes of devas and humans, all went together to inquire after his illness, yet Ānanda did not even hear [them].
This was because he was not within the inner chamber. Later in the text, Ānanda asks the Tathāgata, "What is this fragrance?
The Buddha replies, "This is the fragrance of the fragrant rice eaten by that bodhisattva; it is the fragrance from his pores. If it were otherwise...
Because it is so, we know that Ānanda was not within the inner chamber; this is because there were two assemblies where he heard twice and did not hear once.

Thus, it is both hearing and not hearing that is referred to as "I have heard. Question: It is understandable to refer to what one has heard as "I have heard," but since there was something he did not hear, how can it also be called "I have heard"?
Answer: Although he did not hear [it], Ānanda [was present] at a distance.

Because he has received [the teachings], he is entitled to say, "I have heard. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Ānanda, as a man of great learning (*bahuśruta*), shall naturally understand and comprehend.
The *Mahāvajragarbha Sūtra* states: "Ānanda has attained the Samādhi of Awakening to the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).

How could it be that he does not hear [the teachings] yet does not comprehend them in advance? Furthermore, the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā Sūtra* states: "Ānanda has attained the dhyāna of non-forgetfulness; the Buddha has awakened him."
This is obscure. Furthermore, Shi Dao’an stated that Ānanda attained the Buddha-mind Samādhi.

According to the *Bao’en jing* (Sūtra on Repaying Kindness), when Ānanda served as the attendant, he sought four vows; the final vow was: "Regarding the sūtras I have not yet heard, I pray that the Buddha will speak them for me once more.
If this is so, then although he did not hear them previously, he subsequently obtained them again. Moreover, regarding this hearing...
To hear the inconceivable Dharma is itself inconceivable hearing; this inconceivable hearing is to hear by means of non-hearing.
Now, there were three Ānandas who upheld the Tripiṭaka, and there was yet another Ānanda who upheld the Tripiṭaka.
This present Ānanda has been a companion to the Buddha; because Śākyamuni was diligent and he was of great learning, he became the Buddha’s Ānanda.
He upholds the Buddha-dharma. [The interlocutor] asks: "If that is so, what was the intention behind his reprimand? [The Master] explains: "It was for the sake of opening the Way together.

However, the Way itself is neither gain nor loss; it is only those who can gain or lose [it]. He who speaks of the inconceivable is named the Layman; he who upholds the inconceivable is named Ānanda."
"Once upon a time" (ekasmin samaye) refers to the third matter; this is not a single instance, but now it shall be briefly elucidated. "Once upon a time" may be understood in two senses:
first, the time when the conditions of the faculties (*indriya*) were awakened; second, the time when Ānanda attained realization.
The awakening of the conditions of the faculties is precisely this [primary] time, whereas Ānanda’s realization of this meaning is secondary. Why is this so? As follows:
The purpose of coming to that teaching is precisely to develop sentient beings; it is for this reason that the Bodhisattva expounds the teaching. This intention is the primary meaning.
If Ānanda has attained realization, it is simply so that he may establish others in faith after the Tathāgata has passed away.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "It is by speaking of the time, place, and person that people are led to believe. Therefore, this is secondary. Furthermore...
Master Zhaò said: "The Dharma King has initiated his auspicious career; this is a time of sublime gathering. As for "Buddha," it is the fourth matter.
"Buddha" refers to the Master who expounds the teachings. In foreign lands [Sanskrit] they say *buddha*; here [in China] it is translated as "the Awakened One" (*jùzhě*).
Foreigners designate the Buddha as the "Celestial Drum. Why is this? Among the Thirty-three Heavens there is a drum; when thieves approach, [the drum sounds].
However, even when the "Crying Thief" departs, he cries; at that time, the various devas are as courageous as the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma, as explained in other passages (etc.).
In the city of Vaiśālī, the fifth section below clarifies the dwelling place, which is also called the country of Vaiśālī. This is...
Among the six great cities, it is one great city; among the sixteen great nations, it is one great nation.
Vaiśālī—also called Viśālī or Vṛśālī—is here translated as "Vast, Pure, and Adorned," also as "Excellent Rice," and further as "Excellent Accomplishment.
One should understand that there are two locations, general and specific, broad and narrow. The Āmra Garden refers specifically to the latter.
The location is also called the Āmrapālī Garden. This matter is similar to that of the Jeta Grove;
while the Jeta Grove was purchased by the Elder Anāthapiṇḍika to build a vihāra for the Buddha, this place was offered by Āmrapālī herself to build a vihāra for the Buddha.
Furthermore, there were six vihāras in Rājagṛha, whereas there are three vihāras in Vaiśālī, one of which is located within the city.
The inner name is Mihuòtuó (Mihodha), located south of the city; this was the multi-storied lecture hall (*kūṭāgāra-śālā*).
Today it is located north of the city, two *li* away, and is called the Nalanda Garden Monastery (*Nalanda-vihāra*).
The circumstances regarding Nalanda are found in the *Nalanda-sūtra*, as explained therein.
○ Regarding the section "The Great Assembly of Bhikṣus" below, the sixth item: Now, there are two types of assemblies.

First, those that testify to Ānanda’s freedom from the error of hearsay, so as to inspire confidence in later generations. Since it was previously stated, "Thus have I heard," this implies either that Ānanda heard it himself or that he heard it together with others.
If he had heard it alone, it might not be fully trustworthy; for this reason, the assembly of co-hearers is now listed.

This clarifies that Ānanda did not hear [the teaching] alone, but heard it together with immeasurable people; this serves as a witness to prove that Ānanda was free from the error of hearsay, and thus he is trustworthy.
Second, previously it was clarified that the Buddha is the teacher who expounds the doctrine and the Āmrapālī Grove is the place where the doctrine is expounded;
now, by listing the assembly, the text identifies those for whom the teaching is intended. Within this context, the listing of the assembly serves as follows:

Second, regarding the assembly in the first row, there are two parts: first, the assembly that takes its place, and second, the assembly that forms the connection. Within the assembly that takes its place, there are three sections:

first, the listing of the *śrāvakas*; second, the listing of the *bodhisattvas*; and third, the listing of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Although they do not follow a sequential order, there is a numerical significance:

first, it is to demonstrate that the teaching clarifies the superiority of both the mind and the form of the *śrāvaka*, and thus places them before the *bodhisattva*, whose mind alone is not yet fixed in superiority.
Because their physical forms are inferior, ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) occupy a middle position; because both [physical form and spiritual capacity] are inferior, they are placed last.

Second, *śrāvakas* delight in *nirvāṇa* and fear *saṃsāra*, whereas ordinary persons delight in *saṃsāra* and fear *nirvāṇa*. *Śrāvakas* abide in *nirvāṇa* while ordinary persons are stuck in *saṃsāra*; both are thus extremes.
Because they represent these two extremes, they are placed before and after [the Bodhisattvas]. Bodhisattvas do not cling to either extreme.
Because it occupies a middle position, the text states: "It is not the practice of ordinary beings, nor is it the practice of noble ones; it is the practice of Bodhisattvas. Question:

What is the intent behind citing the Śrāvakas here, rather than praising their virtues? The traditional explanation says: This is the third instance of the "teaching of suppression and exaltation" (*yiyang jiao*), wherein the Śrāvakas are suppressed and the Bodhisattvas are exalted.
This serves as the gradual preparation for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Lotus Sūtra); thus, it is said that [this teaching] is intended to assemble the assembly.
Because they ultimately converge upon a single principle, you praise ordinary beings and further disparage the śrāvakas as being like rotten seeds;

for this reason, you do not praise the śrāvakas. Now I clarify that this is not so: if you look up to the śrāvakas while holding the bodhisattvas in high esteem, yet you criticize the śrāvakas without criticizing the bodhisattvas, then since you criticize the śrāvakas and do not praise them, you should likewise criticize the bodhisattvas.
Sengzao did not praise the *Bodhisattva-klāpya*, nor did he praise the *Klāpya* that praises [the bodhisattvas];

furthermore, he used the *Dharmapada* to criticize this sutra for its disparagement of the śrāvakas, yet he did not praise the śrāvaka teachings of the *Dharmapada*, which refutes the śrāvakas (and so forth).

Furthermore, one school says there are "only Small" and "only Great" [teachings], and because the "only Small" is what is criticized, this interpretation also fails to resolve the difficulty. What [is the solution]?

Since this [criticism] already rebukes the "not merely small" while failing to praise the "not merely small," and fails to praise the "not merely small" while failing to rebuke the "not merely small"—and even rebukes the "not merely small" while failing to praise the "not merely large"—if one says that praising the "not merely large" should likewise involve praising the "not merely small," then the shallow difficulty [is as follows] (*etc.*).
However, the meanings of "but not" (*bu dan*) differ; what is clarified here is the interpretation from the Guanzhong school, which, compared to the previous presentation, reveals [the following].
The teaching can thus be understood as follows: What is the distinction? It is said that in Guanzhong, it is held that *śrāvakas* do not require praise while *bodhisattvas* do. Why is this?
Because the appearance and demeanor of *śrāvakas* are superior to those of ordinary people, and all believe them; therefore, they are praised at times and not praised at others.
The appearance of *bodhisattvas*, however, is not fixed, and not everyone believes them; therefore, they must always be praised. Furthermore, among the ignorant there are many who possess wisdom.
External forms are easily recognized, whereas internal virtues are difficult to know. Because external forms are easily recognized, there is no need to praise the *śrāvakas*;

because internal virtues are difficult to know, it is necessary to praise the *bodhisattvas*. Furthermore, since the assembly of *śrāvakas* is constant and consists of no others, there is no need to praise them;
however, since the assembly of *bodhisattvas* is not constant and includes others, it is necessary to praise them.
He was accompanied by a great assembly of eight thousand bhikṣus.
Among the three chapters, this is the first: the listing of the śrāvaka assembly of great bhikṣus, explained as usual.
There were thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas, renowned to all, who had fully accomplished the fundamental practices of great wisdom and were established by the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas.
They protected the city of the Dharma, upheld the true Dharma, and were able to roar the lion’s roar;
their fame reached the ten directions, and as uninvited friends to all people, they brought them peace and security, ensuring that the Three Jewels would flourish and never be extinguished.
Having subdued the hosts of Māra and the various non-Buddhists, they are entirely purified and forever free from the hindrances and entanglements;
their minds dwell constantly in unimpeded liberation, with mindfulness, concentration, dhāraṇī, and eloquence never ceasing.

They are fully endowed with generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, and the power of skillful means, having attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena through the realization of non-attainment.
Having already been able to accord with and turn the non-retrogressive wheel, they are well-versed in the knowledge of dharmas and understand the faculties and roots of sentient beings;

they have attained fearlessness before the great assemblies through their merit and wisdom, and have cultivated their minds. Their physical marks and signs adorn their bodies, and their appearance is supreme;
they have abandoned all worldly ornaments, and their fame is loftier than Mount Sumeru. Their deep faith is firm and unshakable.
Like the vajra-like jewel of the Dharma, it shines universally and rains down nectar upon all; its vocal tones are subtle, wondrous, and supreme, penetrating deeply into dependent origination.
It severs all false views and the two extremes of existence and non-existence, leaving no further residual habits.
Its fearless exposition of the Dharma is like the roar of a lion; its preaching is like the crashing of thunder, immeasurable, transcending all measure, and gathering a vast assembly.
The Dharma Jewel is like a sea-captain who thoroughly understands the profound and subtle meanings of all phenomena;
he well knows the destinations of beings’ comings and goings as well as the movements of their minds.

He draws near to the peerless wisdom of the Buddhas—the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities—and while closing the gates to all evil realms, he manifests his body within the five destinies for the sake of great beings.
As a King of Physicians, he skillfully cures all ailments, providing medicine according to the disease so that it may be taken and applied.
He has fully accomplished immeasurable merits and purified immeasurable Buddha-lands; those who see or hear him do not fail to receive benefit, and whatever he does is never in vain.
Thus, he is completely endowed with all such meritorious qualities.
"Thirty-two thousand Bodhisattvas" marks the second section. Listing the names of the assembly of Bodhisattvas constitutes the fifth [section], consisting of five parts:

(1) the general designation of their names; (2) the proclamation of their number; (3) the praise of their virtues; (4) the listing of their individual names; and (5) the concluding summary of the Bodhisattvas.

"Thirty-two thousand" is the proclamation of the number. "Known by all" is the third part, the praise of their virtues. However, regarding this praise of their virtues, there has been no traditional commentary from ancient times.
A single master explains this according to its stages: these two lines refer to the first stage (*bhūmi*), while the following lines praise the second stage and so forth.

Subsequently, various masters of the Central Kingdom (China) directly analyzed the phrases to provide their explanations. What is clarified here does not exceed two types: those who have left the household life and those who remain at home.
Furthermore, there are two types: those from other regions and those from this land. Again, there are two types: the first...

Regarding the two types of bodies—the body of karmic bonds and the body of dharma-nature—the *Vyākhyā* (Commentary) states: "Upon attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) in the seventh stage, one abandons the fleshly body and attains the dharma-body.
Although this is the case, what is being praised here is specifically the dharma-body of the Bodhisattva. This dharma-body encompasses both the monastic and the lay, as well as the new and the old.
Furthermore, the praise herein does not exceed two aspects: first, the mutual generation of the hook and the clasp; second, that which is appropriate [to the occasion].
Regarding the generation of characteristics through phrases: in the former case, the preceding phrase generates the subsequent phrase, and the subsequent phrase explains the preceding phrase;

this is what is meant by "the phrase itself generating [the next] in succession. It is not so in the case of "the phrase itself generating [the next] independently. Therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states that there are two kinds of dharma-exposition:

first, according to the sequence of meaning (*artha-anukrama*); second, according to circumstances (*pratyaya-anukrama*). "According to the sequence of meaning" refers to the mutual establishment of preceding and succeeding elements, whereas "according to circumstances" does not necessarily follow such a sequence.
Thus, in the present text, this [phrase] exists in its complete form. Regarding those who are "known by the multitude," there are differing interpretations of this phrase.

Some say that "the thirty-two thousand followers known by the multitude" constitutes a single compound, clarifying that these thirty-two thousand are those known by the multitude, thereby making clear the immeasurable nature of the bodhisattvas. Others say that "bodhisattva" [is the subject].
The general title "thirty thousand" and so forth indicates the enumeration; "known by the multitude" is a praise of his virtues.
Now it is clarified that this phrase belongs to the praise of virtues.
Regarding the expression "known by the multitude," there are several meanings: first, to know the internal virtues of a bodhisattva constitutes "knowing."

Regarding the distinction between *jñāna* (knowledge) and *vijñāna* (consciousness): first, they are distinguished by their objects; *jñāna* cognizes that which is distant from the multitude [of ordinary beings], while *vijñāna* cognizes that which is near to the multitude. This is like a person who, when near, perceives both the name and the form, whereas when distant, they know only the name but do not perceive the form. Second, the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, in the "Chapter on the Categories of Dharmas" (*Dharmapada-paṭala*), states: "Knowledge is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), while consciousness is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Since conventional truth is shallow, it is termed *vijñāna*; the ultimate is termed *jñāna*. Third, they are distinguished by their nature: *jñāna* is true wisdom, while *vijñāna* is false wisdom. False wisdom is termed *vijñāna*, while true wisdom is termed *jñāna*. Fourth, they are distinguished by their function: *jñāna* functions as the antidote to ignorance, while *vijñāna* functions as the antidote to delusion. Ignorance is termed *jñāna*, while delusion is termed *vijñāna*. Fifth, they are distinguished by their essence: *jñāna* is the essence of liberation, while *vijñāna* is the essence of bondage. Liberation is termed *jñāna*, while bondage is termed *vijñāna*. Sixth, they are distinguished by their fruit: *jñāna* is the fruit of the path, while *vijñāna* is the fruit of the world. The fruit of the path is termed *jñāna*, while the fruit of the world is termed *vijñāna*. Seventh, they are distinguished by their basis: *jñāna* relies upon the noble ones, while *vijñāna* relies upon ordinary beings. Noble ones are termed *jñāna*, while ordinary beings are termed *vijñāna*. Eighth, they are distinguished by their time: *jñāna* pertains to the future, while *vijñāna* pertains to the present. The future is termed *jñāna*, while the present is termed *vijñāna*. Ninth, they are distinguished by their realm: *jñāna* belongs to the supramundane, while *vijñāna* belongs to the mundane. The supramundane is termed *jñāna*, while the mundane is termed *vijñāna*. Tenth, they are distinguished by their cause: *jñāna* arises from the cause of cultivation, while *vijñāna* arises from the cause of birth. Cultivation is termed *jñāna*, while birth is termed *vijñāna*. Eleventh, they are distinguished by their aspect: *jñāna* is the aspect of non-discrimination, while *vijñāna* is the aspect of discrimination. Non-discrimination is termed *jñāna*, while discrimination is termed *vijñāna*. Twelfth, they are distinguished by their object: *jñāna* takes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its object, while *vijñāna* takes the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) as its object. The unconditioned is termed *jñāna*, while the conditioned is termed *vijñāna*. Thirteenth, they are distinguished by their support: *jñāna* is supported by the Dharma-body, while *vijñāna* is supported by the body born of parents. The Dharma-body is termed *jñāna*, while the body born of parents is termed *vijñāna*. Fourteenth, they are distinguished by their activity: *jñāna* performs the activity of liberation, while *vijñāna* performs the activity of bondage. Liberation is termed *jñāna*, while bondage is termed *vijñāna*. Fifteenth, they are distinguished by their nature: *jñāna* is the nature of purity, while *vijñāna* is the nature of defilement. Purity is termed *jñāna*, while defilement is termed *vijñāna*. Sixteenth, they are distinguished by their power: *jñāna* possesses the power of mastery, while *vijñāna* lacks the power of mastery. Mastery is termed *jñāna*, while lack of mastery is termed *vijñāna*. Seventeenth, they are distinguished by their stage: *jñāna* resides in the stages of the noble ones, while *vijñāna* resides in the stages of ordinary beings. The noble stages are termed *jñāna*, while the ordinary stages are termed *vijñāna*. Eighteenth, they are distinguished by their result: *jñāna* is the result of the cessation of suffering, while *vijñāna* is the result of the origin of suffering. Cessation is termed *jñāna*, while origin is termed *vijñāna*. Nineteenth, they are distinguished by their characteristic: *jñāna* has the characteristic of permanence, while *vijñāna* has the characteristic of impermanence. Permanence is termed *jñāna*, while impermanence is termed *vijñāna*. Twentieth, they are distinguished by their essence: *jñāna* is the essence of the Buddha, while *vijñāna* is the essence of sentient beings. The Buddha is termed *jñāna*, while sentient beings are termed *vijñāna*. Twenty-first, they are distinguished by their function: *jñāna* functions to sever the afflictions, while *vijñāna* functions to increase the afflictions. Severing is termed *jñāna*, while increasing is termed *vijñāna*. Twenty-second, they are distinguished by their nature: *jñāna* is the nature of nirvana, while *vijñāna* is the nature of samsara. Nirvana is termed *jñāna*, while samsara is termed *vijñāna*. Twenty-third, they are distinguished by their aspect: *jñāna* is the aspect of emptiness, while *vijñāna* is the aspect of existence. Emptiness is termed *jñāna*, while existence is termed *vijñāna*. Twenty-fourth, they are distinguished by their object: *jñāna* takes the ultimate truth as its object, while *vijñāna* takes the conventional truth as its object. Ultimate truth is termed *jñāna*, while conventional truth is termed *vijñāna*. Twenty-fifth, they are distinguished by their essence: *jñāna* is the essence of the path, while *vijñāna* is the essence of the world. The path is termed *jñāna*, while the world is termed *vijñāna*. Twenty-sixth, they are distinguished by their fruit: *jñāna* is the fruit of the path, while *vijñāna* is the fruit of the world. The fruit of the path is termed *jñāna*, while the fruit of the world is termed *vijñāna*. Twenty-seventh, they are distinguished by their basis: *jñāna* relies upon the noble ones, while *vijñāna* relies upon ordinary beings. Noble ones are termed *jñāna*, while ordinary beings are termed *vijñāna*. Twenty-eighth, they are distinguished by their time: *jñāna* pertains to the future, while *vijñāna* pertains to the present. The future is termed *jñāna*, while the present is termed *vijñāna*. Twenty-ninth, they are distinguished by their realm: *jñāna* belongs to the supramundane, while *vijñāna* belongs to the mundane. The supramundane is termed *jñāna*, while the mundane is termed *vijñāna*. Thirtieth, they are distinguished by their cause: *jñāna* arises from the cause of cultivation, while *vijñāna* arises from the cause of birth. Cultivation is termed *jñāna*, while birth is termed *vijñāna*. Thirty-first, they are distinguished by their aspect: *jñāna* is the aspect of non-discrimination, while *vijñāna* is the aspect of discrimination. Non-discrimination is termed *jñāna*, while discrimination is termed *vijñāna*. Thirty-second, they are distinguished by their object: *jñāna* takes the unconditioned as its object, while *vijñāna* takes the conditioned as its object. The unconditioned is termed *jñāna*, while the conditioned is termed *vijñāna*. Thirty-third, they are distinguished by their support: *jñāna* is supported by the Dharma-body, while *vijñāna* is supported by the body born of parents. The Dharma-body is termed *jñāna*, while the body born of parents

The profound truth consists in knowing that a bodhisattva possesses the wisdom of the two truths; thus it is said they "know consciousness. Fourth, regarding the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), they are categorized as follows:
the six organs do not transcend seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing. The eyes see, the ears hear, and the three organs of nose, tongue, and body constitute sensing;
the mental organ (*manas*) constitutes cognizing. Furthermore, there are four permutations: first, knowing without recognizing; second, recognizing without knowing.
The third case is both knowing and cognizing; the fourth is neither knowing nor cognizing.
"Knowing but not cognizing" refers to people today who know that Avalokiteśvara and Maitreya possess great virtuous conduct, yet do not truly cognize it.

"Cognizing but not knowing" refers to those who personally recognize this bodhisattva but do not understand their inner virtues. Thus, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra says: "There are people who see the Buddha..."
It is said that he was merely a śramaṇa of fine appearance; as for the "three who knew him," it means they recognized his inner virtue while perceiving his outward form.
This is neither true knowledge nor mere perception, and thus it is not accepted in the present context. Furthermore, Master Zhao’s commentary states:
"The Great Being dwells in the world like the sun rising in the sky; among those with eyes, who would not know and recognize him? Question:
Why is it that when Bodhisattvas appear in the world, they are known and understood by all? The explanation is this: within, the Bodhisattva possesses great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*);
without, they manifest all forms and utter all teachings, desiring to deliver all beings.

As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "What is the great matter for which the Bodhisattva arises? It is said to be the deliverance of all sentient beings. Having already delivered all sentient beings...
How could all sentient beings not recognize [the Bodhisattva]? Furthermore, if one recognizes the manifest but does not recognize the obscure, one cannot be called a "knower of the multitude.

Because they recognize both the obscure and the manifest, it is said that they are "known by the multitude. Question: Since the Bodhisattva universally acts for the sake of all, why are there those who are not saved?
Answer: This must necessarily depend on internal causes. If there are no internal causes, the Bodhisattva [cannot save them].
Although it would ultimately be of no benefit to oneself, just as rain falling upon withered wood is not received, so it is with the Bodhisattva;
yet, when there is a cause, there must be a corresponding result.
As for the phrase "the Great Wisdom and Fundamental Practices are all fully accomplished," this refers to those renowned among the superior assembly, manifesting his external virtues.
The fundamental practice of great wisdom is arrayed within his internal virtues, and thus he has attained liberation. For what reason is he known by the multitude?

It is precisely because he possesses the fundamental practice of great wisdom that he is recognized and known by the multitude. If he lacked internal virtuous conduct, how could he be known by others?
By means of the impartial wisdom of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time—
Therefore, it is said that "Great Wisdom" is so called because the *Lotus Sūtra* states that "Equal Great Wisdom preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
This "Original Practice" refers to the Bodhisattva; this practice is the foundation of Great Wisdom, for by cultivating this practice one attains Great Wisdom.
Thus, "Great Wisdom's Original Practice" is precisely a praise of the causal practice. The preceding phrase praised his virtues, while this phrase extols his practice.
The first phrase indicates the subject, and this phrase indicates the explanation;
these two pairs clarify both the cultivation of superior dharmas and the meeting with superior persons.
The former phrase clarifies the cultivation of superior causes, while this phrase clarifies the meeting with superior conditions. Although Bodhisattvas cultivate the causes...
All Buddhas must bestow their empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) so that [the practitioner] may achieve success. There are two kinds of empowerment:
the proximate and the remote. Regarding the proximate, it refers to such cases as when Vajragarbha and others are granted eloquence (*pratibhāna*) to enable them to preach the Dharma.
Regarding the remote, it refers to the empowerment of all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) from the initial generation of the bodhicitta until the final attainment of Buddhahood.

It is universally taught that [the attainment] is accomplished, using the analogy of a fish-mother who achieves it through her mindfulness of her offspring. Question: Fish eggs are born from the mother’s womb, where the sinews and blood separate to allow for their development;
how can Bodhisattvas, who are not born from a Buddha’s womb, achieve accomplishment through the Buddha’s protective empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*)?

Explanation: According to one school of thought, there is the principle of "original purity" (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*); the Buddha and sentient beings [are fundamentally identical]. Thus, although they are not born from the Buddha’s womb, they achieve accomplishment through his empowerment.

Since their source is the same, they are interconnected; regarding these two in terms of their activities as well, they are interconnected because it is through the Buddha’s teaching that there are bodhisattvas, who are thus born from the Buddha’s mouth and transformed by the Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "those who protect the city of the Dharma": the preceding clause clarifies that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas rely upon this [Dharma], while this clause clarifies that Bodhisattvas act as conditions for the Buddhas.
The preceding clause clarifies that because all Buddhas establish their protective empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the Bodhisattva’s practice is perfected;

now, since the Bodhisattva’s practice has been accomplished, they repay the Buddha’s kindness by acting as a city to protect the Dharma. Furthermore, there are two meanings here, both of which are valid.

First, because the True Dharma is taken as a city, a sutra says: "The precious city of the True Dharma. Because Bodhisattvas protect this city of the Dharma, it is said they act "to protect the city of the Dharma.
Second, "wei" (為) means "to act as. Because Bodhisattvas act as the city of the Dharma, there is a worldly saying:

"This person can serve as a fence. The latter meaning is correct here. Furthermore, there are two kinds of cities: first, [the city of the Dharma]; second, [the city of the world]. (Note: The text appears to be incomplete at the end.)
The Dharma-city of the Bodhisattva King of Peace, who wards off enemies, is likewise twofold: first, it wards off the heterodox; second, it establishes the orthodox.
Therefore, it is called a "Dharma-city.
Regarding the phrase "upholding the True Dharma," previously this was praised as the external virtue of Bodhisattvas for protecting the Dharma-city; now it is stated that they "uphold" it.
The praise of the Bodhisattva’s inner virtues regarding the True Dharma (*saddharma*) also explains the preceding phrase: "By what means can one protect the city of the Dharma?

It is precisely because of upholding the True Dharma. "Receiving" (*udgrahaṇa*) refers to initially taking it into one's mind; "upholding" (*dhāraṇa*) refers to maintaining it in good health without forgetting.
Thus, there is first receiving and subsequently upholding.
Regarding the phrase "one who can roar the lion’s roar," Zhaoti says this is a praise for Bodhisattvas of the ninth stage (*navamī-bhūmi*). How do we know this is so?

He cites the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, which states that Bodhisattvas of the ninth stage possess the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*) and thus fall into the rank of Dharma-preachers;

since it is said here that they "can roar the lion’s roar," it must refer to the ninth stage. Now, I shall clarify that this is not so: Bodhisattvas of the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) are also able to roar the lion’s roar.
"Subhūti (Zi Kong) is capable of the lion’s roar even up to the tenth stage; why should he be restricted merely to the ninth stage?

Ultimately, he is a Bodhisattva who has attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). For a Bodhisattva of the patience of non-arising, this patience is itself universal penetration.
Previously, his upholding of the True Dharma praised his internal virtue; now, his ability to roar like a lion praises his external virtue. This is also an explanation."
This is primarily because, by internally upholding the True Dharma, one is able to externally expound it.
The lion’s roar is as explained in detail in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Saṃghāṭasūtra*.
Regarding "fame reaching the ten directions," the former [the lion’s roar] praises the cause, while fame reaching the ten directions praises the fruit; this is also due to...
Because he is able to roar the lion’s roar, his name is heard throughout the ten directions. Question:
It was already stated previously that he is "known by all," so why is it said again here that his "name is heard throughout the ten directions"? Explanation:
The previous "being known by all" is narrow, whereas the present "name heard throughout the ten directions" is broad. Why? Because being "known by all" previously refers only to a single [assembly].
The "world" refers to the world under heaven and the four quarters; now, because one hears of the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions, it is explained extensively.
For this reason, there is a difference between the former and the latter.
Although people do not request it, the Great Sūtra says that one should establish them as friends and not incite [them] to speak what is not [right].
Regarding the statement that "there is no teaching without being requested," one might ask: why does this sutra now say there is "teaching without being requested"? The explanation is as follows:

That sutra praises teaching upon request, while this sutra praises teaching without being requested. Since there are specific reasons for both requesting and not requesting, one must not interpret them as being categorically contradictory.
As for the present mention of "teaching without being requested," Sengzhao says: "A true friend does not wait for a request, just as a compassionate mother hastens to her child's side."
Just as a compassionate mother does not wait for her infant to request it before the wet nurse provides milk, so too is the Bodhisattva:
he does not wait for sentient beings to request his teaching before speaking. Rather, he brings peace to them according to what is appropriate;

he brings them peace as humans or devas where human or deva status is appropriate, and he brings them peace through the Three Vehicles where the Three Vehicles are appropriate. Thus, he brings them peace by befriending them. "Befriending" refers to paternal compassion.

It is said that a son is filial and an elder brother is affectionate, while a younger brother is respectful; furthermore, those of the same gate are called *peng* (companions), and those of the same aspiration are called *you* (friends).

Because Bodhisattvas and sentient beings share the same aspiration in seeking the Buddha-way, they are called friends. Moreover, among Bodhisattvas, those who attained awakening earlier are considered elder brothers, and those who attained awakening later are considered younger brothers.
It is not based on seniority of age, but rather on the sequence of their awakening that brothers are distinguished; therefore, it is so stated.

"To befriend and bring peace" means that while the preceding phrase clarifies that there is a standard to which one conforms below, this phrase clarifies that there is an inspiration to be aroused above—
namely, to cause the Three Jewels to flourish so that they are never severed. It is possible to cause the Three Jewels to flourish.
There are two [types of flourishing]: first, flourishing within the causal stage; second, flourishing at the stage of fruition.

Regarding "flourishing in the causal stage," this refers to the lineage of Nāgārjuna and Āryadeva, who refuted the heterodox Three Jewels to manifest the orthodox Three Jewels, and refuted the Three Jewels of attainment to propagate the Three Jewels of non-attainment.

Regarding "flourishing at the stage of fruition," this clarifies that Bodhisattvas cultivate the contemplation of non-attainment without ceasing, thereby awakening to the non-arising of all phenomena.
Having attained the patience of birth (*utpatti-kṣānti*) and achieved Buddhahood, he now returns here to awaken those sentient beings who have not yet awakened;
because the Three Jewels are never exhausted and never severed, it is said that they shall "not be interrupted."

The preceding phrase praised the manifestation of the correct [Dharma], while this present phrase praises the refutation of the heterodox to clarify the Bodhisattva’s virtue that transcends the three realms.
Thus, because his virtue surpasses those of the three realms, he is invincible to them; because his virtue surpasses that of the heavenly Māras, no Māra can oppose him;

and because his virtue surpasses that of non-Buddhists, no human being can oppose him. Since neither gods nor humans can oppose him, it follows that he is likewise invincible to those in the four miserable destinies.
Since this is not being discussed here, it is said that he "subdues the demonic enemies" and "restrains the heterodox.
To strike them with awe is called "subduing," while to overcome them through debate is called "restraining.
The phrase "all by means of purity, forever departing from the hindrances and entanglements" praises the Bodhisattva for having eternally departed from the celestial Māras.

This phrase praises the Bodhisattva for being internally free from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and the fetters (*paryavasthāna*). "Hindrances" refers to the five hindrances, while "all fetters" refers to the ten fetters and the immeasurable fetters; the Bodhisattva is free from all of these.

Regarding the phrase "the mind constantly dwells in unimpeded liberation," the preceding section clarified the permanent departure from hindrances and fetters, whereas this praises the Bodhisattva’s state of being free [from them].
This passage clarifies that the mind constantly dwells in unimpeded liberation (*anāvaraṇa-vimukti*).

Regarding the Bodhisattva’s attainment of such unimpeded liberation, the *Śāstra* (Treatise) explains it differently from other enumerations as "unimpeded severance-liberation" (*anāvaraṇa-prahāṇa-vimukti*).

Furthermore, the "Chapter on Distinctions" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattva proceeds within the path of unimpeded realization (*anāvaraṇa-mārga*) and attains the liberations of all Buddhas."

Regarding the practice within the Path, if one were to judge it according to cause and effect, the preceding thought-moment would be "unhindered" (ānantarya) and the succeeding thought-moment would be called "liberation" (vimukti).
However, what is clarified here is not explained in this way;
rather, "unhindered" itself is designated as "liberation," which is precisely the inconceivable liberation. Therefore, it is called "unhindered liberation."
"Recollection, concentration, dhāraṇī, and uninterrupted eloquence"—this refers to four dharmas as a praise:
"recollection" constitutes one phrase, "concentration" one phrase, "dhāraṇī" one phrase, and "eloquence" another phrase. "Uninterrupted" pervades the aforementioned four phrases;
for when recollection is uninterrupted, wisdom surpasses in clarity; when concentration is uninterrupted, the mind is constantly unified; and when dhāraṇī is uninterrupted, [wisdom] is sustained.

The continuity of mindfulness, cognition, eloquence, and transformation constitutes unimpededness. The reason these four factors are uninterrupted is that they distinguish the ordinary person from the sage.
The ordinary person forgets [the experience] immediately upon passing through the womb; the practitioner of the Two Vehicles does not undergo rebirth again;

whereas the Bodhisattva does not forget [the experience] while passing through the womb, and their wisdom increases further with each successive kalpa. Therefore, it is said that mindfulness, concentration, dhāraṇī, and eloquence are uninterrupted.

In the lower section on praising the Bodhisattva’s two types of wisdom, it is stated that these two types of wisdom are manifold; herein, the six perfections are the provisional, while wisdom is the real.

Because the real is the skillful means (*upāya*) and the skillful means is the real, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Wisdom as skillful means—only when a Bodhisattva possesses the practice of wisdom as skillful means does their practice become perfected;
if they lack the practice of wisdom as skillful means, their practice is not perfected. If there is no [wisdom], [the practice] is not perfected.
If there are six matters, one immediately falls into the view of emptiness; if there are six matters, one immediately establishes the view of existence.
Therefore, skillful means and wisdom are required. It is the same here: without skillful means, the six perfections are not fulfilled;
without the six perfections, skillful means is not fulfilled. Since both of these two things are now present, it is said that there is nothing that is not fulfilled.

Regarding "attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas through non-apprehension": "attaining" means reaching; "non-apprehension" refers to that which is not grasped, as clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
As for the "patience of the non-arising of dharmas," this is the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

However, there are different interpretations of this: according to the Three Great Dharma Masters, the simultaneous contemplation of both the ultimate and conventional truths at the eighth stage is called "non-arising."

Now, it is clarified that this is not so; the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) is itself true non-arising (*anutpāda*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "The seven stages and so forth are the stages of samādhi and wisdom.
Furthermore, the seventh stage is the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), which is precisely non-arising.

Moreover, regarding the Arhat, the Sūtra says there are three kinds of non-arising, which refers to the affairs of the Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage. *Pratyutpanna-samādhi* belongs to the eighth stage.
