For this reason, he manifests the skillful means of illness, yet does not manifest the two forms of decline—aging and death.

Furthermore, the reason for manifesting the skillful means of illness is to clarify the meaning of "Vimalakīrti" (Stainless Fame); this intent is extremely vast and profound, universally transforming all those of the two vehicles, as well as all ordinary beings and sages.
Therefore, he manifests illness; this chapter is precisely for the purpose of transforming all ordinary people by means of the layman.
Because he was ill, all the people came to him and asked the householder about his illness; for their sake, he preached the Dharma by means of his own sickness.
Second, because of that illness, he summoned five hundred śrāvakas, but all five hundred śrāvakas declined, saying they were unable to comply;
he then disparaged the śrāvakas and highly extolled the bodhisattvas, thereby transforming the śrāvakas. Third, next...
He commanded eight thousand bodhisattvas, but they all declined, saying they were unable to manifest the virtue of Vimalakīrti. Therefore, he manifested as a bodhisattva;

wishing to transform these beings, he appeared with an illness. Furthermore, the reason for manifesting illness was his desire to transform sickness through sickness—just as a woman transforms a woman, so too does a man transform a man.
It is not the case that a man would fail to transform a woman; it is likewise here. Now, by means of this...
If one who has been transformed as ill were to use that transformation of health to speak of the faults and perils of illness, the actual patient would not believe or accept it;

yet, when one who is currently ill speaks of the faults and perils of illness, they immediately believe it. This clarifies that while a layperson’s body was originally healthy, it has now suddenly fallen ill;
likewise, although all sentient beings are currently healthy, they too are ill, because the layperson is ill. Thus, all sentient beings [are also ill].
Birth is entirely illness. Furthermore, it extends to sentient beings and householders who are not ill; yet they are ill because there is no place that is not ill.
Because sentient beings are [the locus of] illness, they are ill; because they are not ill, they are not ill. Although they are not ill, this very state is illness.
For this reason, he manifests illness. According to the text, there are four sections: first, the actual manifestation of illness; second, the question of the people of the country.
Third, because people came to inquire about his illness, the Virtuous One preached the Dharma for them;
fourth, because he preached the Dharma, they attained realization of the Way.
Thus, through skillful means, he manifested himself as having a sickness. Because of this illness, kings, ministers, elders, and householders...
Kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, various princes, and countless thousands of other officials and attendants all went to inquire after his illness.
By means of this skillful expedient, he manifested that he was ill; this was the foremost and true manifestation of sickness. Because of this illness—
From the king and his ministers down to the second-class citizens, the householders, and the virtuous and disciplined—
all who are currently ill, who would not go to the chamber of the Master to inquire after his illness?
○ Regarding the previous section, "Vimalakīrti uses his own physical illness to preach the Dharma," this third part, "Preaching the Dharma," is divided into two sections:
first, preaching on the impermanence of birth and death to inspire weary detachment; second, praising the merits of the Dharma-body.
There are briefly two reasons for preaching these two teachings: first, to transform ordinary beings and to censure the [self-conceited] sages.
Regarding the phrase "transforming the ordinary," it refers to ordinary sentient beings who claim that birth and death are permanent and possess a joy worth pursuing;
therefore, this view is now refuted to clarify that birth and death are impermanent, suffering, empty, and impure, and are thus deeply to be dreaded and loathed.

Regarding the "reproving of the Two Vehicles," it refers to those of the Two Vehicles who, upon seeing that birth and death are impermanent, suffering, empty, and impure, immediately desire to abandon birth and death.
Regarding the entry into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*: as for why Arhats enter *nirupadhiśeṣa*, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states that prior to entering *nirupadhiśeṣa*, Arhats still possess a body;
because they possess a body, there is hunger, cold, and illness. Therefore, they cultivate the profound *śūnyatā-samādhi* and enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Now, Vimalakīrti turns his mind away from this and cannot enter it.

Although both *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and *saṃsāra* are impermanent and thus objects of wearying aversion, there is nevertheless a subtle and wondrous body—namely, the Buddha, the World-Honored One—who possesses a wondrous body of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
This is truly something to be rejoiced in; one ought to rejoice in the Buddha-body. How could one enter *nirupadhiśeṇa-nirvāṇa*?
This is said because [the Buddha] rebukes the two views of ordinary beings and sages, and thus expounds these two kinds of Dharma-gates.
Regarding the second meaning: the "door of pressing" refers to the preceding clarification that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is impermanent;
the "door of drawing forth" refers to the subsequent explanation of the merits of the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*). These two doors are opened for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
Yet, when one discusses *saṃsāra* and *nirvāṇa*, how could there ever be two? For the sake of sentient beings, what is non-dual is forcibly described as two paths.

Birth and death are impermanent, while the Buddha-ground is eternal and blissful; this is simply because the former is not like the latter. Birth and death and the Buddha-ground are definitively two [states];
abandoning birth and death and attaining the fruit of Buddhahood is the mental activity of the practice of taking and abandoning.
In the past, Vimalakīrti used his own physical illness as an occasion to extensively preach the Dharma:
"O virtuous ones, this body is impermanent, lacking strength, lacking power, and lacking solidity; it is a thing that quickly decays and cannot be relied upon.
It is suffering and affliction, a gathering place for manifold maladies. O virtuous ones, such a body is not trusted by the wise; this body is like a mass of foam."
This body cannot be grasped or rubbed; it is like a bubble that cannot endure for long. This body is like a flame, born from craving and thirst.
This body is like a plantain tree, having no solidity within. This body is like an illusion, arising from perversion. This body is like a dream, consisting of false perceptions.
This body is like a shadow, appearing through the conditions of karma. This body is like an echo, dependent upon various causes.
This body is conditioned like a floating cloud, changing and perishing in an instant; this body is like lightning, not abiding for even a single thought-moment.
This body has no master, being like the earth; this body has no self, being like fire; this body has no life-span, being like wind;
this body has no person, being like water. This body is unreal, with the four great elements as its home; this body is empty, devoid of a self.
This body of mine is insentient, like grass, wood, tiles, or pebbles; this body is inactive, driven by the power of the wind;
this body is impure, filled with filth and evil; this body is deceptive, for though it is provisionally sustained by bathing, food, and clothing, it must ultimately return to decay;
this body is a calamity, afflicted by one hundred and one maladies; this body is like a dilapidated well, beset by old age.

This body is without permanence; it must inevitably die. This body is like a venomous snake, like a hostile thief, and like an empty village—a composite formation of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
O worthy ones, this is something to be weary of and loathe.
Within these two chapters, this first section clarifies that birth and death are to be loathed. O virtuous ones, this body is impermanent and lacks strength;
it lacks strength because what was once healthy has now fallen ill—thus it is impermanent and lacks strength.
It is suffering, comprising the eight sufferings as its specific instances and the nine general categories as its summary. It lacks power, for it cannot dispel illness; therefore, it is empty.
Power is also such that the body has no master; it is like the earth, clarifying that there is no difference between the four great elements (mahābhūta) of the internal and external.
External great elements, such as mountains, rivers, and trees, and internal great elements, such as the four limbs and hundred members of the body, are not two distinct things.

When the external four great elements aggregate, they become the internal four great elements; when the internal four great elements disintegrate, they return to becoming the external four great elements. Thus, the external great elements are not different from the internal.
Since the great external earth element has no master, the internal [earth element] likewise has no master. Thus, this body is selfless and is like fire.

The preceding passage clarified that the external earth element is not different from the internal earth element. Regarding this, it is said: while the external earth element is insentient and cannot act, yet is forcibly treated as having a master;
the internal [earth element], being sentient and capable of purposeful action—such as coming and going, speaking and remaining silent—is likewise without a master.
How could these [elements] possibly be without a master? Therefore, it is now clarified that because fire has fuel, when there is no fuel, the fire is extinguished;
small fuel produces a small fire, and large fuel produces a large fire. When burning bamboo or wood, various sounds are produced.

Since the external element of fire is not independent, it is without self (*anātman*); the internal element is likewise so. Following favorable conditions results in greed, while encountering adverse conditions results in anger. It is not autonomous.
Regarding the statement, "In this body there is neither self nor permanence, yet it is certain that one must die": Question: Since there is no permanence, why is it further said that one "must" die?

If death is certain, why is it called "uncertain"? Explanation: These two phrases—"no permanence" and "one must die"—constitute a single unit. "The body has no permanence" clarifies that [the duration of] youth or old age is not fixed.

"It is certain that one must die" means that while the specific time of death is uncertain, the fact that death will inevitably occur is itself a certainty. Thus, although the time is indefinite, the necessity is definite. Therefore, these two aspects together form a single point.
The middle age is not fixed; although there is no fixed certainty regarding whether one is old or young, tall or short, death must inevitably occur.

Furthermore, this lack of certainty means that those who die do so in different ways—whether by water or fire, or dying naturally or by the hand of another—and thus it is uncertain. Nevertheless, death is certain.
"O virtuous ones, this is something to be weary of and loathe"—this concludes the preceding section.
One should take delight in the Buddha-body. Why is this? The Buddha-body is precisely the Dharma-body. It is born from immeasurable merit and wisdom;
it is born from precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; it is born from loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;
and it is born from generosity, upholding the precepts, patience, gentleness, diligent application, vigor, meditative concentration, liberation, and various samādhis.

One hears that wisdom and the various pāramitās arise from skillful means; they arise from the six supernormal powers, the three types of clear knowledge, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and śamatha and vipaśyanā;
they arise from the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they arise from the abandonment of all unwholesome dharmas and the accumulation of all wholesome dharmas; and they arise from reality.
The Tathāgata’s body arises from non-negligence; it arises from such immeasurable, pure dharmas.
O noble ones, those who wish to attain the Buddha-body and sever the illnesses of all sentient beings should resolve their minds toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Regarding the section "One should delight in the Buddha-body," the second part clarifies the merits of the Buddha’s Dharma-body.

There may be three types of people who feel weary and disgusted [with the body]: first, worldly ordinary beings who, although they know this body is impure, feel weary and disgusted yet do not abandon it;
second, those of the Two Vehicles who feel weary and disgusted with birth and death, and thus abandon birth and death to enter forever into [nirvana].

Regarding the three aspects of *nirvāṇa without remainder*: it is because Bodhisattvas loathe the impermanence and impurity of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) that they seek the Buddha-body’s merits of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Here, this specifically refutes the Two Vehicles, urging them instead to delight in the Buddha-body. Why is this so?
Because the Buddha-body is precisely the Dharma-body—this explains why one should delight in the Buddha-body. However, as for those who have come from the past...
If one does not understand this, how can one proceed? The Hinayana school says that the Buddha was born in the royal palace, lived for eighty years, and passed away between the twin śāla trees;
this constitutes the three marks of his final lifespan (*mahākāla*). Within this, there are further three marks occurring in every moment (*kṣaṇa*), which are no different from those of an Arhat.
The only difference lies in the coarseness or subtlety of the body. As for the three marks that press upon us, there is no further distinction. If it were as [the Hinayanists claim]...
How can this be considered sufficient for joy? Regarding the five periods of teaching on the meaning of the Dharma as understood in this region:

the first period of eighty years is the Buddha’s second major category of teaching. Kaishan says that these are still the eighty years of the Buddha’s first period of teaching, but that in the first period the physical body (*rūpakāya*) was taken as the Buddha, whereas in the second period the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) was taken as the Buddha. Zhaoti says that the distinction lies merely in the veneration of the Honored One.

The third [position], the teaching of Vimalakīrti and Siyi, maintains that the Buddha is defined solely by the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), yet his lifespan lasts only seven hundred *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
This interpretation ultimately remains impermanent; what difference, then, is there between this and [ordinary] impermanence?

Since it is thus insufficient to be joyful about, the Mahāyāna Sūtra says: "The first analogy is excrement—whether much or little, both are foul-smelling; the lifespans of those who live long or short are likewise so."
Traditionally, it has been explained that this section is merely the introduction (*nidāna*) and not the actual teaching of Vimalakīrti;

thus, the difficult passages representing the actual teaching were considered the core of the sutra while the introduction was deemed non-canonical. However, since both the introduction and the main teaching are equally part of the sutra, we know that this traditional interpretation has missed the mark by a great deal.
Now, the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa explains: "The Buddha-body is the Dharma-body," clarifying that there is no distinction between saṃsāra and [nirvāṇa].

One should always take heed that the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of the Buddha-ground is characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity; because one rejoices in these qualities, it is said that "the Buddha-body is the Dharma-body.
Herein, the Dharma-body is elucidated as that which is clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin): the Dharma-body has neither coming nor going.

It is also like what is stated in the "Vajra-body Chapter" (*Vajrakāya-parivarta*) of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*: it is not "not-not" among a hundred negations, and it is not "is-is" among a thousand affirmations. This is the present Dharma.
The body is likewise thus: it clarifies that the Buddha-body is neither born nor extinguished, neither departing nor arriving, for it is ultimately pure.
Master Zhao said: "If one follows it, its tracks cannot be found; if one meets it head-on, its crown cannot be seen.

The four realms of existence have no means to constrain its life-force, and even the power of the wind has no means to transform its substance. This is the Dharma-body, and therefore it is worthy of joy.
The phrase "also born from immeasurable merit" explains the cause for attaining Buddhahood. If you wish to attain this Dharma-body, you should practice its causes and so forth.
O virtuous ones, those who wish to attain the Buddha-body and sever all the illnesses of sentient beings should resolve their minds [to seek enlightenment].

This is a general exhortation to resolve the mind; for the resolution of the mind is the foundation of all practices, and therefore it is exhorted that one must resolve the mind. Exhortation to resolve the mind. Exhortation to resolve the mind.
He caused them to practice so as to attain the body of a Buddha.
Thus, the elder Vimalakīrti taught the Dharma appropriately to those who had come to inquire after his illness,
causing countless thousands of people to all resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Thus, regarding the various visitors who came to inquire after the householder’s illness, from the fourth period onward, the assembly heard the Dharma and attained the Way as described in the text.
Chapter Three: The Disciples.
Indeed, this chapter ought to follow immediately after the "Buddha-land" chapter; there is no intermediate section on skillful means.
How do we know this to be so? In the "Vihāra" chapter, the Tathāgata expounded the causes and effects of the Pure Land;

once that section was concluded, it was necessary to dispatch someone to inquire after his illness. Why? Because the five hundred members of the Ratnākara assembly and Vimalakīrti are equal companions in the city of Dharma.
In every matter, they open the Way for one another; there is no occasion when they do not gather together to investigate the profound mysteries. Now, these five hundred have all come to Vimalakīrti.
Since he did not arrive, we know he was ill; being ill, he should have sent someone to inquire after his health rather than appearing in person.

Furthermore, the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (*Upāya-paryāya*) belongs to the first assembly of Vimalakīrti, as he had already been ill and had finished preaching the Dharma for the elders and laypeople even before the Buddha had gathered the assembly.
Therefore, it should not follow after the "Chapter on the Buddha-land" (*Buddhakṣetra-paryāya*).
Those who are now at the end [of this section] are the compilers of the sutra; desiring to complete this single scripture, they have placed this here as a transitional insertion.

As for the reason for making this insertion: when the Buddha was at the Āmrapālī Grove and the great assembly gathered like clouds to hear him preach the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, five hundred elders all arrived, yet Vimalakīrti alone did not come. Thus we know he was ill. Since he was ill, there was no...
When the person being measured asked about his illness, Vimalakīrti used that very physical ailment as the occasion to preach the Dharma; this was because he knew the cause of the illness.
Therefore, following the "Buddha-kṣetra" chapter and the "Skillful Means" chapter, there follows the chapter on the disciples and others.

This is because while the kings, elders, and others have all already inquired after the Tathāgata’s health, the Tathāgata has not yet been inquired after; it is now time to command those who inquire after his health.
The "Chapter on Disciples and Others" corresponds to the *loka-vyavahāra* (worldly) *sarvato-mukha* (universal) gate;

Vimalakīrti was once a great elder who now lies with his head upon his pillow, and while everyone else has come to inquire after his illness, the Tathāgata has not yet visited—therefore, he now commands [Mañjuśrī] to inquire after his illness.
Furthermore, the reason why the "Chapter on Disciples" follows the "Chapter on Expedient Means" is that it serves as the *pratipakṣa-sarvato-mukha* (remedial universal) gate.

The preliminary expedient means previously destroyed the illnesses of ordinary persons; now it destroys the illnesses of noble ones. Within the category of noble ones, there are two types: minor and major illnesses.
Because three kinds of illnesses are destroyed, there are three grades of preliminary expedient means. To destroy the illnesses of ordinary persons:

"ordinary persons" refers to those who believe this body possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Although they do not claim it has a manifest, eternal constancy, they maintain that it will last for a hundred years.

Because they constantly delight themselves in the five desires, taking them to be permanent and pleasurable, the Bodhisattva destroys this affliction by clarifying that this body is impermanent, characterized by suffering and vexation, and is utterly loathsome;
one should instead rejoice in the Buddha-body. Regarding the destruction of the views of the Śrāvakas:
the Śrāvaka views that saṃsāra should be abandoned and nirvāṇa can be attained, because they possess four kinds of knowledge and attain two kinds of nirvāṇa.
Now, the Bodhisattvas have all shattered [the notions of] dhyāna and prajñā, as well as the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—all of which are deviations.

To "shatter the Bodhisattva" means that they refute the claim that there are ten thousand practices (*daśasahasra-caryā*) to be cultivated, that a Buddha-fruit can be attained, that there are predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) to be received, or that there is a person who can attain them.
Vimalakīrti shatters them all; when examined, nothing remains. This is explained at length in the text. Is this not so?
Thus, there are three grades. Question: Since both Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas are disciples (*śiṣya*), for what reason are Śrāvakas called "disciples" while Bodhisattvas are not designated as such?
Explanation: While the general rule would suggest otherwise, it is not so because Śrāvakas personally attend upon the physical form of the Buddha;
their demeanor is in accordance with the Dharma, and thus they are called "disciples. The forms of Bodhisattvas are not fixed, and they act contrary to the conventional norm.
To harmonize with the Way is like Mañjuśrī’s drawing his sword to strike the Buddha; because this was not the dharma of a disciple, he could not be called a "disciple.
As for why he is nevertheless called a "disciple," an external text states: "The Master regarded his gate-disciples as younger brothers and placed himself among them as an elder brother;
the disciples loved the Master as a father and placed themselves among him as sons. Thus, teacher and student were raised together as a single unit.
It is said that the Buddha-Dharma penetrates sentient beings, such that one approaches the Buddha as a father and positions oneself as a son;
the Buddha likewise regards sentient beings as his children and positions himself as their parent. Therefore, it is said: "I am the father of the world, and all sentient beings are my children.

Those who attained awakening first are the elder brothers, while those who attained awakening later are the younger brothers; thus, they are called "disciples" (*śrāvaka*). This is according to this text.
The middle section consists of two parts: first, the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) manifests illness; second, the Tathāgata sends a messenger.
The reason for these two parts is that both serve as conditions to benefit sentient beings. These two sages observe one another: Vimalakīrti is an ancient Buddha and Śākyamuni is a present Buddha;
Vimalakīrti is in the secular world and Śākyamuni is in the Way; Vimalakīrti is ill and Śākyamuni is not ill—all such instances are likewise [for the purpose of benefiting others].
It is for the sake of benefiting sentient beings through skillful means.
At that time, the elder Vimalakīrti thought to himself: "I am currently bedridden with illness; will the World-Honored One, in his great compassion, not deign to show me pity?"
Now, the first section—“Vimalakīrti Manifests Illness”—is as presented in the text.

○ Regarding the passage “The Buddha, knowing his intention,” the second section—“The Buddha Commands an Inquiry into the Illness”—is divided into two parts: first, the command to the Śrāvakas; second, the command to the Bodhisattvas.
Within the section on the Śrāvakas, there are two further divisions: first, the individual commands to ten persons; second, the collective command to five.
The hundred [disciples] now constitute the first group of ten. These ten people are further divided into two types; within these two types, there are three groups.
Regarding the "two types" and the "three": the first four are the four great *śrāvakas*; the next three are the three great Dharma-masters—Pūrṇa, who understands the *Sūtra*;
Vatsīputra (Candana), who understands the *Abhidharma*; and Upāli, who understands the *Vinaya*—while the remainder...
Third, they are the Buddha’s own kinsmen. Furthermore, there are three types: Śāriputra is a person of the superior grade, while Maudgalyāyana is a person of the middling grade.
Thus, the Sūtra says that Śāriputra attained awakening upon hearing [the Dharma] once, whereas Maudgalyāyana attained awakening only after hearing it twice.
Moreover, for every one thing Śāriputra understood, Maudgalyāyana understood five hundred; the rest are persons of the inferior grade. This refers to the second [category].
Regarding the two types of lineage: the former two refer to those who are left and right attendants, while the latter refers to those who are not attendants;
furthermore, the latter three belong to the royal caste, whereas the former consist of a mixture of noble and humble origins.
The Buddha, knowing their thoughts, addressed Śāriputra: "Go to Vimalakīrti and inquire after his illness."
Among the ten [disciples], he is now the foremost; Śāriputra was sent to inquire after his illness.
This man is the foremost in wisdom among the śrāvakas and is the one who turned the Wheel of Dharma for the second time. Thus, the treatise says:

"Of all forms of wisdom, with the exception of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, if one were to compare [any other] to Śāriputra, it would not equal even one-sixteenth part. [This refers to] the foreigner.
All were prostrated by his divine wisdom; for this reason, the preceding command constitutes two parts according to the text:
first, the command to inquire after his illness, and second, the refusal on the grounds of incapacity. What follows now is the initial command to inquire after his illness.
"Śāriputra" is translated here as "Son of Body" (Shenzi), a name derived from his mother; because his mother was of great intelligence and her fame spread far and wide, he was named after her.
Because his mother’s name was similar to that of the śāri bird, he is called Śāriputra; this is explained in detail in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.”

Śāriputra addressed the Buddha: [This concludes] the second section on declining to accept, which consists of three parts: first, the heading indicating the inability; second, the explanation of that inability;
and third, the conclusion regarding that inability. This present passage is the first part, the heading indicating the inability.
Why is this? I recall that in the past, while I was sitting in meditation beneath a tree in the forest, Vimalakīrti came to me and said:
"O Śāriputra, it is not merely by such sitting that one is said to be 'sitting in meditation. As for true sitting in meditation:

it is when one does not manifest body or mind within the three realms; this is sitting in meditation. It is when one manifests various majestic postures without arising from the meditative concentration of cessation."
To sit in meditation while not abandoning the Dharma yet manifesting the affairs of ordinary people—this is sitting in meditation.

For the mind to dwell neither within nor without—this is sitting in meditation. To remain unmoved by all views while practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—this is sitting in meditation.
To enter nirvana without severing the afflictions—this is sitting in meditation. If...

"One who can sit in this manner is approved by the Buddha. At that time, I, the World-Honored One, hearing these words, remained silent and ceased speaking, unable to offer a further reply. Why was this?
[This concludes] the second explanation of being unable to respond; [now follows] the first section on being rebuked.
By means of the second illumination, the purport of the rebuke is established; by the third, the submission [of Śāriputra] is shown. Now, first, the reason for being rebuked is presented:
Śāriputra was rebuked because he suffered from the agitation of body and mind and desired to dwell in mountains and marshes;
therefore, he was rebuked. At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me: [the following section] presents the second point, the one who is able to rebuke.
The reason why those who follow the Śrāvaka path are rebuked is that they have three layers of attachments. First, they possess both body and mind;
this constitutes one layer of attachment. Furthermore, seeing this body as something real, they seek to find peace for it within forests and marshes;
seeing this mind as something real, they seek to guard it in a single state of concentration. Thus, they see this scattering as something to be abandoned and strive to eliminate it.

There is meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) that can also be settled, which is the second stage. Upon reaching it, one perceives dispersion and perceives stillness; one perceives arising and perceives cessation.
Dispersion cannot employ stillness, and stillness cannot employ dispersion; arising cannot employ cessation, and cessation cannot employ arising;
arising and cessation together cannot employ the absence of arising and cessation. Thus, dispersion and stillness obstruct one another.
Because the characteristics of arising and ceasing obstruct non-arising and non-ceasing, there is attainment; because there is obstruction, there is attainment.
One who thus possesses attainment is not a disciple of the Buddha but a member of Māra’s retinue; therefore, he is rebuked. It is not necessarily those who sit [in meditation] who are meant here;

Śāriputra must sit in this manner because he perceives his body and mind as agitated and restless, and thus requires to dwell in mountain forests to settle the body and collect the mind into a single object.
Vimalakīrti rebuked him, saying that sitting in this manner does not constitute "sitting in meditation" (*yàn-zuò*).

Furthermore, regarding the insistence on sitting, although Śāriputra’s sitting here was indeed the ultimate superior sitting, Vimalakīrti’s is not merely the first kind of sitting. (The pronunciation of *yàn* is *yàn*.
Now, as for "sitting in meditation," it means not manifesting body or mind within the three realms; the former [criticism] was a general rebuke, while this is a specific one.
The previous rebuke concerned the sitting posture of the Śrāvakas; now, it demonstrates the sitting posture of the Bodhisattvas.

When it says, "He does not manifest his body or mind within the three realms," it clarifies that although Śāriputra entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and extinguished his mind, he could not extinguish the afflictions of his body.

While the mind within the three realms was extinguished, the afflictions of the body within the three realms were not extinguished; thus, the body could not be extinguished. For this reason, Vimalakīrti rebuked him. Since [Śāriputra] desired...

If the cessation of the mind should entail the cessation of the body, then since the body is not ceased, the mind likewise should not be ceased. Yet Śāriputra, though he universally ceases the mind, cannot cease the body;
therefore, this is not true "sitting in meditation. For a Bodhisattva it is not so: when manifesting, they manifest both simultaneously; when ceasing, they cease both simultaneously. Question:
Why is it said that they are "both" [simultaneous], given that the Bodhisattva ceases the mind because there is no mind, and ceases the body because there is no body?
Is it not the case that cessation is otherwise? The explanation says: It is not so. The tradition of Guanzhong states:

A Bodhisattva takes the Dharma-body as his body, pervading all places yet remaining outside the three realms; he takes wondrous wisdom as his mind, universally conditioning all objects while remaining eternally quiescent.

Because he pervades all places yet remains outside the three realms, and because he universally conditions all objects while remaining eternally quiescent, when these are manifested, they are manifested together, and when they cease, they cease together.

It is cessation; yet, because the Bodhisattva has never been characterized by either "together" or "not together"—in order to shatter the notion of one appearing while another does not—the text says that for the Bodhisattva, both appear together and both do not appear together.
If there were no state of being "not together," there would likewise be no Bodhisattva who is "together";

they are simply transcendent and pure. As for manifesting majestic deportment without arising from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), this was previously explained as mastery over body and mind.

Now, it is explained that stillness and distraction are unimpeded. Those of the Two Vehicles who enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) cannot manifest majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*), and those who manifest majestic deportment cannot enter the meditative absorption of cessation.
This is because stillness obstructs distraction and distraction obstructs stillness; therefore, they are not disciples.

When a Bodhisattva enters the meditative absorption of cessation and yet manifests majestic deportment, their movement is capable of the function of stillness, and so forth. They do not abandon the dharmas of the Path while manifesting [these states].

"Ordinary people attend to this" and below clarifies that there is no obstruction between the secular and the monastic. "The mind does not dwell within" means being sovereign over both internal and external;
not relying on the six internal sense organs (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) and not relying on the six external objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) constitutes *yansan* (seated meditation).

"Remaining unmoved amidst various views while practicing the factors of the path" means that while Śrāvakas are moved by various views when practicing the factors of the path, [the Bodhisattva] practices the factors of the path while remaining unmoved.

Regarding the various views (*dṛṣṭi*): which ones move through the three, four, two, or five [categories]? The various views and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are severed by the single [path] of the Truths (*satya*), or severed by the single [path] of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Or rather, it is precisely because they move through the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) that the various views are not [separate from them];

for the Bodhisattva in meditative seclusion (*pratisaṃlayana*) is not otherwise. Are the various views themselves the factors of the path? Yes, because they are unimpeded. Yet, they do not sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Entering into nirvana is likewise as described in the text. If one can sit in this manner, it is clearly approved by the Buddha;
if one can sit thus, one is a disciple of the Buddha, whereas if one cannot do so, one is not a disciple and is not approved by the Buddha.
At that time, [the opponent] was humiliated for the third time.
Therefore, I am not fit to go and inquire after his illness.
Thus, I am unable; I cannot bear the third entanglement. There are five reasons why Śāriputra was unable:
first, because of the difference between the Great and Small Vehicles, he was unable; second, because this is the dwelling place of present-day śrāvakas...
First, these śrāvakas are disciples of past Buddhas; how could they possibly question a present Buddha?

Second, there is a difference between "attainment" and "non-attainment": how could śrāvakas who have attained anything possibly question a Bodhisattva who has no attainment? These two points are to be compared.
Third, these śrāvakas have already been rebuked by the householder; since they were previously unable to answer him, they do not [speak] now.

Regarding the five who were worthy of being questioned: these are all individuals who have realized the Way (*tīdào*), employing the skillful means (*upāya*) of contraction and extension to suit their respective faculties and conditions.
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana: This is the second section, "Commanding Maudgalyāyana. As for why Śāriputra was commanded first and Maudgalyāyana afterwards: [it was because]... (text continues).
Furthermore, it is because these two individuals possessed profound and heavy vows from past lives that were perfectly synchronized;
thus, after Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana was next summoned. Moreover, these two are the Buddha’s disciples who stand at his left and right sides:
if Śāriputra is on the right side, then Maudgalyāyana is on the left side. In this context, the left is honored while the right is considered inferior, as is the case with the left hand.
The Left Vice-Director (You Puyue) is inferior to the Right Vice-Director (Shi Puyue). If one follows foreign customs, the right is honored and the left is held in low esteem;
therefore, Śāriputra was on the right and Maudgalyāyana was on the left. Thus, the Pure Name previously rebuked this person, for he had violated [the protocol].
Furthermore, while Śāriputra is a sage who remains silent, Maudgalyāyana is a sage who preaches the Dharma; the Buddha commanded his disciples to always practice in this manner.
Second, now Vimalakīrti refutes Śāriputra’s holy silence, showing that his holy silence does not constitute true holy silence;

he refutes Maudgalyāyana’s holy preaching of the Dharma, showing that his holy preaching of the Dharma does not constitute true holy preaching. Since neither his holy silence nor his holy preaching constitutes true holiness, he is no longer a disciple of the Buddha.
Furthermore, previously he refuted Śāriputra’s silence, showing it was not true silence; now he refutes Maudgalyāyana’s speech.

Whether in silence or in speech, all such conventional expressions fail to be established, just as in the Mahāyāna Sūtra it is said that shaving one's head and begging for alms are likewise not established.
Furthermore, this refutes the three karmas of the Śrāvakas, all of which are impure. Previously, the impurity of the mental karma of Śāriputra was refuted while he was practicing dhyāna;
now, the impurity of the verbal karma of Maudgalyāyana is refuted while he is preaching the Dharma. Next...

In the *Pójiāshè qǐshí* (Breaking the Kāśyapa’s Begging), it is said that his physical karma was impure; [it is taught that] while the three karmas of śrāvakas are all impure, those of bodhisattvas are entirely pure.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "When a bodhisattva practices prajñā, their physical karma is pure, up to and including the purity of mental karma.
As for what is called "impurity," it refers to seeing the body, speech, and mind as impure. Why? Because one sees the body...
Because one perceives the views of body, speech, and mind, they are impure; if one does not perceive the karma of body, speech, and mind, it is pure.
Previously, Śāriputra perceived the mind, and thus his mind was impure; now, Maudgalyāyana perceives that there are dharmas to be spoken, and thus his speech is impure.
At times, the Great Master further advanced his argument to refute Śāriputra, but he refuted only the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Now, having refuted the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), one further refutes the conventional designation (*prajñapti*). Regarding the previous refutation of intrinsic nature:

there is nothing that cannot function when it is quiescent, yet it cannot function when it is dispersed; this is the meaning of "nature. Now, in refuting both nature and designation, the refutation of nature is no different from the aforementioned refutation of designation.
Thus the text says: "Dharmas have no comparison because they are without mutual dependence," thereby clarifying the long-standing relationship between existence and non-existence.

The meaning of "short" and "long" being mutually dependent is that of provisional designation (*upādāya-prajñapti*). Now, when one seeks for existence, it cannot be found; when one examines non-existence, there is nothing from which it can arise.
Thus, since the long and the short—both subject and object—cannot be established, what thing could there be to depend upon?

Therefore, it is said: "Dharmas have no comparison; they are without mutual dependence. Question: While the nature [of things] may be refuted, how can the meaning of provisional designation be refuted? Answer: There is. It is explained as follows: there is.

Since there is only provisional designation because of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and since intrinsic nature does not exist, how can there be provisional designation? Because there is that which is dependent, there is that which is non-dependent;
since there is no dependence, there is also no non-dependence. Thus, both dependence and non-dependence are pure, for the two vehicles do not participate in the realm of the Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, above I refuted Śāriputra by challenging his own practice; now I refute Maudgalyāyana by challenging his...
While he himself practices meditation in secluded places to transform others, he now preaches for the sake of the lay devotees; this is what it means to transform others through preaching.
What Dharma does he preach? He preaches the Dharma of giving and so forth. Furthermore, this refutation of the Śrāvakas is precisely the instruction for Bodhisattvas.
The Buddha said to Mahāmaudgalyāyana, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
According to the text, this also consists of two parts: first, the command; second, the refusal of the inability. Now follows the first part, the command to Maudgalyāyana (and so forth).
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.
Maudgalyāyana’s second refusal consists of three parts: first, the indication of his unfitness;
second, the explanation of his unfitness; and third, the conclusion. This section is the indication of his unfitness.
Why is this? I recall that in the past, when I had entered the great city of Vaiśālī and was teaching the Dharma to the lay devotees in the streets and alleys,
Vimalakīrti came to me and said, "O Mahāmaudgalyāyana, you should not teach the Dharma to lay devotees as you have just done."
Why is this so? Below, the second section explains the inability [to teach], which also has three parts: first, the reason for being rebuked; second, the purport of the one capable of rebuking;
and third, the acceptance of defeat. This is now the first: the reason for being rebuked. For what reason was he rebuked?
It was because he was preaching the Dharma for a layperson (*gṛhapati*). The Great Master said: "This chapter is precisely..."

If a Dharma-preacher who holds some attainment is refuted by Vimalakīrti, or if one claims there is a person who is the speaker and that which is spoken, a teacher who can teach and a recipient who is taught, or a speaker and a listener—these are all refuted by Vimalakīrti.
He exhorts and transforms them toward non-reliance and non-attainment, because he asks about the teaching. Thus, the subsequent text says: "As for his teaching..."
The Dharma is without speech and without demonstration; those who hear the Dharma neither hear nor attain it. It is preached like an illusion, and it is preached as an illusion.
When preaching like an illusion, there is nothing preached; when hearing like an illusion, there is nothing heard. One should establish this intention.
At that time, Vimalakīrti arrived and spoke—this is the second instance of his coming forth to set forth the principle of "able censure."
In general, the reproach that what has been said is inappropriate contains several meanings. First, "inappropriate" refers to speech that is contradictory;
because you have made such a statement, it is contradictory, and thus it is called inappropriate.
Furthermore, "inappropriate" means that you possess a mind of attainment while speaking of the Tathāgata’s dharma of non-attainment; for the Tathāgata is without...

Regarding "attaining": within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), there is the mind that attains, yet the dharmas attained are non-attainable. To establish dharmas as having something to be attained is to destroy the characteristics of all dharmas;
therefore, it is a calamity and an anomaly. Furthermore, "inappropriate" (*budō*) is of two kinds: first, being inappropriate regarding the conditions of the sense faculties (*indriya-pratyaya*);
second, being inappropriate regarding the characteristics of dharmas (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*). Hence, it is called "inappropriate."
Now, one who preaches the Dharma should preach the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma: because it is devoid of sentient beings, the Dharma is free from the defilement of sentient beings;
because it is devoid of a self, the Dharma is free from the defilement of the self; because it is devoid of life-span, the Dharma is free from birth and death;

because it is devoid of a person, the Dharma is severed at its prior and subsequent limits. The Dharma is eternally quiescent, for it extinguishes all marks; the Dharma is free from marks, for it has no object of perception. The Dharma...

Because names and speech are severed, dharmas are beyond verbal expression; because they are free from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), dharmas have no form or characteristic, being like empty space;
because they are ultimately empty, dharmas are free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); because they are devoid of "mine," dharmas have no sense of possession;

because they are free from all consciousnesses, dharmas are without discrimination; because they are without comparison, dharmas have no counterpart; and because they do not belong to causes, dharmas are... [not subject to conditions].

Because phenomena arise through conditions, they accord with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); because phenomena enter into all things, they follow suchness (*tathatā*) without following anything;

because phenomena abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), they do not move toward any extremes; because phenomena are without agitation, they do not rely on the six sense objects; because phenomena have no coming or going, they never abide;

because phenomena conform to emptiness, follow signlessness (*animitta*), and correspond to wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), they are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and free from beauty and ugliness; thus, phenomena are without [intrinsic nature].

The Dharma is free from increase or decrease; it is a dharma without arising or ceasing; it is a dharma that has no place of return; it is a dharma that transcends the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind;
it is a dharma without high or low; it is a dharma eternally abiding and immovable; it is a dharma detached from all contemplative practices.
O Mahāmaudgalyāyana, such is the nature of dharmas—how could it ever be described?
Now, one who expounds the Dharma should do so in accordance with the Dharma; this exhortation to expound in accordance with the Dharma means that it is impossible to establish a duality here.
First is the refutation of the person (*pudgala*), and second is the refutation of dharmas (*dharma*). "Person" refers to the person who acts as the agent or the object of action;
"dharmas" refers to the dharmas of the teaching gate. These two chapters encompass everything exhaustively. If one perceives a person or perceives dharmas, [it is not in accordance with the Dharma].
What are these two views that you claim constitute an Arhat? For this reason, I shall now refute these two types. Within the two chapters, this is the first:
the refutation of the view of a person (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*). You say there is a person who is acted upon; who is this person who is acted upon?
You say there is a person who acts as a speaker; who is this person who speaks? If you do not perceive the person who is the object of action, [how can you establish such a self?]
One who is capable [of teaching] is itself purity; if one perceives the one who can speak and the one to whom it is spoken, this is defilement.

Therefore, the Dharma has no sentient beings, because it is free from the defilements of sentient beings. "The Dharma is eternally quiescent" marks the second section, which refutes views regarding the Dharma.
To say "the Dharma is eternally quiescent" means that, as explained above, there is no person, no life-span, no agent, and no object. It is not...
This is the True Dharma that dispels [all things] so they become non-existent; since the original nature of all dharmas is eternally thus, it is said that "dharmas are eternally quiescent.
Furthermore, the intent is this: when you now preach the Dharma, do you preach for the sake of persons or for the sake of dharmas?

If you preach for the sake of persons, since there are no persons, how can you preach for persons? If you preach for the sake of dharmas, since there are no dharmas, how can you preach dharmas? This is precisely the purification of persons.
The Dharma is the two-fold emptiness of person and phenomena for the wise;

that "the Dharma is free from marks because there is nothing to be apprehended" means that while Maudgalyāyana possessed a mind capable of apprehension, here it is clarified that being free from marks, there is nothing to be apprehended.

Since there is nothing to be apprehended, there is likewise no such thing as an apprehending subject. That "the Dharma has no name" refers to the aforementioned refutation of the substantiality of dharmas. This is...
Regarding the "Destruction of Dharmas" (Pofa), Master Zhao said: "Names have no power to grasp objects, and objects have no reality to correspond to names.
Since there is neither name nor object, where do names and objects reside? Dharmas have no speech; they are beyond conceptualization (*vitarka*) and discernment (*vicāra*).

Although Maudgalyāyana had dharmas he could speak of, his current destruction [of them] arises from internal conceptualization and discernment, whereby external speech-dharmas appear. Yet even conceptualization and discernment themselves do not exist."

As for the statement, "Where could there be a teaching that what was originally non-existent now exists? For dharmas are free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) because they are ultimately empty," this means that to claim there is a dharma that can be taught or a person who can teach it constitutes conceptual proliferation.

Now it is clarified that there is neither a subject nor an object, and thus no conceptual proliferation, being like space. That dharmas have no comparison and no mutual dependence has already been explained.
The previous explanation is also like the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*’s treatment of fire and fuel: phenomena do not belong to causes and do not reside in conditions.
For example, if one seeks a sprout within a grain, it cannot be found; seeking it within water or soil, it likewise cannot be found.

Because it cannot be found within the grain, it does not belong to the cause; because it cannot be found in the water or soil, it does not reside in the conditions. Thus, phenomena are eternally abiding and immovable.
"Phenomena are free from all modes of contemplation"—these final two phrases conclude the refutation of the permanence and immobility of external phenomena.

"Free from all modes of contemplation, they are eternally quiescent and immovable"—this concludes the refutation of the internal as well. "Conditions being exhausted, they are free from all modes of contemplation; purity encompasses both internal and external;

object and contemplation are both stilled. This means that when conditions are exhausted, one is free from all modes of contemplation, such that purity pervades both the internal and external, and both the objective referent and the contemplative observation are simultaneously tranquilized.
"Only Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the characteristics of dharmas are thus"—this concludes the summary and reproach as in the text.

Now, one who preaches the Dharma has neither speaking nor showing; those who listen to the Dharma have neither hearing nor attainment. It is as if a phantom person were preaching the Dharma for a phantom person.
One should establish this intention when preaching the Dharma, and one should understand that the faculties of sentient beings are either sharp or dull.

Being dull in wisdom yet unimpeded in knowledge and vision, one should praise the Mahāyāna with a heart of great compassion, remain mindful of repaying the Buddha’s kindness, and ensure that the Three Jewels are never interrupted;
only then should one preach the Dharma.
Now, as for the one who preaches the Dharma, "no preaching and no demonstrating" is an exhortation to preach in such a manner; it is also a turning of the pivot to break [delusions].
Why? Because when those hearers above were told that there is no person and no dharma, and no agent and no object, they immediately concluded that both agent and object are entirely non-existent.
Therefore, the pivot is now turned to clarify that the preacher of the Dharma has no preaching, and the listener of the Dharma has no listening.
There is no hearing; there is no such thing as hearing what is preached as an illusion. One merely hears what is preached as an illusion, and in hearing, there is nothing heard;
one merely speaks what is preached as an illusion, and in speaking, there is nothing spoken. When will there ever be neither speaking nor hearing?
One must understand that the faculties of sentient beings are either sharp or dull; this, moreover, is a turning point to clarify that there is no speaking and no hearing in speaking and hearing.
One should speak of things as being like an illusion and listen to them as being like an illusion; one must not speak at random. One should observe the faculties of others.

If one were to explain it directly in this way [from the beginning], why did Śākyamuni Tathāgata, at the outset, not immediately teach this Dharma, but instead taught the vehicles of humans and devas, up to the three vehicles and so forth?
Therefore, one must know whether their faculties are sharp or dull and preach the Dharma accordingly; one must not [preach indiscriminately].
To say that he turned [the meaning] in such a way was simply because Maudgalyāyana proceeded to provide this interpretation,
which is why Vimalakīrti subsequently refuted it.
When Vimalakīrti preached this Dharma, eight hundred lay devotees (gṛhapati) resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Maudgalyāyana thought to himself, "I have no such eloquence as this.
When Vimalakīrti preached this Dharma, Maudgalyāyana was humbled for the third time, and eight hundred lay devotees attained the Way.
Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
This concludes the third section, which summarizes the inability [to go].
Next, the third [section] commands Kāśyapa; it addresses Kāśyapa: "Why is it that you, an Elder, are here with Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana?"
Later, Liai’s commentary states: Although Kāśyapa’s seniority in the precepts (*śīla-varṣa*) was great, his wisdom was not necessarily superior to that of the two preceding individuals.
Regarding the distribution of food by means of counting sticks (*śalākā*), the foremost elder asks first, followed by the junior elder.
Since one who inquires after illness must possess wisdom and eloquence (*pratibhāna*), the Buddha first summoned Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, and subsequently summoned Kāśyapa.
Question: "Kāśyapa, there are further elders who do not understand; you say that above Kāśyapa there are over a thousand people.

Why then do you speak of 'elders' [only] as the ten great disciples and the four great śrāvakas? It is like the Master [Confucius], who led three thousand disciples, yet among them only seventy-two entered the inner chamber.
Among the heroic and outstanding, there were eighty-nine; now it is the same—there are one thousand and two."
There were one hundred and fifty arhats and five hundred śrāvakas, including the ten great disciples and the four great śrāvakas.
[The Buddha] asked why he was sending two people to inquire after his illness. The explanation is as follows: He wished to demonstrate compassion by making a universal proclamation;

furthermore, he wished to provide a comprehensive critique; furthermore, he wished to bring extensive benefit. What was previously taught was merely for the sake of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) to benefit those of the Small Vehicle.

Today, within this great assembly, he speaks again for the sake of further benefiting the multitude. The reason his censure differs from the previous instance is that he discusses the three types of action (*trikarma*).

Previously, he censured Śāriputra, which was a censure of the mental action (*manaskarma*) of the śrāvakas; next, he censured Maudgalyāyana, which was a censure of the vocal action (*vākkarma*) of the śrāvakas;
now, he censures Kāśyapa, which is a censure of the bodily action (*kāyakarma*) of the śrāvakas—specifically, regarding his holding of the alms-bowl while begging for food.
This is also a matter of bodily action. Previously, he rebuked Maudgalyāyana for preaching the Dharma, which was a rebuke of the gate of the śrāvakas' wisdom;
now he rebukes Kāśyapa, which is a rebuke of the gate of the śrāvakas' merit—namely, the merit of begging for alms out of compassion.
Thus, he clarifies that whether it be the wisdom or the merit of the śrāvakas, both are inadequate. Furthermore, having previously rebuked Maudgalyāyana, he now rebukes his patron.
Previously, he rebuked Kāśyapa for his field of merit; now, with Maudgalyāyana preaching the Dharma for the sake of conversion, he rebukes his gift of the Dharma.

Now that Kāśyapa is begging for alms, he is indeed a field of merit; therefore, the previous rebuke concerned the śrāvaka donor, not the donor, while the current rebuke concerns the śrāvaka field of merit, not the field of merit.
Furthermore, the previous rebuke of Maudgalyāyana concerned the wisdom of the śrāvakas.

Now, Prajñāśrī rebukes Kāśyapa; he rebukes the śrāvakas who possess the virtue of cessation. Whether it be their wisdom or their cessation, for the śrāvakas, neither is true wisdom nor true cessation.
Furthermore, previously he rebuked Śāriputra; he rebuked all meditation masters who have attained something;
he rebuked Maudgalyāyana; he rebuked all dharma masters who have attained something; and he rebuked Kāśyapa, the master of moral conduct who has attained something. This is Kāśyapa.
"Because he practices the Way and virtue yet does not rely on the Buddha’s instructions, this chapter has come into being for this reason.
The Buddha said to Mahākāśyapa, "Go to Vimalakīrti and inquire after his illness."
As for Kāśyapa, his nature was that of a tortoise; he was a great being from a foreign land, comparable to the "Gou-long" (river-dragon) of this land or the "Xi-zhu" (western boar).
Thus, the "tortoise" represents a great being from abroad. Regarding his name, many people do not know it; it must have been Potala.
His family was immensely wealthy, such that even a thousandth part of the kingdom of Magadha would fall short of their riches, yet they had no son.
The parents prayed to the devas, saying, "There is no one capable of becoming a son for our family. At that time, out of compassion, Brahmā Devendra was born into their household;
his body was of a true golden color, and his wife was likewise golden-colored. The details of these causal conditions are as previously described in the preceding sections.
Now, this is the first instance of being commanded to inquire after his illness.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness. Why is this?
I recall that in the past, I was wandering for alms in a poor neighborhood."

Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: [The following section] is the second part, which consists of three headings: declining the capacity, explaining the reason for the decline, and concluding the argument.
Herein, we first mark the inability. Why is this so? [The following section] is the second part, the explanation of the inability, which is divided into two:
first, setting forth the cause for being rebuked; second, clarifying the purport of the rebuke. Herein, we first set forth the cause for being rebuked.
The reason he was rebuked was that in the past he had gone to beg for alms in poor neighborhoods;
it was because of this that he was rebuked. There are several reasons why Kāśyapa enters poor neighborhoods to beg: first, to avoid worldly suspicion.
If people were to see Kāśyapa frequently visiting wealthy households and seeking alms there, they might suspect that he is coveting their offerings.
For this reason, one abandons the wealthy to follow the poor. Second, regarding abandoning the wealthy to follow the greedy:

Kāśyapa possesses a heart of compassion equal toward the poor; seeing that those without clothing or food are immediately afflicted by suffering, Kāśyapa accepts alms from them, thereby enabling them to obtain the fruits of the present life.
This is why one should make offerings to those who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Regarding "attaining retribution in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*): Kāśyapa was one who had attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that when Kāśyapa went to a certain household to beg for food, he received neither food nor drink, but obtained only a single bowl of water.

Kāśyapa used it to rinse his mouth and wash his bowl; when he looked at it afterward, it had turned entirely white. This is an instance of retribution in the present life. Furthermore, there is another account.
Kāśyapa went to a poor old woman and begged from her a bowl of dregs; Kāśyapa accepted it and drank it.

Later, the old woman was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven as the goddess Rasanā, the Mistress of the Tongues of the Gods. Desiring to repay his kindness, she descended to transform an old man and the old woman.
When Kāśyapa came to beg from them, the old man and old woman immediately opened a golden jar, and its fragrance pervaded the entire kingdom. Kāśyapa did not accept it.
Third, as for those who fly away: the reason the poor are poor is truly because they did not practice giving in the past; thus they are poor now.
If they do not give now, they will be poor in the future. Fearing that their poverty will never end, they beg from the poor.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me: "O Mahākāśyapa, you possess a heart of compassion, yet you do not practice universal equanimity by begging from the poor while avoiding the wealthy.
Kāśyapa, you should dwell in the dharma of equality and beg for alms in regular succession. You should go on almsround for the sake of non-eating;
you should accept morsel-food for the sake of destroying the perception of composite things; you should receive food for the sake of non-acceptance."
Receiving that food with the perception of it as an empty village, he enters the town: whatever forms he sees are like those of a blind man;

whatever sounds he hears are like echoes; whatever fragrances he smells are like the wind; regarding tastes he eats, he does not discriminate; and as for all tactile sensations, he experiences them as they are realized by wisdom:
that all phenomena are like illusions, lacking intrinsic nature and lacking extrinsic nature, being fundamentally non-arisen and now non-existent.
Kāśyapa, if you can enter the eight liberations without abandoning the eight heterodoxies, and enter the true Dharma through the characteristics of the heterodox;
if you can offer a single meal to all beings as an offering to all Buddhas and the assembly of worthy sages, only then may you eat such food.
One who eats such food has neither afflictions nor is free from afflictions; they have neither entered a state of meditative concentration nor arisen from it; they do not abide in the world.

"In the interim, one does not abide in nirvāṇa; for whoever gives, there is neither great merit nor small merit, it is neither beneficial nor detrimental—this is the correct entry into the Buddha-way, not relying on the śrāvakas.
Kāśyapa, if one eats in this manner, one does not eat the alms of others in vain.

At that time, our World-Honored One, hearing these words, attained what he had never experienced before, and immediately [at that single...]* *Note: The source text appears to be truncated at "即於一". This translation reflects the available portion.*
All the bodhisattvas gave rise to profound reverence and further thought: "One who possesses such a name as this, and such eloquence and wisdom, is truly capable of this.
Who would not resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Since that time, I have no longer exhorted others toward the practices of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. For this reason, I am not fit to go there to inquire.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and addressed [Kāśyapa]. This is the second instance of the principle of being able to censure him:

while Kāśyapa was begging for alms in a poor neighborhood, Vimalakīrti immediately came to censure him, noting that although Kāśyapa possessed a heart of compassion, it was not universal, as he avoided wealthy families.

Regarding the statement that [the practice] is not universal because it proceeds from the poor: there is both the horizontal and the vertical. As for the horizontal not being universal, it means abandoning the wealthy to beg from the poor.
If there is compassion, then there is the Great [Vehicle]; if there is no Great [Vehicle], then there is no compassion.

If there were the Great [Vehicle], one would beg universally from both the poor and the wealthy; because one abandons the wealthy to beg from the poor, it is not universal. (And so forth. This is the vertical.
Regarding "not universal," Kāśyapa, it is because one sees only the poor of the past who failed to practice giving;

seeing that they are poor now, one does not see the wealthy of the present practicing giving, and thus fails to see those who will be poor in future lives. Because one perceives what is near but not what is far, it is called "not universal.

Furthermore, the compassion (*maitrī*) of the *śrāvakas* is not universal because their great compassion is limited. Why? Because the compassion of the *śrāvakas* is like the compassion for eunuchs or the compassion for those without roots of virtue.

The great compassion of a bodhisattva is not [limited] great compassion; rather, it universally delivers all sentient beings from birth-and-death within and without the triple world and bestows upon them the bliss of Great Nirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa, it merely desires to equalize those who suffer from lack of support and lack of food by providing them with clothing, food, and drink;
because it cannot ultimately deliver them and grant them ultimate bliss, it is said to be "not universal. As for the "Dharma of equality":

To beg for alms in successive order without distinguishing between the poor and the wealthy is called "equal begging. Kāśyapa’s practice of abandoning the wealthy to follow the poor is not equal, and therefore it is not compassion.
For one who should practice begging for food because they do not eat [at home], the former [criticism] was for abandoning the wealthy to follow the poor; now the criticism is directed at him.
Previously, he was criticized for his failure to transform others; now, he is criticized for his failure in his own practice. Therefore, he is now rebuked for begging for food.
One who should practice begging must not go without eating. Why?
Because although the minds of śrāvakas are free from outflows (anāsrava), their bodies still require sustenance. Thus, they must eat; this is why Vimalakīrti now rebukes him.
How does this differ from that of an ordinary person? An ordinary person also begs for food, and you likewise beg for food;
therefore, you are no different from an ordinary person. If there were a difference, then while the ordinary person begs for food, you should not beg for food.
To "cherish the harmony of the aggregates" means that harmony is the harmony of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Ordinary persons act to increase the five [aggregates].
The grasping for food by means of the body of the aggregates—you now likewise perform this grasping for food that prolongs the five aggregates, no different from ordinary worldlings;
you should extinguish this grasping for food of the five aggregates. As for "kabalīṅkāra-āhāra" (morsel-food), it refers to food taken by grasping and chewing.

However, while rice possesses four subtle elements (*tanmātra*), only three subtle elements sustain the body; the element of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) does not sustain the body. One should enter a village with the perception of it as an empty village.
Those who have fallen—the śrāvakas—cannot be thus; they cannot simultaneously [comprehend] true emptiness while entering a village.
Entering a village necessarily pertains to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya). Because they enter a village, they cannot simultaneously [comprehend] true reality.
Therefore, it is now rebuked: as if entering a village that is like an empty village, one enters the village; yet entering the village is precisely like an empty village.
"This village is ultimately empty; it is the ultimate empty, quiescent dwelling. Knowing it to be thus, one may go for alms.
Regarding the phrase "the forms seen are equal to those of the blind," this next section rebukes the six sense faculties; however, in this passage, Kāśyapa has reached three levels [of meaning].
The first inversion is to abandon the wealthy and follow the poor out of a heart of compassion.
The second is to think that wherever one treads, the village is what is trodden upon, and the body is that which treads;

furthermore, upon entering the village, one again sees with the eyes forms—square, round, long, short, beautiful, or ugly—and hears sounds with the ears. For these reasons, Vimalakīrti rebuked him in successive order.
Now, first of all, one must reprove the eye for seeing forms, treating them as equal to those who are blind; only then may one take food. Śrāvakas cannot do this. Why?
Because when they enter the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), they are like the blind and cannot see;

yet if they were to see while not having entered that absorption, their seeing would not be like that of the blind. If it were otherwise, how would they differ from ordinary people? For ordinary people also act in this way.
"This view of yours is just like the view of ordinary worldlings; you are not a field of merit, nor am I a field of merit.
How can one who begs for alms see as one who is blind? To see as one who is blind is to see while seeing nothing;
to see while seeing nothing—only if you can do so may you receive this food. You should experience all contacts as one who has realized through wisdom."

When the wisdom of the śrāvaka realizes the true nature of reality (dharmatā), there is neither contact nor non-contact; therefore, it is said that "experiencing all contacts" is like the realization of wisdom.

If there were no other-nature (parabhāva) apart from self-nature (svabhāva), Kāśyapa would regard himself as the beggar and others as the object of begging, or himself as the one being measured and others as the standard by which he is measured;
it is because of these two views that [the distinction between self and other] exists.
If one can, without abandoning the eight classes of beings, enter the eight liberations, then one simultaneously strikes both the ordinary person and the sage without abandoning the eight [realms].
As for the two vehicles, do they abandon the eight [realms] to enter the eight liberations? Ordinary persons abandon the eight liberations to take up the eight [realms];
do the two vehicles abandon the eight [realms] to take up the eight liberations? Ordinary persons likewise take up and abandon, and the two vehicles likewise take up and abandon; they are the same.

Grasping and abandoning are equally possessed of afflictions and equally devoid of wisdom; yet the Bodhisattva is not so—he does not abandon the eight [wrong paths], yet he enters the eight liberations.
Entering the eight liberations, he is no ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); not abandoning the eight [wrong paths], he is no follower of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* or *pratyekabuddha*).

This is the practice of the Bodhisattva: neither the conduct of an ordinary person nor the conduct of a noble one (*ārya*). When one thoroughly realizes the eight [wrong paths], they are precisely the eight liberations. Thus it is.
Only by practicing in this way can one go forth to beg for food. To offer a single meal to all beings as a supreme offering to all Buddhas—such a thing a śrāvaka cannot do.

To give a single meal downward to all beings and upward to the Triple Gem, giving downward to all beings and equalizing them with the four modes of birth while offering it upward to the Triple Gem so as to cause the Triple Gem to flourish—this is not the way of a śrāvaka.
If there were neither such an event nor such a thought, then the Bodhisattva’s act of taking food from the Incense Accumulation [Heaven] would not have occurred;
it was precisely because there was both an event and a thought that he took food from the Incense Accumulation—that is, the single meal offered to the immeasurable assembly.
One who eats in this manner neither possesses afflictions nor is free from afflictions; they simultaneously negate both the ordinary and the holy.

For an ordinary person, a single meal gives rise to the three poisons. Although those of the Two Vehicles do not give rise to the three poisons, they ultimately fail to see that food is neither possessing afflictions, nor being free from afflictions, nor being non-saintly. Only if it is like this can it truly be so.
This refers to begging for alms.
Regarding those who give, whether their merit be great or small, it is said that one who gives to a person who has entered the *nirodhasamāpatti* (attainment of cessation) obtains immeasurable merit.
Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Because one enters an immeasurable concentration, one obtains immeasurable merit. This is considered great.
Regarding the giving of merit to ordinary people for the sake of small merit, it is now refuted by saying there is neither great merit nor small merit.

As for the claim that "it neither benefits nor harms": we see in the present that when one begs for food and receives it, one obtains the five fruits [of the monastic life], which constitutes benefit;
when one begs for food and does not receive it, the absence of those five fruits constitutes harm. How, then, can you say it neither benefits nor harms?
Duan Ye’s commentary says: "Ordinary people are also like this; they cannot be considered 'dedicated' (dūna), but can be considered 'beneficial' (yì).

You are now also like this, no different from ordinary people, and thus are not a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). If you were different from ordinary people, then you would not be merely dedicated or beneficial.
If you eat in such a manner, it constitutes not eating the alms of others in vain. If Kāśyapa cannot do so, then his [eating] is in vain."
Kāśyapa, whose moral virtue was such that he was foremost among the twelve dhūta practices, still ate the food offered out of faith by others;
how much more so those of the present day? If one does not embody the Way, how can they be called virtuous? It is because one embodies the Way that it is called virtue;
if one does not embody the Way, how can it be named virtue? Since even upholding the precepts is insufficient, how much less so breaking them!
If within each of the various provinces one harbors this [view], it is not that Kāśyapa is being disparaged, but rather that the words are addressed to Kāśyapa;
if there is such a mental path, one immediately falls into this ruin.
At that time, World-Honored One, having heard these words, I praised and revered the bodhisattva. [I thought:

"If an arhat who has long since emerged were to look down upon a bodhisattva, it would be clear that the arhat śrāmaṇera is superior to a bodhisattva bound for the stage of succession (samyak-saṃbodhi). Why?

Because the arhat śrāmaṇera has already severed all afflictions, whereas the bodhisattva bound for succession is still an ordinary person (pṛthagjana). Therefore, today I praise the śrāmaṇera as being superior to the bodhisattva.

The Bodhisattva’s virtue is lofty while the Śrāvaka’s path is shallow; this person known by the name of his family is Vimalakīrti, a lay Bodhisattva whose joyful reputation has spread far and wide, hence he is called "one renowned by the name of his family. The remaining phrases and sentences are as they appear in the text.
○ Fourth, he addresses Subhūti. This person has attained the Samādhi of Non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*) and is foremost in the understanding of emptiness;
as he is the fourth among the four great śrāvakas, he is addressed here as the fourth. As for why Subhūti was rebuked:
previously, it was simply stated that Kāśyapa abandoned the wealthy for the poor; now, Subhūti [is shown to] abandon...
Kāśyapa went from poverty to wealth because he wished to relieve the suffering of those in immediate distress; thus he followed the path of poverty.
Now, Subhūti goes from wealth to poverty to clarify that although you are currently wealthy and noble, if you do not practice giving now, you will become poor again in future lives;
