therefore, he follows the path of wealth. Since these two individuals are both unequal [in their circumstances], they are both subject to [the cycle of rebirth].

Kātyāyanīputra now says that this is not necessarily so; how could Subhūti, having attained the Samādhi of Non-contention and being able to teach the Prajñāpāramitā himself, have been unaware of Vimalakīrti’s virtuous conduct and yet go to him to beg?
Here it is clarified why Subhūti went to him to beg: while Vimalakīrti was in the city of Vaiśālī, there were five hundred arhats...
Regarding those who dared to peer into his courtyard: Subhūti considered himself one who had attained the Samādhi of Non-contention and was foremost in the realization of emptiness;
internally he possessed wisdom that relies on nothing, and externally he possessed unimpeded eloquence.

Because he was foremost in understanding emptiness and sufficient in his eloquence at that time, when [Mahākāśyapa] arrived at his dwelling, he was thus rebuked. As for "must receive the former," it refers to the sound of the previous reprimand.
Having previously criticized the śrāvakas for their concentration, he now criticizes Śāriputra;

having previously criticized Maudgalyāyana for his supernormal powers, he now criticizes him for preaching the Dharma—thus criticizing the śrāvakas for their concentration and wisdom, which implies that concentration and wisdom are a pair.
Next, he criticizes Kāśyapa for his ascetic practices (dhūta-guṇa), and now he criticizes Subhūti for his understanding of emptiness; this means that practice and understanding are one.

The two śrāvakas—whether in terms of concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), or conduct (*caryā*)—are all rebuked for this reason; they are rebuked because of this very meaning.

Furthermore, these four persons are great arhats who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Making offerings to these four persons yields present retribution. The *Vibhāṣā* states that making offerings to five persons yields great fruit:
first, those in cessation absorption; second, [those in the path of seeing]; third, [those in the path of cultivation]; fourth, [those in the path of no-more-learning]; and fifth, the Buddha.

Through the three samādhis of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), the three states of non-contention (*araṇā*), the first attainment of the lower fruit, and the attainment of the higher fruit—by encountering these five causes and making offerings to these five persons, one obtains a great fruit. Why is this so? There are two meanings:

first, because the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) enters universally into all concentrations and resembles the fruit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one obtains great merit.
The Buddha said to Subhūti, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
The textual passage is as before; now he specifically commands Subhūti—also known as Śubhakarmā, Śubhabuddhi, or Śubhamati—to go and inquire after his illness.
Regarding the karmic conditions for his birth alongside Sudhana (and so forth), that man’s virtuous conduct is inconceivable.
Some call him Buddha Qinglongta (Azure Dragon), while others call him Bodhisattva Aweiyen; Aweiyen is a bodhisattva in his final birth before buddhahood.
Subhūti said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.”
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "I am reluctant to undertake this task; it is for the purpose of introducing, explaining, and concluding [the discourse].
To explain why: I recall that in the past, when I entered his house to beg for alms, Vimalakīrti took my bowl, filled it with food, and said to me:
'Subhūti, if you can regard food as equal to all dharmas...'"
Furthermore, those who are equal to all dharmas are also equal regarding food; practicing alms-gathering in this manner, one may accept food.
Subhūti, if one does not sever lust, anger, and ignorance, yet does not dwell with them; if one does not destroy the body, yet conforms to the single mark;

if one does not extinguish delusion and craving, yet gives rise to liberation; and if one attains liberation through the marks of the five heinous crimes—then such a person is neither liberated nor bound.
He does not see the Four Noble Truths, yet it is not that he does not see the Truths; he has neither attained the fruit nor failed to attain the fruit;

he is neither an ordinary person nor apart from the dharmas of an ordinary person; he is neither a noble one nor not a noble one. Although he accomplishes all dharmas, he is detached from the marks of all dharmas—only then may he take the food.
Subhūti, if he did not see the Buddha and did not hear the Dharma, he would be one of the six heretical teachers.
Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Sañjaya Vairaṭīputra, Ajita Keśakambalin, Kakuda Kātyāyana, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra—these were your teachers.
Because you left the household life under them, you have fallen wherever those teachers fell; only then can you be accepted.
"Eat! If you, Subhūti, enter into various wrong views and do not reach the other shore; if you dwell in the eight difficulties and do not attain freedom from them;

if you are identical to afflictions and separated from pure dharmas—then those who give to you shall not be called fields of merit, and those who make offerings to you shall fall into the three evil realms."
"To join hands with the various Māras and act as their companion in toil; to be no different from the various Māras and the afflictions (*kleśa*);
to harbor enmity toward all sentient beings, to slander the Buddhas, and to destroy the Dharma;
to be excluded from the ranks of the assembly and never attain *nirvāṇa*—if you are thus, only then may you take this food. When my World-Honored One heard this, he said:
Stupefied and not knowing what these words meant, nor how to answer, he set down his bowl and was about to leave the house.
Vimalakīrti said, "Subhūti, take up your bowl; do not be afraid. What do you think?

If a person created by the Tathāgata through his transformative power were questioned on this matter, would they feel any fear? I replied, "No. Vimalakīrti said, "All [beings are likewise like that]."
All dharmas have the characteristic of being like illusions and transformations; you should not feel any fear regarding them now. Why is this?
All verbal expressions do not depart from these characteristics. However, for the wise, they do not cling to words; therefore, they have nothing to fear. Why is this? The nature of words is detached;
there are no words, and this is liberation. The characteristic of liberation is precisely all dharmas.
When Vimalakīrti preached this Dharma, two hundred devaputras attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire after his illness.
Why is this? [The following section] explains the inability [to go], which clarifies the reason for being rebuked.
At that time, Vimalakīrti took my bowl and filled it from the second [vessel] that had come forth; this was the purport of his censure.
However, there may be three reasons why Vimalakīrti—addressing those of discerning wisdom—took Subhūti’s bowl and filled it with food but did not give him any:
first, to fill the bowl completely before speaking, thereby silencing the criticisms of those who accuse him of stinginess; for had he not filled the bowl...
The reprimand states that the householder was stingy with the food and would not give it;

however, if Subhūti had been in his hand, he might have been intimidated and departed before the force of the discourse could be fully exhausted. Thus, [the householder] did not give it and rebuked him. Furthermore, regarding the fact that he filled the bowl but did not give it:
filling the bowl clarifies that the Bodhisattva is the donor, while the rebuke of Subhūti reveals the nature of the Śrāvaka.
The *Pifutiandulunjie Wangshengpin* (Explanation of the Non-field of Merit, Chapter on Rebirth) states: "One who has first resolved for enlightenment is capable of being a field for an Arhat.
If this is so, then how could an Arhat today be capable of being a field for a Dharma-body Bodhisattva?

Furthermore, [the text] shows that filling a bowl with rice represents the Bodhisattva’s material giving (*āmiṣadāna*), while grasping the bowl and questioning [the recipient] represents the Bodhisattva’s ability to practice the Dharma-giving (*dharmadāna*). Again, grasping the rice and asking: "If..."
Regarding the equality of food and so forth, all phenomena are likewise equal. This single point of inquiry leaves one speechless: if they are equal, one should not come to beg;

if they are unequal, one should likewise not come to beg. If the rice in the bowl were equal to the dirt in the bowl, one would not discard the dirt to take the rice; therefore, it is improper to come to beg.
If they are unequal, one discards the dirt and takes the rice—discarding the foul and taking that which is pure. Thus, [the objection] does not hold.

Purity refers to the purification of the mind’s activities of grasping and rejecting; if one holds the dual views of purity and impurity, one is fully possessed of afflictions. Why is it called a field of merit?
Therefore, one should not accept food. If one can understand that the earth is identical to the rice, such that purity and impurity are non-dual, then one may accept the food.
"Not severing lust, anger, and delusion, yet not being accompanied by them" means that both the ordinary person and the sage are simultaneously negated.

If an ordinary person is accompanied by afflictions, and the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) have severed afflictions so as not to be accompanied by them, then this [teaching] clarifies that one does not sever afflictions—thus differing from the two vehicles—and yet is not accompanied by them—thus differing from the ordinary person. That the two vehicles cannot do so is what is called "ordinary."
If one has afflictions, there is the view [of existence]; if the two vehicles have no afflictions, there is the view [of non-existence].

How can these dual views of existence and non-existence be called the foremost understanding of emptiness? To "not destroy the body while conforming to the single mark" means that previously he rebuked the severance of afflictions and rebuked *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder);
now he rebukes the destruction of the marks of the body and rebukes *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder).

The statement that Nirvana does not destroy the body while conforming to a single characteristic clarifies that those of the Two Vehicles destroy the five aggregates of the body to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*;
if they do not destroy the five aggregates of the body, they cannot enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, it is now rebuked [that] one can enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* without destroying the body; [yet] to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* without destroying [the body] is impossible.
The body may indeed be taken as food, yet Subhūti cannot do so; furthermore, he does not enter into the remainderless (*anupadhiśeṣa*). To have a body and views is the view of permanence;

to enter the remainderless is to be without body and without views, which is the view of annihilation. Thus, he is fully endowed with both the views of permanence and annihilation, as well as existence and non-existence.
What is meant by "wisdom that abandons"? What is meant by "understanding emptiness"? For this reason, it is said that he is indestructible.
Within the body, there is a single characteristic; this single characteristic is *nirvāṇa* without remainder. Since this phrase is thus, the remaining phrases are likewise so:
ignorance and craving do not cease, yet they give rise to clarity and liberation. Clarity is the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*);
clarity and liberation are compassionate perception, the ninth liberation. Because ignorance obscures and craving obstructs liberation, by extinguishing ignorance one attains clarity.
Because one attains liberation by severing craving, the Bodhisattva here rebukes the failure to extinguish delusive craving and instead gives rise to the clarity of liberation.

By thoroughly understanding this delusive craving, one immediately realizes that clarity and liberation; since bondage and non-bondage are identical, and awakening and non-awakening are identical, it is said that there is neither bondage nor liberation.

Next, the five heinous crimes (pañcānantarya) are explained as being liberation itself. Previously, the critique was directed toward afflictions; now, the critique is directed toward karma. This was clarified previously.

Regarding the non-obstruction between bondage and liberation, it is now clarified that there is non-obstruction between good and evil: simply to realize these five heinous acts (*pañcānantarya*) is itself liberation.
As when Mañjuśrī pierced the Buddha with his sword, this very act is birthlessness, the absence of agent and object, and ultimate purity.
Why do ordinary people and those of the two vehicles regard liberation as being like the five heinous acts? For liberation is not such as they claim.
To do so would be to harm the True Dharma; the offense of harming the True Dharma exceeds even that of the five heinous crimes.
Subhūti, if you neither see the Buddha nor hear the Dharma, it is because your very nature is such that you say you see the Buddha and hear the Dharma;
yet those in the eight difficult circumstances neither see the Buddha nor hear the Dharma, and the Buddha himself has declared that they do not see him.

Regarding the hearing of the Dharma: When the Buddha first descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven after finishing his preaching for his mother and returned to Jambudvīpa, all people wished to see him.
There was a nun named Utpalavarṇā who desired to go forward to see the Buddha; she transformed herself into a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*).

Everyone thought he was the Wheel-Turning King and all stepped aside to clear the road. When the nun Utpalavarṇā reached the place where the Buddha was, the Buddha said, "It is not you who should come forward."
"Venerable One, you have already paid homage to me; why did Subhūti pay homage to me first? Subhūti was in his stone cave contemplating the Buddha’s Dharma-body;
this is truly paying homage to the Buddha. For this reason, Vimalakīrti rebuked him below, saying: 'To see the Buddha and hear the Dharma is for the sake of realization;
if one sees them but does not realize them, that seeing is false. If it were realization, then there would be neither Buddha nor [Dharma].'"
There is no Buddha and no Dharma, and because there is no Dharma, there is no non-Dharma; thus, there is neither seeing nor hearing.

In this state of delusion, one cannot see the Buddha or hear the Dharma, and even in awakening, one cannot see the Buddha or hear the Dharma. How can you say that you see the Buddha and hear the Dharma?
If one does not know this, then there is no wisdom; where there is no wisdom, there is no severance. Without wisdom and severance, there is nothing to be attained.
Because he is not a disciple of the Buddha’s Dharma, it is said: "Subhūti, if you do not see the Buddha and do not hear the Dharma, only then may you accept this food.
By stating that the six heretical teachers are your teachers, it clarifies that the six teachers are the seven Buddhas and the seven Buddhas are the six teachers.
If one can understand it in this way, only then may one accept the food; Subhūti was unable to do so.
Thus, hearing of the seven Buddhas is correct, whereas hearing of the six teachers is false; because the false and the correct are two, and the internal and external are two, this censure is issued.
When it says "the teacher falls and you fall with him," it clarifies that the followers of those external paths fall into false views in the present life and will fall into hell in the future;
therefore, it is called "falling. To say "the teacher falls and you fall" means:
"He has now fallen into wrong views, and you too should fall into wrong views;
he shall fall into hell, and you too shall fall into hell. Yet, falling into wrong views is itself falling into right contemplation, and falling into hell is itself falling into nirvana.
Why? Because the two causes—wrong and right—are not different, and how could the two results—hell and nirvana—be distinct?
If one can penetrate and understand it in this way, then one may take the food; however, the Śrāvakas cannot do so.

This refers to those who have attained the first fruit of either the heterodox or the orthodox path and have already departed from the three miserable realms—how could an Arhat possibly fall into hell?

In this way, is it that false views are identical to right view, or that right view is distinct from false views? Is it that within false views there exists right view? Or is it that within right view there exists false view?
If one immediately adheres to right view as ultimate, or ultimately adheres to dualistic views, one is not a field of merit.

Why? As the Sūtra says: "Wherever there is duality, there is no Path and no fruit. Furthermore, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra states: "Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa—these two are delusions; the path of the worthy and the sages is otherwise.
If this were the case, where would the samādhi of non-contention and the understanding of emptiness be? This is why I offer this reprimand against such errors.
This rebuke of Subhūti is merely entrusted with a provisional meaning. Is Subhūti truly the Buddha Śākyamuni?
How could he possess these two views? It is that sentient beings possess these two views, and Subhūti manifests them for their sake.
That "the sickness of sentient beings is the sickness of the Bodhisattva" refers precisely to this matter.
"To join hands with all the Māras and act as their fellow laborers"—this means to be of one kind with the Māras, joining hands to lift them up;
it is like using one hand to weave silk. "Subhūti, can you do this? [The Buddha asked. "No, World-Honored One, I cannot; I am incapable of taking food.
At that time, when the World-Honored One heard this, he was taken aback; Subhūti had been rebuked most severely.
What is meant by this? While the aforementioned individuals had only one fault, Subhūti here has two faults. Regarding these two faults:
first, he came when he should not have come; second, he departed when he should not have departed.
As for the phrases "not knowing what to say" and "not knowing how to answer," since the previous reprimand reached his mind in such a manner, [he was thus unable to respond].

Not knowing what these words meant, he could not respond and remained bewildered, unable to give an answer; he then wished to set down his bowl and depart. Vimalakīrti immediately seized him, saying, "You cannot go!
Are you afraid in your heart? Of whom are you afraid now? Who is it that can rebuke you, and who is the object of the rebuke?
Since neither the agent nor the object exists, of what are you afraid? Therefore, he said, "Take your bowl; do not be afraid."
The Tathāgata creates emanated beings; next, he uses this analogy to enlighten them: What capacity does an illusory or emanated person have to revile, and what is there to be reviled?
What capacity has he to speak, and who is there to listen? What is spoken by an illusion, and what is there to be spoken?
What is reviled by an illusion, and what is there to be reviled? If this is so, why should one fear? If one does not realize the nature of illusion, then one is not a disciple of the Buddha.
Therefore it is said that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations; one should not harbor fear. The remaining phrases may be sought elsewhere.

Regarding the two hundred devaputras who attained the Dharma-eye: was this attained prior to hearing [the teaching], or was it attained after hearing? The interpretation is that it was attained upon hearing.
Regarding "attaining the Way later": Subhūti did not understand previously; how could he have attained it then? He only attained the Way later.
The fifth time [the Buddha] summons Pūrṇa: Having finished summoning the four great śrāvakas, he next summons him again.
Regarding that person, the commentary explains that because there were great Dharma masters outside of the four great śrāvakas, he was summoned next.
That person was foremost in preaching the Dharma; both the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* state that he was foremost in preaching the Dharma.
Master Kumārajīva said, "He was foremost in understanding the Abhidharma. [Question: Subhūti is also foremost in preaching the Dharma; why is it now [said to be] Puṇya...?
Rāhula is also said to be foremost in preaching the Dharma; how does this differ [from Subhūti]?

As for Subhūti being foremost in preaching the Dharma, this appears in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Chapter on Encouraging Study (*Kuan-hsüeh p'in*), where Śāriputra praises Subhūti as being the very best among those who preach the Dharma because he has attained the *araṇā-samādhi*.
Nāgārjuna explains that Subhūti is foremost in preaching the Dharma because...
Regarding the fact that Pūrṇa is foremost among those who understand emptiness, he is distinct from Subhūti because he is foremost among those who understand all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
However, being foremost among those who understand all phenomena does not necessarily mean one surpasses Subhūti, who is foremost in the understanding of emptiness. Why is this?
Because there are various types of people, each capable of excelling in their own particular field; some may be preeminent in one area while another is preeminent in another. Now, as for Pūrṇa...
Although he understands all understandings and his realization of emptiness is certainly not inferior to that of Subhūti, why was Pūrṇa rebuked?
The answer is: although Pūrṇa is foremost among all dharmas, this refers to his status as foremost among the śrāvakas and not as a bodhisattva;
therefore, he was rebuked. Furthermore, Pūrṇa is indeed a bodhisattva.
Because he employed skillful means for the sake of appearing as a śrāvaka, the Sūtra says:
"Pūrṇa secretly maintained the practices of a bodhisattva while outwardly manifesting as a śrāvaka with few desires who was weary of birth and death; yet in reality, he purified Buddha-fields.
This was his skillful means of appearing as a śrāvaka and his skillful means of accepting humiliation. Question: At what point was Pūrṇa rebuked? Explanation: It was because he did not understand.

Because of the faculties, [the Buddha] was rebuked: if one possesses the faculty-nature of the Hīnayāna, one should be taught the Hīnayāna Dharma; if one possesses the faculty-nature of the Mahāyāna, one should be taught the Mahāyāna Dharma.

Teaching the Hīnayāna Dharma to one with the faculty-nature of the Hīnayāna—this is the correspondence between the object and the teaching (ālambana-śāsana-saṃvāda). The teaching is the object, and the object is the teaching;

when the object and the teaching correspond, it is the same for the Mahāyāna object as well. This is precisely what is meant by the correspondence between the object and the teaching, and all such cases are alike.
The benefit is like treating a disease with compassion; this is why the Buddha and Jīvaka divided the treatment.
However, because Pūrṇa preached the Dharma of the Hīnayāna for those with the capacity for the Mahāyāna, he was consequently rebuked.
The Buddha said to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
This text also consists of two parts; this is the first, the command to inquire after the illness. *Pūrṇa* means "one whose vows are fulfilled";
*Maitrāyaṇī* means "a woman of good knowledge"; *putra* means "son. Thus, he is the son of a woman who is a woman of fulfilled vows and of noble wisdom.
"Cloud-Maitrāyaṇīputra" refers to those such as Śāriputra.
Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness."
Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha [to decline the request], marking his second refusal and inability to fulfill it; this section now specifically indicates that he is incapable. Why is this?
He recalled: "In the past, while I was in a great forest beneath a tree for the sake of various newly initiated learners..."
While the bhikṣu was preaching the Dharma, Vimalakīrti came and said to me:
"Pūrṇa, you should first enter meditative concentration and observe the minds of these people before preaching the Dharma. Do not place foul food into a precious vessel;
you must know the thoughts within this bhikṣu’s mind. Do not treat lapis lazuli as if it were common crystal; you are unable to understand sentient beings."
From the very beginning, they have not conceived the aspiration for the Lesser Vehicle; they are like those who have no sores themselves—do not wound them.
If you wish to travel the Great Path, do not show them the narrow byway; do not try to contain the great ocean within a cow’s footprint, and do not equate the light of the sun with that of a firefly.
Pūrṇa, this bhikṣu long ago gave rise to the mind of the Mahāyāna, yet he has forgotten this intention.
"Why do you instruct them using the teachings of the Hīnayāna?
I observe that the wisdom of the Hīnayāna is shallow and limited, like a person born blind who cannot distinguish between the sharpness and dullness of the faculties of all sentient beings.
At that moment, Vimalakīrti entered a samādhi, causing these bhikṣus to recognize their own past lives and the roots of merit they had planted under five hundred buddhas.
They dedicated [their merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and immediately their minds were suddenly opened as they recovered their original nature.
Thereupon, those bhikṣus bowed their heads at the feet of Vimalakīrti.
At that time, Vimalakīrti preached the Dharma for them, so that they no longer regressed from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. I reflect that the śrāvakas do not contemplate...
One who lacks the spiritual faculties (indriya) should not preach the Dharma. Why is this?
[The following provides] the second explanation of why he is unfit for the four [tasks]: first, it sets forth the reason for his being rebuked;

second, it clarifies the purport of the one capable of rebuking him; third, it shows how the assembly at that time attained the Path; fourth, it concerns his receiving of defeat. Now, this is [the first].
The reason for the first instance of being rebuked is as follows:

he was rebuked because in the past, while preaching the Dharma to beginners in the Great Forest (Mahāvana), this bhikṣu—whose spiritual disposition was that of the Mahāyāna—taught the Hinayāna Dharma; therefore, he was rebuked.
As for the "Great Forest," it refers to the Great Forest within the city of Vaiśālī, which contains the Monkey Pond (Markaṭahrada).
In the vihāra, Pūrṇa was preaching the Dharma there.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me: [The following section] secondly clarifies the principle of being able to reprove, which is divided into two parts:
first, the actual clarification of being able to reprove; second, the explanation of the meaning of the reproach. This is now the first part, which is further divided into two. First...

First, explaining how the teaching does not accord with conditions and criticizing the failure to recognize the teaching; second, explaining how conditions do not accord with the teaching and criticizing the failure to recognize conditions.
Now, regarding the first—criticizing the failure to recognize the teaching because it does not accord with conditions—there are three dharmas and three parables which constitute three chapters.
Regarding the failure to recognize the three periods of time, this is now the first: the failure to recognize the future faculties and dispositions.
Rāhula should have first entered meditative concentration to observe the faculties and dispositions of that person before preaching the Dharma to them.
Since this person was fit to hear the Great Dharma, yet he did not observe their faculties and instead preached the Lesser Dharma out of arrogance, it was improper.
"One should not place foul food in a precious vessel" is a metaphor where the precious vessel represents the faculties for the Mahāyāna and the foul food represents the Lesser [Dharma].
The vessel for the Dharma-jewel of the Mahāyāna should hold fragrant and pure food; it should not hold foul food.
One whose root-nature is that of the Mahāyāna should be taught the Mahāyāna Dharma; one should not be taught the Hīnayāna.
You should know that this bhikṣu’s mental intention is what is meant by the second "not knowing"—namely, the present mental state of this bhikṣu. Do not use lapis lazuli [for this purpose].
The second analogy of the crystal compares the cheapness of crystal to the preciousness of lapis lazuli; this illustrates the relative worth of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
"You cannot know the root-source of sentient beings" is the third rebuke of the fault of the bhikṣu’s ignorance:
"This bhikṣu has long since resolved upon the Mahāyāna mind; how could he have given rise to the Hīnayāna? Do not cause him to incur such a wound.
"To wound it" refers to the third analogy: since the body of the Mahāyāna has no wound from the Hīnayāna, how could the claws of the Hīnayāna tear through the body of the Mahāyāna?
Because those who have not yet studied have attained the Hīnayāna, they have no wound;
yet to speak of the Hīnayāna today wounds their very bodies. This concludes the second section on "Wishing to Practice the Great Path."

Regarding the passage that criticizes the failure to understand conditions by stating that "conditions do not conform to the teaching," there should likewise be three dharmas and three analogies as in the preceding section;
though the text is abbreviated, there are indeed three analogies, which correspond to the three [stages]: first, the arousal of the bodhicitta;
second, the universal deliverance of sentient beings; and third, the cultivation of all practices. The conduct of a bodhisattva does not transcend these three points.

It is improper for Pūrṇa to turn others away from the Great Vehicle so that they might instead give rise to the mind of the Two Vehicles, cultivate the practices of the Two Vehicles, and seek only their own self-discipline and self-deliverance.
Thus Master Sengzhao said: "To turn a dragon-elephant onto a rabbit path, or to pour the great ocean into a cow’s footprint"—this refers precisely to such an act.
"If you wish to travel the Great Way, do not show them the small shortcut"; this is the first step in giving rise to the Bodhicitta.
Furthermore, it is not because the great ocean immediately crosses over sentient beings for a second time that it is called the "Great Mind.
Nor is it because the sunlight descends for a third time that it is called the "Cultivation of All Practices. How could it be possible to teach the practices of the Two Vehicles?
It is simply not so.
Pūrṇa, this bhikṣu’s [fault] is explained secondly as the reason for the censure. As for why he was censured:

although this bhikṣu long ago resolved upon the Mahāyāna mind, he has forgotten that intention. You should have instead taught him the Mahāyāna Dharma, yet because you taught him the Hīnayāna, he was censured.
Regarding "long ago resolving upon the Mahāyāna mind but forgetting that intention": [it refers to his initial aspiration].
This is no different from the analogy of the jewel fastened [to the robe] in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
At that time, Vimalakīrti entered samādhi; this concludes the third section on the benefits received by the assembly. [The benefit] of Vimalakīrti’s two kinds of "honey" consists of:

first, the benefit of the "honey of mind" through entering samādhi; second, the benefit of the "honey of speech" through preaching the Dharma for their sake; and third, the praise of the bodhisattvas.

There are three types of benefit for the śrāvakas, which they did not previously possess. Vimalakīrti benefits the bhikṣus with two kinds of "honey" (mystic teachings), and they likewise obtain two benefits:
first, the old benefit; second, the new benefit. Recognizing their own past lives and thereby regaining their original minds constitutes the old benefit;
because he then preaches the Dharma for them so that they do not regress from bodhi, this constitutes the new benefit. As stated in the text.
I recall that among the śrāvakas, the fourth [rank] is the lowest in terms of being subject to defeat;
for this reason, I am not fit to go there to inquire about his illness.
Thus, "not fit" is the third concluding statement of incapacity.

Next, regarding the sixth point concerning the summoning of Kātyāyana: The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that Kātyāyana is a person of middling faculties while Pūrṇa is a person of inferior faculties.
Why, then, was Pūrṇa summoned first and Kātyāyana later? There is a specific reason for this distinction, which shall be explained separately.
This concerns the second section on the person’s understanding of the meaning of the Sūtras and Śāstras.
Regarding the *Kun-le lun* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra), it is said to consist of two hundred thousand verses. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the *Kun-le lun* has two gates:
first, the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and second, the gate of existence (*bhava*). Entering the gate of emptiness, the exposition of its meaning is inexhaustible.

If this were so, then even while the Buddha was in the world, there already existed sūtras and śāstras on bamboo and silk. As for why that person [the author of the Vibhāṣā] was rebuked, it was because he did not discuss the teachings [of the Buddha]. Therefore, he was rebuked.
Previously, although Pūrṇa was equally ignorant of the teachings on conditions (*pratyaya*), he was rebuked precisely because he did not recognize those conditions.
Thus, the preceding passage states: "Do not place a precious vessel in filthy food.

Just as a king examining his own treasury might suddenly pour stinking excrement into a celestial *pārijāta* flower or a vessel of human ambrosia (*amṛta*), [Pūrṇa] failed to recognize the capacities of sentient beings (*indriya-gotra*). Now, Kātyāyana...
Yaśas and Śāriputra both failed to understand the teaching; this is precisely because they did not understand the teaching. As the text says:

"Do not use a mind that functions through arising and ceasing to explain the Dharma of the True Mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa)," for they did not understand the teaching. Question: Previously, Maudgalyāyana also preached the Dharma; how does this differ from the present case? Answer:
Previously, Maudgalyāyana lost both the literal meaning and the intended sense. Now, Yaśas has grasped the Buddha’s words but has not grasped the Buddha’s [intended] meaning.
It is different because of the intention.
The Buddha told Mahākātyāyana, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
According to the text, this also consists of two parts; here is the first: the command to inquire after the illness. Kātyāyana is his family name.
“Excellent eyebrows!
Kātyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness. Why is this?
I recall that in the past, when the Buddha had briefly explained the essential Dharma for the bhikṣus, I subsequently elaborated upon it.”
Its meaning refers to the meaning of impermanence, the meaning of suffering, the meaning of emptiness, the meaning of non-self, and the meaning of cessation.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me: "Kātyāyana, do not use a mind characterized by arising and ceasing to explain the Dharma of the true mark.
Kātyāyana, the ultimate non-arising and non-ceasing of all dharmas is the meaning of impermanence; the thorough penetration of the five aggregates of clinging as empty is [the meaning of suffering]."
That there is nothing that arises is the meaning of suffering; that all phenomena are ultimately non-existent is the meaning of emptiness;
that "self" and "non-self" are non-dual is the meaning of selflessness; and that dharmas were originally not ignited and thus now do not extinguish is the meaning of cessation.
When this Dharma was taught, the minds of those bhikṣus attained liberation. Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire after his illness.

Kātyāyana addressed the Buddha [regarding] the second part of his refusal, which consists of two sections: first, the indication of the inability to explain; now, this is the indication of that inability.
As for why [he was unable], the following explains the inability in two parts; now, this is the first, setting forth the reason for being rebuked.
The reason he was rebuked was that in the past, when the Buddha had preached the Dharma for the bhikṣus, they returned and concealed it.

The Buddha’s words were thus rebuked. When asked whether he was reciting the Buddha’s words from the Hīnayāna or the Buddha’s words from the Mahāyāna, the explanation given was that he was reciting the Buddha’s words from the Hīnayāna;
because he did not understand the Buddha’s intent, he erred.

The reason he did not understand the meaning of the Hīnayāna was that he wished to be like a Śrāvaka who has attained depth—meaning it was clear that he had indeed attained the Hīnayāna, not merely...
If one does not understand the meaning of the Great Vehicle, nor the meaning of the Small Vehicle, why is this?

Since one does not understand the Small or the Great, how could one recognize the distinction between them? If a Bodhisattva recognizes both the Small and the Great, they then recognize the distinction between the two;

thus, for a Bodhisattva, both exist, whereas for a Śrāvaka, both are absent. Furthermore, it is not only that they do not grasp the meaning, but they also do not grasp the words; they do not grasp the words.
The text below asks: "How can one understand the meaning of the words above? Whether great or small, whether intention or speech, all have lost their essential reason.
This is because [the author] wishes to manifest that there are, in truth, no two vehicles. Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:

"In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle. Question: If the Śrāvakas possess the realization of attainment yet preach the Dharma of non-attainment, how is it that they have already been...?
If it is argued that the Buddha’s teaching of the existence of attainment while possessing a mind of non-attainment should likewise be censured, the explanation is as follows:

this is not comparable to [the case where] one with a mind of attainment teaches the dharma of non-attainment. The dharma of non-attainment is established as the opposite of attainment; therefore, it is subject to censure.

If the Buddha, while possessing a mind of non-attainment, teaches the dharma of attainment, his intention does not lie in attainment itself; he teaches attainment only for the sake of establishing non-attainment.

Because he has attained this, he is not subject to reproach. As for the statement that "the Buddha briefly taught the Dharma and entrusted me to expound its meaning later," it means that in the past the Buddha briefly taught two dharmas:
first, the dharma of birth-and-death; second, the dharma of nirvana.

Birth-and-death is the conditioned and impermanent dharma, while nirvana is the unconditioned and permanent dharma. These two dharmas are further expanded into three dharmas, namely: [birth-and-death, the path, and nirvana].
The three Dharma seals are as follows: the seal of nirvāṇa as quiescence; the seal of impermanence regarding the conditioned phenomena of saṃsāra;
and the seal of non-self regarding all phenomena. These extend to both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. Furthermore, the three seals are expanded into five:
the four aspects of impermanence within saṃsāra—namely, suffering, emptiness, and so forth—and the quiescence of nirvāṇa as Buddhahood. This is the brief summary.
Regarding the statement that the three Kātyāyanas provide extensive explanations: when the Buddha briefly explains two [points], the two Kātyāyanas provide extensive explanations;

likewise, up to when the Buddha briefly explains five, their extensive explanations of those five—such as the meaning of impermanence, the meaning of flux, and the meaning of arising and ceasing—are called "elaborating upon their meanings. Thus, it is said that they expound their significance.
At that time, Vimalakīrti descended. Second, this clarifies the purport of his censure: "Do not preach the dharma of the true mark with a mind of arising and ceasing.
Regarding this, commentators differ; here, I shall provide a direct interpretation: the dharma of the true mark is precisely non-attainment.
Because Kātyāyana preached with a mind of arising and ceasing based on attainment, [Vimalakīrti] said, "Do not [preach] with a mind of arising and ceasing."

This explains the Dharma of the true mark (*dharmatā*). Regarding the statement that "all dharmas are ultimately neither born nor extinguished" as the meaning of impermanence (*anityatā*), this phrase is difficult to understand.
Now, let us inquire: if non-arising and non-extinction constitute the meaning of impermanence, then arising and extinction should likewise constitute the meaning of permanence.

Furthermore, [the text] concludes (etc.). Herein, it is clarified that the meaning of impermanence—namely, that all dharmas are ultimately neither born nor extinguished—is precisely this very impermanence.
What, then, is the meaning of neither arising nor ceasing? What is now called "impermanence" does not mean that there is impermanence;
rather, it means that there is no permanence. Therefore, one speaks of "impermanence" precisely because this negates permanence.
Since permanence does not exist, where could impermanence exist? Thus, impermanence is itself without impermanence, being ultimately neither arising nor ceasing.
This is the meaning of impermanence (*anitya*). Because this meaning is difficult to practice, it must be extensively established through the scriptures and treatises.
Master Zhao of Guanzhong also held this view; thus he said: "To say that things are 'not existent' clarifies that they are not [substantially] existent;
it does not mean they are non-existent. The same applies to saying they are 'not permanent': it clarifies that they are not [substantially] permanent. It does not mean they are impermanent.
This refers to the fact that [all things] are impermanent. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that there are two kinds of impermanence:

first, that which lacks skillful means (*upāya*), and second, that which possesses skillful means. Regarding impermanence lacking skillful means, it is the case where permanence does not exist, yet impermanence still exists.
As for impermanence possessing skillful means, impermanence fundamentally serves as the remedy for permanence; since permanence no longer exists, one thereby realizes [the truth].
The two phrases "neither impermanence nor permanence" are already purified; because they proceed downward until ultimately nothing remains, this text serves as the proof.
That is to say, since impermanence refutes permanence, and since permanence no longer exists, impermanence likewise ceases to exist.
Therefore, it is said that "non-arising and non-ceasing" is the meaning of impermanence. Question: Why does the Buddha not state both [terms] together?
"Is there no impermanence, or is there simply one impermanence? The explanation says: To speak of "one non-existence" is to mean all things are non-existent;

to speak of "all things being non-existent" is for those of dull faculties. If one speaks of "one non-existence" and thereby understands that all things are non-existent, such a person possesses sharp faculties.
As for saying "one non-existence" means "all things are non-existent," once [the nature of] impermanence is understood, one knows [this].
Since there is no "non-impermanence," and impermanence itself does not exist, one knows that nothing at all exists; thus it is said that the non-existence of one is the non-existence of all.
Now, although Kātyāyana knew that there is no permanence, he still perceived the existence of impermanence, which is why he was rebuked.
This principle applies to all other statements as well. When this Dharma was being taught, the bhikṣus...
Regarding those who have attained liberation: although the bhikṣus know that there is no permanence, they still speak of "impermanence";

thus, they remain bound by the view of impermanence. Now, by breaking through impermanence, they are liberated from the view of permanence; and by being without impermanence, they are liberated from the view of impermanence.
To be free from these two views is called attaining liberation; it is not that one attains liberation without a basis. Other cases are to be understood accordingly (*etc.*).
Next, at one time, [the Buddha] selected from above that "neither arising nor ceasing" is the meaning of impermanence.

If a householder says that "neither arising nor ceasing" is impermanence, what was the Buddha’s intention in saying, "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are dharmas of arising and ceasing"?
If this is so, Cāṇūra attained the dharma while the householder attained the meaning. The householder explained, saying: "Cāṇūra attained the words, and he also attained the meaning."
The Sūtra says: "Arising and ceasing, non-arising and non-ceasing, arising and ceasing...
(and so forth). Next, the seventh [case] concerns why Aniruddha was rebuked. Previously, Pūrṇa was rebuked because he did not recognize the nature of the faculties;
next, Kātyāyana was rebuked because he did not recognize the intent of the teaching; now, Aniruddha... [was rebuked because he did not recognize the heavenly realms].
Because of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), he was rebuked for clarifying that the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) of the *śrāvakas* are not true supernatural powers.

Furthermore, whereas Cāṇakya previously taught the Dharma through speech, Āniruddha now teaches the Dharma through supernatural power. Thus, wisdom is supernatural power and merit is the teaching of the Dharma;
it is not that there is no teaching of the Dharma. From what does wisdom arise? If supernatural power is not [true] supernatural power, from what cause does merit arise? Therefore—
There is now this section.
The Buddha said to Aniruddha, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
This passage consists of two parts; first, the Tathāgata’s command to inquire after the illness, and second, [the response of] Aniruddha, also known as Aniruddha.
He is also named Arhaddatta and Aniruddha; these are merely different names. This term [Aniruddha] also means "Free from Poverty," "As One Wishes," or "Good Intention.
He was of the Kṣatriya caste and was among the Buddha’s disciples foremost in the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
A sūtra states that his divine eye extended across half a head. Regarding this "divine eye extending across half a head," there are two interpretations. The first says it is an abbreviation.
"Half-head vision" refers to seeing like an ordinary person who sees only the half of another's head;
because both [the ordinary person and the Buddha] see one half of the head, it is called "half-head vision. The Buddha, however, sees the entire head.

As for those who have attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), they have fallen into the wombs of snails and clams for five hundred lifetimes, and thus in this life their eyes remain constantly closed.
A bhikṣu ridiculed him, whereupon [the bhikṣu] immediately encircled his eyes with bamboo rings; his eyes then became blind.

Later, through the cultivation of dhyāna-samādhi, he attained the four great elements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and delighted his body, whereby he was able to see the trichiliocosm as clearly as looking at a fruit in the palm of one's hand—like an *āmala* fruit, transparent both inside and out—and he saw it thus.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that this is the case for those of extremely sharp faculties.
The Pratyekabuddha raises the following point: In the trichiliocosm, it is asked whether the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and the physical eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) function simultaneously.
The answer is that they do not. It is explained that if one intends to see during the day, both eyes function; however, at night, only the divine eye sees.

Furthermore, it is asked whether the divine eye must turn toward an object in order to see it in the future. The explanation is that it does not turn; rather, as soon as one forms the intention, one sees. Therefore...
This is because the eyelids of his divine eye are intact and cannot obstruct it.
Aniruddha said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness. Why is this?
I recall that in the past, while I was walking in meditation at a certain place, a Brahma King named Śuddhavimala, together with ten thousand..."
Then Brahmā, emitting pure light from both [his eyes], came to where I was, prostrated himself in homage, and asked me:
"To what extent, Ānanda, does the divine eye perceive? I replied:
"Venerable sir, I see this trichiliocosm, the buddha-field of Śākyamuni Buddha, as clearly as one would look at an *āmala* fruit held in the palm of one's hand. At that time, Vimalakīrti—
They came and said to me, "Aniruddha, is that which is seen by your divine eye a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta*) or an unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta*)?

If it were a conditioned phenomenon, it would be equal to the five supernatural powers of the non-Buddhists; if it were an unconditioned phenomenon, it would be unconditioned and thus there should be no seeing.
World-Honored One, at that time I remained silent. When those Brahmās heard these words, they attained what they had never experienced before.
They paid homage to him and asked, "In this world, who possesses true divine vision? Vimalakīrti replied, "There is the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who has attained true divine vision;
he always abides in samādhi and perceives all buddha-fields without the duality of signs.
Thereupon, the Brahmā King Śuddhāvāsa and his retinue of five hundred Brahmās all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Having prostrated at the feet of Vimalakīrti with the thought of supreme enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), he suddenly vanished.
Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire after his illness.
Aniruddha addressed the Buddha, saying: [The second refusal, consisting of three parts—statement, explanation, and conclusion—now follows.]
Regarding the question "What is the reason for this? and so forth, the second section provides an explanation of why [the Buddha] was unable to do so, which is divided into two parts.

First, it sets forth the cause for being rebuked: the intention behind the rebuke arose because Brahmā questioned him regarding his vision; he replied that it was the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), and it was on this account that the rebuke ensued.
At that time, Vimalakīrti descended. This second section clarifies the principle of being able to censure [the opponent], which is divided into two parts:

first, establishing the two points of contention; second, resolving the two difficulties. Now, both points of contention are established simultaneously: is it a conditioned mark (*saṃskṛta-nimitta*) or an unconditioned mark (*asaṃskṛta-nimitta*)?
To say it is a conditioned mark is to take shapes such as square or round as the conditioned mark, and to take colors such as blue or yellow as the perceived object.

Regarding the perception of forms: not apprehending squareness, roundness, blue, or yellow constitutes the mark of non-action (*anabhisamskāra*). As for the perception of duality: where there is an eye, it is the agent of seeing and form is the object seen;
this constitutes the mark of action because there is both an agent and an object. Where there is no eye, there is the ability to see and yet no form to be seen;
this constitutes the mark of non-action because there is neither an agent nor an object. Therefore, we now challenge the position that perception is an act of construction.
This is the view of the mark of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Suppose it were the mark of action; this is the second pair of conclusions that resolve the objection.

If it were the mark of action, it would be identical to the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Why? Because the non-Buddhists also produce the views of squares, circles, blue, and yellow, as well as the subject and object of seeing.

You now likewise produce the views of squares, circles, blue, and yellow, as well as the subject and object of seeing. Since you see blue and yellow identically, you are the same as the non-Buddhists.
You say that the perception of blue and yellow is internal; since that perception of blue and yellow is also internal, it is equal to the internal.
This equality of the internal constitutes the third difficulty, which is difficult to resolve. If there were no characteristic of activity (*kāritra-lakṣaṇa*), then as for the second difficulty:
if there were no characteristic of activity, one would not see blue, yellow, square, or round; thus, there would be no blue, yellow, square, or round. If that were so, then...

This unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) should not be visible; furthermore, it encounters three difficulties. Since you see blue and yellow, yet space lacks blue and yellow, space should likewise be visible.
This is the third difficulty regarding "reaching" [the object]: if you see space but do not see [its qualities], then space should also not see what you do not see.
Next, another difficulty follows: if you treat [space] as having characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), then you are identical to the outsiders (*bāhya*).

If the Way is different from that of the non-Buddhists, it is without action and without the marks of action; there is nothing seen, nor is there an eye. How then can one say that the divine eye sees?
Because [the opponent] remained silent and offered no response to these two points, Master Sengzhao said: "He lost his footing at that time and was humiliated by the two difficulties.
Furthermore, if there are marks of action, there is seeing; if there is no action, there is no seeing. This is the dichotomy of existence and non-existence.
Second, one may also reprove the Brahmā King regarding his ears, for the Brahmā King is a disciple of the Buddha.

When the various kings heard these words, they experienced what they had never known before and immediately prostrated themselves. Because those Brahmās had heard this discourse on "startling the ears," they uttered an exclamation of unprecedented wonder.
Furthermore, these Brahmās also possess the divine eye and see a thousand worlds; having heard [the sounds] of their inhabitants...
The Licchavi, exclaiming in wonder at this unprecedented event, asked: "Is there anyone in the world who possesses true divine vision?
Between myself and Aniruddha—who is the one with true divine vision in this world? Vimalakīrti replied: "There is.
When the King of the Brahmā Heaven asked if there was anyone with true divine vision, he answered: 'The Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses true divine vision.'"
The heading above indicates that there are those who exist now; they constantly abide in samādhi and behold the various Buddha-lands without dualistic characteristics.

Next, the explanation of "seeing the various Buddha-lands with the true divine eye without dualistic characteristics" clarifies that while seeing the various lands as vividly present, there is nothing seen;
and while there is nothing seen, one sees them vividly. Thus, seeing does not obstruct non-seeing.
"Non-seeing does not obstruct seeing because it is not characterized by duality; therefore, he was not rebuked.
Ānanda, however, cannot see in this manner; since he cannot achieve non-seeing, and non-seeing cannot function as seeing, he was rebuked.
The remaining phrases may be sought elsewhere in the text.
Next, the eighth [section] concerns the exhortation of Upāli. The reason he was rebuked was because he upheld the Vinaya.

This rebuke clarifies that for Śrāvakas, wisdom is not true wisdom, supernormal powers are not true supernormal powers, upholding the Vinaya is not true upholding of the Vinaya, and repentance is not true repentance.
Why is this? Because within the Hīnayāna, there are five categories and seven groups; the first of these five categories is...
There are four categories that are universally irredeemable and seven categories that are redeemable. Regarding the first category, it is irredeemable; the remaining six categories are redeemable.
The first category is like cutting off the crown of a *tāla* tree, or like a hole in the eye of a needle, or like a dead person who can never be cured.
However, if one performs the repentance according to the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras, all such offenses are entirely extinguished. Now they are extinguished. Now, [the *upāsaka*...]
Upāli performed a Hinayana repentance for this bhikṣu, who was of Mahayana lineage and should have heard a Mahayana repentance;
because Upāli performed a Hinayana repentance instead, he was rebuked.
The Buddha told Upāli, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.

According to the text, this section also consists of two parts; here, first, is the command to inquire after his illness. Upāli—here translated as "Foremost"—was once a lowly man of Rājagṛha who has now attained arhatship.
Since there is no distinction between noble and base when one abides in the Way, he is now honored; therefore, the Buddha now commands him.
Thus it was.
Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness. Why is this?
I recall that in the past there were two bhikṣus who had violated the disciplinary rules; feeling ashamed, they did not dare to ask the Buddha, so they came to me to ask."

I said, "O Upāli, we have indeed transgressed the Vinaya and truly feel ashamed; we do not dare to question the Buddha ourselves, but we pray that you will resolve our doubts and remorse so that we may be freed from this fault.
I then explained the Dharma for them according to the rules.
Upāli’s second section of the initial inquiry concerning the inability [to explain] begins here; this is the formal introduction. Why is this so?
The second section, the explanation of the inability, is divided into two parts; this is the first, which sets forth the reasons for being rebuked.
There were two bhikṣus who had violated the rules of discipline. When questioned, "What offense have these bhikṣus committed? the text does not [explicitly state].
Regarding the explanation of the gravity [of offenses], it has traditionally been said that one commits the second *pārājika* offense. Why?
Because if it were the first *pārājika*, it would be irredeemable; since he now seeks atonement, we know it is the second *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Furthermore, because it resembles the violation of the first [pārājika], the bhikṣu’s mind was filled with doubt, fearing it might belong to the first category. Thus, he did not dare ask the Buddha himself, but instead questioned Upāli.
Regarding the question addressed to Upāli, there are four reasons: first, because the Buddha’s majestic virtue is as venerable as a dragon or a fire, one must not dare to question him lightly;
second, having received the precepts from the Buddha, one now commits an offense that violates his original vow;

though he personally declared he could uphold them, since he has now committed an offense, he does not dare to question him; third, the Buddha possesses precise knowledge of the characteristics of offenses.

Fearing that this might be the first type of transgression which is ultimately and absolutely irredeemable; fourth, had he gone to question the Buddha, it would have been made manifest before the great assembly.
Now, because he pays homage and questions Upāli, it is said: "I do not dare to question the Buddha; I come to question Upāli.
Upāli then explained for him according to the methods of the five categories and seven groups of offenses, before Upāli himself had even finished [speaking].
The layman who spoke these words immediately came to rebuke him. He asked: "Since Pāṭieṇa understands the Vinaya, he can extinguish offenses;
if he did not understand it, he could not extinguish them. Thus, one cannot say that Pāṭieṇa does not understand the Vinaya, for in reality he does understand it.
He further asked: "If he understands the Vinaya, then Pāṭieṇa relies upon the Vinaya to extinguish offenses. If this were the case, then to rebuke Pāṭieṇa in such a manner would be impossible."

The statement that "extinguishing transgressions" is a criticism of the Vinaya means that it cannot extinguish transgressions; the statement that "it is not a criticism of the Buddha" means that the Buddha cannot be blamed for the transgressions.

There are two meanings to this explanation: first, it clarifies that while some are suited to hearing the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) for the extinction of transgressions, this bhikṣu possesses the spiritual capacity (gotra) of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) and is thus suited to hearing the teachings of the Great Vehicle to eliminate them; yet, Upāli preached the Small Vehicle for him instead.
Therefore, why was he rebuked? It concerns the World-Honored One. Second, regarding the great and the small: the Tathāgata’s skillful means open the great as the small.
Since Upāli neither recognized the great nor recognized the small, he was rebuked.

If a bodhisattva were fully endowed with the understanding of the great and the understanding of the small, then both the great and the small would be the Tathāgata’s skillful means of opening [the truth].

Since both [the *Vinaya*] and the *Mahāyāna* are the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Tathāgata, there is a reason for this. As a sutra says: "One who studies the *vinaya* is one who studies the Mahāyāna.
If that were so, there would be no Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) at all;
therefore, it is Upāli’s fault for preaching the Dharma of the Small Vehicle—how could it be the fault of the Tathāgata?
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me, "O Upāli, do not further increase the offenses of these two bhikṣus;
you should simply extinguish them and not disturb their minds. Why is this? The nature of those offenses is neither within, nor without, nor in between.
As the Buddha has taught: 'Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled; because the mind is pure, sentient beings are pure.'"
The pure mind is neither within, nor without, nor in between. As it is with the mind, so it is with defilements;
as it is with all phenomena, they do not transcend suchness (*tathatā*). "Upāli, when one attains liberation through the characteristic of the mind, is there still any defilement?
I replied, "No. Vimalakīrti said, "The characteristic of the minds of all sentient beings is inherently free from defilement."
It is also thus: only conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), Upāli, is defilement; the absence of conceptual construction is purity.
Inversion is defilement; the absence of inversion is purity. Grasping at a self is defilement; not grasping at a self is purity.
Upāli, all phenomena arise and perish without abiding, like illusions and like lightning; phenomena do not wait for one another, not even for a single thought-moment.
"All dharmas are false perceptions, like dreams, like mirages, like the moon reflected in water, like images in a mirror;
they arise from deluded thought. He who knows this is called one who upholds the Vinaya; he who knows this is called one who well understands it.
Then the two bhikṣus said, "How sublime is his wisdom! This is beyond the reach of Upāli; he is the supreme among those who uphold the Vinaya."
When I was able to explain this, I replied: "Since the Tathāgata’s own passing, no śrāvaka or bodhisattva has been able to restrain his eloquence in preaching.

His wisdom and insight are as penetrating as this. At that time, the doubts and regrets of the two bhikṣus were immediately dispelled, and they resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, making this vow: "May it be so for all sentient beings."
All have attained such eloquence; therefore, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.
At that time, Vimalakīrti descended. Second, this clarifies the purport of his censure: "Do not further increase the offenses of these bhikṣus.
Upāli had indeed increased the offenses of these bhikṣus; for this reason, he censured him, saying, "Do not further increase their offenses. First.
First, it clarifies that one who has committed an offense with a perverted mind perceives the existence of a mind capable of committing offenses;
once the act is completed, Upāli further explains the characteristics of the offense for him, which is why it is said to "further increase" [the perception].

Second, regarding the previous commission of an offense where one perceived the arising of an offense, now Upāli acts to extinguish the offense, leading to the perception of the extinction of the offense; the former perception was of its arising, whereas [the latter] is of its extinction.
Because the view that exists is extinguished by the very seeing [of it], there is no further view; thus, it is increased.

That which should be directly severed is what Pāli calls "turning back to sever" (*paryāvṛtti-prahāṇa*), while the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* calls it "direct severance. Pāli’s "turning back to sever" is equivalent to the *Vimalakīrti*’s "direct severance," which is right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*).

Right contemplation is the contemplation of the Vaipulya [sūtras], such as the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna-sūtra*, which constitute the repentance [rites].

Therefore, in the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra, Jīvaka said: "Great King, if you hear what the Tathāgata has taught regarding the absence of agency and the absence of receiving [karmic results], the king’s grave offenses will surely be extinguished.
The King asked: "When one commits an offense, is it committed by the mind, by the body, by the person, or by the dharmas?
If it is committed by the mind, what is this 'mind'? If it is committed by the body, what is this 'body' or 'person'?"
"The Dharma is also like this. The King said, "If one must undergo punishment, who is it that undergoes the punishment? Is it the mind that undergoes it, or is it the body that undergoes it?

Is it the person or the Dharma that undergoes it? If it is the mind that undergoes it, what is this mind? If it is the body that undergoes it, what is this body? As for the person and the Dharma, they are likewise thus.
Since there is neither agent nor recipient, the King’s offense is immediately purified. [The King] asked Jīvaka: "Is it also..."
It is said that there is neither action nor recipient; the six heretical teachers also say there is neither action nor recipient.

Therefore, the text states: "There is no black karma, and no retribution for black karma. What is the difference [in interpretation]? The explanation says: they are vastly different. Why? To answer by citing the sutra:
the sutra says that one who holds the view of emptiness is "not existent," while one who holds the view of existence is "not non-existent. However, this...
This is not yet sufficient to resolve the difficulty; now we shall clarify that those of sharp faculties attain sudden awakening.
Why is this? If one were fixedly attached to existence, they would not see emptiness; if one were fixedly attached to emptiness, they would not see existence.
Therefore, it is known that there is neither fixed existence nor fixed non-existence; being neither existent nor non-existent, it is ultimately pure.
Purity is also as stated in the *Universal Worthy’s Contemplation*: "If one wishes to perform repentance, sit upright and contemplate the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
The true mark is the cessation of all mental activities; it is neither arising nor ceasing, quiescent and like *nirvāṇa*.

How could this be the same as the 'view of non-existence' held by the six heretical teachers? Therefore, it is said that one should directly eliminate and sever [defilements]. Why is this so? Because of the nature of sin..."
The statement that [the offense] "does not exist within, without, or in between" explains the previous point that there is no basis for further increasing one's guilt.
Now, it clarifies that since guilt is ultimately unattainable, how could one further describe the characteristics of guilt?

To say it does not exist within, without, or in between means that the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) are "within," the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) are "without," and the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) are "in between. Within these six sense organs, [guilt] does not exist.

Because of sin, it does not exist within the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*); because there is no sin, it does not exist within the six consciousnesses (*ṣadvijñāna*). Since it does not exist, it does not exist in between;
for when even the six faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) and the six sense objects do not exist, how could it possibly exist within the six consciousnesses?

Second, "self" constitutes the internal and "other" constitutes the external, while the union of self and other constitutes the middle. For example, if a pure object gives rise to greed, is it from the internal?
Does birth arise from the external, or does it arise from the intermediate? If it arose from within, there would be birth even in the absence of objects;

if it arose from the external, there would be birth even in the absence of mind. Since there is no intermediate state apart from the internal and the external, there is no [source] from which it arises.
As the Buddha said: "Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled. This implies that if there were no transgressions (*āpatti*), how could there be a mind? For the mind is the root.

Since the root is already tranquil, there can be no branches; therefore, we now further refute the root as we did the branches, examining it from the internal, external, and intermediate perspectives.

As it is with the mind, so it is with defilements and stains, and so it is with all phenomena (*dharma*); "all phenomena" refers broadly to the fact that just as the former has no difference, the latter likewise has no distinction.
When the characteristics of the mind are liberated, O Pūrṇa, could there possibly be any stain?
"No," he replied. "That refers to the noble mind; how could it be so for an ordinary person? Therefore, I now ask you, Pāṭali:
at the moment you attained the ninth liberation of arhatship, was there any defilement? He said, "No.
"If you attained the ninth liberation, could there possibly be defilement? This is merely using what is accepted as non-existent to illustrate what is accepted as existent."
Because that which is believed to exist is the same as that which is believed not to exist, the mental characteristics of all sentient beings are likewise so.
"Only the delusive marks, Upāli, are defilements" is intended to resolve a doubt. The doubt is as follows:

"If all sentient beings are without defilement, then they should not be seen [as such] now; yet we currently see them as having defilement. How can you say they are without defilement? Furthermore, it is not...
It is said that liberation consists in the elimination of deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*); thus, the absence of deluded thoughts is purity. This encompasses the three "arrivals":

the arrival of thought (*citta*) is the elimination of deluded thoughts; the arrival of mind (*manas*) is the elimination of defilement; and the arrival of vision (*darśana*) is the elimination of grasping at a self.
Next, an analogy is provided; the remainder may be sought according to the text.
○ Ninth: The Exhortation to Rāhula. Rāhula was the son of the Buddha and foremost in the observance of the precepts.

For what reason did [the Buddha] further reprimand him? The explanation says: It was because he ultimately possessed the notion of attainment (*upalambha*) and was thus subject to inversion (*viparyāsa*);

for this reason, he was reprimanded. Question: On account of what matter was he reprimanded? Was he reprimanded because of his renunciation (*pravrajyā*)? Question: Does this reprimand apply to Rāhula’s renunciation?
[Question: Is it not the case that the household life is not so? [Answer: The explanation says: It was not Rāhula who was rebuked;
rather, he was rebuked because he did not understand the reason for leaving the household life. Why was this? Because the suffering of desire is profound even for a Śrāvaka.

This clarifies that for a person of the Śrāvaka vehicle, [practicing] wisdom, meditative concentration, begging for food, and leaving the household life are all [insufficient]. [Question: Rāhula is the grandson and Ānanda is his uncle. How can this be?
Why was the uncle not mentioned first and his grandson mentioned second, rather than the grandson being mentioned first?
The explanation says that although there is a distinction between an uncle and a grandson, as for Rāhula—whether from the perspective of the Path or the world—he is greater than Ānanda.
In worldly terms, he is greater because Ānanda and Rāhula were both born on the night they attained the Path, yet Rāhula was six years older.
Regarding the years: first, because he was in the womb for six years; second, because Rāhula holds the rank of sovereign while Ānanda holds the rank of minister.
Why? Because Rāhula is the Buddha’s son, and the Buddha ought to have been a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin).
Since Rāhula is the Golden-Wheel Crown Prince who succeeds to the position of sovereign, whereas Mahā-Ānanda is merely a king.
For these reasons, Rāhula is listed first and Ānanda second. Regarding the greatness of their paths:
Rāhula has attained the highest fruit (*phala*), whereas Ānanda remains on the stage of training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*) and has attained only the first fruit.

Furthermore, Rāhula left the household life early, while Ānanda left late, beginning his renunciation at the age of twenty-five. Moreover, according to another interpretation, Rāhula was originally a renunciant.
Observing the precepts is the foundation; for this reason, he first commanded Rāhula and subsequently commanded Ānanda.
As for why Rāhula is called "the one who covers and obstructs," it is because he was covered by the womb for six years, and thus he is called "the one who covers and obstructs.
Regarding the reason he remained in the womb for six years, tradition says that in the past, he blocked a mouse hole with his body.

Therefore, it is said that he remained in the womb for six years. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: There was a rishi who entered the king’s kingdom, took the king’s drinking water, and used the king’s willow branch.
Having committed the offense of taking what was not given, he went before the king to confess and accept punishment.

Upon seeing him, the king immediately retired into his inner chambers for six days, indulging himself in the five desires and forgetting the rishi outside. The rishi said, "It is only right that you punish me in this manner."
Because he remained inside for six days without coming out to see the seers, he was born after remaining in the womb for six years. [Question:
Was Rāhula born because Siddhārtha performed worldly affairs, or was Rāhula born because he did not perform worldly affairs?
[Answer: There is an interpretation which says that he did not perform worldly affairs; rather, Siddhārtha merely touched his abdomen with his finger and [the child emerged].
There is another tradition which explains that the Buddha left home on the night of the eighth day of the fourth month.
On that day, a physiognomist said to King Wen: "Tonight you must provide excellent protection; Prince Siddhārtha will leave home tonight.
If he does not leave home, tomorrow the seven treasures and the golden wheel will arrive spontaneously. Upon hearing this, the father-king [acted accordingly].
The music and dancing girls were increased even further, and Prince Siddhārtha’s desire was immediately stirred.

When the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens saw this, they feared he would sink forever into the ocean of suffering with no one to rescue him; they descended and transformed the dancing girls so that they appeared like corpses, causing the prince to give rise to a sense of revulsion.
Thereupon, they escorted the Bodhisattva away, while the Four Heavenly Kings supported the hooves of the horse.
He left the city because that very night he intended to depart; it was at that moment that Yaśodharā conceived Rāhula.
Furthermore, Rāhula is also called "Born in the Palace. He is so called because while the Buddha was practicing austerities for six years, Yaśodharā became pregnant.
The Śākyas feared that if Yaśodharā were to give birth after the Buddha had passed away, the offspring might resemble the son of another man.

Because he attained [realization], it is said that he was born in the palace. Question: The Buddha renounced the position of a Cakravartin king; he renounced the position of a Golden Wheel-turning King.

Rāhula also renounced the position of a Cakravartin king—what kind of wheel-position did he renounce? Explanation: Had the Buddha not left the household life, he would have obtained the status of a Golden Wheel-turning King;
had Rāhula not left the household life, he would have obtained the status of an Iron Wheel-turning King, ruling over one world-system. (From the Tripiṭaka Section).

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states that when a Cakravartin King of the Iron Wheel appears in the world, there is a white parasol covering the entire world-system, extending ten yojanas through the space above and the earth below, over which gods and spirits have jurisdiction.
Therefore, Rāhula ought to have obtained the status of an Iron Wheel-turning King, and since the Iron Wheel also turns, it is said that he "renounced the turning of the wheel.
If even one who renounces such wealth and honor to leave the household life is still subject to reproach, how much more so [is this the case for others]?

"Are these not merely lowly ordinary people? Yet nowadays among the worldlings, those who are clever and intelligent remain to inherit the family business, while the dull and ignorant leave the household life. Such as this must not be tolerated."
The Buddha said to Rāhula, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
[The passage continues as before; now follows the initial command.
Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness. Why is this?"
I recall that in the past, the sons of the elders of Vaiśālī came to where I was, prostrated themselves at my feet, and asked me, saying:
"Rāhula, you are the son of the Buddha; having renounced the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch, you have left the household life to practice the Way.
