Nor is this taken as the "straight mind. Again, it was asked: "Is taking the ten evils as the 'turning mind' and the ten virtues as the 'straight mind' not so?
The explanation says: This is also not it. This is merely a discussion of crookedness and straightness among ordinary people;
within the Holy Path, both are "turnings. This is a "turning" within turning, and "good" within evil; therefore, it is also not the straight mind.

He asked again: "In the Abhidharma (*Vibhāṣā*), it is held that one realizes the principle of the Four Truths; in the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, it is taught that they converge upon the single Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

It clarifies that the three types of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) equally realize cessation and equally attain non-arising (*anutpāda*). Is this to be understood as the 'direct mind' (*ṛju-citta*), or not? The explanation says: This is also not so.

Rather, this refers to the mind of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-citta*) of the two vehicles. As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states regarding the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas: [They possess a mind of arising and ceasing.]
If one turns back from seeing [the truth], why would one not attain Bodhi? If one turns back from seeing [the truth], can one then attain Bodhi?

Furthermore, there is the Mahāyāna, which is also called "turning back from seeing. Therefore, it is said that those who have "something to be attained" are characterized by ignorance (*avidyā*) within the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
Thus, what is here called the "direct mind" (*ṛju-citta*) is named "directness" because it is the upright contemplation that is without attainment and without dependence.
The mind that is free from all views of attainment is called the "straight mind. This straight mind is the cause for attaining Buddhahood and the foundation from which the Way arises;
therefore, it is said that "the straight mind is the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Because it is devoid of artifice, it is "without falsehood";
this means it is free from all attainments of existence and the false delusions of annihilationism and eternalism—thus it is said to be "without falsehood. To set forth and practice [this] is...
The bodhimanda is that which can distinguish phenomena; the practice arising from the right contemplation of non-attainment is what constitutes the accomplishment of practice.
As clarified in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, one practices the myriad deeds with the *prajñā*-mind, and thereby accomplishes those deeds.
Because these deeds are accomplished, one is able to distinguish the unsurpassed fruit; therefore, it is said that "the arousal of practice is the bodhimanda for distinguishing phenomena."

Therefore, regarding "the profound mind is the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*): the preceding section clarified the "straight mind" (*ṛjukacitta*), yet there are two kinds of straight mind—the shallow straight mind and the profound straight mind.
Thus, this clarifies that it is the profound [mind]. Regarding "the bodhicitta is the site of enlightenment":
although the straight and profound minds were clarified above, this mind is not necessarily great; therefore, the following is clarified next.
The "Great Mind" is precisely the bodhicitta. Next, it is taught that the six perfections and myriad practices constitute the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Regarding the statement, "Patience is the site of enlightenment because the mind is unimpeded," this clarifies that when the mind is free from anger, it is unimpeded;
whereas if there is impediment, there is anger, and if there is anger, all matters are ruined. Within the Bodhisattva precepts, anger is considered a grave offense.

Furthermore, son of good family, if a bodhisattva, in accordance with the various *pāramitās*, teaches and transforms sentient beings such that every lifting and placing of their feet proceeds from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), this clarifies that the bodhisattva lifts and places their feet by means of the mind of *prajñā*;

because every lifting and placing of their feet is itself *prajñā*. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "One does not perceive worldly affairs of production as being anything other than *prajñā*."
Therefore, because the Bodhisattva’s prajñā-mind performs all activities, all things are prajñā.
If the mind of perversion performs all activities, then all things are perversions. Why? Because one perceives that the body and mind can perform all activities;
seeing them as objects of action and perceiving coming and going and so forth—all such things are [perversions]. Thus, they are all [perversions].
If one perceives inversion through correct contemplation, then because of its coming and going and so forth, it is entirely *prajñā* and entirely the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
At that time, the assembly realized the Way as described in the text.
Third, he commands the Bodhisattva Lokadhara to see the first Maitreya before the renunciant Bodhisattvas.
The virtuous qualities of the renunciant bodhisattva follow after those of the householder bodhisattva.
This is because, although the previous examples of Maitreya as a renunciant and Guangyan as a householder exhaustively encompass all cases, they do so only in broad outline;

therefore, two renunciant bodhisattvas and two householders are cited. Generally speaking, renunciant bodhisattvas are subsumed under Maitreya, while householders are subsumed under Jie-shi (Lokadhara). As for renunciant bodhisattvas, they follow Maitreya; as for householders, they follow Jie-shi. Thus they are subsumed.

The Bodhisattva of the House (Gṛhapati) follows the Radiance-Adorned One of Good Virtue (*Prabhāvyūha*). Among these, the former [section] subsumes the single [type], while the present [section] subsumes both;

thus, these four persons represent the sequence of distinguishing between the laity and the clergy. Furthermore, previously, Maitreya was criticized for having what is "attained," thereby showing that his prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) is not a true prediction.
Next, Radiance-Adorned was criticized for having what is "the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*), thereby showing that it is not a true site of enlightenment. Now, [Śāriputra] is criticized...
"World-Upholder, 'having something to attain,' 'subduing Māra,' and 'not subduing Māra'—these three items are the extreme practices of bodhisattvas.

Therefore, Vimalakīrti refutes these three types [of views] to clarify that there is nothing to be attained; that the path of prediction is not prediction; that the site of enlightenment is not the site of enlightenment;
and that subduing Māra is not subduing Māra. Why? Because Māra can be subdued by one who recognizes him; since he does not recognize Māra, he conversely becomes [Māra]."
The subduing by Māra is for the purpose of subduing those who subdue Māra, which is identical to the Bodhisattva; now, why is it that the Bodhisattva’s turn is identical to Māra?
It is because the world upholds [the notion of] Māra out of fear of him; thus, Māra obtains an advantage over the world. As the Sūtra says:
"For example, when a person is afraid, non-human beings take advantage of them. Therefore, if the Bodhisattva who is subdued by Māra has nothing to gain, then he is indeed [a true Bodhisattva].
How is it that one can subdue Māra? It is because one recognizes Māra. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"When a Bodhisattva sees the four Māras coming, they abide within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); by realizing that Māra is itself the limit of reality, [they subdue him]. Furthermore, the *Ratnaketuparivarta Sūtra* (Renwang jing) says: "Afflictions are themselves bodhi.
Moreover, as for those who possess attainment, they cannot subdue Māra; for that very possession of attainment is itself Māra—how could they possibly [subdue him]?
When one has not yet subdued Māra, Māra is able to subdue one; because there is something to be attained, one cannot subdue Māra.
Only when there is no attainment can one truly subdue him.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīdhara: "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness."
"Now, it is the first time you have been called 'World-Upholder' (Jagatīdhara).
Jagatīdhara addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness. Why is this?
I recall that in the past, while I was dwelling in a quiet chamber, Māra Pāpīyān approached with twelve thousand celestial maidens whose appearances were like..."
Śakra, Lord of Devas, accompanied by his retinue, came to where I was with the beating of drums, music, and singing.
He bowed his head at my feet, joined his palms in reverence, and stood to one side. I thought he was Śakra, so I spoke to him, saying: "Welcome, Kauśika!
Although you possess the fruits of merit, you should not be self-indulgent; you should contemplate the impermanence of the five desires and seek the root of goodness."
While practicing the steadfast Dharma with body, life, and wealth, he spoke to me, saying, "Virtuous man, accept these twelve thousand celestial maidens to serve as your attendants.
I replied, "Kauśika, do not offer such unrighteous things to me;
I am a śramaṇa, a disciple of the Śākya, and this is not suitable for me."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra addressed the Buddha with words of humble apology, immediately indicating his inability [to fulfill the task].

As for the reason why—this is the second section explaining that inability. First, regarding the cause for being rebuked: at that time, Dhṛtarāṣṭra was in a quiet room, remaining silent, either contemplating impermanence or reflecting on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Then Māra approached him in the form of Śakra, King of Devas, and disturbed Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
The reason he manifested as Śakra was that Śakra is a donor to the Buddha among the devas who has attained the first fruit [of the path];
since such a person can never cause disturbance to the Buddha-dharma, he transformed himself into Śakra.

Holding the world in his care, he spoke as if it were Śakra’s voice, saying, "Welcome," and then preached the Dharma for him. This clarifies that although one may possess merit, one must not indulge in self-indulgence.
You have cultivated merit in the past and now obtained the retribution of the five desires;
yet this retribution must inevitably perish and is bound to be impermanent. You should not indulge yourself in the five desires.

One who cultivates the "firm dharma" regarding body, life, and wealth—where "firm" refers to the three firm things—should understand that in the world, the body dies, life is transient, and wealth is lost to the five families if one is negligent.
Because one practices physically by renouncing wealth, and because one's body, life, and wealth remain firm and indestructible thereafter, these are called the "Three Firm Dharmas.
He then said to me: "To accept twelve thousand celestial maidens reveals that you, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, have fallen into the belly of Māra.
Why? Because you personally exhorted me to cultivate the Three Firm Dharmas and to relinquish my wealth; I now offer [this to you]."
If one is commanded to renounce [something] but does not accept it, this constitutes the fault of violating one’s word; if one accepts it, one immediately breaks the precepts.

Now, since you have exhorted him to renounce it and he does not accept it, this is the fault of violating one’s word. Question: At what stage of development is this person who does not recognize Māra? Answer:

It is explained that this is a Bodhisattva with a complete body who has not yet attained the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*); therefore, he does not recognize [Māra]. Even if he were to attain the five supernatural powers, [he might still fail to recognize him].

He does not enter meditative concentration, nor does he possess discernment; as for why he does not accept [the food], it is because he is unable to accept it without being defiled, and because he cannot accept it in the manner that Siddhārtha did; therefore, he does not accept it.
Before he had finished speaking, Vimalakīrti arrived and said to me, "This is not Śakra; it is Māra who has come to harass and trouble you.
He then said to Māra, "You may give these maidens to me; I am worthy to receive them.
Māra was immediately struck with fear and thought, "Vimalakīrti will surely torment me," and wishing to vanish from sight, he tried to become invisible but could not.
Exhausting all his supernatural powers, Māra was still unable to depart. Then he heard a voice from the air saying, "Pāpīyān, give these women to him, and only then may you go.
Out of fear, Māra reluctantly gave them. At that time, Vimalakīrti said to the women, "Māra has given you to me;
now you should all resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
He focused their minds and taught them the Dharma according to their needs so that they might resolve to attain the Way.
He further said, "Now that you have resolved to attain the Way, there is the joy of the Dharma with which you may find delight; you should no longer take pleasure in the five desires.

The goddess then asked, "What is meant by the joy of the Dharma? He replied, "It is the joy of constant faith in the Buddha, the joy of desiring to hear the Dharma, and the joy of making offerings to the Sangha."
Delighting in detachment from the five desires; delighting in viewing the five aggregates as enemies and robbers; delighting in viewing the four great elements as venomous serpents;

delighting in viewing the internal sense bases as an empty village; delighting in following and protecting the resolve for the Path; delighting in benefiting sentient beings; delighting in reverently supporting teachers;

delighting in extensively practicing giving; delighting in firmly upholding the precepts; delighting in patience, gentleness, and flexibility; delighting in diligently accumulating roots of goodness; and delighting in meditative concentration.
The joy of bringing disorder to pleasure; the joy of being free from defilement; the joy of clear wisdom; the joy of expanding the bodhicitta;

the joy of subduing all māras; the joy of severing all afflictions; the joy of purifying buddha-fields; the joy of cultivating all meritorious virtues for the sake of accomplishing the marks and signs of excellence;

the joy of adorning the site of enlightenment; the joy of hearing the profound Dharma without fear; the joy of the three gates of liberation; the joy of not delighting in improper times; and the joy of associating with fellow students.
To have no heart of resentment or obstruction toward those who are not fellow students; to delight in protecting against evil associates; to delight in associating with virtuous friends;
and to delight in a mind that is joyful and pure while cultivating the immeasurable factors of the path—this is the Dharma-delight of a bodhisattva.
Thereupon, Pāpīyān said to the women, "I wish to return with you all to the celestial palace. The women replied: "By means of..."
"We and this householder share the joy of the Dharma; we find great delight in it and no longer take pleasure in the delights of the five senses.
Māra said, "Householder, you may release these women and give them all to him; that is what constitutes a bodhisattva.
Vimalakīrti replied, "I have already relinquished them. You may take them away and let all sentient beings obtain their aspirations for the Dharma."
When those women were thus fully assembled, they asked Vimalakīrti, "How do we dwell in the palace of Māra?
Vimalakīrti replied, "Sisters, there is a Dharma-door called the 'Inexhaustible Lamp' (Akṣayapradīpa); you should study it.
Sisters, as for example when one lamp lights hundreds of thousands of lamps, the darkness is dispelled and all become bright, yet the original lamp is never exhausted; such, sisters, is the case."
A single bodhisattva guides hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet their own resolve for the Way is not extinguished;
as they preach the Dharma according to the needs of others, they themselves increase all wholesome dharmas.
This is called the "Inexhaustible Lamp. Although you currently dwell in the palace of Māra, by means of this Inexhaustible Lamp, you shall cause [others] to be without [suffering].
The many devaputras and devakanyās who had resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* did so both to repay the Buddha’s kindness and to bring great benefit to all sentient beings.
At that time, the devakanyās bowed their heads at the feet of Vimalakīrti and returned to the palace with Māra;
suddenly, they vanished from sight. World-Honored One, Vimalakīrti possesses such sovereign spiritual power.
"Because of his wisdom and eloquence, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
Before he had finished speaking, Vimalakīrti came and rebuked Dharmodgata for two faults:
first, that he could not distinguish between the true and the false, or the heterodox and the orthodox; second, [that he did not understand the nature of illness].
He failed because he could not accept what was urged for him; thus he lost [the opportunity]. He then spoke to Māra: "Go down before me and rebuke the Holder-of-the-World (Dharaṇīdhara).
Now, having subdued Pāpīyān, I shall speak to Māra: 'You may give it to me, for I am fit to receive it. Dharaṇīdhara has left the household life and cannot receive it;
I am a householder and should be able to receive it. Māra’s hesitation resulted in two losses: if he gave it, he would lose [his power].

"If the woman does not give [herself], she will violate her previous promise to renounce [her attachment]. Fearing this, she wishes to hide her form and depart, yet though she exhausts all her supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), she cannot leave.
Previously she was submissive in speech; now she is subdued by his majesty. Previously she was submissive in mouth;
now she is submissive in mind. Previously her mouth was defeated; now her mind is defeated. Why? Because of his supernatural power, she wishes to depart from Vimalakīrti."
Because his supernatural power could not restrain her so that she might leave, he was subdued in spirit. A voice from the sky said:
"If you release the woman, you shall be able to depart. Since the Māra’s supernatural power was insufficient, he released the woman.

The reason the Māra feared was not only the loss of the woman, but also the dread of being bound by the five fetters. Next, Vimalakīrti accepted the woman and caused her to generate [the aspiration for enlightenment].
The mind preaches the Dharma for them. Regarding those who possess the joy of the Dharma (*dharmarati*), the nature of women generally dwells in pleasure;

thus, although they may have resolved their minds on the Way, one fears they might still delight in the pleasures of the five desires (*pañcakāmaguṇa*). Therefore, the joy of the Dharma is used to replace them. The goddess asked, "What is meant by the joy of the Dharma?
She inquired about the characteristics of the joy of the Dharma. He replied: "The joy of always having faith in the Buddha means clearly understanding the Three Jewels."
This is the foundation of all virtues; therefore, as previously stated, the remainder is as the text says: "One delights in the three gates of liberation and does not delight in the untimely.
The three gates of liberation are emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).

"Does not delight in the untimely" clarifies that the two vehicles do not delight [in them] because it is not the time for them to attain the fruit. Thereupon, Pāpīyas spoke to the women, saying: "Previously, his majesty..."
"My power was unable to take you away; now I have come again to entice these women back to the celestial palace.
As for those among the women who refused to go, first, they could not leave because they were already under the care of others, and second, they refused to leave because they delighted in the Dharma.
Māra said, "Householder, you may let go of these women; they came here previously with two intentions, and now this is the second time they wish to depart."
The householder Śreṣṭhidāraka requested that he relinquish his daughter. "Śreṣṭhin" means to entreat: "Since you are a bodhisattva, you ought to relinquish this daughter.
As a bodhisattva, you should not even begrudge your own wife and children; how much less would you be stingy with another's daughter?
Therefore, it is said that one who 'ought to relinquish her' is a bodhisattva. Vimalakīrti said, "I have already relinquished her. Vimalakīrti relinquished [her].

The woman asked: "Since you have already taken [them] as a Bodhisattva, why do you now abandon them? If you abandoned them previously, you should not have taken them now. The explanation is that there are several meanings:

first, it is intended to clarify that the Way of the Bodhisattva proceeds through both awe-inspiring power (*wei*) and benevolence (*en*). What was taken previously was by means of awe-inspiring power; what is abandoned now is by means of benevolence.
This clarifies the inconceivable and sovereign power of the Bodhisattva: if he wishes to take, he takes; if he wishes to... [abandon].

Regarding "renunciation," it means renouncing with a mind free from obstruction and desiring that all sentient beings—both those who have attained the state of a Bodhisattva and those who are Śrāvakas—may study this inconceivable path of mastery. As for why what was previously accepted is now renounced:

the previous section clarified that Bodhisattvas are worthy recipients of offerings (fields of merit), whereas the present section clarifies their capacity to act as donors; the former explained those who have attained everything.
Furthermore, those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) are not fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*); they may not receive even a single hair’s breadth [of offerings].
Only the Bodhisattva who has attained non-attainment (*anupalambha*) is a field of merit capable of receiving them. It is the same now: those who have attained the two vehicles cannot act as donors;
only the Bodhisattva can act as a donor. Moreover, the "taking by majestic power" mentioned previously is not like the worldly taking by majestic power which takes everything indiscriminately.
The Bodhisattva does not take [the celestial maidens] for the sake of the pleasures of the five desires;

rather, the reason he takes them is to transform those goddesses so that they may obtain the benefit of the joy of the Dharma. He takes them with the intention of transforming them, and thus he later abandons them.
Question: If the goddesses obtain benefit while Māra suffers great anguish, how can he take them? Answer: It is precisely [for this reason].

Regarding the desire to subdue Māra so that he may be made to submit to the path of the Bodhisattva: although Māra has never previously submitted to the path of the Bodhisattva, his submission now to the path of the Bodhisattva is indeed a benefit.

As for a general explanation of what karma constitutes Māra, other sources state that because [the Buddha] formerly held a single *asaṃkhya* (unrestricted) assembly, he obtained the karmic retribution of the palace of the Sovereign Heaven (*Īśvara*). Therefore, the Bodhisattva...
When you sat at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), the Māra manifested his play; now the Māra observes your past causes.

Because you practiced the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) without obstruction for immeasurable eons as a bodhisattva in the past, this is not comparable [to ordinary acts]. Furthermore, regarding the taking of a woman and the subsequent abandoning of that woman:

"taking" refers to the time of Jyotipāla (Dīpaṃkara), while "abandoning" refers to the transmission of the lamp, so that he might propagate the teaching. If he did not abandon her, [the lineage would not have been transmitted].

This woman has attained benefit, yet she was unable to extensively transform all men and women; now she desires to extensively transform them within the celestial palace—this is renunciation (*tyāga*). Question:
For what reason does she not transform them through transcendence (*dhyāna*) but instead takes them as her own? Explanation: A woman possesses the principle of "following three others.
If she were not taken into one's own possession, the path of transformation would not be facilitated; because she is taken into one's own possession, she then follows.

This was the transformation of Vimalakīrti. Furthermore, taking her now and then relinquishing her clarifies that because the Bodhisattva’s practices and vows are fully perfected, the very act of taking the woman is the Bodhisattva’s practice, and the moment of relinquishing her is the making of the vow, which is the Bodhisattva’s vow. Why?

Since Māra had lost his daughter and vowed that she be returned to him now that the layman relinquished her, that vow was fulfilled; thus, the Bodhisattva has thereby brought forth [the fulfillment of his own vow].
"I vow that all sentient beings shall attain the fulfillment of their aspirations for the Dharma.

Because there are such benefits as these, the Bodhisattva takes up [the path] and now relinquishes it; this taking up and relinquishing are both for the sake of providing conditions and opening the way. Therefore, he previously praised [them], saying:
"There are none among those who see or hear [this] who do not receive benefit; whatever is done is never in vain. Thus, all...

The woman asked the householder: "How can one dwell in the palace of Māra? This was because the celestial maiden had originally delighted in the five desires, but now, having heard the joy of the Dharma, she was about to return to the palace of Māra;
she asked this question out of a desire to know by what karma this was possible. Furthermore, this celestial maiden no longer respected Māra but instead mocked him.
Regarding Māra, the non-Buddhists call him "Flower-Arrow," while in the Buddha-dharma he is called "The One Who Slayes with Wisdom."
Because life is taken, it is called "killing. Now, although this [act] is also termed an ultimate evil, one no longer respects that [life]; for this reason, it is called "evil.
Next, he explained to the layman the method of returning to the palace; this is the method of inexhaustibility and also conveys the intent of transformative teaching.
This may be sought according to the text.
Next, as for the four who were successively exhorted: the first, Bhadrapāla Bodhisattva, was Maitreya, who had left the household life;
the second, Prabhāvyūha, was a householder; the third, Lokadhara, was one who had left the household life;
and now the fourth, Bhadrajyotis, is a householder. It is impossible to list all bodhisattvas in detail; these four individuals briefly encompass all bodhisattvas. If...

The renunciant bodhisattva is included within Maitreya’s *Lokadhara*, while the householder bodhisattva is included within Prabhāvyūha and Śubhavyūha. Question: Why are the two renunciants not paired with one another, nor are the two householders paired with one another? Why is Maitreya addressed as "Lokadhara" (Holder of the World) and Prabhāvyūha addressed as "Śubhavyūha" (Virtuous Splendor), rather than using distinct titles for each? Answer: [To explain: The renunciant Maitreya is called "Lokadhara" because he sustains the world through his teaching; the householder Prabhāvyūha is called "Śubhavyūha" because he sustains the world through his magnificent splendor. Furthermore, the renunciant Maitreya is called "Lokadhara" because he upholds the world by means of the Dharma; the householder Prabhāvyūha is called "Śubhavyūha" because he upholds the world by means of material wealth. Moreover, the renunciant Maitreya is called "Lokadhara" because he sustains the world by means of the Great Vehicle; the householder Prabhāvyūha is called "Śubhavyūha" because he sustains the world by means of the Small Vehicle. Furthermore, the renunciant Maitreya is called "Lokadhara" because he sustains the world by means of the Mahāyāna precepts; the householder Prabhāvyūha is called "Śubhavyūha" because he sustains the world by means of the Śrāvaka precepts. Furthermore, the renunciant Maitreya is called "Lokadhara" because he sustains the world by means of the Bodhisattva path; the householder Prabhāvyūha is called "Śubhavyūha" because he sustains the world by means of the Śrāvaka path. Furthermore, the renunciant Maitreya is called "Lokadhara" because he sustains the world by means of the Buddha-fruit; the householder Prabhāvyūha is called "Śubhavyūha" because he sustains the world by means of the Arhat-fruit. Furthermore, the renunciant Maitreya is called "Lokadhara" because he sustains the world by means of the three vehicles; the householder Prabhāvyūha is called "Śubhavyūha" because he sustains the world by means of the single vehicle. Furthermore, the renunciant Maitreya is called "Lokadhara" because he sustains the world by means of the ten stages (*bhūmi*); the householder Prabhāvyūha is called "Śubhavyūha" because he sustains the world by means of the seven stages. Furthermore, the renunciant Maitreya is called "Lokadhara" because he sustains the world by means of the six perfections (*pāramitā*); the householder Prabhāvyūha is called "Śubhavyūha" because he sustains the world by means of the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*). Furthermore, the renunciant Maitreya is called "Lokadhara" because he sustains the world by means of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*); the householder Prabhāvyūha is called "Śubhavyūha" because he sustains the world by means of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). Furthermore, the renunciant Maitreya is called "Lokadhara" because he sustains the world by means of the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*); the householder Prabhāvyūha is called "Śubhavyūha" because he sustains the world by means of the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*). Furthermore, the renunciant Maitreya is called "Lokadhara" because he sustains the world by means of the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*); the householder Prabhāvyūha is called "Śubhavyūha" because he sustains the world by means of the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*). Furthermore, the renunciant Maitreya is called "Lokadhara" because he sustains the world by means of the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); the householder Prabhāvyūha is called "Śubhavyūha" because he sustains the world by means of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). Furthermore, the renunciant Maitreya is called "Lokadhara" because he sustains the world by means of the ten powers (*bala*); the householder Prabhāvyūha is called "Śubhavyūha" because he sustains the world by means of the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). Furthermore, the renunciant Maitreya is called "Lokadhara" because he sustains the world by means of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*); the householder Prabhāvyūha is called "Śubhavyūha" because he sustains the world by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, the renunciant Maitreya is called "Lokadhara" because he sustains the world by means of the eighty minor marks (*anuvyañjana*); the householder Prabhāvyūha is called "Śubhavyūha" because he sustains the world by means of the ten powers of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*). Furthermore, the renunciant Maitreya is called "Lokadhara" because he sustains the world by means of the four reliances (*pratisaraṇa*); the householder Prabhāvyūha is called "Śubhavyūha" because he sustains the world by means of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). Furthermore, the renunciant Maitreya is called "Lokadhara" because he sustains the world by means of the four ways of attracting disciples (*saṃgrahavastu*); the householder Prabhāvyūha is called "Śubhavyūha" because he sustains the world by means of the four methods of conversion (*pariṇāmanā*). Furthermore, the renunciant Maitreya is called "Lokadhara" because he sustains the world by means of the four types of eloquence (*pratibhāna*); the householder Prabhāvyūha is called "Śubhavyūha" because he sustains the world by means of the four types of faith (*śraddhā*). Furthermore, the renunciant Maitreya is called "Lokadhara" because he sustains the world by means of the four types of mindfulness (*smṛti*); the householder Prabhāvyūha is called "Śubhavyūha" because he sustains the world by means of the four types of concentration (*samādhi*). Furthermore, the renunciant Maitreya is called "Lokadhara" because he sustains the world by means of the four types of wisdom (*prajñā*); the householder Prabhāvyūha is called "Śubhavyūha" because he sustains the world by means of the four types of liberation (*vimukti*). Furthermore, the renunciant Maitreya is called "Lokadhara" because he sustains the world by means of the four types of knowledge (*jñāna*); the householder Prabhāvyūha is called "Śubhavyūha" because he sustains the world by means of the four types of realization (*abhisamaya*). Furthermore, the renunciant Maitreya is called "Lokadhara" because he sustains the world by means of the four types of cultivation (*bhāvanā*); the householder Prabhāvyūha is called "Śubhavyūha" because he sustains the world by means of the four types of abandonment (*prahāṇa*). Furthermore, the renunciant Maitreya is called "Lokadhara" because he sustains the world by means of the four types of attainment (*prāpti*); the householder Prabhāvyūha is called "Śubhavyūha" because he sustains the world by means of the four types of non-attainment (*aprāpti*). Furthermore, the renunciant Maitreya is called "Lokadhara" because he sustains the world by means of the four types of mastery (*vaśitā*); the householder Prabhāvyūha is called "Śubhavyūha

It is said that when he was first commanded to leave the household life, he was unable to do so; fearing that he might be capable while remaining at home, he was next commanded again, yet he was still unable.
Fearing that he might be capable after leaving the household life, he was finally commanded, and thus he was distinguished as one who had departed.

Furthermore, the reason this passage appears is that, following the first censure of Maitreya—which clarified that there are those who have received the prediction and those who have not—it now clarifies the command given to Prabhāvyūha.
The fourth [chapter] clarifies that for one who perceives attainment, the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) is not a site of enlightenment;

it clarifies that for one who perceives attainment through sequential maintenance of the world, one does not recognize Māra and thus cannot subdue Māra. Now, the fourth [section] addresses the life of Śubhavyūha, explaining that for one who perceives attainment, giving does not constitute true giving.
These four points are the essential practices of a bodhisattva; therefore, Vimalakīrti rebukes these four points to reveal [the truth].
There is nothing to be attained. Furthermore, what was previously most profound now reaches its ultimate shallowness; from beginning to end, the profound and the shallow are fully encompassed.
The Buddha said to the son of a householder, Śrīgupta: "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness."
Regarding the text, there are two parts; now, the first concerns the command to visit Sudāsa to inquire after his illness.
Sudāsa addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness. Why is this?
I recall that in the past, while at my father’s house, I established a great assembly for almsgiving to provide offerings to all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas."
The gates and all the non-Buddhists, the poor, the lowly, the solitary, and the beggars waited for seven days to be fulfilled.

Then, Śubhavyūha addressed the Buddha, saying: [This marks the second section, the "Refusal," which consists of two parts: first, the heading indicating the inability to explain; second, the explanation of that inability. As for the phrase "Why is this so?
it begins the second part, the explanation of the inability, which is divided into two sections. This is the first: the reason for being rebuked.]

The reason he was rebuked was that he held a giving assembly at his father’s house; thus he was rebuked. Regarding the statement "he himself held a giving assembly at his father’s house," there are two meanings:

first, to distinguish it from impure wealth, for while one might have wealth acquired through improper means, here Śubhavyūha’s father held the assembly with his own wealth, which constitutes a pure gift;
therefore, it says "he himself held a giving assembly at his father’s house."
Furthermore, because his ancestors had successively performed [these rites] at Changhui, it is said that he did so "in his father's house.

This assembly involved gathering wealth for three years and practicing giving (*dāna*) for seven days. They erected banners, and from the four directions, people gathered from the three fields (*kṣetra*), all of whom were given equal gifts.
Regarding the "three fields": first, the field of compassion (*karuṇākṣetra*); second, the field of respect (*gurukṣetra*); third, those who are both... [the text is incomplete].
The field of compassion (*karuṇā-kṣetra*) refers to all sentient beings who are impoverished or afflicted by illness.
The field of reverence (*guru-kṣetra*) refers to arhats, parents, and the Three Jewels. Those who are both objects of compassion and reverence include sick arhats, monks, and aged or infirm parents.
In foreign lands, there are two kinds of giving: the first is based on the four Vedas, such as giving through song and dance, or giving through sacrificial offerings (*yajña*).
This directly demonstrates the practice of giving; the present excellence of attainment is not the dharma-giving of non-Buddhists (tīrthika), but rather giving as a direct demonstration.
Furthermore, the reason the state performs this giving is the desire to seek the merit of Brahmā and the merit of Maheśvara (Īśvara).
As clarified previously, when Māra performed an unobstructed great sacrifice (mahā-dāna), he obtained the fruit of Maheśvara and became an adversary to the Bodhisattva.
At that time, Vimalakīrti entered the assembly and said to me, "O son of a householder, a great assembly of giving should not be like the one you have arranged;
it should be an assembly for the gift of Dharma. What is the use of this assembly of material gifts?
I asked him, "Householder, what is meant by an assembly for the gift of Dharma? As for an assembly for the gift of Dharma, there is no before and no after; it is a single offering made all at once."

To regard all sentient beings as such is called the assembly for the gift of Dharma. What does this mean? It means: to give rise to a mind of loving-kindness by means of bodhicitta in order to rescue sentient beings;

to give rise to a mind of great compassion in order to uphold the true Dharma; to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy in order to gather wisdom; to practice equanimity in order to gather [beings] through wisdom;

to give rise to the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) in order to gather those who are stingy and greedy; and to give rise to the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) in order to transform those who violate the precepts.
The perfection of giving arises through the dharma of non-self; the perfection of patience arises through detachment from the marks of body and mind;
the perfection of vigor arises through the mark of bodhi; the perfection of meditation arises through all-knowledge;
and the perfection of wisdom arises through the transformation of sentient beings, through emptiness, and through not abandoning conditioned phenomena.
Manifesting birth through the signless; giving rise to effortless protection and upholding of the True Dharma; giving rise to the power of skillful means to deliver sentient beings;
giving rise to the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to respectfully serve all; giving rise to the method of removing pride regarding body, life, and wealth;
giving rise to the three firm dharmas within the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*); and giving rise to a mind of sincerity and rectitude within the six points of reverent harmony.
Practicing wholesome dharmas arises from a mind of pure livelihood; a mind of purity and joy arises from drawing near to the noble ones and not harboring malice toward others;
a mind of self-discipline arises from the dharma of renunciation; a profound mind arises from practicing according to the teaching; great learning arises from the dharma of non-contention;
the inclination toward the Buddha’s wisdom arises from dwelling in seclusion; and the liberation of sentient beings from their bonds arises from meditative seclusion.
The stage of cultivation gives rise to the karma of merit by perfecting the primary and secondary marks and purifying the Buddha-fields;

it gives rise to the karma of wisdom by knowing the mental activities of all sentient beings and preaching the Dharma according to their needs; it gives rise to the karma of insight by knowing all phenomena without grasping or rejecting, entering the gateway of the single characteristic;
and it gives rise to [the karma of liberation] by severing all afflictions, all obstacles, and all unwholesome dharmas.
All wholesome karmas are for the sake of attaining all-encompassing wisdom; all wholesome dharmas give rise to all factors that assist the path to Buddhahood.
Thus, noble son, this is the assembly of the gift of Dharma.
If a bodhisattva abides in this assembly of the gift of Dharma, they become a great donor and a field of merit for all the world. Thus spoke Vimalakīrti to the World-Honored One.
At that time, two hundred people from among the assembly of Brahmins all resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
My mind was then purified, and I marveled at this unprecedented occurrence.
I prostrated at the feet of Vimalakīrti and offered him a necklace worth hundreds of thousands, yet he would not accept it. I said, "Householder, please, by all means—"
Having accepted whatever was offered according to his wish, Vimalakīrti took the necklace and divided it into two parts.
He held one part and gave it to the lowliest beggar in this assembly; he held the other part and offered it to that Tathāgata Durjayanta.
All the members of the assembly saw the land of the Tathāgata Durjayanta, and they also saw the jeweled necklace above that Buddha.
It transformed into a precious dais with four pillars, its four sides exquisitely adorned and not obstructing one another.
When Vimalakīrti had manifested this supernatural transformation, he spoke these words:

"If a donor gives with an impartial mind even to the lowliest beggar, regarding them as identical to the field of merit of the Tathāgata—without making distinctions, equalizing them through great compassion, and seeking no karmic reward—this is called [the true gift]."
He said, "In the city of Dharmadatta, even the most lowly beggar beholds this supernatural power and hears these teachings,
and all resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Therefore, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness."
At that time, Vimalakīrti entered the assembly. This is the second section clarifying his ability to censure and question. When asked, "Vimalakīrti, at what time did you come?

he replied, "I came when the seven days were complete. When further questioned, "Vimalakīrti, knowing that this giving was improper, for what reason did you not refute it on the first day, but instead waited until the seventh day to refute it?
The explanation says: this is ultimately for the sake of mutual completion; they complete one another.
There are two meanings: first, he skillfully obtained the wealth for seven days;

having fulfilled the giving of material wealth, and being about to practice the giving of the Dharma, he first criticized the giving of material wealth as a means to lead toward the giving of the Dharma.
For this reason, it was only at the conclusion of the seven days that he came to offer his criticism. Second, he had already accumulated wealth for three years.
Having practiced giving for seven days, his merit has become complete; yet he fears becoming attached to this merit and forming the notion of "attainment.
If there is attainment, merit is not true merit. Why? Because merit involving attainment is not the merit of permanence;
it merely yields the fruits of the human and celestial realms, which are bound to perish and fade away. Therefore, Vimalakīrti now employs the dharma of non-attainment.
The merit obtained by applying [the ointment] becomes the merit of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), for it cannot be destroyed.

Thus, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is said that when an immortal (*ṛṣi*) stores medicinal herbs in a stone chamber, they cannot be broken even if covered with diamond (*vajra*). The merit of non-apprehension is likewise.
It is also like a man who eats a small amount of diamond; it is not digested throughout the entire day. This is also as described in the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*.
"Can the eastern direction be measured? "No, World-Honored One. "Giving with the mark of non-abiding is equal to the emptiness of the ten directions.
Herein, it is precisely because giving the Dharma without attainment is used to censure giving wealth with attainment that it says:

"It should not be as you have proposed; you should instead establish an assembly for the giving of the Dharma. However, within this, there may be four propositions (catuṣkoṭi), which cannot [be avoided].
If one dogmatically clings to the notion that both one's own wealth and dharmas are non-existent, one is neither censured for one's wealth nor for one's dharmas;
if one is censured for both one's own wealth and dharmas, it is because one has something to grasp.

When both wealth and dharmas are censured, all six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) that involve grasping are censured and cannot move one toward transcendence; however, the six perfections practiced through non-grasping (anupalambha) can indeed move one.
To be able to emerge without being rebuked, and to move with immediate flexibility, is to emerge into non-arising. Regarding material wealth and the Dharma:

the Dharma is not rebuked while material wealth is rebuked; this is the textual principle. When material wealth is rebuked and the Dharma is not, it refers to the gift of these five stalks of flowers.

These five flowers surpass immeasurable gifts of the Dharma that involve grasping at attainment. Herein, [the text] directly censures the Dharma involving grasping at attainment and praises the Dharma free from grasping.
Because he wishes to reveal the dharma of non-attainment, [the Buddha] first censured the wealth of attainment.
Next, Vimalakīrti was skillfully questioned regarding the gift of dharma. In his response, Vimalakīrti stated that the gift of dharma has no sequence of before or after;
it clarifies the distinction between material wealth and the gift of dharma through ten different types of offerings, as already explained in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
What is meant by "clarifying"? It means that one gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness through bodhicitta.

Previously, it was clarified that the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*) are the intended practice for practicing giving, because one practices giving due to the presence of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), great pity, and great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*). Now, having clarified the purpose of giving, the four immeasurables are established as the path.
Herein, this loving-kindness is not the loving-kindness of ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles; although they possess loving-kindness, it is not [this kind].
It is able to universally deliver all beings and bestow great bliss; it grants happiness to humans and devas. The Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) is not called "Great Compassion" (*mahāmaitrī*);
even if its practitioners possess such a mind, they lack the corresponding action, nor do they possess the compassion of non-attainment (*anupalambha-maitrī*).

The compassion spoken of here is the objectless Great Compassion (*animitta-mahāmaitrī*); therefore, it is said that one arouses the mind of compassion through Bodhi. Bodhi is the Path. It is the Right Path, the Great Compassion.

Furthermore, regarding the arousal of the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*) by means of gathering wisdom: it clarifies that after painful sensations (*duḥkhavedanā*), aversion (*dveṣa*) mostly arises; after pleasant sensations (*sukhavedanā*), greed (*rāga*) mostly arises;
and after neutral sensations (*upekṣā*), delusion (*moha*) mostly arises. Therefore, it clarifies that the mind of equanimity gathers wisdom.
Regarding the arousal of *vīrya* (diligence) by means of detaching from the characteristics of body and mind: if one says that diligence of body and mind is not true diligence, then if one can...
Diligence that is detached from body and mind is true diligence. Regarding the six points of harmonious respect (*ṣaḍ-ānulomikāḥ saṃvāsāḥ*), one gives rise to a mind of straightforwardness.

As for the "six harmonies," they consist of commonality of benefit, commonality of view, and commonality of precepts; together with kindness of body, kindness of speech, and kindness of mind—these three [types of kindness] constitute the six kinds of harmony.
Because there is no turning away from sentient beings, it is said that one gives rise to [this mind] regarding the six points of harmonious respect.

The "sincere and straightforward mind" is the arising of *prajñā* through all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); the arising of *prajñā* corresponds to the mind of omniscience (*sarvajña*), as clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The World-Honored One and Vimalakīrti taught the Dharma so that two hundred people attained the Way.

The preceding section clarified the benefit of material giving; this section clarifies the benefit of the gift of Dharma. Because of these two benefits, gain and loss intersect. This is the virtue of goodness.
Having heard this unprecedented Dharma, he immediately removed his pearl necklace;

Vimalakīrti then accepted it and divided it into two parts—one for the honored one and one for the lowly—treating them as equal, like the Great Compassionate Tathāgata, for whom there is no distinction between fields of merit.

This is what is called being fully endowed with the gift of Dharma. Above, the two gifts of wealth and Dharma were distinguished: wealth was criticized while the Dharma was praised, thereby clarifying that through the latter, realization is attained.

Wealth and the Dharma are now united; wealth and the Dharma are not different. Since there is no wealth that is not attained as the Dharma, it is said that "possessing [wealth] is itself the fulfillment of the Dharma.
Furthermore, when taking the pearl necklace and offering it before [the Buddha], this demonstrates the gift of the Dharma; now, demonstrating the gift of material wealth is itself the Dharma.
In this manner, each of these bodhisattvas spoke to the Buddha regarding their own past causes and conditions, recounting the words spoken by Vimalakīrti, and all said,
"We are not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.
Thus ends the second major section, concerning the inability [of the bodhisattvas].
The Fifth Chapter: Mañjuśrī Inquires after the Illness.

Regarding the fifth chapter, "Mañjuśrī Inquires after the Illness," it has been traditionally said that the preceding four chapters constitute the introductory exposition (*nidāna*), while this present section constitutes the second part, the main exposition (*sūtra-deśanā*).
However, this is not so; for as previously stated, the section on dhyāna has already concluded above, and what follows here is the account of the City of Vaiśālī.

This is the second assembly within the inner chamber. The reason why this present collection follows the "Chapter on the Bodhisattvas, the Disciples" is to clarify that the preceding two chapters constitute the preliminary expedient means for inquiring after the illness, whereas these current six chapters constitute the actual inquiry after the illness;
furthermore, while previously he commanded the search for one to inquire after the illness, it is now in these six chapters that those who inquire after the illness are obtained.
Regarding the person sent to inquire after his illness: this refers to the person sent by [the Buddha] to inquire after his health.
The various disciples and bodhisattvas praised Vimalakīrti’s teaching of the past; these six chapters praise Vimalakīrti’s teaching of the present.
The praise of the past teaching describes various dharma-gates, while the praise of the present teaching describes a single dharma-gate. In the past, he subdued five hundred śrāvakas.
The eight thousand bodhisattvas represent eight thousand Dharma-gates;
because today only the single Dharma-gate of illness is manifested, it is said that whereas previously various Dharma-gates were praised, now a single Dharma-gate is praised.

Furthermore, the underlying intent is that one must first, through the preceding two chapters, refute and dismantle the notions of attainment within both the Great and Small Vehicles before one can discern the inconceivable Dharma and enter [the ultimate truth].
Regarding the chamber of inconceivability: this chamber is produced by uncontaminated karma (*anāsrava-karma*).
If one does not shatter the mind that seeks attainment, one cannot enter it, nor is one capable of hearing of its inconceivable practices.
For this reason, the present text follows the two preceding chapters. Question: Why were the bodhisattvas and others of the previous sections incapable of receiving the present text?

Regarding the statement that Mañjuśrī is capable while [Vimalakīrti] was not: it is because there is a distinction between "attainment" and "non-attainment. Where there is attainment, there is obstruction; where there is non-attainment, there is no obstruction.
Therefore, whereas previously he was not capable, now Mañjuśrī is capable. Furthermore, regarding the previous incapacity:

Vimalakīrti and Mañjuśrī had both already attained Buddhahood, whereas Maitreya and the others were still bodhisattvas who were yet to attain Buddhahood; thus, he is capable now. Moreover, regarding the previous incapacity: the assembly...
Since the arising [of this resolve] depends specifically on Mañjuśrī, it was previously stated that [the others] were incapable while only Mañjuśrī was capable.

Furthermore, it causes one to give rise to a sense of rarity and the thought of a difficult encounter, thereby honoring the person and respecting the Dharma; for this reason, those who were previously incapable are now capable through Mañjuśrī.
Regarding this section, there are six chapters divided into two parts; first, this chapter provides a brief [explanation].
The second section, "Elucidating the Two Wisdoms," consists of five chapters that extensively explain these two wisdoms.

Because the inconceivable Dharma cannot be elucidated all at once, the preceding section provided only a brief explanation; now, as that brief explanation is concluded, the second section provides an extensive clarification.
Regarding the first chapter here, titled "Mañjuśrī," it is named after the person who inquires about the illness; therefore, it is called "Mañjuśrī."
In the "Chapter on Inquiring after Illness," it is stated that the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī who wanders through various lands is inconceivable.
In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, within the narrative of Sudhana, it is clarified that this person is a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Originally, from Mañjuśrī down to Maitreya, Sudhana encounters as many spiritual friends as there are atoms in three thousand great thousandfold world systems. Mañjuśrī is the root; how could it be otherwise? Mañjuśrī is indeed the source.
He is the mother of all Buddhas of the ten directions; because all Buddhas of the ten directions are born from Mañjuśrī, he is inconceivable.
Furthermore, the *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra* states: "Mañjuśrī is the Buddha Ratnākara-pramuditagarbha-maṇi;
Aṅgulimāla is the Buddha Sarvasattva-darśana-rati-vīrya; [and] all sentient beings..."
Hearing of these two Buddhas extinguishes the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*).

Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states that Mañjuśrī is the seventh among the fifty-three Buddhas, his name being as previously mentioned, and he currently resides in the world of Constant Joy (*Sadāpramudita*) in the northern direction.
Moreover, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that he is the ninth patriarch of Śākyamuni. Additionally, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* refers to him as "Dragon Seed" (*Nāgabija*).

Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Radiance of Awakening," states that Mañjuśrī is the Bodhisattva of the Stage of Succession (*kṣetrapratyaya*) in the Golden World of the Buddha Akṣobhya of the East; he shall succeed this Buddha in his place.
Based on this, it is explained that Mañjuśrī is neither a past Buddha nor a past Bodhisattva, yet he is capable of being both a Buddha and a Bodhisattva. Thus, he is called Mañjuśrī.
Some call him Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, some call him Mañjuśrī; "Mañju" means "Wondrous Virtue" (Miao-de), while "Śrī" is translated here as "Venerable Head" (Jingshou) or "Scholarly Head" (Rushou).
Because he is named from this [quality], it is called the "Mañjuśrī Chapter."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī: "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.

This chapter is divided into two parts: first, the command to inquire after the illness; second, Mañjuśrī’s acceptance of the command. The present section concerns the Tathāgata’s command to inquire after the illness.

○ Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha. [The section] "Below" is the second part, which corresponds to the command [to visit]. This is divided into three: first, the preliminary matters before the inquiry after illness;

second, the actual inquiry after illness; and third, the matters following the inquiry after illness. Within the first [section], the preliminary matters before the inquiry after illness, there are two further divisions.

First, the causal origin of the inquiry after illness; second, the actual inquiry after illness; and third, the benefits following the inquiry after illness. Regarding the preliminary matters before the inquiry after illness, there are two parts. First...
Regarding the two chapters, "The Arrival of Mañjuśrī" and "The Second Mañjuśrī’s Arrival," each contains four sections.
In the first chapter, the first section praises the virtue of Vimalakīrti; the second is his receiving the command; the third is his desire to depart; and the fourth is his actual departure.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, that noble person is difficult to engage in debate.
He has profoundly penetrated the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and is skilled in expounding the essential teachings. His eloquence is unimpeded and his wisdom is without obstruction.
He fully knows all the rules and methods of the bodhisattvas and enters the secret treasury of all Buddhas without exception. He subdues all demons and sports with divine transformations."
[He] has attained mastery. His wisdom and skillful means have both already reached the further shore.

Now, this first eulogy—regarding why he offers praise—is intended to engender a heart of reverence in sentient beings and to give rise to the realization that [such a person] is difficult to encounter;
thus, he praises the virtues of Vimalakīrti. Within this eulogy, there are three parts: a general eulogy, a specific conclusion, and now, the general eulogy.

Section Two: Praising the Profound Realization of the True Reality (*tathatā*). This section provides a specific praise and also serves as an explanation of the preceding praise. It states that it is difficult to extol;
however, for those who do not yet know how it is difficult to extol, this explanation is now provided. Within this, there are four pairs of praises. The first pair concerns the internal and external:
namely, internally awakening to the true reality and externally possessing sufficient eloquence (*pratibhāna*). Regarding "eloquence being unimpeded," [the following follows].

Second, internally illuminating without obstruction and externally explaining without impediment: although it was previously stated that one internally penetrates the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), there may still be points of obstruction;
therefore, it is now clarified that there is neither obstruction nor impediment. Regarding all Bodhisattva dharmas, one either knows them all completely (the third [point] is twofold:
knowing the cause through knowledge of the fruit), or one knows them all completely by knowing the cause—that is, the secret treasury of all Buddhas.

"Attaining entry" refers to the fruit of consciousness. "Subduing the various Māras" [is the fourth point], which consists of two pairs: first, subduing the various Māras, which is the departure from worldly play;
second, attaining supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), which is the attainment of wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*). All have already attained deliverance.
This concludes the third section of the praise, which summarizes and returns to the two types of wisdom. Although there are many different praises above, they are nothing other than these two.
Because their two types of wisdom have thoroughly penetrated and investigated all things without remainder, it is said that they have all already attained deliverance.
Nevertheless, you should now follow the Buddha’s holy command and go to him to inquire about his illness.
Thereupon, among the assembly, the various bodhisattvas, great disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings all had this thought: "Now these two great beings, Mañjuśrī and [Vimalakīrti]..."

As Mañjuśrī conversed with him, he inevitably expounded the wondrous Dharma; immediately, eight thousand bodhisattvas, five hundred śrāvakas, and hundreds of thousands of devas and humans all desired to follow him.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, together with the assembly of bodhisattvas, great disciples, and devas and humans, respectfully surrounded by them, entered the great city of Vaiśālī.
Although the third person in the assembly below, Vimalakīrti, possesses virtues that are difficult to rival, we shall now rely upon the Buddha’s power to go to him and inquire after his illness.
Since even Mañjuśrī, who was a Buddha in the past, declared himself unable to do so, we must rely on the Buddha’s power;
thus we know that Vimalakīrti’s inconceivability is merely for the sake of sentient beings. At that time, among the assembly, the third...
Mañjuśrī, having received the command, was about to depart. Mañjuśrī’s inquiry after the illness was precisely for the sake of sentient beings;

since sentient beings were departing, the Bodhisattva wished to go as well. Mañjuśrī and the various Bodhisattvas descended [from the sky]; the fourth section, "The Actual Departure," is as stated in the text.
At that time, the elder Vimalakīrti thought to himself, "Now Mañjuśrī is coming together with a great assembly.
He immediately employed his supernatural powers to empty the interior of his room, removing all furnishings and attendants, leaving only a single couch upon which he lay as if ill.
At that time, the second section concerning the Elder begins with Mañjuśrī, who states: "He does not come, yet he comes;
he is unmoving, yet he moves; his movement is a non-movement. Thus he comes from the *bodhimaṇḍa* and thus arrives at the *dharmadhātu*.
Within this arrival at the *dharmadhātu*, there are also four phrases. The first clarifies the empty room, as well as this [state] and worldly sentiment.
When guests arrive in the world, one spreads out a bed and sets out mats; yet now, Vimalakīrti has descended alone into a place where there is nothing at all—what is the meaning of this?
The explanation says that its significance is immeasurable. First, although the room has no attendants, he employs the skillful means (*upāya*) of actually lying upon a single bed;
this is the reality of skillful means. Therefore, the previous praise stated: "His wisdom and skillful means are both perfected."
Having attained deliverance, one now understands that these two—the empty room and all things being empty—are the reality; they have never been either swift or not swift.

To manifest illness by lying on a bed is skillful means and wisdom. This is not like the two types of wisdom previously perceived, where emptiness was taken as the reality and skillful means as something else.
Now, the reality is pointed out as skillful means, and skillful means are pointed out as reality.
This is indeed the causal condition for skillful means. Why? Because the empty room is intended to demonstrate the meaning of emptiness. Since the room is empty, my illness is also empty;
Mañjuśrī’s coming is also empty, and the question and answer are both empty. By means of the emptiness of the question and answer, the question and answer reveal the fundamental nature.
Furthermore, the empty room is intended to show that this room is equal to the Buddha-fields of the ten directions; since this room is empty, the ten directions [are also empty].
That the Buddha-lands are all empty, and furthermore that the room is empty, clarifies that the celestial Māras throughout the worlds of the ten directions are all my attendants;
if they were not empty, there would be no questioning, and if there were no questioning, there would be no such answer. Thus, the empty room is intended to manifest this meaning.
Moreover, the empty room serves as the basis for the subsequent chapters, so that when seats are required, one may borrow them from King Dīpaṃkara, and when food is needed, it is obtained from him.

Therefore, he was able to request a meal at the Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhavyūha) Hall. Furthermore, because he has no retinue, there is the question regarding the Universal Manifestation of the Physical Body (Vairocana-rūpa-kāya).
Vimalakīrti answers that his retinue is equal [to the Dharma-body]. For this reason, the room is empty. As for the fact that only a single couch is placed therein:

the previous emptiness was a provisional means, while the present presence is also a provisional means. The previous emptiness is "emptiness within existence," and the present presence is "existence within emptiness."
This emptiness and existence do not obstruct one another. Why? Within an empty house there is a bed; the bed is within the empty house.
While the empty house contains the bed, emptiness does not obstruct the existence of the bed within the empty house, nor does existence obstruct emptiness.

This is "expedient means arising within expedient means," and "skillful means established within skillful means. To say that expedient means arises within expedient means clarifies the *vimala* (purity).
The Bodhisattva has never had a body, nor has he ever abandoned it; yet now there is a body and there is abandonment. This is a provisional within the provisional:
he manifests illness through a provisional body and empties his dwelling through a provisional abandonment. Thus, within this provisional, he further gives rise to the provisional.
Although he possesses a body and a dwelling, the Bodhisattva has never truly possessed a body or abandoned it; that he is neither body nor dwelling reveals the fundamental reality.
When Mañjuśrī entered the house, he saw that the room was empty and devoid of all possessions, with only a single bed for solitary rest.
Once Mañjuśrī had entered, the second Mañjuśrī silently took his place at the eastern side, and the former Vimalakīrti silently took his place at the western side.
As these two divine beings silently reflected upon one another, this was their silent inquiry and silent response: "Which of us is the one who previously resided here?"

When the gentleman perceived the room as empty, he immediately realized that the provisional mind was ill and lay down; when the provisional [mind] appeared as a pair, the present pair perceived the room as empty.
Thus, the provisional [mind] alone slept upon the single bed, realizing its own existence as provisional. Why is this so?
Because the two were mutually reflected in each other; the Way was present in their very meeting of eyes.
Then Vimalakīrti said, "Welcome, Mañjuśrī! You have come with the characteristic of non-coming; you have seen with the characteristic of non-seeing.
Then Vimalakīrti spoke—this concludes the third section on the householder’s words questioning the previous householder’s silence.
Mañjuśrī silently accepted the words of the layman. The layman asked Mañjuśrī, and Mañjuśrī replied:
"Whether speaking or remaining silent, both serve as conditions for opening the Way and benefiting others. Regarding the statement, "Coming with the characteristic of not coming":

as the ancient scriptures say, "Coming with the characteristic of not coming" means that while the sequence of arrival is not seen, one attains the characteristic of seeing. This current version is a skillful translation by Master Kumārajīva.
"The principle is that where there is no coming, there is coming; where there is no seeing, there is seeing.

This refers to the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly standpoint), wherein host and guest exchange greetings and inquiries; thus, it is through the worldly standpoint that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is revealed.
However, interpretations of this differ: some say that while the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) does not come, the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) does come; others interpret it as follows:

According to the *Zhendi* (Paramārtha-satya), there is no coming; according to the *shisdi* (Saṃvṛti-satya), there is coming. It is also said that true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) does not come, while expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) does come.
Furthermore, during the early Liang dynasty, Zhuangyan was renowned for lecturing on this sutra in Pengcheng, and his lectures were considered the foremost there.
His interpretation states: "The provisional name (*prajñapti-nāma*) comes, but the real dharma (*dharmatā*) does not come. Therefore, he cites this treatise [to support his view].
The text states: "Because the burning of the railing is a conventional designation for coming and going, there is no real dharma; this is the school of the Teacher.
How could those of the Lesser Vehicle who are Arhats understand the profound and subtle meaning of the 'non-attainment' of the Mahāyāna?
If even such individuals as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were refuted, how can you use the meaning of 'a-hari' (not taking) to explain it?"

Because of this sūtra, [the former view] is not acceptable. Next, a master of the *Dilun* school says: "The essence of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) has no coming or going; it is the function of the dharma-realm that comes and goes.
Furthermore, a master of the Middle Way and the Provisional (Zhongjia) says: "In its essence, it neither goes nor comes; in its provisional function, it both goes and comes.
Its essence neither goes nor comes, while its function both goes and comes. Question: If the interpretation of the *Dilun* is thus, what now [is the case]?
The Great Master Yeshan said: "If there were any further interpretations at this time, they would merely be enough to carry passengers.

How could there be any other interpretation? Now, I shall simply read the scripture directly. All the previous commentaries have broken the phrasing when reading the scripture and divided the text to explain the meaning;
their transgression is not light. Here I clarify that it is precisely 'coming without the aspect of coming,' and that 'there is no place from which one comes.'"
"Coming and coming—what is the meaning of these words? This was spoken precisely to shatter the views of the assembly at that time.
When the members of the assembly saw Mañjuśrī coming from the hermitage garden and arriving at the abbot’s quarters to meet the layman, they gave rise to this initial [delusion].
To break through this view, it is clarified that "coming" is a non-coming; one comes without coming. It is not that there is no coming, but because there is no coming, it is called "not-coming."
Nor does one come because of coming; it is simply that coming is non-coming. Non-coming and coming are seen in this same way. Non-coming is coming; correctly contemplate coming.
Non-moving is moving; correctly contemplate moving. Why? Because one correctly contemplates coming and moving, therefore both coming and moving are correctly contemplated.
If one comes and moves with a perverted mind, both coming and moving are perverted. As stated previously: "Whether lifting the foot or setting it down, all..."
Because they have come from the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and abide in the Buddha-dharma, their coming and movement are all seen through right contemplation;
it is also as stated in the text. Mañjuśrī said: "It is thus, householder, that if one has already come, there is no further coming; if one has already gone, there is no further going."
Why is this so? That which departs comes from nowhere, and that which arrives goes nowhere;
what can be seen cannot be seen again.
Mañjuśrī, it is thus. This concludes the fourth passage. Mañjuśrī spoke in response: "It is truly as you have said; it is indeed as you have stated."
The high intent of the statement "having already come, one does not come again" is explained briefly by means of the gate of "already.

To explain the absence of coming by means of the gate of "already": when the assembly saw that Mañjuśrī had already arrived at the chamber, they therefore now refute [the notion] that having already come, he comes again, and that having already gone, he goes again. This concerns Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* speaks of "coming without coming," which is precisely what Mañjuśrī here describes as "coming and not coming.
Why is this? That which comes has nowhere from which it comes; having explained "coming," "not coming" clarifies that it is not simply non-coming.
Thus, "not coming" is in fact "coming," because there is nowhere to which one comes. Master Sengzhao says: "By observing the directions, one knows that there is going; yet the goer does not [go]."
Furthermore, it is as stated in the "Treatise on the Non-Transmigration of Things": "The sun and moon traverse the heavens yet do not complete a circuit;
the rivers rush toward one another yet do not flow. This is precisely that matter; seeing is also like this.

Setting aside this matter for now, the first section—elucidating the events prior to the inquiry regarding the illness—is concluded. Now begins the second section: the actual inquiry regarding the illness, which is divided into two parts.
First, a discussion on Vimalakīrti’s illness; second, a discussion on the illnesses of others.

The discussion on Vimalakīrti’s illness is, in fact, a discussion on the illness of Bodhisattvas. The discussion on the illnesses of others is a discussion on the illnesses of sentient beings. Vimalakīrti’s illness is [the illness of] illness itself.
For the sake of sentient beings, one is afflicted by their afflictions; being thus afflicted, one breaks through these afflictions.

This is the same as the non-affliction of a Bodhisattva’s affliction. Regarding the first [section], there are three parts: first, questioning the substance of the illness; second, questioning the empty room;

and third, questioning the characteristics of the illness. These three sections consist of only two topics: first, discussing the illness, and second, discussing the emptiness. Discussing these two, in turn—
The preceding discussion of the first two matters served as the introduction to the latter two matters.
Setting those aside for now, we shall now address the first [of the remaining topics]:
the illness of Vimalakīrti. This consists of two parts: first, setting aside collateral arguments; second, the primary argument.

Vimalakīrti now urgently requests that this digression be halted; terms such as "not coming" and "coming" are precisely the profound meaning of the Vaipulya sūtras and the great tenet of the Buddha-dharma.
However, because the Sage’s intent has not yet been fully proclaimed, he sets aside the digression; thus it is said, "Let us for now set this matter aside."

Regarding the expression "to inquire with earnestness" in the third section that correctly proclaims the Sage’s intent:

it is "earnest" because he commands five hundred śrāvakas and eighty bodhisattvas, and commands all those of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna to inquire after his illness; furthermore, it is "earnest" because he inquires now once again after having already inquired previously.
"Householder, from what cause does this illness arise? How long has it been since it first appeared? How shall it be extinguished?

The Tathāgata says that it is likewise now; he commands Mañjuśrī to inquire, yet this inquiry by Mañjuśrī is in fact the inquiry of the Tathāgata himself.
