The Prefect of the Heavenly Realm recalled the Master of Elephants’ mind, whereupon the Master addressed the King’s minister: "I am only able to train the body of an elephant, but I cannot train the mind of an elephant.
The King asked, "Who is able to train the minds of sentient beings? The minister replied, "Only the Buddha is able to train the minds of sentient beings.
Therefore, we know that only Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can train the minds of sentient beings. Regarding this chapter, the preceding question was as follows:
As in the text, Vimalakīrti says that a bodhisattva should form this thought; then, below, Vimalakīrti answers, saying:
"This illness arises from the delusions and afflictions of past lives; there is no substantial dharma therein. Your present illness is entirely due to the causes of past delusions and afflictions.
Since the cause is merely delusion and non-existent, the fruit is likewise illusory and non-existent."

The beginning is empty and false, having no real existence; the end is also empty and false, having no real existence. Since both the beginning and the end—cause and effect—are entirely non-existent, who is sick?
Who suffers? Who is afraid? Who is anxious? Therefore, it is said that there is no real dharma;
who is it that receives illness? Why is this so? Because the four great elements combine, they are provisionally named a "body. Thus [it is explained] above.
If one seeks for a self within the four great elements of this very life, it cannot be found;

who then is it that suffers from illness? If you say there is a self, yet apart from these five aggregates there are no five aggregates—there being only the four great elements—then because the four great elements have no master, and because the four great elements have no master, the body has no self. Furthermore, this illness arises entirely from...
Regarding those who cling to a self, I shall explain the reason for their illness and the reason for my refutation. As for the reason for explaining the illness: why are you ill?
It is solely because of the self that you are ill. As for the reason for my refutation: with what intention do I now refute the self?
It is only because of your clinging that I refute the self. Once you know the root of the illness, you will immediately eliminate the notion of a self.

Regarding those who give rise to the perception of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*): herein, one borrows the phenomenon to dismantle the self. If one does not first give rise to the perception of phenomena, there is no means by which the self can be extinguished.
For the sake of extinguishing the self, one first gives rise to the perception of phenomena; once the perception of the self is removed, the perception of phenomena is likewise eliminated.
As the Dharma Master says: "It is like a person who nurtures an enemy; both individuals regard themselves as enemies, and yet both are enemies to one another."
If one has an enemy, by killing one enemy, one nurtures another enemy who will kill that first enemy; once that enemy has been killed, one must still further eliminate this [new] enemy.
Therefore, as for myself and the Dharma, I wish to cease my own enmity and instead nurture the "enemy" that is the Dharma, so that the enemy which is the Dharma may kill my enemy.
Once the intention to kill my enemy is eliminated, the enemy which is the Dharma is also removed. Furthermore, there is the foreign horseman.
The analogy of the son is likewise: when one rides a lion to cross over tigers and wolves, once the tigers and wolves have been crossed, one abandons the lion.
Myself and the Dharma are also like this: the Dharma arises for the sake of ceasing the self; once the self has ceased, one abandons the Dharma.

As stated in the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, there are no sixteen kinds of self, yet in conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), dharmas such as the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*) truly exist. Some people say they do not truly exist.
I possess only the dharmas such as the aggregates (skandhas) and elements (dhātus), just as there is no water in a jar yet the jar itself is not non-existent;

likewise, while there is no self within the aggregates, the aggregates themselves are not non-existent. Now, by borrowing these dharmas to refute the self, it is said that "the notion of self is removed and the notion of dharmas arises.
This indicates that this body is merely a composite formed from the various dharmas, clarifying that it is only the four great elements and so forth that combine to form this body.
Arising consists solely of the arising of the four great elements, and ceasing consists solely of the ceasing of the four great elements; there is no self that arises or ceases.

Furthermore, as for their mutual unawareness: when the earth element arises, it does not call out to the water element to arise, and when the water element arises, it does not call out to the earth element to arise;
therefore, it is said that they are mutually unaware of one another.
That sick bodhisattva, in order to eliminate the notion of dharmas, should form this thought: "This notion of dharmas is itself a perversion;
perversion is precisely a great affliction. I should abandon it. How does one abandon it? One abandons "I" and "mine. How does one abandon "I" and "mine"?
It means abandoning dualistic dharmas. How does one abandon dualistic dharmas? It means not being mindful of the internal or the external.
All dharmas proceed in equality; what is this equality? It is the equality of the self and the equality of nirvāṇa.
Why is this so? Because both this self and nirvāṇa are empty. By what are they empty? They are empty merely by way of designation.
Thus, these two dharmas lack any determinate nature.
At that time, a sick bodhisattva, in order to eliminate the notion of dharmas (*dharmasaṃjñā*), should form this thought: [This is the second section on subduing the view of dharmas.
By relying on the dharma to pacify the self, and by the pacification of the self, the dharma is immediately purified and revealed.
Because there is a self, there is the view of a self; now that there is the dharma, there is the view of dharmas. Since the view of a self is inverted, the view of dharmas is likewise inverted.
Since perversion is identical to inversion, both must be abandoned; once the self (*ātman*) is abandoned, that which belongs to the self (*ātmīya*) is also abandoned.

This differs from the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, which holds that the provisional is transcended by means of the real, and the real is transcended by means of emptiness—wherein both the real and the empty are considered aspects of liberation.

Here, we clarify that in the state of equality, both must be abandoned. How is the self abandoned? That which is called "self" refers to the two dharmas; one does not dwell upon the internal or the external.

Since one's own person is internal and others are external, and the six sense organs are internal while the six sense objects are external, it is said that one does not dwell upon the internal or the external.
Furthermore, one practices equanimity. Again, it was asked: "What is meant by 'equanimity,' such as the equality of the self and nirvana? [The answer is:
Humans are the lowest of beings, while nirvana is the supreme dharma; yet the teaching establishes them as equal, so that high and low are no longer distinguished.
Second, why were these two established to be equal? They were established as equal because they were originally unequal. Now, by establishing these two, all things are encompassed:
when the lowest level is raised, persons are included along with the Dharma; when the highest level is raised, the Dharma is included along with persons.
Therefore, by establishing these two, everything is made equal. Why is this so? It is to explain equality. In which chapter is equality discussed? It is in the Chapter on Equality.
It is because I realize that both the self and nirvana are empty, and therefore they are equal.
Having attained this equality, there is no remaining ailment except for the ailment of emptiness; yet even the ailment of emptiness is empty.

"There is no other illness, only the illness of emptiness; even the illness of emptiness is empty. This concludes the third section, which subdues the view of emptiness so that the view of emptiness ceases.
Above, it was clarified that there is no person, no phenomena, no self, and no nirvana—all are equal.
Consequently, one might form a conceptualization of equality or a conceptualization of emptiness. For this reason, it further clarifies that "emptiness is also empty," as stated in the Treatise.
It is said: "If there were a phenomenon that is not empty, then there would have to be a phenomenon that is empty.
Since emptiness itself does not exist, how could anything else exist? Furthermore, it is said: "The Great Sage taught the Dharma of emptiness in order to bring an end to all views.

If one were to become attached to emptiness, the Buddhas would not convert such a person. Thus, the Dharma of emptiness was taught to bring an end to all views; once all views have been extinguished, emptiness itself is exhausted.
Since the Dharma is itself pure, how could one further cling to the Dharma of emptiness? Now this case is also like that: once the illness is empty, the illness of emptiness is further emptied.
This sick bodhisattva accepts all sensations by means of non-appropriation; yet, until the Buddha-dharmas are fully perfected, they do not extinguish [the sensation].
This refers to receiving [the teaching] and attaining realization.
This section on the sick bodhisattva explains, through the absence of "receiving," the second point: clarifying the subduing of others after first clarifying the subduing of oneself.

Regarding the former—subduing oneself—there are three aspects: the emptiness of sentient beings, the emptiness of dharmas, and the emptiness of illness itself. Now, this section clarifies the subduing of others.
There are also three chapters on subduing [sentient beings]: first, receiving a body for the sake of sentient beings without having previously received one;
second, undergoing suffering for the sake of sentient beings; and third, transforming and guiding sentient beings. These three chapters also follow a sequential order. Why is this?

It is because a bodhisattva has never before received a body for the sake of sentient beings; therefore, they receive a body for the sake of sentient beings. What is meant by "receiving a body for the sake of sentient beings"?
The reason for acting on behalf of sentient beings is that Bodhisattvas share the suffering of sentient beings; because they share their suffering, they cannot remain silent.
Those who share their suffering do so with the desire to transform and guide them so that they may be freed from suffering.
Among the three chapters, this is now the first: "Why is it that one undergoes all sensations without being affected by them? It is always thus. This is as follows:
"Nothing is accepted; I do not accept a self, I do not accept dharmas, I do not accept existence, and I do not accept non-existence. There is nothing whatsoever that is accepted.

Fearing that one might misunderstand this "non-acceptance" as a mere nihilistic void and thereby fall into the stage of the Two Vehicles, the Sūtra asks: "For what reason does it say one falls into the stage of the Two Vehicles?
One who falls into the view of emptiness regarding non-acceptance is said to have fallen into the stage of the Two Vehicles. For this reason, the text now clarifies the meaning of non-acceptance.
Yet one experiences both the two "bounces" (the two views) and non-experience; the ordinary person experiences the bounce, while the follower of the Two Vehicles experiences non-experience.
Now, the Bodhisattva purifies both and does not experience them—neither experiencing experience nor experiencing non-experience.
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "One does not practice, nor does one experience; one does not even experience non-experiencing. This is called the Bodhisattva’s non-experience.
The reception of samādhi is not shared with the two vehicles. Question: The Bodhisattva’s “reception of non-reception” is attained;

the ordinary person also attains “non-reception of reception,” yet they do not understand it. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva “receives while in non-reception,” and the ordinary person likewise “receives while in non-reception.
Why is this so? As the Sūtra says: “Sentient beings and Bodhisattvas are ultimately non-existent, yet sentient beings...”
There are many such inversions; thus, that which does not exist [as a self] is present among sentient beings.
Because they are fundamentally the same as sentient beings, they become non-sentient beings, and because they do not accept [this state], the Bodhisattva does not accept it.

Yet, the Bodhisattva accepts in order to transform sentient beings; he accepts so as to cause them to share the Bodhisattva’s non-acceptance. Therefore, it is said that there is "nothing to be accepted."
Furthermore, while the various feelings (*vedanā*) have not yet fulfilled the Buddha-dharma, one does not realize enlightenment by extinguishing those feelings;

this clarifies that as long as the Buddha-dharma is not fulfilled, one never extinguishes feeling to personally attain realization. Those of the Two Vehicles do not act for the sake of sentient beings, but instead personally extinguish and abandon feeling to realize *nirvāṇa*.
Now, the Bodhisattva should, by means of the two wisdoms, transform sentient beings so as to bring them to Buddhahood.
If the Dharma is not yet complete, one does not extinguish the Buddha-dharmas nor realize them while still undergoing [suffering].

Even if the body experiences pain, one should contemplate sentient beings in the evil realms and give rise to great compassion, thinking: "Once I have been tamed, I shall likewise tame all sentient beings;
I shall only remove their illness, but not the illness itself."
If one experiences suffering oneself and contemplates sentient beings in the evil realms, this is the second [point]:
that as sentient beings experience suffering in their physical bodies, the Bodhisattva likewise experiences suffering in his own body.

Since the Bodhisattva has a body and experiences suffering while constantly contemplating that sentient beings have bodies and experience suffering, and since the Bodhisattva’s own suffering is already used to subdue the suffering of sentient beings through emptiness, it should likewise [be applied].
The reason for employing the three gates of emptiness to subdue sentient beings is that this Dharma-gate is primarily intended for bodhisattvas who have newly begun their practice.
Since you have already used the three gates of emptiness to discipline yourself, you should likewise employ the three gates of emptiness to subdue sentient beings;
thus it is said, "Having disciplined yourself, you should also discipline sentient beings. One merely removes their afflictions.
As for "not removing dharmas," this arises from the self-regulation of the three preceding emptinesses. Why?
Because the preceding [emptinesses] destroy the view of a self, destroy the view of dharmas, and destroy the view of emptiness; otherwise, one might say there are three dharmas that must be removed.

Therefore, it is now clarified that while deluded views are removed, in reality there are no three dharmas to be removed, and never has there been a sentient being who was not afflicted by the sickness of sentient beings.
When one observes sentient beings who are afflicted by illness, there are in reality no sentient beings to be removed; the same applies to phenomena (*dharma*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Therefore, one merely removes their illness, as there are no three dharmas to be removed. Thus it is said that "one does not remove the dharma. To provide an analogy:
it is like flowers in the sky seen by those with an eye disease; one merely removes the eye disease, for in reality there are no flowers to be removed. This is also stated in the *Śata-śāstra*.
The opponent says: "This refutation [of our position] refutes itself; if [things] are inherently empty from the beginning, then they should not be refuted.
The treatise replies by providing an analogy: "It is like a person who sees a mirage and says, 'This is water. A wise person tells them, 'In reality, this is not water.
This merely refutes the perception, for there is no water to be refuted. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Like a thirsty deer, because of its thirst..."
Seeing a mirage, one says it is water and runs toward it, yet no actual water can be found;
this case is exactly like that—only the sickness of the perception is destroyed, for there is actually no dharma to be removed.
He instructs them in order to sever the root of illness. What is called the root of illness? It is having objects of attachment (*ālambana*).

From having objects of attachment, there is the root of illness. To what are they attached? They are attached to the three realms (*tridhātu*). How does one sever these attachments? By means of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
If there is no apprehension, then there are no attachments. What is meant by non-apprehension? It is being free from the two views (*dvaya-dṛṣṭi*).
What are the two views? They are the view of the internal and the view of the external; these are non-apprehendable.
Mañjuśrī, this is how a sick bodhisattva disciplines his mind.
To sever the root of illness, he provides guidance from the slope [of the path]. Herein, the third section clarifies how the bodhisattva, sharing the same illness, provides guidance.

Since their suffering is identical, one cannot remain silent; there must be transformative guidance. Now, having departed from the root of illness—if the root of illness is purified, then the fruit of illness will not exist.
This consists of two parts: first, the indication of the root of illness, and second, the two chapters of transformative guidance, as per the text.
What is meant by the "root of illness"? It refers to having objects of attachment (*ālambana*). Below is the second part, the explanation of these two chapters. That is to say: [text follows].

To distinguish between these two, we now turn to the introductory section on the examination of illness. That which is called "having an object of clinging" (ālambana) refers simply to having something attained:
clinging to persons, clinging to dharmas, clinging to existence, or clinging to non-existence. To cling to the ordinary or the holy, even for the slightest thought of a mind, is itself clinging.
Therefore, a sutra says: "Movement is the net of Māra; non-movement is the Dharma-seal. To give rise to a mind is movement."
Thought is precisely the grasping at objects; because there is grasping, there is illness. Thus, grasping is the root of illness. What is it that is grasped?
It refers to the three realms (*dhātu*). Because there is grasping, one transmigrates through the three realms and cannot escape.
Even while within the burning house, though one encounters great suffering, one does not regard it as a calamity. All such things arise from this.
Because there is that which is grasped as an object of dependence, one cannot escape the twenty-five states of existence characterized by birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Therefore, a sutra says: "That which has something to be attained is called ignorance; the non-attainment of the twenty-five states of existence is called wisdom and is termed Great Nirvana.
That which has something to be attained takes ignorance as its primary characteristic, resulting in birth within these twenty [states].
Because the five aggregates possess fruits, they are called "objects of clinging," which refers to the three realms. How does one sever these objects of clinging?

The second section below, the Chapter on Teaching and Guidance, explains this: "How does one sever objects of clinging? By means of non-attainment. One severs objects of clinging through non-attainment;
it should be known that 'attainment' is itself an object of clinging, and as long as there is an object of clinging consisting of attainment, one cannot be free from it."

Because of the three realms, one experiences bodily sensation and the body, and thus there is suffering. Because there is nothing to be attained, the攀緣 (pān-yuan; cognitive objectification/attachment) is severed.
Because there is no cause, and because there is neither cause nor fruit, [suffering ceases], and so forth. How is it that cognitive objectification is severed by means of non-attainment?
What is meant by "non-attainment"? It refers to the two views: the view of the internal and the view of the external, and the view of existence and the view of non-existence. That is to say—

If there is something to be attained, yet one can neither see the internal nor see the external, neither see existence nor see non-existence—when these two views are fully understood, there is nothing to be attained;
this is precisely *prajñā*. It is not that there is a "non-attainment" apart from these two views.
Now it is clarified that the very understanding of these two views is itself the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and right contemplation (*samyagdarśana*). This is the contemplation of the body.
The contemplation of the Buddha through the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is likewise. What are called the two views? They are the view of the internal and the view of the external.

The mind is internal and the body is external; one’s own body is internal and another’s body is external; those categorized as sentient beings are internal and those not categorized as sentient beings are external.
If one can shatter these two views of internal and external, there will be nothing to be attained, and [the views] will be severed.
Because of objective conditions (*ālambana*), one speaks of internal views and external views; these are non-apprehendable (*anupalabdha*).
To sever the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death is the bodhi of a bodhisattva. If it were not thus, what one has cultivated and refined would be without wisdom or benefit.
For example, only by overcoming an enemy can one be called brave; likewise, only by simultaneously eliminating old age, sickness, and death is one [truly a bodhisattva].
This is what "sattva" means.
To sever the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death is the bodhi of a bodhisattva. [The third pair:
Regarding the preceding section on one's own practice, there were three instances; regarding the subsequent section on transforming others, there were also three. Now, this is the pair.

Regarding the practice of benefiting oneself and others, there are also three parts: first, the teaching on the Dharma; second, the teaching by way of analogy; and third, the application of the analogy.
Here, the first—the teaching on the Dharma—states that "the bodhi of a bodhisattva is for the sake of severing old age, sickness, and death.

This clarifies that one severs the afflictions of the mind and the old age and death of the body within oneself, and is further able to sever the afflictions of the mind and the old age and death of the body in others.
Because they are able to sever [defilements] within themselves and cause others to sever them as well, it is called the Bodhi of a Bodhisattva.

Question: The followers of the Two Vehicles are also able to sever old age, sickness, and death; should this not also be called Bodhi? Answer: It is explained that the followers of the Two Vehicles are only able to sever [defilements] for themselves and cannot sever them for others;
therefore, it is not Bodhi. Because Bodhisattvas sever [defilements] for themselves and cause others to sever them as well, it is called Bodhi. Question: If a Bodhisattva...
Question: One should sever the afflictions such as the three poisons; why then is it said that one severs the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death?
Answer: This is a case of explaining the effect by means of the cause; it clarifies that because the cause is absent, the effect is likewise absent.

Furthermore, old age, sickness, and death are themselves the three poisons. Why? Because greed is old age, hatred is sickness, and delusion is death. Therefore, by severing the three poisons, one severs old age.
If one dies without being thus, the merit one has cultivated is of no benefit because it lacks wisdom. One who cannot sever [defilements] for oneself is of no benefit;
one who cannot sever them for others lacks wisdom. One who can sever them for oneself possesses benefit; one who can sever them for others possesses wisdom.
Therefore, it is said that if one is not thus, the merit one has cultivated is of no benefit because it lacks wisdom. This is an analogy.
Regarding the second analogy, which states that one can only be called brave after having conquered one's enemies:
this clarifies that one can only be considered brave when capable of eliminating the two types of enmity—both within oneself and toward others.

Just as a person in the world is deemed strong and brave for being able to defeat external adversaries, so too is it with the Bodhisattva; having shattered all afflictions within themselves, they are further able to destroy those of others.
It is called "Powerful and Courageous" because it is like a brave man who leads the elderly and the weak across all perilous difficulties;
such is the description of a Bodhisattva who simultaneously eliminates old age, sickness, and death. Third, the combined analogy:
because he not only eliminates his own old age, sickness, and death, but is also able to eliminate those of others, it is said that he "simultaneously eliminates" them.
That sick bodhisattva should further form this thought: "Just as my own illness is neither real nor existent, so too the illnesses of all sentient beings are neither real nor existent.
That sick bodhisattva should further form this thought. [This concludes] the second major section within the chapter on Subduing.

Regarding the clarification of the gains and losses of self-cultivation and transforming others: above, it was only clarified that there is self-cultivation and transforming others; however, within self-cultivation and transforming others, there are further cases of gain and loss.
There is gain when there is skillful means, and loss when there is no skillful means.

Because of this point, the second section clarifies the gains and losses of self-cultivation and transforming others, which also serves to distinguish the meaning of self-cultivation and transforming others from what preceded.
In this regard, there are also three [sections]: first, clarifying the gains and losses of one's own practice; second, clarifying the gains and losses of transforming others;
and third, clarifying the gains and losses of both one's own practice and transforming others. These also serve to establish the preceding [three]. Why is this?
First, clarifying the gains and losses of one's own practice establishes the first [point], one's own practice; second, clarifying the gains and losses of transforming others establishes...

The previous second [section] was the transformation of the third, which was the fulfillment of the first; now, this is the first [section], clarifying that one's own practice (*svayam-caryā*) alone attains only what is faultless.
The second [section] concerns others, and the third concerns both attainment and loss. Now, regarding the first [section] on one's own practice, it should logically involve both attainment and loss;
however, the fact that only attainment is clarified while loss is not is simply because they are mutually inclusive. Thus it is for the Bodhisattva.
"You should reflect that my illness is neither real nor existent, and that the illnesses of all sentient beings are likewise neither real nor existent.

This is the correct teaching for a bodhisattva who has first set out on the path; as you have realized that your own illness is neither real nor existent, you should also know that the illnesses of all sentient beings are neither real nor existent.
Question: What is the difference between "not real" (*amṛṣā*) and "not existent" (*abhūta*)? How should this be explained?
To say that there is something different, something not different, or something neither different nor not different is merely this sickness; it does not truly exist.
To speak of "difference" is neither true nor real existence; it is neither non-existence nor provisional existence.

To know that this sickness is neither real existence nor provisional existence—if one were to say that the sickness is not real existence but is provisional existence, that would still be a bondage. Why? Because they are the same.
Since both this [bodhisattva’s] condition and that [of sentient beings] are illnesses, it is now clarified that this illness is neither substantially existent nor nominally existent.

Question: If the bodhisattva’s illness is neither substantial nor nominal, and the illnesses of sentient beings are likewise neither substantial nor nominal, what further difference is there between sentient beings and the bodhisattva?
Answer: Between the bodhisattva and sentient beings, in the ultimate sense, what further difference could there be?
Therefore, there is the principle of a single source within one family; this is the principle that Buddhas and sentient beings share a common origin.
From where does this single source emerge? Guanzhong says: "Heaven and earth share the same root as I; all things are of one body with me.
Herein, too, it is that Bodhisattvas and sentient beings are identical—neither true nor existent.
When practicing this contemplation, if one gives rise to a great compassion based on attachment or views toward sentient beings, one should immediately abandon it. Why is this?

Because a bodhisattva eliminates adventitious afflictions to give rise to great compassion; however, one who possesses compassion based on attachment or views will have a mind of weariness and exhaustion regarding birth and death.
If one can remain free from this, there will be no weariness or exhaustion, and in whatever place one is born, [one will not be stained].
They are shrouded by craving and views. One who is born without bonds is able to preach the Dharma for sentient beings to untie their bonds, as the Buddha has taught.
It is impossible that one who is themselves bound could untie the bonds of others;
it is possible that one who is themselves without bonds can untie the bonds of others. Therefore, a bodhisattva should not give rise to bonds. What is meant by "bonds"? What is meant by...?
To be attached to the flavor of meditative absorption is the bondage of a bodhisattva; to be born through skillful means is the liberation of a bodhisattva.
When making this observation, the second section follows, which clarifies the gains and losses regarding the transformation of others.
This section is divided into two parts: first, the simultaneous presentation of gain and loss; second, the explanation of gain and loss. Now, the first part clarifies the loss of the bodhisattva.
When one performs this contemplation, to give rise to "compassion based on affection and views" toward sentient beings is precisely what constitutes an error. Question:
Previously it was stated that a bodhisattva knows their own illness to be neither real nor existent, and knows the illnesses of sentient beings to likewise be neither real nor existent;
having realized that both are ultimately empty and non-existent, why now does one give rise to "compassion based on affection and views"?

The commentary explains: What is the meaning of "being bound"? It clarifies that although the Bodhisattva knows for himself that both sentient beings and the Bodhisattva are neither real nor existent, he nevertheless conceives of sentient beings as being truly real and exerts effort toward them. This very understanding is precisely what constitutes the Bodhisattva’s "great compassion of attachment and views. Why?
Because while he claims to have realized that sentient beings and himself are non-existent, he nonetheless regards [them as existing].
Sentient beings cannot know that which is non-existent, yet they claim it exists; whereas Bodhisattvas can fully understand this.

While sentient beings cannot comprehend what is to be saved, Bodhisattvas can save them. To perceive sentient beings and to perceive great compassion for sentient beings—because these constitute the two types of attachment and views—it is said that "great compassion born of attachment and views" is called a failure. This is precisely what should be [avoided].
To abandon this is precisely to attain; if one acts according to what has been seen above, it is precisely a loss.
Since abandoning this understanding is itself attainment, it is said that "one should immediately abandon it. Why is this so? The second part below explains gain and loss.
Having clarified gain and loss here, the text next cites bondage and liberation to provide an explanation. Now, first explaining loss: if one sees...

If there is a bodhisattva who regards those who can deliver sentient beings as the "deliverers" and those who are delivered as the "delivered," this constitutes a great compassion born of attachment and views (*sneha-dṛṣṭi-mahākaruṇā*).
If one possesses such a great compassion born of attachment and views, one will experience weariness and exhaustion within saṃsāra, as clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Such a bodhisattva who clings to objective attainment (*upalambha*) thinks, "Saṃsāra is long and sentient beings are many; when will they ever be delivered? and consequently regresses from the bodhisattva path.
As for the practice, it was like that of the Bodhisattva Śāriputra: when a person came to beg for his eyes, he gave them immediately.
Once the Brahmin had obtained the eyes and stepped on them, Śāriputra withdrew and returned. Those of the Two Vehicles likewise all possess the view of a sentient being;
because they perceive birth and death, they harbor fear and revulsion toward birth and death. Therefore, those whose compassion arises from craving and views are [limited] regarding birth.
There is a mind of weariness regarding death; if one can depart from this, there will be no weariness, and one will attain discernment.
One does not see the Bodhisattva as either the one who delivers sentient beings or the sentient beings being delivered, for delivering sentient beings is like delivering empty space.
Thus, the "Chapter on Dream Vows" says: "The Bodhisattva establishes the vow to deliver sentient beings, yet the nature of sentient beings is like empty space."
If emptiness and space cannot be exhausted, then the Bodhisattva’s deliverance of sentient beings likewise cannot be exhausted.

Although they deliver sentient beings, it is like delivering space—there is nothing delivered; yet this delivery is like the *Vajra-prajñā*, which universally delivers all while there is nothing delivered.
Therefore it is said: "If one can remain free from this [delusion], there will be no weariness," as found in the sixth [chapter].
The Way does not bind one through attachment and views, but is able to liberate one from bondage. Next, citing the Buddha’s words, he exhorts the abandonment of what is lost, as in the text:
"What is called bondage? What is called liberation? He then explains bondage and liberation: "Attachment to the flavor of dhyāna is the bondage of a bodhisattva.
This refers to the fact that while the flavor of dhyāna is a bondage for the two vehicles, it is precisely this that constitutes being bound by dhyāna for a bodhisattva. Why is this so?

Seeing both stillness (*śamatha*) and distraction (*vikṣepa*), one abandons distraction and takes up stillness. Since stillness is fundamentally distracted and distraction is already non-existent, one should abandon even stillness;
yet, if one now abandons distraction while clinging to stillness, one is bound by stillness. Thus, craving the flavor of meditative absorption (*dhyāna-rasa*) is a bondage for the bodhisattva.
To "arise through skillful means" is to explain and resolve that which arises through skillful means: it is to fundamentally use stillness to rest from distraction.
To disperse the breath, to still the fatigue, and to neither cling to stillness nor cling to dispersion is liberation.
○ Furthermore, regarding the section on "Gain and Loss" concerning "Wisdom Bound by Lack of Skillful Means," there are three sections;

having already covered two, this is now the third, which clarifies simultaneously the gain and loss of self-cultivation and the transformation of others. This is further divided into two parts, the first of which is general.
Regarding the second section, which clarifies gain and loss with respect to the two types of wisdom, there are three parts:
first, the dual presentation of the two chapters on gain and loss; second, the dual explanation of gain and loss;
and third, the conclusion and exhortation. This current section is the first: the dual presentation of the gain and loss of the two wisdoms. Now, as for the names of these two wisdoms:

These are not the same: one is the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*) and the other is the wisdom of reality (*tattva-jñāna*). Both of these appear in the *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (Renwang jing), which states:

"The merit of the wisdom of skillful means and the merit of the wisdom of reality. Furthermore, the treatise distinguishes two kinds of *prajñā*: first, the path of *prajñā*, and second, the path of skillful means.
The *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin) says: "The wisdom of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), the wisdom of the aspects of the path (*mārgākāra-jñāna*), all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), and..."
Terms such as "all-encompassing wisdom" (*sarvajñatā*) are all of one category. Now, in this context, it simply says "expedient means and wisdom," which are the names for these two types of wisdom.
As Master Zhao said: "In unifying all practices, provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) is taken as primary;
'provisional' refers to provisional wisdom, and 'wisdom' refers to ultimate wisdom (*jñāna*). It is the same here: "expedient means" is expedient wisdom, and "wisdom" is ultimate wisdom.
The Master Huiran asked: "Why did Master Zhaolun say this? [The respondent] said: "Since he annotated this sutra and saw that its textual phrasing was skillful and concise, he held this view.
Question: Based on what dharmas does this section judge the two types of wisdom? Explanation:

Herein, correctly illuminating the conditioned for the sake of transforming others is the provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), while contemplating emptiness for one's own cultivation is the true wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*).

However, Master Kumārajīva’s commentary explains: "Illuminating emptiness without clinging to it is called 'expedient wisdom' (*upāya-prajñā*); directly illuminating emptiness without clinging to existence is called 'real wisdom' (*bhūta-prajñā*.
When asked where this interpretation originates, Master Kumārajīva replied: "It appears in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, in the chapter on 'Non-Realization' (*Aprativedha-parivarta*).
It uses the analogies of a bird with wings and a skilled archer to illustrate how a bodhisattva studies emptiness without realizing [nirvāṇa] prematurely, just as a bird flies through the air."
Just as one who is skilled at archery does not let the arrow rest in empty space, so it is here: the subsequent arrow shoots the preceding arrow, yet the preceding arrow does not fall.

Likewise, the wisdom of skillful means shoots the wisdom of reality; the wisdom of reality does not fall to the level of the two vehicles. That master sets forth this meaning to explain [the point], yet another immediately raises an objection:
"If you observe emptiness without attachment and illuminate existence without obstruction as the time of skillful means, then it should also follow that..."

If directly illuminating conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) is true wisdom, then now, while directly illuminating emptiness as real, one should likewise directly illuminate conditioned phenomena as skillful means (*upāya*).
Since you have already observed that being unattached to existence is skillful means, you should likewise observe that not realizing emptiness is true wisdom.
The commentary explains: Why must we judge both types of wisdom by applying this same principle in all its various aspects? Although the Master Kumārajīva’s interpretation is as follows...
To say that there is a difficulty while intending it to be excellent is like merely using "emptiness" and "existence" to distinguish between the two types of wisdom;

although this lacks difficulty, it is not excellent in intent. For now, following what Master Kumārajīva has clarified, we take the non-attachment to emptiness and the unimpeded illumination of existence as the skillful means, and direct contemplation of emptiness as the reality.

Furthermore, wisdom without skillful means is bondage, while wisdom with skillful means is liberation; likewise, skillful means without wisdom is bondage, while skillful means with wisdom is liberation.
Now, regarding this first heading, there are four propositions forming two pairs; the first clarifies the attainment and loss of actual wisdom.
Next, the gains and losses regarding skillful means (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are explained. Now, first, the gains and losses regarding true wisdom (*bhūtaprajñā*) are clarified:

when there is no skillful means, wisdom is bound; this refers to the loss of true wisdom. Because true wisdom lacks skillful means, true wisdom itself becomes a bondage. Why is this? This emptiness is [the emptiness of] existence;
since there is no existence to support this emptiness, this emptiness does not constitute emptiness. Therefore, it is said: [it is not true emptiness].
Wisdom without skillful means is bondage; wisdom with skillful means is liberation. This clarifies that through the attainment of true wisdom, one acquires these skillful means.
Since true wisdom exists for the sake of attainment, and since there is the emptiness of having resources, emptiness itself becomes empty.
Therefore, wisdom with skillful means is liberation. One can understand the attainment and loss of wisdom with skillful means from this.

What is called "the bondage of wisdom lacking skillful means"? It refers to a bodhisattva who, with a mind of attachment and views, adorns buddha-fields and brings sentient beings to maturity, yet seeks to discipline himself within the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; this is called the bondage of wisdom lacking skillful means.

What is called "the liberation of wisdom accompanied by skillful means"? It refers to not adorning buddha-fields or bringing sentient beings to maturity with a mind of attachment and views... [and so forth].

To discipline oneself within the states of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness regarding sentient beings, without becoming weary or disheartened, is called "liberation through wisdom accompanied by skillful means.
What is meant by "bondage through wisdom lacking skillful means"? This concludes the second pair of explanations concerning the gains and losses of these two types of wisdom.
First, the explanation of the gains and losses regarding ultimate wisdom; second, the explanation of the gains and losses regarding skillful means wisdom.

The first explanation of the gains and losses regarding ultimate wisdom is based on profound practice; the subsequent explanation of the gains and losses regarding skillful means is based on shallow practice.

Since both apply to the ultimate, and as the explanation of skillful means already applies to the profound, it should likewise apply to the shallow; and since the explanation of ultimate wisdom already applies to the profound, it should also apply to the shallow.
Now, while actual wisdom (*bhūtaprajñā*) relies upon profound skillful means (*upāya*), this text merely interchanges the descriptions for the sake of those at a shallow level.

Although each of the two chapters contains both gains and losses, and although these two sections should properly be combined into two chapters within the treatise, we shall now proceed with the first chapter to clarify the gains and losses of actual wisdom;
what was previously explained was the loss of actual wisdom. The question asks: "How does a Bodhisattva purify the Buddha-land?"
Regarding sentient beings who discipline themselves within emptiness and signlessness, what constitutes a failure? The explanation says: this itself is the failure. Why?
Because this bodhisattva is skillful regarding emptiness and unimpeded therein, yet unskilled regarding existence and unable to remain unmoved by it.
This bodhisattva contemplates emptiness without becoming attached to emptiness; thus, emptiness does not obstruct them, and they emerge from emptiness to accomplish the cultivation of the multitudes.

To be born in a pure Buddha-land while being unable to see it as unimpeded, seeing instead that there is a land to be adorned and people to be saved, constitutes a state of "attainment" (*upalambha*);
therefore, it is considered a failure. Question: To what stage of practice does this person belong? Answer:

According to the tradition inherited from Guanzhong, this refers to those who have just begun their practice (*ādikarmika*) at the sixth stage (*bhūmi*) or below, and who have not yet entered into emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
To be attached to emptiness while being obstructed by phenomena is a failure, for it cannot be without obstruction. What is meant by "liberation through skillful means and wisdom"?
The second explanation states that through true wisdom, this bodhisattva is unobstructed regarding emptiness and immovable regarding existence.
Ultimate emptiness does not obstruct existence, and existence does not obstruct ultimate emptiness; thus, although they adorn the lands, there is no land to be adorned.
Although one delivers sentient beings, there are no sentient beings to be delivered; therefore, this [realization] is attained. This refers to the Bodhisattva of the Seventh Ground.

As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "In the stage of equal concentration and wisdom, one is able to contemplate both emptiness and existence simultaneously. Contemplating emptiness does not obstruct existence, and contemplating existence does not obstruct emptiness;
therefore, there is the liberation of skillful means and wisdom."

What is called "bondage through lack of wisdom and skillful means"? It refers to a bodhisattva who, while abiding in various afflictions such as desire, hatred, and wrong views, plants the roots of all virtues;
this is called bondage through lack of wisdom and skillful means. What is called "liberation through wisdom and skillful means"?
It refers to one who, having abandoned various afflictions such as desire, hatred, and wrong views, plants the roots of all virtues and dedicates them [toward enlightenment].
To be directed toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is called "liberation through wisdom and skillful means.
What is meant by "bondage through lack of wisdom and skillful means"? Second, the gain and loss of skillful means and wisdom are now explained;
this first section clarifies the loss of skillful means and wisdom. This refers to those of shallow practice who are unable to contemplate emptiness and thus remain [attached].
Question: It is a loss to practice various spiritual practices while harboring afflictions; therefore, it is a failure.

Previously, it was stated that the loss regarding true wisdom (*prajñā*) consists in being skillful at emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and unimpeded, yet clumsy regarding existence (*bhava*) and immovability (*akopya*). Now, regarding the loss of expedient wisdom (*upāya-prajñā*), one should likewise be skillful regarding existence and unimpeded, yet clumsy regarding emptiness and immovability.
How is this to be understood? Answer: One cannot be skillful at emptiness and unimpeded while being clumsy regarding existence.
Movement is skillful regarding existence but clumsy regarding emptiness; non-movement is the opposite. Why? Because emptiness is easy while existence is difficult;

it is easy to understand existence at first but difficult to understand emptiness, whereas it is easy to understand emptiness but difficult to understand existence—this is because of the reversal between what is understood and what is not.

Furthermore, since previously one could neither adorn the lands nor bring sentient beings to maturity, the present statement that one "plants the roots of all virtues" clarifies that one now purifies the Pure Land and delivers sentient beings.

Those who have been born here are practitioners of profound conduct, whereas those of shallow practice cannot even accomplish the merit of various deeds; how much less could they cultivate profound conduct?
For this reason, it is said directly that they "plant the roots of all virtues. What is meant by "the liberation of wisdom through skillful means"?
The second explanation is that while one attains skillful means and wisdom, although one contemplates all phenomena as ultimately empty, one does not...

Question: Because it obstructs the cultivation of the myriad practices, it is called "attainment" (*prāpti*). What is the difference between the loss of true wisdom (*prajñā*) and the loss of skillful means (*upāya*), both being losses?
And what is the difference between the attainment of true wisdom and the attainment of skillful means, both being attainments? Answer: Regarding the difference between the two losses:
the loss of true wisdom is profound, while the loss of skillful means is shallow. As for the attainment of both wisdoms, they are equal; that is, they are attained in common.
This is because of the two kinds of wisdom.
Mañjuśrī, a sick bodhisattva should contemplate all dharmas in this manner.
Mañjuśrī, one should contemplate in this way; this is the third contemplation on the knots.
Furthermore, to contemplate that the body is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self is called wisdom;
yet, although the body is ill, to remain constantly within the cycle of birth and death to benefit all beings without weariness is called skillful means.

Furthermore, to contemplate that the body is not separate from illness and illness is not separate from the body—that this illness and this body are neither new nor old—is called wisdom. Even if the body...
To have an illness without it being eternally extinguished is called skillful means (*upāya*).

Furthermore, observing the body as impermanent constitutes the second section, which specifically clarifies the gains and losses of the two types of wisdom. Herein, the distinction between these two wisdoms differs from what preceded:
this [wisdom] takes the observation of the body as impermanent and so forth as "real wisdom" (*bhūtaprajñā*), while manifesting the body as having an illness is the "skillful means."
Furthermore, as the text states, one contemplates the body: the body is not separate from illness, and illness is not separate from the body. This establishes two types of wisdom:

contemplating that the body is not separate from illness and that illness is not separate from the body is designated as "real wisdom" (*bhūtaprajñā*); not extinguishing the body is designated as "expedient wisdom" (*upāyaprajñā*).
To say that the body is not separate from illness and illness is not separate from the body clarifies that where there is a body, there is illness; where there is illness, there is a body.
The body is illness; because the body is ill, the body does not depart from illness. Because the body is ill, illness does not depart from the body.
That "this is illness" and "this is the body" are neither new nor old means that the body is considered old and illness is considered new.
Now it is clarified that since the body is ultimately unobtainable, it is not old; and since illness is ultimately unobtainable, it is not new. Therefore, they are neither [old nor new].
Since the new is not inherently diseased and the old is not inherently the body, it is said that this disease and this body are neither new nor old.

Even if the body were to have a disease, it would not perish eternally; for those of the Two Vehicles, being afflicted by the body, they extinguish the body immediately, but the Bodhisattva is not like this—so long as sentient beings have not yet perfected the Buddha-dharma, the Bodhisattva will never perish eternally.
Mañjuśrī, a sick bodhisattva should thus discipline his mind, neither dwelling within it nor dwelling in a mind that is undisciplined.
Why is this? If one dwells in an undisciplined mind, that is the way of fools;
if one dwells in a disciplined mind, that is the way of the śrāvakas. Therefore, a bodhisattva should not dwell in discipline.
The bodhisattva practice is that which does not tame the mind yet remains free from these two dharmas;

it is the bodhisattva practice that dwells within birth and death without being defiled by conduct, yet abides in nirvāṇa without entering final extinction. It is the bodhisattva practice that is neither the practice of ordinary worldlings nor the practice of noble sages;
it is the bodhisattva practice that is neither a defiled practice nor a pure practice. Although it transcends the practices of Māra, it manifests them.
To subdue all māras is the bodhisattva practice; to seek omniscience without seeking it at an improper time is the bodhisattva practice;
to contemplate that all phenomena are unarisen yet not enter the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*) is the bodhisattva practice;

to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination yet enter among those with false views is the bodhisattva practice; and to gather in all sentient beings without attachment is the bodhisattva practice.
This is the bodhisattva practice: though delighting in seclusion, not relying on the exhaustion of body and mind;
this is the bodhisattva practice: though traversing the three realms, not destroying the dharma-nature; this is the bodhisattva practice: though practicing emptiness, planting all roots of virtue;
this is the bodhisattva practice: though practicing signlessness, liberating sentient beings; this is the bodhisattva practice: though practicing wishlessness.
To manifest the reception of a physical body is the bodhisattva practice; to engage in all wholesome deeds while practicing non-arising is the bodhisattva practice;
to practice the six *pāramitās* while thoroughly knowing the minds and mental factors of sentient beings is the bodhisattva practice;

to practice the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) without exhausting the outflows (*āsrava*) is the bodhisattva practice; and to practice the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) while... [is the bodhisattva practice].

To be born in the Brahma world without being attached to it is the bodhisattva practice; to practice dhyāna, liberation, and samādhi without being reborn according to those meditative states is the bodhisattva practice;
to practice the four foundations of mindfulness without ultimately and permanently abandoning body, sensation, mind, and phenomena is the bodhisattva practice;
and to practice the four right efforts without relinquishing physical and mental diligence is the bodhisattva practice.
To practice the four bases of psychic power while attaining mastery over the supernormal faculties is the bodhisattva practice;
to practice the five faculties while discerning the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of sentient beings is the bodhisattva practice;

to practice the five powers while joyfully seeking the ten powers of a Buddha is the bodhisattva practice; and to practice the seven factors of enlightenment while discerning the wisdom of a Buddha is the bodhisattva practice.
Wisdom is the bodhisattva practice: although practicing the Eightfold Noble Path, one delights in practicing the immeasurable path of the Buddhas; this is the bodhisattva practice.
Although practicing the methods of the aids to the path—calm abiding and insight—one does not ultimately fall into cessation; this is the bodhisattva practice.
Although practicing that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing, one adorns the body with the primary and secondary marks; this is the bodhisattva practice.
To manifest the deportment of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas while not abandoning the Buddha-dharma is the bodhisattva practice;
to accord with the ultimately pure characteristics of all phenomena while manifesting a body according to what is appropriate for beings is the bodhisattva practice;
and to contemplate all buddha-fields as eternally quiescent like space while manifesting various kinds of pure buddha-fields is the bodhisattva practice.
To practice such that, although one attains the Buddha-way, turns the wheel of Dharma, and enters nirvana, one does not abandon the path of a bodhisattva—this is the bodhisattva practice.
Mañjuśrī, a sick bodhisattva should discipline themselves in this way. [End of] the second major section: A Sequential Exposition.
Regarding the section on "Subduing through the Illumination of Dharma," which arises from the chapter on Subduing, there are three stages of discourse in total.
First, one uses the three types of emptiness to subdue oneself: (1) subduing the self so that the view of self ceases; (2) subduing dharmas so that the view of dharmas ceases;
and (3) subduing emptiness so that the view of emptiness ceases. Having thus employed these three methods for self-subdual...
Subduing is also accomplished through three dharmas; having attained awakening by means of these three dharmas oneself, one then causes sentient beings to likewise awaken to what one has realized.
In this regard, how does this differ from the Two Vehicles? It is because those of the Two Vehicles are only able to subdue themselves and cannot subdue others.
Why is it that those of the Two Vehicles—who have themselves been subdued—are unable to subdue others?

The Bodhisattva is not like that; he is able to discipline himself and can also cause others to be disciplined. Next, regarding the second section on the meaning of how the Bodhisattva can discipline himself and also discipline others: if one asks how it is that a Bodhisattva can discipline himself, there are sentient beings who are to be disciplined and there are Bodhisattvas who can deliver those sentient beings.
Since what is delivered is not [the self], to make it even clearer: there is a Bodhi... [text fragment].

If there were sentient beings to be disciplined by the Bodhisattva himself, or if there were Bodhisattvas capable of delivering sentient beings who were to be delivered, then the Bodhisattva would immediately fall into the state of "having something to be attained.
This Great Compassion, being inverted by attachment and views, would instead be disciplined by others; how then could he discipline others?
If one can abide in non-attainment—where there is no Bodhisattva capable of self-discipline and no sentient beings to be disciplined—then [true discipline occurs]. Although...
When one is self-disciplined, there is no "self" to be disciplined; when disciplining others, there is no "other" to be disciplined.
Ultimately, because there is nothing that exists and nothing to be attained, this is called discipline. Thirdly, it is clarified:
if there were a bodhisattva who could discipline sentient beings such that the disciplined object became something attained, this would not be true subduing. If one can be without sentient beings...
Those who are to be tamed by birth cannot be tamed by a bodhisattva; for the tamer and the tamed are non-dual—this is what constitutes true subduing.
For this reason, it is further rolled up: it is not that there is something to be attained, nor is there a taming, nor is there a lack of attainment.
The tamer has never tamed, nor has there been no taming; it is neither taming nor non-taming. Therefore, the words state that one does not dwell in a mind of subduing, nor does one...
This refers to dwelling in an untamed mind. Nevertheless, these three modes of taming exist solely because sentient beings possess these three types [of afflictions];
thus, there are these three tamings. For example, to tame a horse, one requires a halter and a tether;
once the horse is tamed, the halter and tether are no longer required. It is the same here as well. Why is this so? [The text] explains: if...
To abide in non-subduing is the way of the fool; to abide in subduing is the way of the Śrāvaka-dharma.
Now, the Bodhisattva is neither of these two, for he is not an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) and thus does not abide in non-subduing, nor is he a Śrāvaka and thus does not abide in subduing.
To be free from these two dharmas is the dharma of a Bodhisattva. Even while remaining within saṃsāra, he is not defiled by its activities.

That is, they simultaneously abandon both and simultaneously employ both; those of the Two Vehicles thus realize a partial [attainment], abiding in what is not yet tamed while failing to abide in taming, and abiding in nirvana while not abiding in saṃsāra. Now, the Bodhisattva is not like this:
when abandoning, he abandons both; when employing, he employs both. Since he abides in nirvana, he does not abandon saṃsāra; though he abides in saṃsāra...
Though one dies, one’s conduct remains unstained; though one dwells in nirvāṇa, one does not undergo eternal extinction;
though one dwells in saṃsāra, there is in reality no saṃsāra to dwell in; though one abides in nirvāṇa, there is in reality no nirvāṇa to abide in. Therefore it is said:
"To be in saṃsāra without being stained by conduct, and to abide in nirvāṇa without undergoing eternal extinction. This is neither the conduct of ordinary beings nor the conduct of sages.
This clarifies that the preceding section on the dual abandonment is concluded. Now, for what reason does this passage appear? The commentary explains:

although the previous section abandoned the three dharmas, this current passage exists because it abandons both persons and dharmas; since "person" and "dharma" are distinct, this present text is provided.
Although one may have transcended the practices of Māra, herein there are four propositions: first, the dual abandonment and dual application; second, the dual abandonment and single application.
Third is abandoning one while employing both; fourth is abandoning one while employing one. "Not abiding in the disciplined" and "not abiding in the undisciplined" constitute abandoning both;
"abiding in saṃsāra" and "abiding in nirvāṇa" constitute employing both. Now, what follows below concerns abandoning one while employing one.
Although he contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination, he enters into various heterodox views. [Question: Why?
To contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination is right contemplation; why then speak of "entering"? The explanation says:

it is the clear realization that the correct does not obstruct the provisional, and the provisional does not obstruct the correct. Since there is thus no obstruction, the person possesses the dharma of non-obstruction.
Although they encompass all sentient beings, they do not harbor attachment. This clarifies that although the Bodhisattva feels compassion for sentient beings, their own bodies may even shed blood.
Because there is truly nothing to pity, it is said that although one gathers in all sentient beings, one does not harbor attachment to them;
and although one delights in seclusion, one does not rely on the exhaustion of body and mind. This clarifies that there are two kinds of seclusion:
first, minor seclusion, and second, major seclusion. There are also two kinds of "hiding" for laypeople: namely, minor hiding, which is hiding in mountain forests, and major hiding.
The concealment of the Buddha-dharma also has two aspects: concealing it within the marketplace is the "lesser concealment," while concealing it within mountain forests is the "greater concealment.

This is because the former involves the agitation of this body and mind, whereas the latter involves the extinction of this body and mind. The Bodhisattva transcends both of these: although they delight in seclusion, it is not the lesser concealment;

yet, though they do not rely on the exhaustion of body and mind, this is not [mere] concealment either. Thus, even while acting within the three realms, they do not destroy the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
This clarifies that although one dwells within the triple world, one remains unmoved; the rest of the text may be sought elsewhere.
When these words were spoken, among the great assembly led by Mañjuśrī, eight thousand devaputras all resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having spoken these words, the third section concludes; this is the benefit following the illness, which is the subsequent skillful means.

The Sixth Chapter: The Inconceivable.
The Sixth Chapter: The Inconceivable. In the second meeting at the square chamber, two chapters are extensively opened.

First, the brief clarification of the two wisdoms is completed; now follows the second, the extensive clarification of the two wisdoms, which consists of five sections. This is now the first [section].

Regarding the "Chapter on the One Inconceivable": If one asks why this sutra is titled the *Acintya-sūtra* (Inconceivable Sutra), and why every chapter is designated as the "Chapter on the Inconceivable," the answer is as follows:

If it were the case that only this chapter is named the "Chapter on the Inconceivable" while the others are not, then it would follow that only this chapter is the *Acintya-sūtra* and the rest are not. [But this is not the case. Therefore, the title applies universally.
The *Yijing* (Discourse on the Discussion) further raises the objection: "This Dharma is inconceivable (*acintya*), and this person is Vimalakīrti.
If one does not understand it in this way, then how can it be difficult? If this Dharma is inconceivable, then while the Dharma permeates a single sutra, there is a chapter titled "Inconceivable";
likewise, since this person is Vimalakīrti, he too should have a chapter titled "Vimalakīrti" throughout the entire sutra. Yet, this person [Vimalakīrti] does not [appear as such].
Regarding the "Chapter on the Distinctive Vimalakīrti" (Bie Weimo Pin): this inconceivable dharma has no distinction; the "Chapter on the Inconceivable" (Bu Siyi Pin) follows next.
As for the "Chapter on the Difficulties of Vimalakīrti" (Nan Weimo Pin), these are solely the penetrations (tong) and lack distinctions (bie).

This would mean that while this inconceivable dharma is only distinct and should have no penetration, there is a distinction that cannot be without penetration, and there is a penetration that cannot be without distinction. This is the meaning.

The term "inconceivable" (*acintya*) applies throughout this chapter.
While it is explained that "inconceivable" refers to specific matters, this sutra is also generally titled "Inconceivable Liberation.
Furthermore, Master Sengzhao states: "Beginning from the Buddha-lands and ending with the nourishment of the Dharma, although the texts differ, they are all inconceivable."
Because it is one, it is a general [title]. Now, this chapter clarifies the specific "inconceivable" (acintya):
that within a room of only ten feet square there are thirty-two thousand lion thrones is precisely an inconceivable matter.
Why not generally title this sutra the *One Inconceivable Sutra* instead of the *One Inconceivable Chapter*? The explanation is that there are both general and specific [titles].
The general title of this scripture is the *Acintya-sūtra*, and the general title of its chapters is the "Inconceivable Chapter" (*Acintya-parivarta*).

Since there are currently no fourteen distinct chapters, and one now wishes to open up fourteen chapters with separate meanings for each, this chapter is universally titled the "Inconceivable Chapter.

Because a person is a single unity and lacks two distinct parts, it cannot serve as an analogy [for multiple chapters within a single title]. Furthermore, there is an objection that the name of this scripture should be the *Acintya-sūtra*.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Inconceivable" (*Acintya-parivarta*): The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is titled *Nirvāṇa*, and it should logically contain a "Chapter on Nirvāṇa.

However, the commentary explains that while this would apply as a general rule, it is not established here because the meaning of *nirvāṇa* has already been clearly elucidated; thus, there is no need to establish a separate "Chapter on Nirvāṇa.
Conversely, since the title of this scripture is *Acintya* (The Inconceivable) and its meaning has not yet been fully revealed, it is necessary to establish the "Chapter on the Inconceivable."
Next, as for the reason why this sutra is generally titled the *Acintya-sūtra* (The Inconceivable Sutra) yet contains a specific chapter titled the "Inconceivable Chapter":
it is intended to use the specific to permeate the general, so that through phenomena one may manifest the principle, and through traces one may manifest the source.

Regarding the phrase "using the specific to permeate the general," this chapter clarifies that the great can enter the small and the small can contain the great; this is the inconceivability of the Bodhisattva.
Regarding the deliberation on other matters: since this one matter is inconceivable, all matters are likewise inconceivable. Why is this?

Because within this chapter, the large and the small are mutually contained; it utterly transcends the sphere of ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles who grasp at attainments, and those of shallow practice.
As for all remaining matters—whether raising a foot or taking a step—they all transcend the sphere of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles who grasp at attainments.
The attainment [of Buddhahood] and the realm of shallow practice are both inconceivable. To speak of manifesting principle through the employment of phenomena:
this very mutual containment of the great and the small is itself an inconceivable matter.

Since the matter transcends the "attainments" of the Two Vehicles and their shallow practices, the principle likewise transcends such realms. As the matter is inconceivable, the principle is also inconceivable.
Since the traces [of the Buddha] are inconceivable, their source is likewise inconceivable; for this reason, this chapter is titled "The Chapter on the Inconceivable" (*Acintya-parivarta*).
Furthermore, because this chapter distinguishes the name "inconceivable," the subsequent text states:
"Bodhisattvas possess a liberation named 'inconceivable'. Thus, by distinguishing its essence, its name, and its functional activity, it is called "inconceivable."
Question: If this chapter is intended to permeate the entire sutra and is titled "The Inconceivable," why is it not explained at the very beginning rather than being clarified only here? Answer:
It is said that because one wishes to connect the preceding and following sections, it is clarified in this middle position. Furthermore, this sutra begins with the manifestation of illness.
Because of the manifestation of illness, there is this single sūtra; for this reason, the manifestation of illness was shown previously.

Because Mañjuśrī inquired on account of the manifestation of illness, the inconceivable matters of the sick person were revealed. Thus, following the inquiry regarding the illness, the inconceivable is elucidated.
Question: If this sutra arises from manifesting illness, why is it not called the *Pratyutpanna-vyādhi-sūtra* (Sutra on Manifest Illness)? Answer: It cannot be named the *Pratyutpanna-vyādhi-sūtra*.

The term "manifest illness" (*pratyutpanna-vyādhi*) is specific, whereas the term "inconceivable" (*acintya*) is universal. Why? Because all illnesses, including those of the Buddhas, are inconceivable;
manifest illness is merely one instance within that which is inconceivable. Therefore, it cannot be named the *Pratyutpanna-vyādhi-sūtra*.

The reason for connecting this to the "Chapter on Inquiring about Illness" (*Vyādhiparipṛcchā*) is that while the "Chapter on Inquiring about Illness" clarifies the single meaning within the immeasurable, what follows below clarifies the immeasurable within the single.
Regarding the "immeasurable within the single" above, it refers merely to the single skillful means regarding illness;

as for the "single within the immeasurable" clarified below, it is because he manifests bodies equal in number to sentient beings and teaches doctrines equal in number to sentient beings. Furthermore, the intention of the preceding [section] is...

The "Chapter on Inquiring after Illness" clarifies the fundamental intention of a bodhisattva in responding to conditions. Now, to clarify the bodhisattva’s original intention in responding to conditions:

there are two kinds of original intentions. First, the original [intention] of sentient beings; second, the original [intention] of the bodhisattva. The original [intention] of sentient beings is ignorance and craving;
the original [intention] of the bodhisattva is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Because of great compassion, the bodhisattva possesses both body and mind. Now, for the purpose of responding...
As for the conditions: since Great Compassion functions through this Great Compassion, what is its purpose? Great Compassion manifests all manner of skillful means for the sake of sentient beings;
it teaches and instructs sentient beings so that they may realize the essence [of reality], just as a Bodhisattva does.
For this reason, this chapter has come forth.
At that time, Śāriputra, seeing that there were no seats within this room, had this thought:
"Where shall these bodhisattvas and the great assembly of disciples sit? The elder Vimalakīrti, knowing his thoughts, said to Śāriputra:
"Venerable sir, have you come for the sake of the Dharma, or do you seek a seat?"

Within this chapter, the subject is broadly divided into two parts: first, the clarification of skillful means (*upāya*) and true wisdom (*prajñā*); second, the clarification of true [wisdom] and skillful means.
Furthermore, "skillful means and reality" refers to the trace and the source, while "true [wisdom] and skillful means" refers to the source and the trace.

Moreover, it is further divided such that the first part rebukes the seeking of a seat, while the second provides a seat; the present section corresponds to the first, which contains several rounds of question and answer.
Now, Śāriputra silently reflected while seated upon his mat, wondering: "Among those present, there are both bodhisattvas and śrāvakas;
for what reason do the śrāvakas think of their seats while the bodhisattvas do not? The explanation states that there is a reason for this.
There are two meanings as to why the bodhisattvas do not think of their seats: first, the bodhisattva takes the *dharmakāya* as his body, and such a body knows no fatigue.
Because of illness, one does not attend to the seat; furthermore, when a Bodhisattva hears the sublime Dharma, their spirit is refreshed and their mind is gladdened, so they do not attend to fatigue.
How is this known to be so? Even when worldly people hear music and the like, they still forget their fatigue;

how much more so for a Bodhisattva who hears this sublime Dharma—how could they possibly experience fatigue? Therefore, they do not attend to the seat. The followers of the Two Vehicles are the opposite.

Why is this? Although the mind of a śrāvaka is free from outflows (anāsrava), their body still possesses the karma of fetters (saṃyojana). Because they possess the karma of fetters, the body remains dependent [on conditions];

therefore, they do not attend to the seat. Second, even if a bodhisattva who has not yet attained the dharma-body (dharmakāya) possesses a body of karmic fetters, when this bodhisattva hears the Dharma and it enters their mind, they do not consciously perceive any affliction;
thus, they do not attend to the seat. Although a śrāvaka hears [the Dharma], [they do not experience it in this way].
The supreme Dharma does not enter the mind, as illustrated by the self-narrative of the Śrāvakas in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which states:
"I have heard that when the Tathāgata speaks of maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields, I feel no joy at all, but only contemplate emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
From this we know it does not enter the mind; because it does not enter the mind, the body becomes weary, and because of this weariness, one thinks of the couch.

Furthermore, the desire to disparage the Śrāvakas while not censuring the Bodhisattvas arises because of his silent contemplation (*tūṣṇīmbhāva*); it is precisely through this silent contemplation that he is able to disparage the Śrāvakas.
Regarding this silence, one asks: why does he not speak openly but instead contemplate in silence? The explanation is as follows:

this is a case where the two sages mutually illuminate one another through their seated meditation; their spiritual powers intersect, such that by the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the layman (Vimalakīrti), the empty room becomes manifest.

The son remained silent and did not speak out for two reasons. First, he was reflecting inwardly and thus did not manifest his words. Second, the discussion was based on the specific circumstances; because he was addressing the Śrāvakas, he did not speak out. Why?
Because the Dharma-body of a Bodhisattva is his body and is free from all afflictions and burdens, whereas the body of a Śrāvaka is subject to afflictions and burdens.
Since [the Buddha] did not manifest his words regarding the failure to see a seat, Śāriputra sat in silent contemplation. Furthermore, this is why Śāriputra reflected upon the seat.
These are all skillful means for opening the gates of the Way: Śāriputra provides the skillful means for the Path, while the householder provides the skillful means for the secular world.
The householder uses the empty room as his skillful means, and Śāriputra uses the thought of the couch as his skillful means.

Because the householder knew that Śāriputra was about to think of the couch, he left the room empty; because Śāriputra knew that the householder intended to borrow a seat, he thought of the couch. Thus it is asked.
Both [the Buddha and the disciples] employ skillful means; for what reason do they cause the śrāvakas to be mindful [of their faults] but not the bodhisattvas?
The explanation says: causing the śrāvakas to be mindful allows them to long attain a certain kind of status. What is this status? It is the long-standing ability to reprove śrāvakas.

If one were to cause the bodhisattvas to be mindful, they would immediately take their seats and would not be able to be reproved. Now, by causing the śrāvakas to be mindful, one causes the śrāvakas to be uplifted.
The Bodhisattvas will only then take their seats. Now, Śāriputra thought to himself: "Śāriputra is the leader of this assembly;
his body is weary and his mind is fatigued. Judging others by his own condition, he wonders where the great disciples among the Bodhisattvas should sit.
