The elder perceived his intention and immediately rebuked him: "You have come for the sake of the Dharma, not for the sake of a seat. Bring two mats!"
This is a question posed by Guan.
Śāriputra said, "I have come for the sake of the Dharma, not for the sake of a bed or seat.
Vimalakīrti replied, "Indeed, Śāriputra, one who seeks the Dharma does not covet even body or life, much less a bed or seat. One who seeks the Dharma has no form or sensation."

The seeking of perception, volitional formations, and consciousness is non-existent; the seeking of the realms and the sense bases is non-existent; the seeking of the desire, form, and formless realms is non-existent.
Śāriputra, one who seeks the Dharma does not cling to the seeking of the Buddha, does not cling to the seeking of the Dharma, and does not cling to the seeking of the Saṅgha.

One who seeks the Dharma has no seeking for the vision of suffering, no seeking for the abandonment of its origin, no seeking for the realization of its cessation, and no seeking for the cultivation of the path.

Why is this? Because there is no conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) regarding any phenomenon. To say, "I shall see suffering, abandon its origin, realize cessation, and cultivate the path," is conceptual proliferation;

it is not the seeking of the Dharma. Śāriputra, the name of the Dharma is "quiescence" (*śānti*). If one practices with arising and ceasing, one is seeking arising and ceasing, not seeking the Dharma.
The name of the Dharma is "stainlessness" (*anāsrava*). If one is stained by phenomena—even up to Nirvāṇa—it is not the seeking of the Dharma.
To be stained by attachment is not to seek the Dharma. The Dharma has no place for practice; if one practices within the Dharma, that is a place of practice and not the seeking of the Dharma.
The Dharma has no taking up or discarding; if one takes up or discards the Dharma, that is taking up and discarding and not the seeking of the Dharma.
The Dharma has no location; if one clings to a location, that is clinging to a location and not the seeking of the Dharma. The Dharma is called signless; if...

To seek according to the characteristics of consciousness is to seek characteristics, not the Dharma. The Dharma cannot be dwelled upon; if one dwells in the Dharma, this is dwelling in phenomena, not seeking the Dharma.
The Dharma cannot be seen, heard, sensed, or known; if one acts through seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, this is seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, not seeking the Dharma.
The Dharma is named the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); if one acts within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), this is seeking [the conditioned].
Conditioned phenomena are not the seeking of the Dharma. Therefore, Śāriputra, one who seeks the Dharma should have no seeking toward any phenomenon.
When these words were spoken, five hundred devaputras attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
Śāriputra replied, "I have come for the sake of the Dharma; it is not that there are no seats in the Āmrapālī Grove Monastery.
The reason I have come now is precisely for the sake of the Dharma. As for what you say regarding 'dying of oneself': suppose we were both here.
If one seeks the Dharma and does not seek a seat, one should contemplate the Dharma and not the seat. Since you contemplate the seat and do not contemplate the Dharma, you should be seeking a seat."
It is not that he does not seek the Dharma; yet, based on the text, you challenge him by saying, "Have you come here seeking the Dharma?"—this statement is again a dead end.
Why? Because if there were a Dharma to be sought, it would not be the seeking of the Dharma; this immediately breaks the logical sequence.

Now, as for those who seek the Dharma, there are two types of "putting aside the seat" mentioned previously: first, as stated before, they do not seek a seat; second, they [do so] for the sake of seeking [the Dharma].
Because it is the Dharma, he has come; for this reason, we now further refute his claim regarding the seeking of the Dharma.

One who seeks the Dharma does not seek it within the five aggregates (*skandha*), because it is clear that the five aggregates are ultimately unobtainable; therefore, one should not seek it in the five aggregates.

Since the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*) are likewise unobtainable, one should not seek it in the elements, bases, and so forth. It is not in the realm of desire or form... [the preceding line is crossed out].
The six realms now vertically exhaust the three worlds. Śāriputra, one who seeks the Dharma does not seek it by clinging to the Buddha;
this clarifies that the six realms of the world are not the seeking of the Dharma. Now it is clarified that even the supramundane Triple Gem is not the seeking of the Dharma.
Since the Triple Gem is ultimately unattainable, how could one cling to the seeking of the Buddha and so forth? As for the remaining text, it may be sought elsewhere.

When the Bodhisattva Ghoṣadatta spoke these words, five hundred people attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. Herein, the rebukes directed at Śāriputra are for the sake of the devas who have attained the Way;
the rebuke of the śrāvakas serves to transform them into bodhisattvas, encompassing both meanings. Furthermore, to issue such a rebuke is itself the mark of the non-attainment of the Jewel;
if there were any attainment or seeking, there would be a basis of reliance, and the mind’s eye would not be clear.
If purity is non-apprehension, this is precisely the awakening of the mind’s eye; because the mind is pure, it is said that one attains the purity of the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣur-viśuddhi*).
Regarding this term "purity of the Dharma-eye": both the Hīnayāna and the Mahāyāna possess the Dharma-eye.

In the Hīnayāna, the Dharma-eye refers to the vision of the Four Truths attained at the first fruit (*prathamaphala*), which is called the Dharma-eye. In the Mahāyāna, the Dharma-eye refers to the attainment of reality (*tattva*) at the first stage (*bhūmi*).

Because it is the dharma of non-arising (*anutpāda-dharma*), it is called the "purification of the Dharma-eye" (*dharma-cakṣur-viśuddhi*). This explanation of the Dharma-eye within the Great Vehicle was composed by Master Zao. Question:
What is the difference between the Dharma-eye mentioned here and the Dharma-eye among the five eyes? Answer:

The difference is that the Dharma-eye spoken of here is simply the Wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) seeing the dharmas of the Four Truths (*catur-ārya-satya*). When the Wisdom-eye opens, it is designated as the "Wisdom-eye. However, [in this context], it is called the "Dharma-eye."
Now, regarding what is called the "Dharma-eye" (*dharmacakṣus*): because it perceives the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, it is termed the Dharma-eye.

Among the five eyes, the Dharma-eye is that which the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) do not possess; it belongs only to the Bodhisattva, who clearly understands the spiritual capacities of those in the three vehicles and accordingly preaches the Dharma—therefore, it is called the Dharma-eye.
At that time, the elder Vimalakīrti asked Mañjuśrī, "O Benevolent One, you travel through immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya lands;
in which buddha-field is there a lion throne endowed with such excellent, sublime, and accomplished merits?"
At that time, the Elder Vimalakīrti asked: "Venerable sir, the first chapter, 'Opening the Lower Grade,' has concluded its explanation of skillful means and true wisdom.
Now, the second chapter explains true wisdom and skillful means. Why are these two types of wisdom explained?
The commentary states: The scriptural text is thus; now we explain according to the scripture. Furthermore, why does the scripture explain these two?
The *Huijie* (Exegesis on Wisdom) states: "This sutra takes the two types of wisdom as its central theme. The preceding chapter briefly clarifies these two knowledges;
from here on, the two knowledges will be explained in detail. For this reason, the previous section elucidated true wisdom (*shihui*), while this chapter elucidates expedient wisdom (*fangbianhui*).
Question: Why is true wisdom explained first and expedient wisdom explained later, rather than explaining expedient wisdom first?

Regarding the phrase "clarifying the wisdom of reality" (*jñāna-tattva*), the commentary states: since this [wisdom] has no fixed location, it was previously clarified as the wisdom of means (*upāya-jñāna*);
yet, having previously clarified the wisdom of reality and subsequently clarifying the wisdom of means, it is so because it follows conditions.

Previously, Śāriputra thought of his seat while seeking the Dharma; therefore, [the Buddha] first destroyed that mind of seeking the Dharma while attached to his seat, thereby clarifying [the wisdom of reality].
Ultimate non-seeking is true wisdom (*bhūtaprajñā*). Now, to clarify that such a small room can contain such a great seat is inclusive wisdom (*saṃgrahaprajñā*).

Furthermore, having previously clarified true wisdom, now, in clarifying inclusive wisdom, it is shown that both this great seat and this small room are the result of the non-reliant and all-pervading pure karma of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Now, in order to clarify the function that is non-reliant and unimpeded, I have previously refuted the mind that possesses reliance and obstruction.
If one refutes that which has attainment and obstruction, one then attains the dharma that is non-reliant and unimpeded;
for this reason, having thoroughly purified the mind that possesses attainment and obstruction through prior refutation, I am now able to clarify the dharma that is non-reliant and unimpeded.
Now, the first layman asks Mañjuśrī, "Where is there a fine, sublime, and foremost seat? I shall fetch it for you. He asks the host to prepare a seat and immediately has one prepared;
why then does he ask where there is a fine, high seat that he might fetch? The explanation is as follows: The reason for this is that... [text continues]... [Note:
The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on a dialogue regarding the nature of the "seat" (āsana) as a metaphor for the state of realization. [End of provided text]
To manifest the inconceivable supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of Vimalakīrti, Mañjuśrī was asked to select [the seat];
thus, it should be said that he "immediately took" it. Furthermore, there are two reasons why Mañjuśrī was questioned:
first, had Mañjuśrī not been asked, if the householder himself were to have prepared such a great seat, one might fear it was a magical creation by the householder rather than something real.

As for the two [points] mentioned above, it is likely that this refers to the most supreme seat within a single room or a single nation, rather than the foremost seat among the lands of the ten directions.
For this reason, he asked Mañjuśrī: "O Benevolent One, as you travel through the ten directions, where is there a foremost seat?
This was intended to test him. Mañjuśrī travels through the ten directions, and all bodhisattvas likewise travel therein.
In all Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as stated in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, Mañjuśrī is present in every place;

thus, Mañjuśrī travels everywhere throughout the ten directions. For this reason, he is questioned. Furthermore, it is not that Vimalakīrti has never traveled through the ten directions—he has—whereas Mañjuśrī does travel through them;
therefore, he is questioned. Now, the one who questions wishes to have Mañjuśrī choose for himself [the appropriate response].

Because he takes [the transformation] as his basis, he asks: "If it is real, how can it be a superior transformation? The explanation says: It is difficult to transform what is real, whereas that which is like an illusion is easy.
For example, a master of illusions entering through a cow's mouth and exiting from its tail—this is considered easy.
Furthermore, while those of the Two Vehicles can also perform transformations, they cannot employ them with actual efficacy; therefore, he asks to seek out why there is no transformation.
Mañjuśrī said, "Householder, to the east, beyond thirty-six Ganges-sands of worlds, there is a world named Sumeru-lakṣaṇa.
Its Buddha is named Sumeru-pradīpa-rāja, who currently resides there.
That Buddha’s body is eighty-four thousand yojanas in height, and his lion throne is eighty-four thousand yojanas high, being the most exquisitely adorned of all."
When the elder Vimalakīrti manifested his supernormal powers, that Buddha immediately dispatched thirty-two thousand lion thrones—lofty, vast, and pure—to enter the room of Vimalakīrti.
The great bodhisattvas, the great disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings had never before seen such a room;
it was so expansive that it could entirely contain all thirty-two thousand.
The thousand lion thrones were without obstruction; neither the city of Vaiśālī nor the four continents of Jambudvīpa were cramped or constricted, all appearing exactly as before.

Mañjuśrī replied to the householder, "One should take [the thrones] as they are spoken of. Then, as the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) entered meditative absorption, that Buddha immediately dispatched [them].
The one seated [there], Vimalakīrti, arrived without taking anything; he also reached [the assembly] without moving, with a mind of perfect intent (and so forth).
His room was vast and expansive, encompassing all the guests. Next, to illustrate this point: it is like a mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru, or Mount Sumeru entering a mustard seed.
Mount Sumeru does not become small, nor does the mustard seed become large. One need not compress the mountain to make it small, nor open the mustard seed to make it large.
If that were so, it would not be inconceivable; for when a mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru, Mount Sumeru does not become small and the mustard seed does not become large.
Likewise, a small room could contain a great throne, and the great throne would not be narrow while the room would not be broad—this is the logic of the analogy.
Yet the current text states: "The room encompasses the great throne. Since the room is already vast and expansive, how can it be said that "a mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru"?
Regarding the phrase "mustard seeds," the Great Master Daiei’s commentary states: "Internally observing is itself vast; externally observing is itself as it is.
Therefore, observing within a room is itself expansive, while going outside and observing is merely within that eight-foot room.

That the internal expansiveness is not obstructed by the external narrowness, and the external narrowness is not obstructed by the internal expansiveness—this very fact is the inconceivable. Thus says the Dharma Master.
Furthermore, Master Yicheng of the Rui-ji Temple explained that because this was a guest room, the hall was not opened as it was in its usual state.
At that time, Vimalakīrti said to Mañjuśrī, "Please take the lion throne together with these eminent bodhisattvas."
As they sat together, each should naturally manifest their own body as being like the form of the seat.
The bodhisattvas who had attained supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) immediately transformed themselves to be forty-two thousand *yojanas* in height and sat upon lion thrones;

however, the bodhisattvas who had newly resolved their minds and the great disciples were all unable to ascend them. At that time, Vimalakīrti said to Śāriputra, "Please take a seat upon the lion throne."
Pūrṇa said, "Householder, this seat is too high and broad; I cannot ascend it.
Vimalakīrti replied, "Śāriputra, you must pay homage to the Tathāgata Sumerudīparāja, and then you will be able to sit upon it.
Thereupon, the bodhisattvas who had newly resolved their minds and the great disciples immediately paid homage to the Tathāgata Sumerudīparāja and were able to sit upon the lion seats.
The bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds, as well as Śāriputra and the others, were all unable to ascend.
Śāriputra replied, "I am unable to ascend. [The Buddha asked,] "What is this 'I' (*mama*)? It is merely another name for the self (*ātman*).
If it is the sense of mastery (*vaśitva*), how can that which lacks mastery be called 'I'? He further questioned Śāriputra: "When an arhat enters into supernormal powers (*abhijñā*),"
If he is able to manifest bodies that fill the trichiliocosm, why could he not ascend this seat?
Some explain it by saying that Vimalakīrti’s supernatural power restrained him so that he could not ascend;

just as it was clarified in the previous "Bodhisattva Chapter" that Māra could not depart because the householder’s supernatural power restrained Māra from leaving, so it is here as well. Śāriputra was actually capable of ascending and occupying the seat.
The layman said, "I am unable to ascend. The Buddha replied, "It is not so.

You should understand that these high seats are all bodies produced from the pure karma free of outflows of the Buddhas; they are not bodies produced from the karma of defilements like yours. Therefore, you cannot ascend.
By prostrating to the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara and borrowing his supernatural power, you may then ascend."
Śāriputra said, “Householder, this is truly marvelous!

That such a small room can accommodate these high and broad seats without obstructing the city of Vaiśālī, nor even crowding the palaces of the devas, nāgas, rājās, ghosts, and spirits throughout the villages, cities, and towns of Jambudvīpa and the four continents. Vimalakīrti replied:
Śāriputra, only the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess a liberation called "inconceivable.
If a Bodhisattva dwells in this liberation, they can place the high and vast Mount Sumeru inside a mustard seed without it increasing or decreasing;
yet the sovereign Mount Sumeru remains as it was in its original form, while the gods of the Four Heavenly Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven remain unaware and unknowing of it.
Only those who are ready to be delivered perceive Mount Sumeru entering into a mustard seed; this is called the Dharma-gate of the inconceivable liberation.

Furthermore, he causes the waters of the four great oceans to enter into a single pore without disturbing the fish, turtles, crocodiles, or any other aquatic creatures, yet the nature of that great ocean remains as it was before, including its dragons, spirits, and asuras.
Unaware and unknowing of their own entry, these sentient beings are likewise not disturbed.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva dwelling in the inconceivable liberation may take up the trichiliocosm like a potter’s wheel and place it in his right palm, casting it beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; yet the sentient beings therein remain unaware and unknowing.

Knowing where those beings reside, he returns them once more to their original places, such that no one perceives any thought of coming or going, while this world remains as it was in its original state.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, there may be sentient beings who delight in dwelling long in the world and can be liberated;
for them, the Bodhisattva manifests seven days as a single kalpa, causing those sentient beings to perceive it as such.
If there are sentient beings who do not wish to dwell for a long kalpa yet can be delivered, the bodhisattva immediately shortens one kalpa to seven days,
causing those sentient beings to perceive it as seven days. Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva dwelling in the inconceivable liberation can gather the magnificent adornments of all buddha-fields into a single land and display them to the assembly.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva places all sentient beings of all buddha-fields upon his right palm and flies to the ten directions, manifesting them everywhere without moving them from their original locations.

Moreover, Śāriputra, whatever offerings sentient beings of the ten directions present to the Buddhas, the bodhisattva causes them all to be seen within a single pore. Furthermore, all the suns in the lands of the ten directions—
Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Bodhisattva can cause the moon and the lunar mansions to be seen within a single pore;
he can also inhale all the winds existing throughout the worlds of the ten directions into his mouth without his body being harmed, nor are the external trees broken or shattered.
Moreover, when the kalpas of the worlds of the ten directions are consumed by fire at the end of time, he can take all those fires into his belly.

The fire remains as it was before and does no harm; furthermore, he passes through Buddha-worlds below as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, takes up a single Buddha-land, and places it above in worlds beyond the sands of the Ganges, as countless as they may be—just as one might pick up a jujube leaf on the point of a needle—without causing any disturbance.
Moreover, Śāriputra, you dwell in this inconceivable liberation.
A Bodhisattva is able, through supernormal powers, to manifest the body of a Buddha, or manifest the body of a Pratyekabuddha,

or manifest the body of a Śrāvaka, or manifest the body of Śakra, or manifest the body of Brahmā, or manifest the body of a world-ruler, or manifest the body of a Wheel-Turning Sage King; furthermore,
they are able to transform all sounds existing throughout the worlds of the ten directions, whether superior, middling, or inferior.

He causes the voice of a Buddha to be produced, emitting sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, as well as the various teachings spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions, so that all may hear them therein.
Śāriputra, I have now briefly described the power of the inconceivable liberation of a bodhisattva; were it to be explained in detail, it would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.
He asked again: "If such great and small [realms] can coexist, only those who have attained deliverance (*yāna*) should be able to see them.
Now, since Śāriputra and the others have already seen this inconceivable [manifestation], they must understand the inconceivable.

He replied: "Śāriputra and the others do not understand. How do we know they do not understand? Therefore, in the passage below, Kāśyapa says to Śāriputra: "Before the blind, he manifests a multitude..."
It is the same for those who appear as śrāvakas: when they hear of the inconceivable, they do not understand it and do not know it.

Now, if it is difficult to understand, one should not see a response; yet seeing [a response], how can it necessarily mean understanding? This matter is like people in the world who create an object of extreme refinement and subtlety;
everyone sees it, yet they do not understand it. Question: What fault is there in understanding? Answer: It is said that sound... [text ends].
If one hears and understands [the Dharma], one immediately possesses the three types of wisdom and is no different from a Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, there may be sentient beings who delight in remaining long in the world and can be delivered; the Bodhisattva then manifests seven days as a single kalpa.
This is yet another kind of inconceivable power. Now, tell me, how does this differ from entering the Small Room while seated on a great throne?
Above, it was clarified that Mount Sumeru enters a mustard seed while Mount Sumeru remains as it was, and the mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru likewise remains as it was.
Now, it is further explained that seven days are expanded into one kalpa while the seven days remain as they were, and one kalpa is contracted into seven days while the kalpa remains as it was.
This principle is subtle and difficult to fathom. If [the two states] were not different, then when seven days are now expanded into one kalpa...
The day is thus lengthened so that one *kalpa* becomes seven days; likewise, one *kalpa* is shortened so that it becomes a single day.
Furthermore, a mustard seed should contain Mount Sumeru, and Mount Sumeru should enter a mustard seed; Mount Sumeru should be small, yet it is not compressed;
the mustard seed should expand, yet it is not extended. To explain this: the text says that seven days are "extended" (*yāna*) to constitute one *kalpa*.
"One kalpa" refers to extending the discourse; it means that the discourse is extended for seven days to constitute one kalpa.

When one speaks of "extending" by stretching seven days to make them long, this is an error regarding the interpretation of the characters; such an understanding is biased. Furthermore, another explanation states:

this clarifies the meaning of the compatibility between the extended and the brief, which differs from the previous [section]. The previous section clarified the inconceivable compatibility between the large and the small.
Now, the "inconceivability of extension and contraction" was explained above as the inconceivability of non-alteration; here, the inconceivability of alteration is explained.
Regarding the inconceivability of alteration explained above: the small can contain the large, and the large can enter the small, yet both the large and the small remain perfectly distinct;
therefore, it is inconceivable. Regarding the inconceivability of alteration explained here: others are unable to alter it. Seventh.
A single day is made into one kalpa, and one kalpa is changed into seven days; that the Bodhisattva can thus change what is not changed is inconceivable.
This demonstrates that the Bodhisattva’s mastery of the Way is not singular, which is why these two passages differ.

Above, it was clarified that the Great and Small Vehicles are mutually inclusive as they were before; now, furthermore, seven days are made into one kalpa, and one kalpa is made into seven days, thereby extending the duration.

As for "stretching" as before: since one has already stretched [the duration] to become long, and shortened the long to become [the duration], one further opens the small to become large and compresses the large to make it small.
This is intended to show that the Bodhisattva’s embrace is not of a single kind; thus there are these two. Question:
Among the five wisdoms, which wisdom is this sovereign wisdom of stretching and shortening? As for the five wisdoms, the first is—
1. Nirvāṇa-knowledge; 2. Knowledge of abiding in the two dharmas; 3. Knowledge of non-contention (*araṇā*); 4. Knowledge of the limit (*prāntakoṭika*);
5. Knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*). Among these five knowledges, the knowledge of the limit possesses the sovereign power to extend or contract [time]. Question:
This is the sovereign mastery of a bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya*), wherein the great and the small are mutually contained. How, then, can one attain liberation at this present time?
The commentary says: To provide an illustration, consider this analogy: even a small mirror can reflect a mountain a hundred *zhang* high;
though the mirror contains the great mountain, it does not become large, and the great mountain remains as it was upon entering the mirror.

Because the Bodhisattva’s essence regards all phenomena as being like dreams, like illusions, and like reflections in a mirror, they are able to act in such a manner. Next, to clarify the extension and contraction, or the length and brevity [of time], it is as follows:
A person sleeps through a dream for a hundred years; the dream of a hundred years is but a single waking sleep.

That the dream of a hundred years is no longer than a single waking sleep, and that the single waking sleep is no different from the dream of a hundred years—others say this dream is inverted and illusory, so how can it serve as a metaphor?
To explain: within a dream, one experiences dreams with vivid clarity upon awakening.
The awakening within is clear and distinct; since the dream is already false and illusory, the waking state is likewise an inversion.

For this reason, the Bodhisattva realizes that all phenomena are like dreams and illusions, and is thus able to act in such a manner. The subsequent passage explains how they perform immeasurable deeds, manifest immeasurable bodies, and accomplish inconceivable tasks;
it asks whether Māra can also transform himself into the body of a Buddha or the body of a Śrāvaka, and so forth.
If all things can now be manifested by a Bodhisattva in this manner, what is there to be considered extraordinary?

The explanation says: the Bodhisattva is able to manifest them perfectly, whereas that [other being] cannot manifest them perfectly. To say that the Bodhisattva is able to manifest them perfectly means they manifest bodies equal in number to all sentient beings;

as the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra states: "They manifest bodies equal in number to the count of sentient beings and preach teachings equal in number to the count of sentient beings. That [other being] cannot do so.

For this reason, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva is inconceivable. When I now briefly explain that a bodhisattva is inconceivable, it is because the matters of inconceivability cannot be fully described; I am merely explaining them in brief. Question: Is this brief explanation exhaustive or not?
Answer: It is both exhaustive and not exhaustive. First, it is exhaustive in being brief, yet not exhaustive in its fullness. Now, it is exhaustive in its completion.
The phrase "briefly exhausted" clarifies that inconceivable matters do not transcend form and sound;
since it is clarified that form and sound encompass all things, it is said to be "briefly exhausted.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, having heard the exposition of the Bodhisattva’s inconceivable Dharma-gate of liberation, marveled at what he had never before experienced.
Some say: "Śāriputra, it is like a person showing various forms and images before someone who is blind; that person cannot see them.
In this same way, all śrāvakas, upon hearing this inconceivable Dharma-door of liberation, are unable to understand it.
When a wise person hears this, who would not resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
"O Venerable Ones, why do you cut off the very roots of this Mahāyāna, becoming like withered seeds?
All Śrāvakas who hear this inconceivable Dharma-door of liberation should weep aloud, their voices shaking the trichiliocosm;
all Bodhisattvas should rejoice greatly and receive this Dharma upon the crowns of their heads. If there be any Bodhisattva who has faith..."
When Mahākāśyapa spoke these words— “Those who understand this inconceivable dharma-gate of liberation cannot be thwarted by any of the hosts of Māras”—
thirty-two thousand devaputras all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, having heard this unprecedented teaching, immediately offered a simile to verify the preceding clarification regarding how śrāvakas see but do not understand.
There are four possible cases: first, those who see, hear, and understand—these are the bodhisattvas;
second, those who see, hear, and do not understand—these are the śrāvakas; third, those who neither see nor hear but now hear—these are the worldlings...
Furthermore, those people who do not see, hear, or understand are the lowest of men. Regarding the phrase "unprecedented" (*anāścarya*), there are two aspects:
first, that which has never been seen before; second, that which has never been heard before.

At that time, Vimalakīrti said to Mahākāśyapa: "O virtuous one, those who act as Māras in the immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions are for the most part bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation;
by the power of skillful means, they manifest as Māras to teach and transform sentient beings. Furthermore, Kāśyapa, there are some immeasurable bodhisattvas in the ten directions..."
If people come to beg for hands, feet, ears, noses, heads, eyes, marrow, brains, blood, flesh, skin, or bones;
or for villages, cities, wives, children, male and female slaves, elephants, horses, chariots;
or for gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral, amber, pearls, conch shells, clothing, food, and drink—those who beg in such ways mostly dwell in the inconceivable liberation.
The Bodhisattva, by means of skillful power (*upāya-bala*), goes to test them and causes them to become firm. Why is this?

Because a Bodhisattva who dwells in the inconceivable liberation (*acintya-vimokṣa*) possesses the power of majestic virtue (*prabhāva*). He performs acts of oppression to demonstrate such difficult tasks to all sentient beings.
Ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*) are inferior and lack the strength or influence to thus oppress a Bodhisattva; it is like a comparison.
"Just as the trampling of a dragon-elephant is not something a donkey can endure, this is called the gate of wisdom and skillful means of a bodhisattva dwelling in the inconceivable liberation.
At that time, Vimalakīrti said to Mahākāśyapa, "O Noble One, those who act as Māras throughout the ten directions— Kāśyapa, you are one of them."
Seeing one and not seeing the other, one merely knows that the Bodhisattva dwells in the inconceivable liberation, while Māra is powerless against him;
yet one does not realize that Māra himself dwells in the inconceivable liberation. Furthermore, the preceding section clarified the "conformity" to the inconceivable and the "conformity" dharma-gate;
this section clarifies the "reversal" of the inconceivable and the "reversal" dharma-gate. The preceding section clarified the dharma-gate of wholesome qualities.

Now, it was previously explained that there are two types of "conformity to the inconceivable" (anuparivartana) in the section on the dharma-gate of evil: first, form; second, sound. Form and sound encompass all such things.

Now, it is explained that there are likewise two types of "contrariety to the inconceivable" (viparivartana): first, celestial beings; second, human beings. These two categories of celestial and human beings encompass all such beings.

Celestial beings and humans encompass everything; even Māras are included among celestial beings, and beggars are included among humans. Thus, celestial beings and humans encompass all without exception.
Furthermore, this beggar is not merely an ordinary person of the world; rather, he is a Bodhisattva dwelling in the inconceivable who is able to perform such a transformation.
Regarding the phrase "begging from those who have reached the river of giving" (*dāna-nadī*), it means begging from those whose river of giving is about to overflow.
As for "from the external"—namely the kingdom, city, wife, and children—and "the internal":
The four limbs and hundred members, if one bestows them as a gift, immediately cross the River of Generosity (*dāna-nadī*);
because the River of Generosity is thus filled, the beggar is an inconceivable person who causes the practitioner to fulfill their practice.

Next, "giving to a dragon-elephant to trample upon is not something a donkey can endure" means that this is what an inconceivable Bodhisattva can give, whereas it is not something a beggar of shallow practice can receive. At times...
It is said that ordinary māras are like donkeys, while the māras of inconceivable bodhisattvas are like dragon-elephants;
this means that inconceivable bodhisattvas are able to understand what ordinary māras cannot. This term "dragon-elephant" refers simply to a single elephant;
it is like calling a fine horse a "dragon-horse" or a fine elephant a "dragon-elephant."
Chapter Seven: Contemplating Sentient Beings.
There are three reasons why this chapter has been included: first, the distant; second, the intermediate;
and third, the proximate. Regarding "distant beings," it is because this sutra is a Bodhisattva sutra that elucidates [this subject].
When a Bodhisattva practices the Bodhisattva path, they resolve to deliver all sentient beings, placing others before themselves.
Thus, the Mahāyāna Sūtra states: "Before one has attained deliverance oneself, one first delivers others. Therefore, I pay homage to this initial generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*).

Having generated the mind with the desire to deliver all sentient beings, one must recognize the characteristics of sentient beings; if one does not recognize sentient beings, [one cannot deliver them].

If one clings to characteristics, one is unable to deliver sentient beings; this is what is clarified here. By observing sentient beings, one causes the Bodhisattva to recognize the characteristic of sentient beings:
although one delivers sentient beings, in reality there are no sentient beings to be delivered. Therefore, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* states:
"One delivers all sentient beings, yet in reality there are no sentient beings to be delivered. This statement applies universally to all cases; thus it is said.
Regarding the statement that "the arising from afar" refers to what arises from the *Glan pa'i dri ba'i le'u* (The Chapter on Inquiring after the Illness), that text says:

"From delusion there is craving; thus my illness arises. Because the illnesses of sentient beings exist, my illness exists; when the illnesses of sentient beings are extinguished, my illness is then extinguished.

Since compassion for the past and future limits is equal, if it is so, then the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of a Bodhisattva exists because of sentient beings; therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: [Great Compassion is so called] because it is great and because it is directed toward sentient beings.
It is said that Prajñāpāramitā is the Mother of the Buddhas; who, then, is the mother of Prajñā? The explanation says: Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) is the mother of Prajñā.
Who is the mother of Great Compassion? Sentient beings are the mother of Great Compassion. Because sentient beings follow delusion, they give rise to craving;
because of craving, they undergo birth; and because of birth, there is sickness. Since sentient beings are sick, the Bodhisattva has the sickness of Great Compassion. Because of this...
Because of compassion, one speaks of Prajñā; therefore, sentient beings are the root of great compassion, and great compassion is the root of Prajñā.
Since the fundamental source arises from sentient beings, one must now observe sentient beings as the foundation.
Because it is named according to what is observed through the correct contemplation of the Bodhisattva, it is called the "Chapter on Observing Sentient Beings. Thus it is said:
That which is "produced from the proximate" is precisely the production of the inconceivable category; the inconceivable is precisely the two types of knowledge.

These two types of knowledge are precisely the subject that contemplates sentient beings, and sentient beings are precisely the object contemplated. Furthermore, the aforementioned inconceivable liberation is precisely the conditions for teaching sentient beings, and sentient beings are precisely the conditions for the teaching.
Although the above clarifies the subject that contemplates and the conditions for the teaching, it has not yet clarified the object.
Regarding the contemplation of the conditions for the teaching: if one clarifies only the teaching and does not clarify the conditions, it is not complete.

For this reason, having clarified the teaching above, we now examine the conditions. Question: Now, when contemplating sentient beings, is one contemplating them as existing, or is one contemplating them as non-existent?
However, on this point, the interpretations of various schools differ. The Sarvāstivādins and others claim that [sentient beings] are real.
There are no sentient beings; there are only dharmas such as the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus). Sentient beings exist only as provisional designations.

These names do not exist in the two periods [of past and future], but exist only in the present because of their conjunction; thus they have a name. Now it is clarified that if sentient beings truly do not exist, then what is "bodhisattva"?
Since a bodhisattva originally resolves to deliver sentient beings, and yet there are no sentient beings to be delivered, how can there be a bodhisattva?
Furthermore, Subhūti, if there were no sentient beings, that would be the view of non-existence; if dharmas truly existed, that would be the view of existence.
Being fully possessed of both the views of existence and non-existence, as well as those of annihilationism and eternalism, how could one be called a bodhisattva? As the Prajñāpāramitā says:
"One who has severed all views is called a bodhisattva. Now, since you have not yet departed from these various views, how can you be called a bodhisattva?
A Bodhisattva is one who embodies the Way (*mārga*). The ancient scriptures designate a Bodhisattva as a "Way-man" (*daoshi*);
because he embodies the Way, he is called a Way-man. Having embodied the Way, he ought to be free from all views (*dṛṣṛti*).
Second, the Vātsīputrīya practitioner says: "Sentient beings exist; sentient beings cannot be non-existent. Why? Because they consist of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*)."
Through the combination of the dharma of the eye, the five aggregates arise; through the combination of the dharma of the person, [the person] arises.
For this reason, it is known that there truly exists the dharma of the person. That [teaching] clarifies the conventional person, which cannot be said to be real;

therefore, it is neither unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), nor does it belong to the three periods of time, nor is it conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). It is contained within the fifth Piṭaka. Now, it is clarified that this [person] is also not a Bodhisattva. Why is this?
It is said that although one delivers all sentient beings, in reality there are no sentient beings who are delivered. Why is this?
If there is a sentient being who perceives a "life-span" (jīva) and so forth, such a perception means they are not a bodhisattva;

not only are they not a bodhisattva, they are also not of the two vehicles, but are rather an ordinary person bound by all fetters (sakalabandhana). This is because the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) is the root of sentient beings. Thus it is stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
It is said that because the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) subsumes the sixty-two views, one is a complete ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Next, Harivarman says: "It both exists and does not exist; it exists according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and does not exist according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Both the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, as well as the biography of Aśvaghoṣa, provide this explanation: the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are the person, and the axle is the chariot; this is according to conventional truth.
Because there is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), it is non-existent; if that were so, this principle would be excellent.

However, those who investigate exhaustively all revere this phrase as the dwelling place for the spirit and the locus for the mind. Now, I clarify that this is still merely the dualistic view of both existence and non-existence.
Why? Because that which exists in your conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) can be made non-existent, yet that which is non-existent in the ultimate truth cannot be made existent.

If conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) were non-existent and ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) were existent, then conventional truth would definitely exist and ultimate truth would definitely not exist;
thus, these would be the dualistic views of existence and non-existence, and one would not be a bodhisattva. Now, observe that all sentient beings are entirely free from such dharmas.
As the text says, they are like a magician who sees an illusion: the illusion exists, yet it is not existent; the illusion exists, yet it is not non-existent. (4)
"Washing both within and without the phrases—this single phrase alone washes away all illnesses. Therefore, the Master said:
"It is merely by means of a single phrase that one destroys all illnesses. Question: "To regard sentient beings as being like a 'fifth great element' (pañcama-mahābhūta) is itself non-existence;
why then do you criticize him? Explanation: "Now, in clarifying that one regards sentient beings as being like a fifth great element, how can [the critic]..."
If one contemplates others as being like the fifth great element (*mahābhūta*), it is like the fifth *kasāyī* (a type of hellish realm);

now, when contemplating sentient beings, they are like the fifth great element—sentient beings appear vividly yet are non-existent. Therefore, it is said that "one contemplates sentient beings as being like the fifth great element.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattva delivers sentient beings as if they were empty space. Question: Could this not be without reality?
Sentient beings should be understood as provisional illusions; yet, because they are perceived as real, the illusion lacks reality—how, then, can there be an illusion?
All four propositions are pure, for this alone is the true mark (*dharmatā*). Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Sentient beings are themselves the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*);
to establish sentient beings in the limit of reality is to establish the limit of reality within the limit of reality. Since the true mark is itself non-existent, [there is no establishment].
Since all sentient beings are likewise non-existent, the Treatise states: "The true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is where mental activity and language cease;
it is without arising and without cessation, quiescent like *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, one may ask:

"If this is so, with what intention does the Sūtra sometimes speak of 'there being persons' and sometimes speak of 'there being no persons'? The explanation is: "The Buddhas sometimes speak of a self, and sometimes speak [of no-self]."
Within the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, which is selfless, there is neither self nor non-self; for this reason, sentient beings are themselves the true mark.
This section consists of two parts: first, Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti observe sentient beings; second, Śāriputra and the goddess.
The female audience observes these four individuals; observing them is equivalent to observing all people. Why?
Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti represent the two types of persons—monastic and lay; the heavenly maiden and Śāriputra represent the two types of beings—heavenly and human.

Thus, there are the two genders (male and female), the two capacities (great and small), and the two realms (hidden and manifest). Observing these four individuals is therefore the observation of all.
This comprehensively encompasses all [the teachings]. Regarding Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti’s contemplation of sentient beings, there are two primary aspects:

first, clarifying the transformation of others; second, clarifying one's own practice. Within the first [aspect], there are two parts: first, discussing the sentient beings who are the objects of contemplation;

second, discussing the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*) which are the means of contemplation. As for why the contemplation of sentient beings is discussed first and the four immeasurables are discussed afterward:

As explained previously, because sentient beings are the foundation of the four immeasurables, the preceding treatise contemplates sentient beings and the subsequent treatise contemplates sentient beings through the four immeasurables.
Having correctly established this, one next causes sentient beings to be free from suffering; thus there is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Next, one bestows great bliss;

thus there is great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*). Because they are freed from suffering and obtain bliss, there is great sympathetic joy (*mahāmuditā*). By realizing that suffering and bliss are non-dual, one attains equanimity (*mahopekṣā*).

Because emptiness is equal, there is great equanimity (*upekṣā*); for this reason, one contemplates sentient beings [through the four immeasurables], as discussed in the subsequent treatise on the four equanimities.
At that time, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti: "How does a bodhisattva contemplate sentient beings? Vimalakīrti replied:
"It is, for example, like a magician who looks upon a person created by his own magic; a bodhisattva’s contemplation of sentient beings is just like this."
The wise see the moon in water as like the reflection of one's face in a mirror, like a mirage in the heat, like an echo, like clouds in the sky,
like a mass of foam on the water, like a bubble on the water, like the solidity of a plantain tree, like lightning’s long duration,
like a fifth great element, like a sixth aggregate, like a seventh sense-faculty, like a thirteenth base, or like a nineteenth [base].
The Bodhisattva Dhātuka contemplates sentient beings as being like this: like form in the formless realm; like the sprout of a parched grain; like the view of a self-body in a stream-enterer;
like the entry into a womb by a non-returner; like the three poisons in an arhat; like greed, anger, and the violation of precepts in a bodhisattva who has attained patience;
like the habitual tendencies of afflictions in a Buddha; like a blind person seeing forms; or like one who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation.
In-and-out breathing is like the tracks of a bird in the sky; it is like the son of a barren woman; it is like a conjured person.

Afflictions are like what is seen in a dream after one has awakened; they are like the taking on of a body by one who has attained parinirvāṇa; they are like a fire without smoke. Thus does the Bodhisattva contemplate sentient beings.
Now, regarding the first passage where Mañjuśrī asks how a bodhisattva should contemplate sentient beings, Vimalakīrti replies: "Like a magician.
This means that because the Bodhisattva clearly realizes that sentient beings have no inherent existence, he employs the ten similes to clarify this point.
In other sections of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin) and throughout the Mahāyāna, these ten similes are likewise used to provide instruction. Thus it says: "Like..."
Regarding the phrase "illusory": it contains the term "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*). As for this exhaustion, sentient beings claim that sentient beings are real and that illusions are false.
Now, the Bodhisattva conversely uses the "false" which they believe in as a metaphor for the "real" which they believe in.

Since he employs their belief in the false to illustrate their belief in the real, once one knows that the real is not real, one immediately knows that the false is not false. This is precisely "exhaustion"; it is not non-exhaustion.
Some may then think: "If this is so, then there would be no real sentient beings, and there must be illusory sentient beings.

This view does not fully exhaust the confusion of those who are deluded; it must be further cleared away. Since one borrows the illusory merely to refute the real, and since there is no real, where could there be an illusory?
Since one borrows the provisional merely to refute the real, once the real is abandoned, the illusory should likewise be abandoned. Why?

In reality, there is nothing further to be attached to, being as empty as Master Zhaoshan described. He said that impermanence is used to refute permanence, yet it is not that impermanence itself exists;
now it is the same here. One takes emptiness to refute substantiality, yet it is not that emptiness itself exists.

Because substantiality is refuted by means of emptiness, both substantiality and emptiness are revealed to be non-existent. Since these two phrases are absent, the four propositions (tetralemma) are gone, and both the internal and external are pure. Question:
If everything—whether non-existent, not non-existent, or even neither non-existent nor existent—were entirely absent, then there would be no sentient beings.
To explain: it is not so. What is now clarified by the statement "all things are non-existent" is that the characteristics of sentient beings are non-existent;
yet the characteristics of sentient beings are manifest while being non-existent. Take the analogy of illusory speech and laughter: they are manifest while being non-existent.

Because [all things] exist, Master Sengzhao’s *Wu zhen kong lun* (Treatise on Emptiness as Not Being Truly Real) states: "A person created by illusion is not non-existent, yet the person created by illusion is not a real person.
The body of that person embodies all dharmas in this manner; therefore, Master Kumārajīva praised him, saying:
"Among the people of Qin, Sengzhao is the foremost in understanding emptiness. This is like seeing the moon in water, which clarifies [the nature of reality].
The wise person sees the moon in the pond as vividly present yet realizes it is nothing at all, and thus does not grasp it;
the fool is like a monkey who, seeing the moon in the water, dives in to seize it. It is the same with a reflected image in a mirror:

the wise person sees the image as vividly present, yet clearly knows it is nothing at all and does not grasp it; the fool is like a rooster who, seeing its own reflection in a mirror, immediately begins to fight it.
The chicken breaks its claws for it, and the tiger breaks its fangs for it; I do not take these as metaphors, but rather take the wise person as the metaphor.

Just as a mirage exists in the heat, this is also comparable to the aforementioned wise person who sees that a reflection in a mirror is truly non-existent, just as the wise person sees that a mirage in the heat is truly non-existent. This may also differ from the superior wisdom described above.
Upon meeting, one knows that nothing exists; now, some may say that there is a difference between the appearance of heat as water and the actual absence of water.
Next, regarding the "fifth great element" up to the "nineteenth realm" and so forth, these have already been explained as before.

Now, to clarify further, there are two intentions: first, the person who understands dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); second, the person who refutes substantial reality (*dravya*). Herein, we clarify the person who understands dependent origination.

Like an illusion, that which exists has no intrinsic existence; yet, because there are two [aspects], the refutation of a real self is for the purpose of clarifying the "disease" of a real self, showing that sentient beings—like the thirteen bases (*āyatana*) and nineteen elements (*dhātu*)—are ultimately non-existent.
When a Bodhisattva contemplates sentient beings as such, this is their very essence. Question: Are sentient beings like the thirteen bases and nineteen elements?

Since ultimately nothing exists, what does the bodhisattva observe? If sentient beings are like the thirteen bases (*āyatana*) and nineteen elements (*dhātu*), then the bodhisattva is also like the thirteen bases and nineteen elements. Since sentient beings do not exist and the bodhisattva also does not exist, who is there to observe?
The commentary explains: As already clarified previously, it is precisely because the characteristics of sentient beings are such as this.
The Bodhisattva observes that sentient beings are fundamentally non-existent; furthermore, since sentient beings themselves know they exist, there is no need for the Bodhisattva to deliver them.

It is only because sentient beings perceive existence within that which is non-existent that the Bodhisattva observes sentient beings as non-existent, causing them to likewise awaken to this non-existence.
Mañjuśrī said, "If a bodhisattva practices contemplation in this way, how does he practice loving-kindness?
Vimalakīrti replied, "Once a bodhisattva has practiced such contemplation, he reflects: 'I shall preach such a Dharma as this for the sake of sentient beings.
This is truly loving-kindness. He practices the loving-kindness of cessation because there is nothing produced; he practices the loving-kindness of non-feverishness because there are no afflictions."

One practices impartial compassion because it is equal throughout the three periods of time; one practices the compassion of non-contention because nothing arises; one practices the compassion of non-duality because there is no union between the internal and external;
one practices unbreakable compassion because it is ultimately exhausted; one practices steadfast compassion because the mind is indestructible;
one practices pure compassion because the nature of all phenomena is pure; one practices boundless compassion because it is like space; one practices the compassion of an Arhat...
The compassion of Hanzi is because it shatters the thieves of the fetters; the compassion of a bodhisattva is because it brings peace to sentient beings;

the compassion of a Tathāgata is because it attains the mark of suchness; the compassion of a Buddha is because it awakens sentient beings; the compassion of spontaneity is because it is attained without cause;
the compassion of bodhi is because it is of one equal flavor; the compassion of the peerless is because it severs all cravings; and the great compassionate love is because it guides with...

Because it is the Mahāyāna, he practices the compassion of tireless application; because he contemplates emptiness and non-self, he practices the compassion of the gift of Dharma without any stinginess;
because he transforms those who violate the precepts, he practices the compassion of upholding the precepts; because he protects both self and others, he practices the compassion of patience;

because he bears the burden of sentient beings, he practices the compassion of meditative concentration without attachment to its flavor; and because there is nothing he does not know, he practices the compassion of wisdom.
At that time, he practices the compassion of skillful means because he manifests all things; he practices the compassion of non-concealment because his straightforward mind is pure;
he practices the compassion of the profound mind because his conduct is unmixed; he practices the compassion of non-deception because it is not false or artificial;
he practices the compassion of peace and happiness because it causes others to attain the bliss of Buddhahood. Such is the compassion of a bodhisattva. Mañjuśrī asked again: "What is..."
What is meant by compassion? It is answered: that all merits performed by a bodhisattva are shared with all sentient beings.
What is meant by joy? It is answered: that there is rejoicing in whatever benefit has been bestowed, without regret. What is meant by equanimity? It is answered:
that regarding the blessings and merits one has performed, there is no expectation of reward or fear.

Regarding the instruction that "Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva should practice contemplation in this way," how does one practice loving-kindness? This is the second section, discussing the ability to contemplate the four immeasurables.
Previously, Mañjuśrī asked about observing sentient beings; once a bodhisattva has observed sentient beings, how does he practice loving-kindness?
Vimalakīrti replied: "One who practices contemplation in this way reflects within himself and thinks, 'I shall preach this Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.'"
This is truly genuine compassion (*bhūta-maitrī*). Herein, the question is easy and the answer is difficult;
the reason for this is that while the question is narrow and restricted, the answer reveals the Path. Thus, the question is easy and the answer is difficult. The previous question asked:
"Since there are no sentient beings, how does a bodhisattva practice compassion? Now, by stating that this is "genuine compassion," it clarifies that the bodhisattva acts in this manner.

Contemplation is precisely the Middle Way’s correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*). Now, if sentient beings awaken to this correct contemplation and attain the bliss of the Dharma-body, this is true compassion (*karuṇā*).
If ordinary persons and those of the two vehicles merely practice the contemplations of annihilation or permanence, they will obtain the fruits of birth and death; this is not true compassion. Why?
Because when ordinary persons perceive existence, they fall into the view of eternalism; when those of the two vehicles perceive non-existence, they fall into [the view of annihilation].
The view of annihilationism is precisely the afflictive view of permanence; it brings about the fruit of birth and death.

To enable Bodhisattvas to simultaneously transcend these two extremes, one contemplates that sentient beings do not exist, thereby abandoning the view of permanence; by contemplating sentient beings while they do not exist, one abandons the view of annihilationism.
Transcending both annihilationism and permanence is the Middle Way and correct contemplation, which enables sentient beings to awaken to this Middle Way.
Because one attains the Dharma-body, this is the compassion of ultimate reality (*bhūta-karuṇā*).
Furthermore, since it is said that this Dharma is the teaching of true compassion, it is called "the compassion of ultimate reality. However, this interpretation is still not easily understood.
Why? Because if there are no sentient beings, then there should be no teaching; how then can such a teaching be called the compassion of ultimate reality?
The commentary explains: If sentient beings were to know that there is nothing whatsoever, then ultimately there would be no Bodhisattva and nothing to be taught.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "If sentient beings were to know ultimate emptiness, the Bodhisattva would have no effort to exert.

This is simply because sentient beings do not exist; yet, while sentient beings are non-existent, there is a Bodhisattva who does exist. Therefore, [the Bodhisattva] acts for the sake of sentient beings who are themselves non-existent.

To speak that which is spoken while there is nothing spoken, and to speak that which has no existence so as to cause sentient beings to realize the non-existence of both existence and non-existence—this teaching of non-existence is true compassion.
As for "compassion of cessation," it is the cessation of all views; this is the compassion of cessation. [The question regarding] the Arhat is twofold.
The gate of transverse compassion is mounted upon loving-kindness; yet this is not the "loving-kindness of fondness. How then can it be said that this is the loving-kindness of an Arhat?
The explanation says: this merely borrows the term "Arhat" to designate this compassion. The name "Arhat" signifies one who has slain the thieves of the fetters (*saṃyojana*);
it clarifies that this compassion is capable of destroying those thieves of the fetters. The practice of the Bodhisattva’s compassion is likewise so; both are merely metaphors.
The remaining three [categories] are as in the text.
Mañjuśrī asked again: "In the face of the fear of birth and death, upon what should a bodhisattva rely? Vimalakīrti replied:
"A bodhisattva, amidst the fear of birth and death, should rely on the power of the Tathāgata’s merits. Mañjuśrī asked again:

Question: Where should a bodhisattva who wishes to rely on the power of the Tathāgata’s merits abide? Answer: A bodhisattva who wishes to rely on the power of the Tathāgata’s merits should abide in the liberation of all sentient beings. Question: What must be eliminated in order to liberate sentient beings? Answer: To liberate sentient beings, one must eliminate their afflictions (*kleśa*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the afflictions? Answer: To eliminate the afflictions, one must eliminate the objects of perception (*ālambana*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the objects of perception? Answer: To eliminate the objects of perception, one must eliminate conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate conceptual proliferation? Answer: To eliminate conceptual proliferation, one must eliminate the mind (*citta*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the mind? Answer: To eliminate the mind, one must eliminate the object of the mind (*cittālambana*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the object of the mind? Answer: To eliminate the object of the mind, one must eliminate the grasping at characteristics (*nimittagrāha*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the grasping at characteristics? Answer: To eliminate the grasping at characteristics, one must eliminate the duality of subject and object (*grāhyagrāhaka*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the duality of subject and object? Answer: To eliminate the duality of subject and object, one must eliminate the view of a self (*ātman*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of a self? Answer: To eliminate the view of a self, one must eliminate the view of phenomena (*dharma*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of phenomena? Answer: To eliminate the view of phenomena, one must eliminate the view of emptiness (*śūnyatādṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of emptiness? Answer: To eliminate the view of emptiness, one must eliminate the view of non-emptiness (*aśūnyatādṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of non-emptiness? Answer: To eliminate the view of non-emptiness, one must eliminate the view of both emptiness and non-emptiness (*śūnyatā-aśūnyatādṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of both emptiness and non-emptiness? Answer: To eliminate the view of both emptiness and non-emptiness, one must eliminate the view of neither emptiness nor non-emptiness (*naiva-śūnyatā-nāśūnyatādṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of neither emptiness nor non-emptiness? Answer: To eliminate the view of neither emptiness nor non-emptiness, one must eliminate the view of permanence (*nityadṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of permanence? Answer: To eliminate the view of permanence, one must eliminate the view of impermanence (*anityadṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of impermanence? Answer: To eliminate the view of impermanence, one must eliminate the view of both permanence and impermanence (*nityānityadṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of both permanence and impermanence? Answer: To eliminate the view of both permanence and impermanence, one must eliminate the view of neither permanence nor impermanence (*naiva-nitya-nānityadṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of neither permanence nor impermanence? Answer: To eliminate the view of neither permanence nor impermanence, one must eliminate the view of existence (*astidṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of existence? Answer: To eliminate the view of existence, one must eliminate the view of non-existence (*nāstidṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of non-existence? Answer: To eliminate the view of non-existence, one must eliminate the view of both existence and non-existence (*astināstidṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of both existence and non-existence? Answer: To eliminate the view of both existence and non-existence, one must eliminate the view of neither existence nor non-existence (*naivāsti-naivāstidṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of neither existence nor non-existence? Answer: To eliminate the view of neither existence nor non-existence, one must eliminate the view of eternity (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of eternity? Answer: To eliminate the view of eternity, one must eliminate the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of annihilation? Answer: To eliminate the view of annihilation, one must eliminate the view of both eternity and annihilation (*śāśvatocchedadṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of both eternity and annihilation? Answer: To eliminate the view of both eternity and annihilation, one must eliminate the view of neither eternity nor annihilation (*naiva-śāśvata-naivocchedadṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of neither eternity nor annihilation? Answer: To eliminate the view of neither eternity nor annihilation, one must eliminate the view of identity (*ekatvadṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of identity? Answer: To eliminate the view of identity, one must eliminate the view of difference (*anyatvadṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of difference? Answer: To eliminate the view of difference, one must eliminate the view of both identity and difference (*ekatvānyatvadṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of both identity and difference? Answer: To eliminate the view of both identity and difference, one must eliminate the view of neither identity nor difference (*naiva-ekatva-naivānyatvadṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of neither identity nor difference? Answer: To eliminate the view of neither identity nor difference, one must eliminate the view of cause (*hetudṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of cause? Answer: To eliminate the view of cause, one must eliminate the view of no-cause (*ahetudṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of no-cause? Answer: To eliminate the view of no-cause, one must eliminate the view of both cause and no-cause (*hetvahetudṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of both cause and no-cause? Answer: To eliminate the view of both cause and no-cause, one must eliminate the view of neither cause nor no-cause (*naiva-hetu-naivāhetudṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of neither cause nor no-cause? Answer: To eliminate the view of neither cause nor no-cause, one must eliminate the view of effect (*phaladṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of effect? Answer: To eliminate the view of effect, one must eliminate the view of no-effect (*aphaladṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of no-effect? Answer: To eliminate the view of no-effect, one must eliminate the view of both effect and no-effect (*phalāphaladṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of both effect and no-effect? Answer: To eliminate the view of both effect and no-effect, one must eliminate the view of neither effect nor no-effect (*naiva-phala-naivāphaladṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be eliminated in order to eliminate the view of neither effect nor no-effect? Answer: To eliminate the view of neither effect nor no-effect, one must eliminate the view of action (*karmadṛṣṭi*). Question: What must be
"Regarding affliction, what should one practice? He replied, "One should practice right mindfulness. He asked again, "How does one practice right mindfulness?
He replied, "One should practice non-arising and non-ceasing. He asked again, "What dharma does not arise? What dharma does not cease?
He replied, "Unwholesome dharmas do not arise; wholesome dharmas do not cease. He asked again, "What is the root of the wholesome and the unwholesome? He replied, "The body is the root."
He asked again, "What is the root of the body? He replied, "Desire and greed are its root. He asked again, "What is the root of desire and greed?
He replied, "False conceptualization is its root. He asked again, "What is the root of false conceptualization?
He replied, "Inverted perception is its root. He asked again, "What is the root of inverted perception? He replied, "Non-abiding is its root. He asked again, "What is the root of non-abiding?"...
"Abiding—what is its basis? He replied, "If there is no abiding, then there is no basis. Mañjuśrī, from the basis of non-abiding, all phenomena are established.
When Mañjuśrī asked, "What should a bodhisattva rely upon regarding the fear of birth and death? this was the first instance of Mañjuśrī [interacting] with the layman.

Regarding the observation of sentient beings as duality, the first section—clarifying the transformation of others—is concluded. Now, for the second section on one’s own practice, this text is further divided into two parts:
first, the question posed by Mañjuśrī, and second, the answer given by Vimalakīrti. This first part concerns the question of Mañjuśrī;
however, this question is specifically asked for the sake of bodhisattvas who have newly begun their practice. Why, then, is there this distinct passage?
Regarding the passage, "To clarify that there is fear in birth and death, on what should a bodhisattva rely? the commentary explains:

The presence of this text contains both general and specific meanings. As for the general meaning, it clarifies here that when a bodhisattva who is a beginner first resolves upon *bodhicitta*, once that *bodhicitta* has been generated, it is inherently distinct from the mind of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*. As for the mind of the *śrāvakas*... [text continues]
One who has attained self-mastery abandons birth and death to enter nirvana;

however, since you are now a bodhisattva who has resolved for enlightenment, you ought to remain within birth and death to deliver all sentient beings. Being within birth and death, that realm is truly terrifying.
Now, as a bodhisattva at the beginning of practice, you have not yet overcome this fear; you dread birth and death, and because you dread birth and death—
Upon what basis does the Bodhisattva ask this question? The underlying intention arises from the preceding passage on the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*):
since the Bodhisattva possesses great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he ought to rescue sentient beings from suffering within birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).

Yet, as birth-and-death is terrifying, upon what should the Bodhisattva rely to persevere despite such fear? Therefore, the question is posed: "Birth-and-death is fearful; O Bodhisattva, upon what do you rely?"
"What should one rely upon? Vimalakīrti replied, "A bodhisattva, amidst the terrors of birth and death, should rely upon the merits of the Tathāgata.
Previously, Mañjuśrī asked, "When there is fear in birth and death, what should one rely upon?
Now he answers, "One should rely upon the merits of the Tathāgata," clarifying that because there is something to rely upon above, there is nothing to fear below. Thus, one relies upon...

The merit of the Tathāgata is precisely the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*. This *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* universally cures all [afflictions]. What constitutes specific remedies and universal remedies? As for specific remedies: for those with much greed, one teaches impurity (*aśubha*); for those with much anger, one teaches loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*); for those with much delusion, one teaches the contemplation of causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*); for those with much attachment to the breath, one teaches counting the breaths (*ānāpānasmṛti*); and for those attached to the self, one teaches [the contemplation of] non-self. As for universal remedies: [the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*] is taught for all. Why? Because it is the most supreme among all dharmas. Furthermore, because the Buddha is the teacher of all dharmas, he is able to cure all afflictions. Therefore, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is like a great king who can subdue all enemies; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great physician who can cure all illnesses; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great fire that can burn all grasses and trees; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great wind that can blow away all dust and dirt; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great rain that can moisten all parched lands; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a bright lamp that can illuminate all darkness; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great mountain that cannot be shaken by any wind; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great ocean that cannot be agitated by any waves; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like the great earth that supports all things; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like empty space that cannot be defiled by any dust; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like the sun that can dispel all cold; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like the moon that can dispel all heat; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great jewel that can fulfill all desires; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great medicine that can cure all poisons; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great armor that can protect against all weapons; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great ship that can carry across all beings; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great bridge that can lead all beings to the other shore; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great path that can lead to the city of Nirvāṇa; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great light that can dispel all ignorance; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great cloud that can shower down the rain of Dharma; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great drum that can awaken all sentient beings; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great conch that can proclaim the sound of the Dharma; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great bell that can ring out the sound of emptiness; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great mirror that can reflect all forms; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great sword that can cut through all fetters; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great net that can bind all demons; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme.
