It is also like a great wind that can scatter all clouds; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great rain that can wash away all filth; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great light that can illuminate all worlds; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great vessel that can hold all jewels; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great treasury that can provide all necessities; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great physician who knows all medicines; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great caravan leader who leads all merchants safely; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great wheel-turning monarch who rules over all lands; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great sage who is honored by all gods; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great hero who conquers all enemies; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great elephant that can trample all foes; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great horse that can gallop across all mountains and rivers; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great chariot that can transport all beings to the city of Nirvāṇa; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great palace that is adorned with all virtues; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great garden that is filled with all flowers and fruits; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great lake that is clear and free from turbidity; thus, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the most supreme. It is also like a great tree that provides shade for all beings; thus, the *buddhā

The skillful means regarding the realms (*dhātu*) are specific, whereas those that treat [afflictions] universally are as follows: when sentient beings equally possess such maladies, they should be taught the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*.
Because the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* universally treats all [afflictions], it causes one to rely upon the merits of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, when a bodhisattva practices the nine-fold contemplation (*navākāra-saṃjñā*), the hairs on the bodhisattva’s body all stand on end.
Just as one causes a fearful mind to engage in the six recollections, so it is here as well. Mañjuśrī asked again:

"Upon what should a bodhisattva rely when dwelling upon the merits of the Tathāgata? This clarifies that while the bodhisattva remains within the terrors of saṃsāra, what is their practice based on reliance upon the Buddha’s merits?
Vimalakīrti replied: "The bodhisattva relies upon the merits of the Tathāgata with the desire to deliver [sentient beings]."
It liberates all sentient beings. Furthermore, "relying above on the Tathāgata’s merits" refers to that which is relied upon above;
"now clearly delivering sentient beings" refers to that which is rescued below. Thus, there is what is propagated above, and now there is what is transformed below.
Moreover, this also explains how, by relying above on the Tathāgata’s merits, one attains fearlessness. Why? Because it is due to the Great [Vehicle].
When the Bodhisattva Diao Xiaoming directs his mind with the desire to universally deliver all sentient beings, since this mind is already so vast, how could he still possess even the slightest fear?
Second, in delivering all sentient beings, he possesses a heart of compassion;
if there is a heart of compassion, there is nothing to fear, and no one can cause the Bodhisattva any affliction. Therefore, the world...
It is said that humans have no intent to harm beasts, and beasts have no intent to harm humans. These three [groups] recite the merit of the Buddha; this is the supreme Dharma.
Since they delight in the supreme Dharma, they forget about things to be feared, and thus they do not fear.
Furthermore, it was asked: "In desiring to deliver sentient beings, what should one eliminate? This clarifies what a Bodhisattva eliminates when delivering sentient beings. The answer is as follows:
The reason for delivering sentient beings is the desire to eliminate their afflictions (*kleśa*). Again, it was asked: "For what reason are afflictions eliminated? He replied:
"One should practice right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). Once afflictions are eliminated, one then practices right contemplation (*samyak-darśana*);

because of this contemplation, one is able to eliminate afflictions. Again, it was asked: "What is right mindfulness? He replied: "It is the attainment of the practice of neither arising nor ceasing."
This statement regarding "non-arising and non-ceasing" does not refer to the "non-arising and non-ceasing" found among the eight negations;
rather, this statement of non-arising and non-ceasing clarifies that unwholesome dharmas do not arise and wholesome dharmas do not cease, and thus it is called non-arising and non-ceasing.

Furthermore, it was asked: "Of what are the wholesome and unwholesome fundamentally rooted? The answer was: "The body is the root. This clarifies that the body is capable of giving rise to the wholesome.

Question: Since unwholesome states arise, why is it said that the body is the root? Answer: The body is rooted in craving. To explain that craving is the root means that because of craving there is craving;
this craving is precisely *tṛṣṇā* (thirsting desire). Because of *tṛṣṇā*, there is the body. Therefore, the Mahāyāna Sūtra says:
"The ultimate limit of birth and death has two aspects: first, ignorance (*avidyā*); second, craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*). Because of craving, one receives a body."
Therefore, sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) is the root of the body. Again, it was asked: "What is the root of sensual desire? The answer was: "False conceptualization (*abhūtaparikalpa*) is its root.
This clarifies that false conceptualization is the root of sensual desire. Again, it was asked: "What is the root of false conceptualization? The answer was:
"Perverted perception (*viparyāsa-saṃjñā*) is its root. Why? Because one discriminates forms (*rūpa*) solely because of the existence of perverted perception.
Therefore, because false discrimination is the cause of inverted perception, inverted perception is taken as the root of discrimination. Again, it was asked: "What is the root of inverted perception?
The answer was: "Non-abiding is its root. This statement is difficult to understand; there are two interpretations within the commentary.
The first interpretation states that "non-abiding is its root" clarifies that inverted deluded perceptions do not abide for even a single thought-moment.

If at any time one attains even a single moment of mental abiding, that is itself the True Dharma; it is only because one fails to attain a single moment of mental abiding that it becomes erroneous and inverted.
To illustrate this with a metaphor: when ripples disturb the water, the water is not still and the reflection is distorted;
when the ripples subside, the water becomes level and the reflection is correct. Inverted states are likewise so: if one fails to attain a single moment [of stillness], one remains in error.
Because it abides, it is said that "non-abiding" is the root of deluded thought and inversion.
Second, to say that non-abiding is the root clarifies that inversion is ultimately non-existent;
because it is ultimately non-existent, yet appears as existence to sentient beings, it is said that non-abiding is the root of the perception of inversion. Question: [Regarding] non-...

That "ripening" (*vipāka*) is based on a "substratum" (*mūla*) is difficult to understand. If one were to say there is no substratum, one would fall into positions such as causelessness (*ahetuka*) or spontaneity (*svabhāva*), which would not differ at all from the views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
To briefly illustrate this by comparing the two schools: first, a non-Buddhist might question which of the eleven faculties (*indriya*) is the root;

if one says the five great elements (*mahābhūta*) are the root, they would then question what the root of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) is, and so on. Finally, they would question what the root of ripening itself is.

The original response [to the question] "What is the root of the *ālayavijñāna*? was that it is "ignorance" (*avidyā*). The subsequent challenge [to that] was: "What is the root of ignorance? The response was: "It is the *bhavāsrava* (outflow of existence). Next, the challenge was:

"What is the root of the *bhavāsrava*? The response was: "It is the *rūparāga* (craving for the realm of form). The challenge was then: "What is the root of the *rūparāga*? The response was: "It is the *kāmarāga* (craving for the realm of desire). The challenge was: "What is the root of the *kāmarāga*? The response was: "It is the *ekadeśasthāvarabhūmi* (the stage of abiding in one place). Regarding the meaning of the five *bhūmis*, when one sees the *ekadeśasthāvarabhūmi*, who is its root? The response was: "Desire-love (*kāmarāga*) is the root.

The challenge was: "What is the root of desire-love? The response was: "Form-love (*rūparāga*) is the root. The challenge was: "What is the root of form-love? The response was: "Existence-love (*bhavarāga*) is the root. Next, the challenge was: "What is the root of existence-love? The response was: "Ignorance."
If one asks why, when questioning the root of ignorance, it is said that ignorance has no root, and now [the same] applies here;

and if from the beginning one questions what is wholesome and unwholesome, and finally one questions non-abiding and the absence of a root—what is the difference? For now, based on two interpretations, this differs from the traditional view in one respect:
first, according to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, there is the doctrine of five stages (*pañca-bhūmi*), whereas the Sāṃkhya system [posits]... [text fragment ends].
There are twenty-five categories of truth (*tattva*), yet the Bodhisattvas have never held such views; rather, they mistakenly claim that sentient beings possess these various phenomena.
Now, the Bodhisattvas refute them by showing they cannot be apprehended, and thus speak of "non-abiding" and "having no root.
At times they employ an analogy: it is like finding money in a dream and drinking wine; while drinking the wine, they fight one another, and this very fighting is what constitutes their consent.
The official asked, "What was your intention in fighting? Since you drank wine, how did you get the money for the wine?

How could you have obtained the money? He simply did not know; even now it is the same. Because he cannot account for this inversion, it is said that there is no fundamental basis. This is a refutation of a position, not the establishment of one.
Second, clarifying that there has never been a cause, yet there has never been an absence of a cause; cause and non-cause [are thus distinguished].
Because they are all based on inverted views—claiming there is a cause while being questioned about that cause—it is said that they have no abiding place and no fundamental basis;
thus, they differ from others.
○ At that time, there was a goddess in Vimalakīrti’s room. (Chapter Two: Śāriputra and the Goddess Discuss)
The reason sentient beings have this woman is ultimately because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest as reflections of one another to provide the conditions for opening the way toward benefit;
previously Vimalakīrti employed the skillful means of a man, while today this goddess employs the skillful means of a woman.
Thus Master Zhaolun said: "As for that which can be both celestial and human, how could it be something that heaven and humanity are capable of producing? It is certainly not so."
Because a deva is not inherently a human, it is able to be a deva and able to be a human; it is the same now as well.
That which can be male or female is not something that males or females themselves can produce; rather, it is that which is neither male nor female that can produce males and females. Question:

As for this heavenly maiden, how does the Śāriputra discourse on sentient beings differ from the previous passage concerning Mañjuśrī and the layman? Answer: Generally speaking, they are not different. Why is this?
Both chapters generally aim to enable one to recognize the true nature of sentient beings;
since ordinary people cannot know the true nature of sentient beings, these two chapters do not differ in this regard. However, there is a distinction in their specific approach. Why is this?

In the preceding section, Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti discuss sentient beings from a general perspective, whereas here, the heavenly maiden and Śāriputra discuss them from a specific perspective. Thus, the statements differ.

The preceding discussion on "pervasion" (sāmānya) directly addressed sentient beings as being like illusions, like mirages, and like the thirteen bases (*āyatana*), because the discourse on sentient beings pervades all things.
Now, the present discussion on "distinction" (viśeṣa) specifically addresses men and women;
it states that "man" is unattainable and "woman" is unattainable, and that "woman" is unattainable and "woman" is unattainable—this is why it is called "distinction."
Furthermore, as for these two types of persons encompassing all people: how so? As already clarified previously, men and women encompass all;
gods and humans encompass all; and monastics and laypeople encompass all. Therefore, these two types of persons encompass all.

Since the two types of persons encompass all, the discourse concerning these two persons is itself the discourse concerning all people. This discourse concerning these two persons cannot be found [as something separate].

"Nothing at all can be apprehended. [Question: Now, in this treatise, why is it that while discussing sentient beings, one discusses men and women? [Answer: It is explained that because of men and women, there exist all sentient beings.
Why is this? Because a man perceives a woman, a woman perceives a man; a woman perceives a man, and a man perceives a woman.
A woman desires a woman, a man desires a man; a man desires a woman, and a woman desires a man. It is by reason of men and women [that all this arises].

Therefore, craving arises from views; because there is craving and views, there is the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*); because there is the Truth of Origination, there is the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

When suffering and origination exist together, this is precisely the cycle of birth and death. Question: A sutra states that the fundamental limit of birth and death consists of two things, namely ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Why, then, do you now say that views and craving are the root? Answer: It is simply because [the sutra] speaks of "views."
Because this ignorance is ignorance, views arise; thus the *Śāstra* says that when delusion (*moha*) is predominant, it is termed "view.
For this reason, this treatise discusses men and women: since a man cannot be apprehended, there is no man;
since a woman cannot be apprehended, there is no woman. With neither man nor woman, there is neither craving nor view; with neither craving nor view, there is nothing [further].
Because sentient beings [distinguish] between these two, the two individuals discussed here are male and female.
At that time, there was a goddess in the room of Vimalakīrti who, seeing the devas and humans and hearing the Dharma he preached,
manifested her form.
Regarding this passage, there are seven sections, which for now shall be divided into three: first, the origin of the doctrinal discussion; second, the actual doctrinal discussion;

and third, the traces of the Buddha. This is the first section. As for the heavenly maiden, Master Kumārajīva said she was the deity of the "Eight Inconceivable Mansions" from the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
When the person reaches emptiness, they become identical to the formless, appearing simultaneously throughout the ten directions without ever ceasing.
There is a dwelling, yet it is not a dwelling, because it conforms to worldly convention; it has never possessed a deity, yet it possesses a deity, because it conforms to worldly convention.
This dwelling differs from the dwellings of ordinary people through eight inconceivable qualities.

Because this deity differs from the deities of ordinary people—being the deity of the *dharmakāya* Bodhisattva—it is said that "there is a heavenly maiden in the chamber. Upon seeing the Great Beings and hearing [them speak],...
There are two intentions regarding the manifestation of the body through the preaching of the Dharma: first, to open the way for those above; second, to rebuke the śrāvakas below.
"Opening the way for those above" refers to making offerings to bodhisattvas and the True Dharma; "rebuking the śrāvakas" refers to the discourse with Śāriputra.
As for the statement, "seeing the Great Man and hearing the preaching of the Dharma," it means seeing Mañjuśrī and the other bodhisattvas.
Because they have come to hear the inconceivable Dharma described above, it is said that they "see the great beings and hear the Dharma they preach.
As for their manifesting their bodies: the devas were originally hidden, but now they appear immediately. Why did the goddesses hide? The layman [Vimalakīrti] said: "The room is empty;
since the objects are empty, the spirits are likewise absent. Now that there are objects in the room, the spirits appear before us. When they were hidden, it was because [the room] was empty."

Having perfected the skillful means of emptiness, he now manifests the skillful means of existence. Whether hidden or manifest, whether revealed or concealed, all are for the purpose of opening the path for sentient beings;
they are all skillful means. Because what was previously concealed is now manifested as a skillful means, it is said that "he manifests his body."
He immediately scattered celestial flowers over the Bodhisattvas and the great disciples;

when the flowers reached the Bodhisattvas, they all fell away, but upon reaching the great disciples, they stuck and did not fall. All the disciples, despite their supernatural powers, were unable to make the flowers fall away.

"Scattering heavenly flowers" constitutes the second section, the Correct Discourse on the Meaning (*samyak-artha-viniścaya*). This is divided into three parts: first, the discourse on the original body;

second, the discourse on the transformed body; and third, the discourse on the restored body. Regarding the first: the phrase "scattering heavenly flowers" indicates that because the flowers were intended as the subject of the discourse, the goddesses scattered them.
Furthermore, the scattering of flowers was intended to demonstrate veneration and also to humble those [who held opposing views].

The "lesser path" (hīnayāna) is thus the scattering of flowers. To speak of the flower as the treatise means that a bodhisattva may rely on either the treatise of the fruit of reliance (*niśraya-phala*) or the treatise of the true fruit (*bhūta-phala*).

The flower is the fruit of reliance, while the body is the true fruit. Within the true fruit, there is either the treatise of the original body, the treatise of the transformed body, or the treatise of the [re-]manifested body;
the three karmas are all for this reason. Why is this so? Because the bodhisattva has no reliance.
The various unimpeded manifestations—whether as worlds, radiance, fragrant flowers, or buddha-fields—are according to the faith of sentient beings.
Just as the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa perceived the Buddha’s eighty chambers as suddenly vast and expansive, and the foul earth as suddenly pure, thereby resolving his doubts;

or as [the Buddha] answered the doubt of Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra: how could a chamber that is narrow not be narrow? Thus one knows that although the lifespan is short, it is not short, and although the light is [dim], it is not dim.
The discourse on illumination (*prabhā-vāda*) is as described in the nineteenth fascicle of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, where a light suddenly appeared amidst the great assembly;
it was not blue when seen as blue, nor yellow when seen as yellow, and so forth—this refers precisely to the refutation by King Śrīdharman.

The discourse on fragrance and flavor (*gandha-rasa-vāda*) corresponds to the "Fragrant Accumulation" chapter (*Gandhavyūha-parivarta*) later in this sutra. Now, within this context, the discourse on scattering flowers (*puṣpa-vikiraṇa-vāda*) involves merely scattering a single flower.
When the flowers were scattered, the Bodhisattvas were challenged by the Bodhisattvas, and the Bodhisattvas were challenged by the Great Disciples;
those who were challenged by the Bodhisattvas all fell away. This was the Bodhisattvas’ unimpeded exchange of questions and answers.
When the flowers were scattered, it was an inquiry based on non-reliance; when the Bodhisattvas could remove the flowers, it was an answer based on non-reliance. This was the unimpeded inquiry.
The question was unimpeded and the answer was unimpeded; because both question and answer were unimpeded, the flower did not adhere to the body.
When it came to the Great Disciples, the question was unimpeded but the answer was obstructed, and thus the flower adhered and did not fall.
Because an unimpeded question met with an obstructed answer, the answer failed to be a true answer; hence it is said.

That the flowers do not depart—whereas all the disciples, through their supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), were unable to make them depart—is precisely because of the supernormal power of mental action (*manas-karma-abhijñā*) surpassing that of the hands.
When the great disciples now use their supernatural powers to remove [the flowers] or not, this is simply a matter of whether their supernormal power of mental action is unimpeded or not.
As for why they can or cannot remove them, this is due to the absence of obstruction.
Because the flower exists, the obstructed mind does not depart; yet the unobstructed flower and the unobstructed mind do not cause the flower to become attached.

Because the obstructed mind exists, the flower immediately becomes attached. It is not only that the unobstructed [mind] is attached to the obstructed [flower], but it is also attached to the unobstructed mind.
It is not only that the unobstructed [mind] is not attached to the obstructed [flower], but it is also not attached to the obstructed mind.
"Those who are unimpeded are all attached to the unimpeded, while those who are impeded are all detached from the unimpeded.
At that time, a deva asked Śāriputra, "For what reason did you remove these flowers? He replied, "These flowers are not in accordance with the Dharma;
therefore, I removed them. The deva said, "Do not say that these flowers are not in accordance with the Dharma. Why is this? Because these flowers have no [attachment]."
"Venerable sir, you have merely given rise to a conceptual discrimination yourself. If one who has gone forth in the Buddha-dharma engages in conceptual discrimination, it is contrary to the Dharma;

if there is no conceptual discrimination, that is in accordance with the Dharma. To observe that the flowers do not adhere to the bodhisattvas is because they have already severed all conceptual discriminations.
It is, for example, like when a person is afraid and non-human spirits find an opportunity to take advantage of them."

Because these disciples fear birth and death, forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and tactile objects gain mastery over them. For one who has already abandoned this fear, all five desires are powerless.
If their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted, the flowers will cling to their bodies; if their habitual tendencies are exhausted, the flowers will not cling.

At that time, a deva asked why he had removed the flowers. Śāriputra, being foremost among the śrāvakas in the exposition of the Dharma through speech, was therefore questioned by the deva as to why he had removed the flowers.
Śāriputra replied, "I removed these flowers because they were not in accordance with the Dharma.
As for what is meant by "not in accordance with the Dharma," it is because flowers are originally things cherished by worldly people and do not belong to the discipline of the Vinaya.

Because it is not the dharma of a śramaṇa, it is called "not according with the Dharma" (*ayathādharma*). Furthermore, when it is said "not according with the Dharma," it means that the *pūrvayāna* (earlier) Dharma departs as soon as it arises;
whereas this [lotus] does not depart even now. Because this is not the *pūrvayāna* Dharma, it is called "not according with the Dharma.
Śakra said: "Do not say that these flowers are not according with the Dharma. Śāriputra said: "The flowers are not according with the Dharma. Śakra said: [They are].
“Daughter, do not say now that the flowers are improper; rather, it is Śāriputra who is improper. Why?
Because flowers have no mind to speak of what is proper or improper. It is because you, O Venerable One, judge them as proper or improper that they appear so.
Whether something is proper or improper depends upon Śāriputra. If one has entered the Buddha-dharma and yet makes such discriminations, [one is not truly a follower].”
Regarding the second section on "that which accords with the Dharma": if one discriminates between what accords with the Dharma and what does not accord with the Dharma, both are non-Dharmic;
if one does not discriminate between what accords with the Dharma and what does not accord with the Dharma, both are Dharmic.

Śāriputra, by discriminating between what accords with the Dharma and what does not accord with the Dharma, all such [discriminations] belong to Śāriputra. A bodhisattva does not discriminate between what accords with the Dharma and what does not.
"Those who act in accordance with the Dharma are all Bodhisattvas. This is like the analogy of a person who, out of fear, does not lift [something];

the preceding part illustrates the point, and the following part provides the application. Now, regarding the statement that when a person is afraid, non-humans find an opportunity to take advantage of them, Master Shi (Kumārajīva) said:
"In foreign lands there are rākṣasas who transform themselves into horses. Someone might ride upon one, and the rākṣasa would speak from its head, saying..."
When the horse is excellent, this person immediately draws his sword and says, "Is the sword not excellent?
This person, because he does not fear the rākṣasa, leaves the rākṣasa with no recourse against him. Likewise, because the disciple fears birth and death, [the following occurs].
Second, the combined analogy has two parts; the first clarifies that because the śrāvaka fears birth and death, [it is like] a flower.

The Bodhisattva who wears [the flowers] does not fear birth and death, and therefore does not wear them. Next, it is said that because the Śrāvakas have not yet exhausted their residual habits (*vāsanā*), the flowers stick to their bodies;
whereas because the Bodhisattvas have exhausted their residual habits, the flowers do not stick to their bodies.

However, this statement is difficult to understand. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "If a Bodhisattva has severed their residual habits and attained Buddhahood, what further thing would they need to sever? Indeed, it is great.
Regarding this treatise, there are two explanations: first, the followers of the Hīnayāna claim that a bodhisattva has not yet severed even a single hair’s breadth of affliction (*kleśa*);

second, the followers of the Mahāyāna claim that a bodhisattva attains non-arising (*anutpāda*) and thus severs the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of afflictions entirely. This treatise now refutes both of these interpretations;
we shall now explain according to reality whether a bodhisattva has severed afflictions entirely or has not yet severed their habit-energies. If it were as [the former] claims...
How can it be said that a bodhisattva has severed their residual habits (*vāsanā*)? Master Kumārajīva had two interpretations. First, he said: "Both śrāvakas and bodhisattvas possess residual habits.
However, when a śrāvaka possesses residual habits, they immediately give rise [to afflictions]; whereas when a bodhisattva possesses residual habits, the habits do not give rise [to afflictions].

Because they arise, one says they exist; because they do not arise, one says they do not exist. Since the mind neither arises nor does not arise, one says they both exist and do not exist; this is not a case of being neither."
Because of the cessation or non-cessation [of these habits], it is said that they exist or do not exist. The commentary explains:

Śrāvakas have the habituation (*vāsanā*) of the three realms, whereas Bodhisattvas lack the habituation within the three realms; they possess the habituation of the merit of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti-guṇa*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that "having habituation" refers to having the habituation of the merit of mindfulness of the Buddha.
This statement that they "lack habituation" means they lack the habituation of the three realms. Thus, the Sūtras and the Śāstras each have their own [perspective].
There is no contradiction in my intention.
Śāriputra asked, "Goddess, how long has it been since you have dwelt in this room? She replied, "I have dwelt in this room for as long as the Venerable One has possessed liberation.
Śāriputra said, "Have you dwelt here for that long? The goddess said, "How long has it been since the Venerable One attained liberation?"
Śāriputra remained silent for a long time without answering. Śāriputra said:
"The goddess has resided in this room for a very long time. Regarding the arrival of these words, there may be two possible intentions:
either she is praising [the Buddha], or she is asking why [the gods] above have been subdued by the supernatural power of this celestial goddess."

Regarding the statement that Śāriputra’s eloquence was surpassed: this eloquence arises because internally he possesses non-reliant wisdom (*anāśrita-prajñā*) and externally he possesses unimpeded eloquence (*apratihata-pratibhāna*).
He must have long cultivated the three bases of merit (*tri-skandha*) while dwelling in his chamber; therefore, he asked, "How long have you been staying in this room?
This is precisely a question concerning the duration of his stay—whether it is long or short. Furthermore, out of astonishment and wonder, he asked, "Who is this goddess?"
Possessing such supernatural power and eloquence—with wisdom that is inwardly independent and eloquence that is outwardly unimpeded—one should no longer receive a female body.
For this reason, he asked: "How long has it been since you stayed in this room?
He replied: "I have stayed in this room for as long as the elder’s liberation has been manifest in his upper body."

The disciple asked how long [the girl] had been there; today, because the heavenly maiden has destroyed the notion of duration, she now answers, "I have dwelt in this chamber as long as you have realized unconditioned liberation.
She addresses Śāriputra as "Venerable One" (*sthavira*); being sixty years of age constitutes being a "Venerable One," for at that time Śāriputra was also old.
An external text states: "At sixty, one is called 'Venerable' (*sthavira*); one no longer exerts oneself but is instead employed by others."
The term "venerable" (*sthavira*) refers to one who has attained liberation. There are two kinds of liberation: first, conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and second, unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Regarding conditioned liberation, it is the liberation of the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcadharmakāya*). As a verse states: "The preceding and all dharmas are subsumed within the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
Here, "the preceding" refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), while the remaining four [of the Dharma-body] are the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). Fifth.
Since the aggregates (*skandhas*) are all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), the fivefold Dharma-body and liberation are also conditioned.
That which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and *nirvāṇa*; this is unconditioned liberation. Now, this question concerns unconditioned liberation.
Śāriputra said, "Have you been staying here for so long? The heavenly maiden replied, "I have been staying in this room for as long as you have realized [your own realization]."
Wuwei said to Śāriputra: "If that is so, then the deva has been in this room for a long time. Why?

Because from the beginningless past, this unconditioned liberation (asaṃskṛta-vimukti) has inherently existed here. Master Zhaolun said: "It transcends all mundane existence with its profound and vast capacity;
it measures the great void with permanence. One follows it but finds no trace of its length; one looks for its head but beholds nothing. Thus it is.
[The Venerable One] said: "I know that my liberation has come long ago; since my liberation has been long, the Deva has also dwelt in this chamber for a long time.
Is it not therefore said that he has dwelt here for a long time? The Deva replied: "Venerable sir, your liberation is likewise as if it were long-standing.

This immediately challenges the notion of the duration of liberation, clarifying that *asaṃskṛta-vimukti* (unconditioned liberation) is the cessation of conceptual proliferation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is without arising or ceasing, without beginning or end, and without duration or non-duration.
"What is near? Is unconditioned liberation long-lasting? If there were duration—whether long or near—it would entail coming and going, arising and ceasing;
yet it is not so. Therefore, the present inquiry asks: "How can liberation also be long-lasting? Śāriputra remained silent and did not answer for two reasons:

first, he did not answer because his position was进退 (进退 *jìntuì*, i.e., whether to advance or retreat); second, had he answered that there is neither duration nor proximity, it would have accorded with the truth.

If one claims that liberation has duration—whether long or short—it contradicts the previous statement and thus constitutes a fault. If one says there is such duration, it does not violate the prior words, yet it harms the nature of liberation.
To contradict the prior words, the celestial maiden previously said, "Is this liberation as long-lived as an elder?

and Śāriputra acknowledged, "It is indeed this long. This clarifies that liberation is eternal. Now, if one were to say that liberation has no duration, it would contradict the aforementioned statement. If one were to say...
There is liberation whether it be long or short, yet he remained silent, not knowing what to say.

Second, since Śāriputra possessed sharp faculties, upon hearing this reprimand, he attained profound awakening to liberation—that there is neither long nor short, nor is there anything that is not long or short;
therefore, he remained silent. Furthermore, there are three grades of silence: inferior, middling, and superior. Inferior silence refers to that of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Because he did not understand the characteristics of dharmas, Śāriputra remained silent. Among various forms of silence, this "silence" refers to Śāriputra’s realization that the Way is ineffable;

fearing that speech might harm the Way, he remained silent. The former "silence" refers to Vimalakīrti’s realization that the Way is ineffable, yet his speech does not contradict the Way, and thus he remained silent.
Now, Śāriputra understands that liberation issues forth from beyond words and speech, and fears that verbal expression might cause injury.
He remained silent because he was liberated.
The deva asked, "How is it that one who is so venerable and possessed of great wisdom remains silent? He replied, "Liberation is beyond verbal expression;
therefore, I do not know what to say. The deva said, "Verbal expressions and written characters are all the very marks of liberation. Why is this so?"
What is liberation? It is neither internal nor external, nor does it abide between the two; even words are neither internal nor external, nor do they abide between the two.
Therefore, Śāriputra, there is no teaching of liberation apart from words. Why is this?
Because all dharmas possess the characteristic of liberation.
The deva said: "How is it that you, an elder of great wisdom, remain silent while coming forward to reproach me for what is right or wrong speech?
This clarifies that the śrāvaka cannot speak the holy Dharma. Now, by reproaching my silence, you clarify that the śrāvaka cannot maintain holy silence.
As for those born above, they obtain neither life nor death; whether in birth or death, whether in speech or silence, all are entirely non-existent."
[The interlocutor] asks: "Since this is so, why does the one of great wisdom remain silent?
He replies: "Liberation is that which cannot be expressed in speech. Śāriputra answers in accordance with liberation, clarifying that liberation is without words or speech;
therefore, he remains silent. The Deva says: "If words and letters are all the characteristics of liberation, this clarifies that Śāriputra perceives the One."
Seeing these two, one knows only liberation as being beyond verbal expression, yet does not know that verbal expression itself is liberation;

therefore, it is said that liberation emerges from the waters of verbal expression. Just as the "self" of the calf [is known] through the *Tattvārthā-alaṃkāra-śāstra*, the *ālayavijñāna* transcends the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*).
Śāriputra was likewise: he knew only liberation as being cut off from the four propositions, but did not know the four propositions themselves.

Because it is liberation itself, it is said that all characters and words are the mark of liberation. Why is this? Because the interpretation of characters and words is itself liberation, as the text states.
Why is this? The statement that "all dharmas are the mark of liberation" is a further explanation clarifying that everything is the mark of liberation.
Since it has been said that all dharmas are the mark of liberation, [so too are] characters and words...
"Is it not the case that a single dharma is liberation? Or rather, that all dharmas are liberation, and liberation is all dharmas?
Śāriputra said, "Does one not further attain liberation by being free from lust, anger, and delusion? The Deva replied, "The Buddha spoke for the sake of those with increased [afflictions]."

Those with overweening pride say that liberation consists merely in being free from lust, anger, and delusion; however, for those without such overweening pride, the Buddha says that the very nature of lust, anger, and delusion is itself liberation.
Śāriputra asked, "Is it not the case that one attains liberation by being free from the three poisons? Śāriputra and others raised this objection.
The goddess said: "If all dharmas were themselves liberation, then the three poisons would also be all dharmas, and the three poisons would also be liberation.
Since the Buddha taught that being free from the three poisons constitutes liberation, if that were so, one should be liberated through the abandonment of all words and letters.
It is for this reason that I ask this question. The goddess replied: "The Buddha spoke thus for those who possess overweening pride."
To be free from the three poisons is liberation alone. However, regarding Śāriputra’s arrival here, there have been four successive instances of being defeated:

first by a flower, second by speech, third by silence, and fourth by both speech and silence—each time he was established in defeat. Now, this is a case of being defeated by citing the Buddha’s own words;
whether by speaking, by remaining silent, or by citing [the scripture], none of these can be established as valid. This is what is meant by "citing the Buddha’s words."
Śāriputra said: "The Buddha has taught that freedom from the three poisons is liberation; why do you say that all dharmas are themselves liberation?
Therefore, the Heavenly One now answers: "The Buddha spoke of freedom from the three poisons as liberation only for those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Why? Because those with overweening pride claim to have severed what they have not severed, and claim to have attained what they have not attained."
The severing of afflictions refers to attaining liberation; for such a person, the Buddha teaches that one attains liberation only when afflictions are completely severed.
However, for a Mahāsattva of profound practice, he teaches that the three poisons are themselves liberation.
Thus, it is said: "Lust is itself the Way; so too are anger and delusion. Within these three dharmas lie the immeasurable paths of all Buddhas."
Since each of these explanations has its own intended meaning, how should one establish a definitive understanding? Therefore, it is said:

"The Buddha taught that for those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*), freedom from the three poisons constitutes liberation; yet if there is no overweening pride, the three poisons themselves are liberation."
Śāriputra said, "Excellent, excellent, O goddess! What have you attained, and by what means have you realized it, that your eloquence is such as this?
The goddess replied, "I have no attainment and no realization; therefore, my eloquence is such as this. Why is this?
If one were to have attainment or realization, one would be considered arrogant regarding the Buddha-dharma."
Śāriputra said, "Excellent, excellent! Śāriputra, knowing himself to be inferior, humbly yielded to the Bodhisattva;
therefore, he praised him, exclaiming, "Excellent, excellent!

Since Śāriputra had been bested by the Goddess’s eloquence, he now questioned her regarding that eloquence, saying: "What have you attained? What have you realized, such that your eloquence is thus? She replied: "I..."
There is nothing to be attained and nothing to be realized; discernment is thus. To critique and praise is the speech of the śrāvaka, while silence is not their speech;

self-deprecation is their praise, while praise is not theirs. For the śrāvaka, all dharmas are entirely non-existent—not only are all dharmas non-existent for the śrāvaka, but the śrāvaka themselves are also entirely non-existent.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there are none..."

There are two vehicles. Question: What constitutes attainment (*prāpti*) and what constitutes realization (*sākṣātkriyā*)? Explanation: Attainment refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), while realization refers to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) is attainment, and the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is realization. For the Śrāvaka, there is both attainment and realization;
that which is attained is "having something to be attained," and having something to be attained implies an external basis as well as an internal [basis].

The Bodhisattva’s state of non-obstruction consists in neither attainment nor realization; because there is nothing to be attained, there is nothing to be grasped externally, and because there is no obstruction internally, there is no reliance.
As the Great Sūtra states: "Those who have something to attain lack the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), while those who have nothing to attain possess the four analytical knowledges.
Thus, the present answer that there is "neither attainment nor realization" is established precisely in this manner. Now, as for the words...

"No attainment and no realization" does not mean that there is nothing to be attained or realized; rather, it clarifies that one attains that which is unattainable and realizes that which is unrealizable, and is thus called "no attainment and no realization.
To claim that there is attainment and realization when all phenomena are without attainment or realization is the mark of one who possesses overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Śāriputra asked the goddess, "In which of the three vehicles do you aspire? The goddess replied, "Because I transform sentient beings through the Dharma of the Śrāvaka, I am a Śrāvaka;
because I transform sentient beings through the Dharma of causes and conditions, I am a Pratyekabuddha;
and because I transform sentient beings through the Dharma of great compassion, I am of the Mahāyāna."
Śāriputra asked the goddess, "In which of the three vehicles do you seek to aspire? The goddess replied, "I have neither attainment nor realization;
therefore, my eloquence is such as this. Śāriputra then asked again, "To which of the three vehicles do you aspire?
Since the Buddha-dharma does not exist outside of the three vehicles, I ask this question. The goddess said, "The Dharma of the śrāvakas is a transformation."
The lower goddess replied: "Please understand my intention: it is neither three nor one, neither great nor small;
you should not ask about being great or small, or three or one.
Śāriputra, it is like a person who enters a campaka grove and smells only the campaka, not other fragrances. Thus, if...
Upon entering this room, one perceives only the fragrance of the Buddha’s merits and takes no pleasure in the fragrance of the merits of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Śāriputra, when Śakras, Brahmās, the Four Heavenly Kings, devas, nāgas, spirits, or ghosts enter this room, they hear this superior person expounding the True Dharma;
they all take pleasure in the fragrance of the Buddha’s merits and resolve their minds [upon enlightenment].
"Śāriputra, I have resided in this room for twelve years, yet I have never heard any teaching on the Dharma of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas;
I have heard only the inconceivable Buddha-Dharma of the Bodhisattvas' great kindness and great compassion."
Śāriputra, it is like a person who enters a campaka grove and perceives only the scent of the campaka;

this illustrates that there is neither three nor one, neither great nor small, and no notion of "no-existence. Therefore, what is clarified here is that although there is neither great nor small, there is no loss of the distinction between great and small;
thus it is said, "entering a campaka grove, one perceives only the scent of the campaka. This corresponds to the analogy in the text.
"Śāriputra, as for my saying 'I have dwelt in this room for twelve years,' this is merely a conventional expression of its duration;

it clarifies that there is neither duration nor non-duration, yet by saying there is neither duration nor non-duration, I thereby clarify that although there is neither duration nor non-duration, one does not lose track of duration and non-duration.
This is why I now say, 'I have dwelt in this room for twelve years. Why do I speak of 'twelve' specifically?"
