What is attained here? At the beginning of this sutra, it is revealed that the householder is the host and the Tathāgata commands him to be the guest;
thus, Mañjuśrī is the guest for the most part, while the householder is the guest less frequently. Here, the increase in number clarifies the meaning as stated in the text:

"The seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) serve as the seeds. Regarding the seven consciousnesses, there are two kinds: first, the seven consciousness-elements (*vijñānadhātu*), and second, the six [consciousnesses].

Consciousness together with the mind-faculty (*manas*) constitutes the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*). Regarding these two [categories], the seven stations of consciousness are as follows: those in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) among humans and devas constitute one;

the three dhyānas constitute three; and the three formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) constitute three. Combined, these make seven stations of consciousness. Question: For what reason are the four miserable destinies (*apāya*) of the desire realm not considered stations of consciousness? Why is the fourth dhyāna of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) not a station? And why are the formless realms, specifically the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), not stations? Explanation: There are four reasons. First, the four miserable destinies lack the stability required for consciousness to dwell; they are characterized by intense suffering and instability.

Second, the fourth dhyāna is a state of extreme tranquility where the movement of consciousness is suspended, rendering it unsuitable as a "station" for active consciousness. Third, the formless realms lack physical form (*rūpa*), and since consciousness requires a basis to dwell upon, they cannot function as stations in the same way. Fourth, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is so subtle that perception itself is nearly extinguished, making it impossible for consciousness to maintain its functional activity there. Thus, these are excluded from the list of stations of consciousness.

Regarding "the realms of existence are not places of abiding": consciousness does not delight in dwelling in the suffering of the four realms of existence; it does not delight in dwelling in the fourth dhyāna or the heaven of non-perception because there is no mental consciousness there;
and it does not delight in dwelling in the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling because the mind and consciousness have been extinguished.
The eight wrong views and nine afflictions may be understood as explained elsewhere, and so forth.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa exclaimed, "Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī! You have spoken these words most skillfully; it is truly as you have said.
The host of afflictions is the seed of the Tathāgata. We can no longer bring ourselves to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
yet even those who have committed the five sins of immediate retribution are still able to give rise to such a thought."
Having been born into the Buddha-dharma, we are now forever unable to give rise to it;

just as a man whose sense organs are destroyed can no longer derive benefit from the five desires, so too for these śrāvakas who have severed their fetters, there is no further benefit within the Buddha-dharma, and they never again aspire to it.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī, ordinary worldlings still possess the capacity for repentance and renewal toward the Buddha-dharma.

The śrāvakas, however, do not possess this. Why is that? Because while ordinary persons, upon hearing the Buddha-dharma, can give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment and ensure the non-interruption of the Three Jewels, even if śrāvakas were to hear of the Buddha’s powers and fearlessnesses throughout their entire lives, they would never be able to produce the intention for unsurpassed enlightenment.

Furthermore, it is said that if Śrāvakas cannot resolve their minds toward enlightenment even after hearing this Dharma for the rest of their lives, these words are likewise difficult to understand. Why?

Because if it is said they cannot resolve their minds for the rest of their lives, for what purpose does the *Lotus Sūtra* bestow predictions of enlightenment upon them? The explanation is as follows:
This is merely a temporary leveling of claims, like comparing it to scolding a child; when a child does something, [the parent] scolds them.
If [Kāśyapa] did not succeed, he was immediately rebuked, saying, "Even if you fail until old age, it is not necessarily that you will never succeed.
This was merely a sudden scolding intended to bring him to awakening. Question: What is the meaning of Kāśyapa’s own statement that he was unable to generate the *bodhicitta*?
Explanation: If Mañjuśrī had spoken this himself as a layman, the *śrāvakas* would not have believed him; therefore, Kāśyapa, being a great *arhat*, spoke for himself.
Because he was unable [to do so], everyone believed him.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana who asked Vimalakīrti, "Householder, who are all these people—your father, mother, wife, children, kinsmen, relatives, officials, commoners, and friends?

And who are your male and female servants, slaves, elephants, [horses, oxen, sheep, goats, poultry, pigs, dogs, monkeys, parrots, mainas, peacocks, pheasants, partridges, quails, and other such creatures]?"
"Where have all the chariots gone?
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly who had attained the lower grade of the first [stage]. First, this explains the meaning of contravening the skillful means;
now, secondly, this text comes to explain the conformity with existence. Having come from afar through the void, he was born in an empty room and remained in that empty room.
All things, as well as retinues, elephants, horses, and so forth, are entirely non-existent; it is for this reason that I now ask.
Furthermore, householder, the reason your room is empty and you have no retinue is yet another kind of skillful means. Why?
Because the perceptions of sentient beings differ. Those who rely on worldly ears and eyes see the Bodhisattva as having parents and possessing [a household].
His wife, children, and others then believed that the Bodhisattva truly had parents, a wife, children, and kinsmen;

yet because the Bodhisattva wished for sentient beings to become like himself and for himself to become like them, he shared in having a family with sentient beings while remaining truly detached from them.
Because sentient beings truly believed the Bodhisattva had a family, he universally manifested this to answer Vimalakīrti extensively.
He replied.
Then Vimalakīrti answered in verse: "The Perfection of Wisdom is the mother of Bodhisattvas; Expedient Means is their father.
All Teachers of the Multitude are born from these."

Regarding the statement that "the Perfection of Wisdom is the mother of Bodhisattvas," the treatises explain that the parents differ. First, the *Fuhui* (Merit and Wisdom) distinction defines the parents:
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter on Non-Realization, states that the six perfections are the parents. The Master of Treatises explains this as follows:
the five perfections constitute the gate of merit (*puṇya*), while the perfection of wisdom constitutes the gate of knowledge (*jñāna*). This is the second [point].
Regarding the classification of Prajñā as the mother and father, and Pratyutpanna Samādhi as the father:
while the two types of wisdom (prajñā) are classified as the mother and father in this very text, the Buddha has two kinds of parents: first, the Dharma-parents; second, the human parents.
What is the meaning of having two sets of parents? The explanation is that there are two bodies: first, the birth-body (janma-kāya); second, [the dharma-body].
Since the Dharma-body possesses two bodies, it likewise has two fathers and mothers. What are they? The Dharma-body of Śākyamuni takes the two wisdoms as its parents;
his birth-body takes Śuddhodana and Māyā as its parents. For the layperson as well, there are two [bodies]:

the Dharma-body takes the two wisdoms as its parents, while the *zuànshìnǚ* (the woman who compiled the commentary) serves as the parents for the birth-body. Thus, both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have two sets of parents.
Birth also has two kinds of parents. What are they? Sentient beings take ignorance as their father and craving as their mother;
these are the fundamental parents. Because of these fundamental parents, there are the "parents" such as Zhang and Wang, who are the derivative parents.
Now, all the teachers of the multitude arise from the wisdom of liberation and skillful means; they are likewise all [the teachers of the multitude].

Birth arises together from ignorance and craving. Furthermore, regarding these two bodies—the Dharma-body and the birth-body—if their parents are identical for the Dharma-body, they are not identical for the birth-body;
what is the reason for this? The explanation is as follows: because the Dharma-body is identical, its parents are identical;
because the birth-body is not identical, its parents are not identical. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
Because the Tathāgatas of the ten directions share a single Dharma-body, their Dharma-bodies are identical;

yet because their birth-bodies may be either sixteen feet or eight thousand feet tall, their birth-bodies are not identical. It is the same for sentient beings: all sentient beings are born from ignorance and craving, and thus they are the same;
yet because there are distinctions such as the noble and the common, or the myriad clans, they are not identical. Question: Why is this so?

One might wonder: in this context, why is "reality" (satya) treated as the mother and "expedient means" (upāya) as the father, rather than treating expedient means as the mother and reality as the father?

The explanation says: Furthermore, one may question the underlying intention behind taking craving (tṛṣṇā) as the mother and ignorance (avidyā) as the father, rather than taking ignorance as the mother and craving as the father.

The response to this objection states: While both alternatives are logically possible, it is not so [in this case]. It is explained that while both would generally be acceptable, it is not done in that way.
This [phrase] pursues the meaning to manifest that actual wisdom (*bhūtaprajñā*) illuminates serenely and is capable of generating the meaning of skillful means (*upāya*).

The teaching and metaphors are such that, just as one who travels through space does not linger and one who traverses existence (*bhava*) does not cling, so too should one be able to teach the meaning and generate the "mother" (the source), and be able to teach and assign the "father" (the progenitor).

Sentient beings are also like this: they are born because of craving (*tṛṣṇā*); it is through the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of ignorance (*avidyā*) that craving arises. Furthermore, regarding actual wisdom...
Internally reflecting, it is still; externally employing skillful means, it moves. The worldly parents correspond to Heaven and Earth: Heaven moves and is Yang, while Earth is still and is Yin.
Therefore, it is said that the six dragons gallop through Heaven; Heaven never rests for even a moment. One horse travels upon the Earth, moving only occasionally;
thus, Heaven is ultimately in motion while the Earth is ultimately still. Now, the two wisdoms are likewise so. By means of...

The movement of embracing and shifting is equal to Yang (the active principle), and thus it corresponds to Heaven; its essential nature is concentrated and still, and being identical to Yin (the passive principle), it is paired with Earth.
Regarding all the teachers of various paths: having previously clarified that the parents can give birth [to the Way], we now clarify the offspring who are born from them.
If one asks how it is said that the two wisdoms give birth to the Buddha, it is because we now employ these two wisdoms alone.

If one asks: "Since the Buddha exists apart from the two wisdoms, how can it be said that the two wisdoms give rise to him? The explanation is as follows: From the perspective of conventional meaning, this is so.
In the world, parents are the "producers" (the agent) and the child is the "produced" (the object).

Now, although the two wisdoms are in reality not different from the Buddha, for the sake of meaning they are divided into two: the two wisdoms are taken as the "Dharma" and the Buddha as the "person. Thus, the Dharma is the producer.
The person (*pudgala*) is that which is produced, and cause and effect are distinguished as two: wisdom is the cause and the Buddha is the fruit.
Because the cause is able to produce the fruit, it is "that which produces" (*janaka*), and [the fruit] is "that which is produced" (*janya*). However, there are three types of this:

first, the person is the cause and the dharmas are what produce the person; the fruit is likewise so. Second, the cause is able to produce the fruit, which is "that which is produced. Question: What is the cause?
How are these two wisdoms attained, and by what method do they arise such that it is said thus? The explanation is as follows:

traditionally it has been said that the Buddha’s two wisdoms expound the two truths. Since the two wisdoms expound the two truths, taking the knowledge itself as the truth, sentient beings receive the two truths and give rise to the two wisdoms;
thus, these two truths serve as the parents [of the wisdoms]. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
Prajñā is the Mother of the Buddhas; Upāya is either the Father or the Teacher. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"Upāyakauśalya is the Great Teacher’s power of skillful means.
Taking the joy of the Dharma as one's wife, the mind of compassion as one's daughter, the sincere and truthful good heart as one's son, and ultimate emptiness and quiescence as one's dwelling.

Regarding "taking Dharma-joy as one's wife": the preceding section clarified the parents; this section now clarifies the wife and children. There are two types of wives; here, Dharma-joy itself is taken as the wife.
In the world, one takes a wife for the sake of joy; here, the Bodhisattva finds delight in the Dharma for himself, and thus it is said that he takes Dharma-joy as his wife.
This does not merely mean taking the hearing of the Dharma as one's wife; rather, it refers to taking all three forms of wisdom (*trividya*) as Dharma-joy.
Regarding the statement that "compassion is the daughter and sincerity is the son," this next section clarifies that offspring likewise consist of two types.

Here, compassion is designated as the daughter and sincerity as the son because compassion is manifest externally and thus paired with the female, while sincerity abides within and is thus assigned to the male.
Furthermore, compassion is soft and yielding, and therefore it is the daughter; sincerity is... [the son].
Because they are active and functional, they are considered male. [Question: Compassion is the gate of merit (*puṇya*), while sincerity is the gate of wisdom (*prajñā*).

For what reason is meditation female and wisdom male? [Answer: The explanation says that as the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra* states: "One who seeks a son seeks wisdom; one who wishes for a daughter seeks physical excellence.
Physical excellence is the gate of merit. This is clarified within the two types of adornment (*saṃbhāra*)—the Lion’s Pores [Sūtra]—wherein it is shown that the adornment of merit is inferior.
Because wisdom distinguishes between the superior and the inferior, it is for the sake of the excellence of women and the equality of men; thus they are both equal and unequal.
Ultimately empty and quiescent, the previous section clarified the person, while this section clarifies the dwelling. It is not that there was first a person and later a dwelling;

rather, the distinction between "before" and "after" is made solely based on the primary and secondary retributions (*pratyaya-phala*). Since the primary fruit is primary, the previous section clarified the dependent fruit (*niśraya-phala*) as a secondary point.

Therefore, in the subsequent discussion of the "dwelling" (*śālā*), there are likewise two types: first, a dwelling of ten feet square; now, ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) is taken as the dwelling.
Just as a worldly dwelling wards off wind and frost and prevents robbery and theft, so too does this dwelling of ultimate emptiness ward off all views and prevent the various heavenly Māras.
Furthermore, while worldly beings take up residence in dwellings, the Bodhisattva takes up residence in ultimate emptiness.
Because it is empty, it is likened to a house.

The various afflictions of the disciples are turned according to one's will; through the spiritual friends of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), one thereby achieves perfect awakening.
As for "the various afflictions of the disciples are turned according to one's will," this means that by means of the three poisons and all afflictions...
Regarding "being turned according to the will of disciples": it means that the three poisons are rendered non-poisonous, just as a disciple follows and obeys [the teacher].
As for the "factors of the path" (*mārga-aṅga*) as "good friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*): previously, the personal retinue was clarified; now, the good friends are clarified.
A good friend is one who demonstrates what is the path and what is not the path; therefore, the factors of the path are considered good friends.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Great Treatise on Wisdom) states: "The factors of the path serve as the gateway to Nirvana, demonstrating the nature of birth-and-death and opening the way to Nirvana.

The various perfections and dharmas are one's companions, while the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) are the courtesans; singing and reciting the words of the Dharma constitute their music."
Regarding the "various perfections as equal companions": previously the good knowledge was clarified; now the companions are clarified. In the world, everyone has companions;
now the Bodhisattva takes the various perfections (*pāramitās*) as his companions.

This is the first true companion. "Abiding" means abiding together; "practicing" means practicing together. The reason it is said that the various perfections are his companions is that "perfection" (*pāramitā*) is [derived from] *pāra*... [text fragment].
Regarding "crossing from this shore to the other shore," since all the *pāramitās* (perfections) accompany the Bodhisattva, they go along with him.
As for the "various *pāramitās*": there are six *prajñā-pāramitās*, and there are eighteen thousand four hundred; because they are not merely one, they are called the "various *pāramitās*.
Regarding "the four means of integration (*saṃgraha-vastu*) as courtesans": worldly people gather exquisite courtesans to delight themselves and others; now, the Bodhi... [text fragment ends]

The Bodhisattva gathers sentient beings through the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), thereby delighting himself and delighting others. When asked how the Bodhisattva also finds delight while gathering sentient beings, the answer is:
because when sentient beings are gathered by the Bodhisattva through these four means, the Bodhisattva’s own mind immediately experiences joy and happiness.
To chant and recite the words of the Dharma is like the worldly songs of the "bright spring" and the "white water."
Exquisite melodies and beautiful sounds are now the Bodhisattva’s chanting of Dharma words as music;
thus there are two kinds of music, the mundane and the supramundane, which likewise constitute two types of sound.
The garden of dhāraṇī contains the forest trees of untainted (anāsrava) dharmas, the pure and wondrous flowers of the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), and the fruits of liberation and wisdom.
The garden of dhāraṇīs is like a worldly garden where trees are planted, flowers bloom, and fruit is produced. Now, the Bodhisattva takes dhāraṇīs as his garden;
by means of them, he maintains all evils so that they do not arise and maintains all virtues so that they are not lost.
Because nothing is lost, the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment bloom and the fruit of liberation is realized. Since there is this garden, [the Bodhisattva’s cultivation is complete].
Since there are forests and trees, next the untainted (anāsrava) forests and trees are explained. Regarding "the factors of enlightenment" (bodhyaṅga), these are the seven awakenings;
among the thirty-seven [auxiliaries], these are the most excellent. The preceding eightfold right path constitutes the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga);

the seven awakenings constitute the Path of Cultivation (bhāvanāmārga); and liberation constitutes the Path of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣamārga). Thus, the eightfold right path is the forest, the seven awakenings are the flowers, and liberation is the fruit; they comprise the three paths.

Furthermore, the fruit of the knowledge and vision of liberation consists of both conditioned and unconditioned fruits; liberation itself is the unconditioned fruit, while knowledge and vision are the conditioned fruit.
Question: This is the Small Vehicle; why does it explain the Great Vehicle? Answer:
Because both the Great and Small Vehicles possess the three paths.

The bathing pool of the eight liberations is filled with the tranquil waters of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), strewn with the flowers of the seven purities, wherein these stainless persons bathe.

Regarding the "bathing pool of the eight liberations": since the preceding section clarified the garden and grove, and there was a pool within that garden, this section now clarifies the bathing pool.

The "eight liberations" refers to the eight *vimokṣas*; alternatively, they are called the eight *pratisarga* (relinquishments). They are termed "liberations" because one is liberated from lower stages.

Regarding "liberation through turning away" (*prātimokṣa-vairāgya*): it is called "turning away" because one turns one's back on the lower stages. Regarding its being likened to a "bathing pool": a pool washes away dust and grime;
since liberation cleanses the afflictions (*kleśa*), it is metaphorically compared to a bathing pool. As for the phrase "the water of concentration is full and serene":

one might ask, "Since the eight liberations encompass all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and there is no concentration existing apart from the eight liberations, why is this further clarified?"
The commentary explains: there is no water apart from the pond; it is simply by taking the water itself as the pond that it is established as the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*).
To speak of them again here is merely to explain them according to their distinct meanings. Washing away all burdens constitutes liberation (*vimukti*);

being perfectly full and tranquil constitutes the water of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). As for "spreading the flowers of the seven purities," since there is already this clear and beautiful water, furthermore—
It scatters the flowers of pure excellence. Regarding the seven purities: first, purity of precepts; second, purity of mind; third, purity of view; fourth, purity through overcoming doubt;

fifth, purity regarding what is and is not the path; sixth, purity of practice; and seventh, purity of abandonment. Because these seven purities are scattered across the three paths, it is called "scattering.
As for the three paths, they are the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, and the path of no-more-learning. Within the path of seeing the truths, there are five [moments].

This means that the purity of precepts leads to the purity of mind; the purity of mind leads to the purity of concentration; the purity of concentration leads to the purity of view, which eliminates the views of self-identity and extremes;

the purity of view leads to the purity of overcoming doubt; and the purity of what is and is not the path eliminates the clinging to rules and rituals. Within the path of cultivation, there is one purity called the purity of practice;
in the stage of no-more-learning, there is likewise one purity called the purity of abandonment.

With the five supernormal powers as elephants and horses, they gallop upon the Great Vehicle as their chariot; with single-mindedness as their driver, they travel the path of the Eightfold Right Path.

Adorned with the primary marks, they beautify their countenance; embellished with the secondary signs, they grace their form. A sense of shame and remorse is their supreme garment; a profound mind is their flower garland.
Regarding "the elephant and horse galloping with the five supernormal powers": the five supernormal powers serve as the elephant and the Great Vehicle serves as the chariot;

a single mind serves as the driver as one traverses the path of the Eightfold Noble Way. Regarding "adorned with the marks to grace the countenance": because the marks range from coarse to subtle, the marks adorn the countenance and the excellence of these graces embellishes the physical form.

To be rich in the seven treasures of wealth means that one should cause them to increase through instruction, as previously explained; practicing according to the teachings and dedicating the merit constitutes the great benefit.

Regarding "being rich in the seven treasures of wealth," the previous section concluded with the explanation of adornment; now, the seven treasures of wealth—faith, ethical discipline, learning, wisdom, renunciation, shame, and dread of blame—are clarified.
As for "causing them to increase through instruction," since one already possesses these material assets...
One must circulate the interest and profit from these seven riches by bestowing them upon others, and those others in turn bestow them upon yet others.
In this way, the riches will never be exhausted; though the four modes of birth may come to an end, the seven riches shall not be depleted.
As it is said, a practitioner who has already bestowed material wealth should now practice the "wealth of the Dharma."
The four dhyānas serve as his seat, born of pure livelihood; extensive learning increases his wisdom, serving as the sound of his self-awakening.
The nectar of the Dharma serves as his food, and the flavor of liberation as his drink. He bathes with a pure mind and uses the factors of morality as his unguent.
Having crushed and destroyed the thieves of affliction, he is valiant and unsurpassed; having subdued the four Māras, he raises the banner of victory at the site of enlightenment.
Regarding "the four dhyānas as the bed and seat": there are two aspects to a bed—being separated from what is below and being securely established upon what is above.

The four dhyānas are likewise; they are separated from the various fetters (saṃyojana) below, and wisdom arises from above. Regarding "much hearing as the sound of awakening": when a noble person of the world wishes to awaken someone whose eyes are closed in sleep, they play music;
so too, when the Bodhisattva Suvarṇa entered the fourth dhyāna, he used the sound of much-heard wisdom to awaken him.
"Taking ambrosia as food and the flavor of liberation as drink": ambrosia is *nirvāṇa*, and *nirvāṇa* is the food;
liberation is the drink. Question: Since *nirvāṇa* is simply liberation, why speak of two? Answer:
They differ in terms of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). The unconditioned is *nirvāṇa*; the conditioned is liberation.
Although one knows there is neither arising nor ceasing, for the sake of instructing others, birth is manifested throughout all lands, just as there is no place where the sun is not seen.
"Although one knows there is neither arising nor ceasing" refers to the preceding section which distinguished the supramundane from the mundane;

now it clarifies that the supramundane transcends the mundane, for such a thing does not exist within the mundane world. The first half of the verse demonstrates birth, while the second half [demonstrates]... [the cessation].
Manifesting birth for the benefit of others, the Bodhisattva appears in the world like the sun in the sky; there is nothing that is not fully seen, and none who do not receive benefit.
He makes offerings to the immeasurable billions of Tathāgatas and Buddhas throughout the ten directions, as well as to his own body, without any thought of discrimination.
Although they know that all Buddha-lands and sentient beings are empty, they constantly cultivate pure lands to transform and guide the multitudes of living beings.
Regarding all classes of sentient beings—their forms, sounds, and deportment—the Bodhisattvas, through their power of fearlessness, can manifest them all at once.
They perceive all the works of Māra and yet demonstrate compliance with their conduct; through the wisdom of skillful means, they are able to manifest anything according to their will.

Or they manifest old age, sickness, and death to bring all beings to accomplishment, so that they may understand all things as being like illusions and transformations, attaining unimpeded penetration.
Although they know that all Buddha-lands and sentient beings are empty—though they know the Buddha-fields are empty yet they cultivate pure lands;
though they know sentient beings are empty yet they constantly deliver them—this is the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of equality. From [this...].

It is said that this refers to the Bodhisattva’s simultaneous contemplation (*pingguan*). Simultaneous contemplation of emptiness and existence, good and evil, motion and stillness, and so forth, constitutes vertical simultaneity;

simultaneous contemplation of these [pairs] constitutes horizontal simultaneity. Because this non-duality of emptiness and existence is without mutual obstruction, it is called "simultaneous contemplation.
One asks: at what stage of the bodhisattva path can one contemplate in such a manner? Others say:

The Bodhisattvas of the Eighth Stage all observe the Master’s critique regarding "simultaneity" (*ping*). Is it that the True and the Conventional are simultaneous, or that they are non-dual yet simultaneous?
The Kai Shan school’s view of the two truths as a single essence is thus criticized: first, how can one speak of simultaneity? Two distinct entities may be discussed in terms of simultaneity;
since they are non-dual, how can one speak of simultaneity? Therefore, this is untenable. As for the Long Guang school’s view of the True and the Conventional as dual...

Regarding the term "both" (*bing*), Master [Zhi]yi says that "both" refers to the pair of the turtle and the crab; though they have two holes each, these are situated on the left and right and are not related to one another.
Furthermore, what is the meaning of "both"? It is simply because of the existence of both emptiness and existence that they are "both.
Since you claim that the two truths are not related, how can you speak of "both"? What is now called "both" is precisely the contemplation of non-duality (*advaya*) from the very beginning.

The moment the mind is aroused, one practices this contemplation of non-duality; both the *Mahāvaipulya* (Great Extensive) Sūtra and the *Avataṃsaka* contain these words, for the two minds are not distinct.
Question: Since the two minds are not distinct, how can there be an initial and a subsequent [realization]? Answer: It is said that the former is simultaneous and the latter is simultaneous;
how then are they not distinct? To provide an analogy: although one is a Buddha from beginning to end, there is still a distinction between the initial and the subsequent states.

Furthermore, what is the intent behind the necessity of presenting these two together? The explanation states: because there are two views regarding sentient beings, the Bodhisattva observes sentient beings by means of both views simultaneously.
It is to shatter these two that the Bodhisattva clarifies non-duality. Thus, the Sūtra says: "The fool speaks of duality; the wise one realizes and penetrates non-duality.
This is precisely the clarification of non-duality in contrast to duality; once duality is removed, non-duality is also gone.
This is purity itself.

Sometimes he manifests the end of an eon, when the heavens and earth are scorched until they are all ablaze; though people harbor notions of permanence, he illuminates them so that they may know impermanence.
Countless billions of sentient beings come together to invite the Bodhisattva, who arrives at their homes all at once to transform them and lead them toward the Buddha-way.
Whether it be the study of scriptures, the recitation of incantations, or the mastery of various crafts and arts, they manifest in all these activities to benefit all living beings.
Among all the worldly paths and dharmas, they may renounce the world; through this, they resolve the delusions of others so that they do not fall into false views.
At times they become the sun or moon, the gods, Brahmā, or the lords of the world; at other times they become earth or water, or again, wind or fire.
In kalpas when epidemics appear, he manifests as various medicinal herbs; those who consume them are cured of illness and their many toxins are eliminated.
In kalpas when famine occurs, he manifests as food and drink, first relieving their hunger and thirst, and subsequently instructing people with the Dharma.
In kalpas when weapons and warfare prevail, he gives rise to compassion for them, transforming those sentient beings and causing them to abide in the ground of non-contention.
If there is a great battle, he establishes it with equal strength; as a Bodhisattva manifesting majestic power, he subdues them and brings peace and harmony to all lands.
To all places where there are hells within all lands, he immediately goes there to relieve their suffering and distress.
Within all lands where animals devour one another, he manifests birth among them to act for their benefit.
They manifest the experience of the five desires and further display the practice of dhyāna, causing the minds of Māras to become confused and agitated so that they cannot find an opportunity.
To produce a lotus flower within fire may be called rare; likewise, to practice dhyāna while remaining amidst desire is equally rare.
They may manifest as courtesans to attract those who lust after beauty, first drawing them in with the hook of desire and subsequently leading them into the Buddha’s wisdom.
I may become a leader of a village, or a guide for merchants, or a national preceptor and great minister, to bring benefit and aid to sentient beings;
to those who are impoverished, I manifest as an inexhaustible treasury to encourage and lead them so that they may resolve upon Bodhicitta.
To those whose minds are arrogant, I manifest as a mighty warrior to subdue all their haughtiness and cause them to abide in the Unsurpassed Way.
For those who are fearful, he stands before them to comfort and reassure them, first bestowing fearlessness and later causing them to resolve upon the Way.

Or, manifesting freedom from lustful desire as a seer possessing the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), he guides all sentient beings, leading them to abide in the precepts, patience, and compassion.
Seeing those who require service, he manifests himself as a servant; having thus gladdened their hearts, he then inspires them with the mind of the Way.
According to whatever they require, they enter the path of the Buddha; through the power of skillful means, they are able to provide for them all sufficiently.
Thus, the Way is immeasurable, their practice is boundless, and their wisdom is limitless as they deliver countless multitudes.
Even if all Buddhas were to praise their merits for countless billions of eons, they still could not exhaustively describe them.
Who, upon hearing such a Dharma, would not resolve to attain bodhicitta—except for those unworthy persons who are deluded, ignorant, and lacking wisdom?
The meaning of the three calamities has already been extensively explained elsewhere. Now, among these three calamities, what is it that Bodhisattvas transform?
Regarding "sentient beings," the commentary says: "The Bodhisattva Vasumitra transforms sentient beings within this [assembly];
this Bodhisattva follows after Maitreya. Shi Dao'an states: "This Bodhisattva is subsequent to Maitreya."
Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Volume Four;

Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Volume Five (In the original manuscript, this volume lacked a title at the beginning and placed the chapter number directly at the end as in Volume Four; following the current convention, the title has been added above).
Composed by Hu Jizang.
Chapter Nine: Entering the Dharma-Gate of Non-Duality.
In the extensive exposition of the two types of wisdom, three chapters have already been concluded;
this is now the fourth chapter, clarifying the entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality. As for the reason why this chapter has come to be: there is... [text continues].
That there are those who say that what is near implies what is distant and that this is the fundamental intent behind Vimalakīrti’s manifestation of skillful means, and furthermore,
that it is the reason why Mañjuśrī inquires after his illness— why it is said to be both the fundamental intent behind Vimalakīrti’s manifestation of illness and the reason for Mañjuśrī’s inquiry—
is explained as follows: if it were not for the purpose of causing sentient beings to enter into non-duality...

Vimalakīrti did not manifest illness and Mañjuśrī likewise did not pose difficult questions; it was solely for the sake of leading sentient beings into the Way of Non-duality that Vimalakīrti manifested illness and Mañjuśrī inquired after his health.
Therefore, this is the original intent of Vimalakīrti and the reason why Mañjuśrī inquired after his illness.
As for the "remote words," they are indeed the true [teaching] of all Buddhas of the three periods and ten directions.
What do you think? Although the words and teachings spoken by the Buddhas of the three periods and ten directions are immeasurable, they ultimately serve to reveal the One Way.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The Dharma of Mañjuśrī is ever thus; the Dharma-King has but one Dharma.
All those who are unimpeded give birth to transcendence from suffering through this One Way. Question: Are the Buddhas of the three periods and ten directions truly only one?
Question: For what reason does the Way preach various teachings? Answer: Although various teachings are preached, they ultimately serve to explain the One Way;
the preaching of variety is not for the sake of variety, but rather to manifest the Dharma of the One Way. As the *Lotus Sūtra* states:
"Although various vehicles are preached, they ultimately lead to the One Vehicle. Therefore, the non-dual Dharma is that of all Buddhas of the three periods and the ten directions.

The fundamental intent is also proximate to the meaning of the two preceding chapters: the "Chapter on Observing Sentient Beings" (Shengqun Zhongsheng) concerns transforming sentient beings, while the "Chapter on the Buddha Way" (Fodao Pin) concerns seeking the Buddha-way above.

This present chapter, however, sublates both; it clarifies that although one transforms sentient beings, in reality there are no sentient beings to be transformed, and although one seeks the Buddha-way, in reality there is no Buddha-way to be sought. It thus reveals the true nature of both sentient beings and the Buddha.
Because there is no duality, it is now clarified that there is non-duality. This is precisely the meaning of "herding" (guiding) into [the truth].

Although there are such skillful means (*upāya*) mentioned above, they all exist for the sake of non-duality; thus, they are the "herder. Looking toward what follows, this is the meaning of "emerging" and "functioning":
because of non-duality, one is able to give rise to all skillful means. Furthermore, both before and after, there are respectively the functions of "emerging" and "herding."
Furthermore, the Great Master has analyzed this chapter as having two types and three types. Regarding the two types:

first, there are the thirty-three bodhisattvas who explain the entry into non-duality, and second, there are the five thousand [bodhisattvas] who realize the entry into non-duality through the explanations of those thirty-three bodhisattvas.
Thus, by means of the thirty-three bodhisattvas explaining the entry into non-duality, the five thousand bodhisattvas attain realization.

Regarding "entering non-duality": because five thousand [bodhisattvas] should enter non-duality, thirty-three [cases] are taught. Entering non-duality is precisely the correspondence between the teaching and its conditions;
it is like administering medicine according to the illness, which one then takes and practices in accordance with the Dharma. Furthermore, there are two types:
first, the thirty-two bodhisattvas manifest non-duality through speech, while Vimalakīrti manifests non-duality through silence. This...
Both speech and silence are gateways of the teaching. Why? Because both are able to open the Way and benefit sentient beings.
While it may seem that speech and silence are not both teachings—whereas others claim that speech is the teaching and silence is not—I now clarify that both are indeed the teaching.
Since one awakens through speech to speech, this is already the teaching; since one awakens through silence to silence, how could this not be the teaching? Therefore, they are both such.
The teaching is precisely this: that speech is non-speech is itself non-duality.
To speak of non-speech is speech; non-speech is speech. Non-speech is not speech, and speech is not non-speech.
Neither speech nor non-speech, neither talk nor silence—this is entry into non-duality. Regarding the three types: as for the first type, there are three.
To clarify these thirty-three bodhisattvas entering non-duality, there are generally three stages:
first, the eleven bodhisattvas speak of entering non-duality from duality; second, Mañjuśrī speaks of entering non-duality from both duality and non-duality—neither dual nor non-dual;
third, Vimalakīrti enters from neither dual nor non-dual, which is neither "not dual" nor "not non-dual. Question: If this is so...
The first thirty-one bodhisattvas have entered non-duality; why, then, is it said here that they all "enter non-duality" in general?
The explanation is as follows: there are two ways of entering non-duality. First, regarding the initial thirty-one bodhisattvas:

taking arising and ceasing as "duality" and taking cessation as "non-duality," they enter from the duality of arising and ceasing into the non-duality of non-arising and non-ceasing. Mañjuśrī [then] stepped forward...
The former two are non-dual, yet together they constitute duality; that which is neither dual nor non-dual is what constitutes non-duality.
From this duality and non-duality, one enters that which is neither dual nor non-dual. In the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, both "neither dual" and "not non-dual" are combined to form duality;
that which is neither the negation of duality nor the negation of non-duality is non-duality. From this state of neither dual nor non-dual, one enters [the ultimate].
"Neither non-duality nor not non-duality"—though these repetitions differ, they ultimately lead from duality into non-duality.
This is like the three successive stages of the two truths: first, conditioned phenomena as conventional truth and unconditioned phenomena as ultimate truth;

next, unconditioned phenomena as conventional truth and neither-conditioned-nor-unconditioned phenomena as ultimate truth; and finally, both duality and non-duality as conventional truth, with neither-duality-nor-non-duality as ultimate truth.
That which is non-dual is not the ultimate truth; although there are three sections, they do not go beyond the two truths.
Regarding the second type of threefold [classification], the first thirty-one bodhisattvas spoke of non-duality because it can be expressed. Thus, Mañjuśrī spoke of non-duality through words.
Knowing that non-duality is ineffable yet speaking of non-duality is to speak of the ineffable. Vimalakīrti knew this... [text ends]... non-duality.
Second, "non-speech" does not speak of non-duality; this non-speech is itself the three phrases.
Thus, while the Bodhisattvas speak, Vimalakīrti is silent, and Mañjuśrī both speaks and is silent.
Therefore, regarding the thirty-one Bodhisattvas who say that non-duality can be spoken of as non-duality, they were those who heard Vimalakīrti’s summons.
To speak of the non-dual assembly of bodhisattvas is itself to speak of non-duality; thus, to speak of non-duality is to speak within speech.
Next, Mañjuśrī knew that non-duality is beyond words, Vimalakīrti had nothing to command, and the assembly of bodhisattvas had nothing to say.
Although they knew this, they could not help but speak of that which is beyond words through speech.
To speak of the ineffable is to speak within that which cannot be spoken; it is the unspeakable. Vimalakīrti, knowing the non-duality of silence, remained silent.
This silence regarding the non-duality of non-duality is the ultimate limit of non-dual non-duality.
As for the third type, the three [preceding categories]: the thirty-one bodhisattvas previously had broken duality and clarified non-duality, yet they were unable to know it.

The subject that negates and the object to be negated are non-dual; likewise, Mañjuśrī realized that birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are non-dual, and he further realized that the subject that negates and the object to be negated are non-dual.
Since there is no duality of the object to be negated, there is no non-duality of the subject that negates.

Although he knows there is no negation, there is neither "negation" nor "non-negation" that can be predicated; yet, while speaking, he speaks of neither negation nor non-negation. Next, Vimalakīrti knew that there is no negation.
One may speak of "breaking" [duality], yet there is no speech regarding this non-speech; there is no non-speech regarding this non-breaking, for it is not broken.
However, entering the gate of non-duality is difficult to understand. Traditionally, it has been said that the gate of non-duality consists of two things being non-two;
because one enters non-duality by means of duality, duality constitutes the gate of non-duality. Now, if it is called the "gate of non-duality," why is this so?
If you say that duality is the gate of non-duality, then one should speak of "entering the gate of duality.
Yet now you say "entering the gate of the non-dual Dharma"—how can duality be the gate of non-duality? This statement contradicts itself.
Furthermore, if you further equate them by saying that entering the gate of the non-dual Dharma means that duality is non-duality, this would be an inconceivable interpretation.
Furthermore, by what means does the Dharma-gate of liberation function as a gate? The inconceivable Dharma-gate of liberation takes that very inconceivable Dharma-gate of liberation as its gate;
it should enter the Dharma-gate of non-duality, taking that very non-dual Dharma as its gate.
If the Dharma-gate of non-duality were to take duality as its gate, then the Dharma-gate of liberation would conversely take bondage as its gate.
[As stated] above: If these two intentions—the intention of Vimalakīrti manifesting illness and the question of Mañjuśrī regarding that illness—are both present, why are only these two mentioned?

It is because the fundamental intention of all Buddhas of the ten directions is also included therein. Question: If one does not employ duality as the gate to non-duality, then does one employ non-duality as the gate?
This too is impossible. If non-duality were the gate, through what would one enter?
From where does one enter this state? If one enters the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), the true mark is simply non-duality;
thus, entering the true mark is entering non-duality. Furthermore, one may ask: from where does one enter this non-duality that is to be entered?
If one does not enter non-duality by means of duality, nor attain realization of the principle through the teachings, then the conclusion is reached as follows:
Now, the explanation possesses three meanings: first, clarifying the cause; second, awakening to and entering non-duality;
and third, because it serves as the gateway to non-duality, it is called "entering the gate of non-duality. Why is this? If these two were truly dual, then duality could not enter non-duality.
If they were not non-dual, they would not be the gate to non-duality. Since this is non-dual, by means of this non-duality, the dual enters.
Because two and non-two are non-dual, the duality of two and non-two constitutes the gate of non-duality. This fully clarifies the relationship between the transformer and the transformed.
If we consider it from the perspective of the transformer, the teaching of "two" expresses non-duality; thus, duality serves as the gate of non-duality.
This is like the thirty-one bodhisattvas expressing non-duality through the teaching of two gates, and also like the Tathāgata’s teaching of the two truths.
The two truths are presented as the gateway to the principle because they manifest the principle of non-duality;

thus, the Mahāyāna Sūtra states: "These two words are for the sake of understanding one word. This refers to the perspective of the transformer (the teacher). From the perspective of those being transformed (the disciples), it means that through these two, one realizes the non-dual.

One realizes the principle by means of the teaching; thus, for the transformer, the manifestation serves as the gateway, while for those being transformed, the realization and entry serve as the gateway. These are the two.
Taking these two as the gate of non-duality—what does this clarify? It clarifies that the noble path is primordially neither dual nor non-dual;
it is neither two nor not-two. Now, "non-duality" is provisionally designated as the "gate" in order to lead one to awaken to the Path.
This may also be understood in terms of the transformer and the transformed: with respect to the transformer, non-duality is spoken of as a signifier.

Because the Way is non-dual, the teaching serves as the gateway to the Way; thus, the Preface to the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "In reality, one does not awaken through names; one proclaims it by relying on the Middle.
This teaching also serves as the gateway to principle, whereby one attains entry into non-duality.
It is neither dual nor non-dual; non-duality is the gateway to being neither dual nor non-dual. For those to be transformed, they awaken through this non-dual teaching.
Because one enters the Way of non-duality, non-duality is the gate. These three [points] take this very non-duality as the Dharma-gate;
it is just as the *Avataṃsaka* has various Dharma-gates. That is, taking non-duality as duality is distinct from the two previous explanations.
Why? Because non-duality itself is the gate, it differs from the two preceding [explanations] which treat non-duality as the gate through which one enters.

Since this non-duality has nothing further to enter, it differs from the second explanation. This current explanation distinguishes the meaning by defining the "Gate of Non-duality" as simply another name for the Way (*mārga*).
This non-dual Way is pervasive and unimpeded, serving as the "gate"; being non-dual, it is that which can be followed as the "Dharma.
To awaken to this non-duality is called "entry," and it also possesses the capacity to transform others.
Regarding the thirty-three bodhisattvas who teach non-duality so that other bodhisattvas may enter into non-duality:
herein, there are thirty-three bodhisattvas who speak as questioners. What is the intention behind having thirty-three bodhisattvas speak in such a sudden manner?
The explanation is that because the delusive illnesses of sentient beings differ, their awakenings are likewise distinct; therefore, it is necessary to provide various methods of instruction.
This is because various medicines cure illnesses.
At that time, Vimalakīrti addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying: "Venerable sirs, how do bodhisattvas enter the gate of non-duality?
