this is inconceivable. Now, the inferior [inconceivability] is that a small amount can satisfy a great multitude, such that the great multitude eats a small amount of rice and yet it is not exhausted;
this is inconceivable. If one were to ask: "If a single small bowl of rice could satisfy a great multitude, then it should also be [the case for other things]."
If a small seat serves as a seat for a large assembly, then since many seats serve as seats for a large assembly, it should likewise follow that many bowls serve as bowls for a large assembly.
The explanation states: this is a general principle; many seats serve as seats for a large assembly, and much rice serves as food for a large assembly.

A single small bowl of rice serves as food for a large assembly, and a single small seat serves as a seat for a large assembly. That it is not so [in the present case] is because they are shown to be different in their mutual application.
It manifests various transformations and various inconceivable matters, and because these are revealed as distinct, they differ [from the previous].
Furthermore, while the aforementioned was an inconceivable response through silent resonance, the present involves sending forth an inconceivable emanation;

both of these transcend the reach of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, and are therefore inconceivable. Question: Since the previous instance involved silent contemplation, why does the Buddha now separately dispatch an emanation?
When [the Buddha] silently thought of food, food immediately arrived; now that he has sent an emanation to request a meal, he also sends an emanation to borrow a seat.

When [Śāriputra] silently thought of ascending the throne, the throne was immediately provided; now that he has sent an emanation to go and request a meal, this too is a mutual manifestation demonstrating various kinds of inconceivability.
Furthermore, as for the title of the chapter, it should be called the "Chapter on the Fragrant Accumulation Buddha."

The Buddha of Fragrant Accumulation performs buddha-work through the Dharma; now he performs buddha-work by means of fragrant food. It should be titled "Chapter on Fragrant Food. The commentary explains:
"Naming it according to its origin—why is there food? Because that Buddha exists, there is food; thus it is named according to its origin. [Objection:
If it is named according to its origin, then from the origin it should be called "Buddha-Work. The commentary explains: "Such fragrant food constitutes buddha-work."
The activity is itself the Buddha-activity. If it were not for that Buddha, by what means could this fragrant food be obtained?
Therefore, this Buddha-activity of the fragrant food is that very Buddha; because he performs this Buddha-activity, the chapter is titled "The Chapter on the Fragrant Accumulation Buddha.

This chapter is divided into two parts: first, the elucidation of material giving (*āmiṣa-dāna*); second, the elucidation of Dharma-giving (*dharma-dāna*). Now, this concerns both material and Dharma [giving].
Because this Dharma is the very wealth that nourishes the Dharma-body and sustains the life of wisdom, this Dharma is wealth;
indeed, this wealth is itself the Dharma.
Thereupon, Śāriputra thought to himself: "As the time for the meal is approaching, where shall these bodhisattvas eat?"
Regarding the first [section], there are three parts: first, mindfulness of food; second, the reproach of mindfulness of food;
and third, the giving of unprecedented food. This present instance is the first. Question: For what reason does Śāriputra practice mindfulness of food while other people do not?
Explanation: There are several reasons. First, there are generally three grades of persons. Those of the lower grade possess afflictions (*kleśa*), and thus their minds are...
To toil the body because of inverted views means that the body has dependencies; this refers to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
Second, those of middle capacity sever afflictions (*kleśa*), so their minds do not toil; yet because they possess a retributive body, it has dependencies—this refers to the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*).
Those of superior capacity have no afflictions within, so their minds do not toil; because the Dharma-body is their body, they have nothing upon which to depend—this is Bodhi.
The Bodhisattva has no internal attachments and his external body has no dependencies; therefore, he does not think of food.
Although Śāriputra has no internal attachments, his external body still has dependencies; therefore, he now thinks of food. Second, the previous section spoke of the Bodhisattva’s dharma;
when the Bodhisattva’s dharma accomplishes sentient beings and purifies the Buddha-land, the Bodhisattva hears this and rejoices so much that he forgets hunger.
Regarding "mindfulness of food": because the śrāvakas hear this and neither understand nor take pleasure in it, they merely practice mindfulness of food.
Thirdly, by virtue of that mindfulness, Vimalakīrti was able to provide the unprecedented food and extensively perform buddha-work for the benefit of sentient beings;
this demonstrates reality and reveals the Path. [The interlocutor] asks: For what reason does he himself not practice mindfulness [of food], yet speaks of the bodhisattvas?
"When should they eat? The commentary explains that Śāriputra himself had food; however, his regular meal was only for the time of the bodhisattvas.
Since it was already late, and according to the dharma of the ancient Buddhas one does not eat after midday, he asked, "When should the bodhisattvas eat?
Now, this mindfulness of food differs from the mindfulness of the seat. Why? Because the mindfulness of the seat is... [text fragment ends]
Because both self and others are included, what was previously stated—that "these bodhisattvas and great disciples shall sit where?"—is not the case here;
it simply says, "Where shall these bodhisattvas eat?"
At that time, Vimalakīrti, knowing his thoughts, spoke to him, saying: "The Buddha has taught the eight liberations;
do you, O Noble One, practice them while partaking of mixed desires and food to hear the Dharma?

He further said: "The Buddha has taught [the following]... [This is the second censure regarding the mindfulness of food, whereas previously it was said that a bodhisattva requires food, whereas a disciple...]
It is not necessary to eat; one should reprove the Bodhisattva but not the Śrāvaka. The explanation is as follows:

if it is necessary for the Śrāvaka but unnecessary for the Bodhisattva, one should not think that it must be taken at every moment. Furthermore, because the Śrāvaka thinks of it while the Bodhisattva does not, the Śrāvaka requires it whereas the Bodhisattva does not.
Because the Bodhisattva does not require it, one does not reprove the Bodhisattva; because the Śrāvaka requires it, one reproves him.
Question: What is the difference between the Śrāvaka’s current reproach regarding food and his previous reproach regarding the seat? Answer:

It is explained that previously he reproached the seat by resorting to lower dharmas, whereas now he reproaches the food by resorting to higher dharmas. Previously, when reproaching the seat by resorting to lower dharmas, it was for the sake of the Dharma coming and the seat coming;
now, when reproaching the Buddha’s teaching by resorting to higher dharmas, he clearly explains the eight liberations, saying: "O Venerable One..."

How could one who practices the teachings listen to the Dharma while being preoccupied with the desire for food? Regarding those who criticize [this practice] based on the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*):

the eight liberations are the eight stages of relinquishment (*aṣṭa-pratipakṣa*). Since these liberations generally involve relinquishing desire and form, how could one still harbor thoughts of food? As for the specific details:

in the first two of the eight liberations, one practices the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), specifically observing the impurity of food; thus, one should not delight in food. You, O virtuous one, should constantly practice this.

The contemplation of impurity consists of these eight types alone; it is the joyful feast of the Dharma-body and the supreme nourishment for the life of wisdom—how could it ever be a meal mixed with sensual desires?
Furthermore, if one hears this sublime Dharma, one should not even begrudge one’s own body or life;
why then would one think of food? Thus he rebuked him.
"If you wish to eat, wait but a moment; I shall cause you to obtain food such as you have never experienced before.
If you wish to eat, [the text] proceeds to the third section on "Giving Food," which contains four parts: first, the promise to give food; second, the indication of its location;
third, the inability of the great assembly to reach it; and fourth, Vimalakīrti’s dispatching of a transformation being to fetch it. Now...
[The Buddha] said: "I shall first give you food; you who must eat, wait a moment, for you shall obtain food such as has never been had before.
Question: Previously he rebuked him; why does he now intend to give him a demonstration? Answer:

Granting or withholding follows what is appropriate, all for the sake of benefiting sentient beings—just as worldly people may scold their children while still giving them food. Question: Regarding his mindfulness of constant eating:
"Why does he not give him his usual food, but rather this unprecedented food? To explain:
it is because he wishes not to contradict the previous statement, and furthermore, to manifest the inconceivable virtue of the Bodhisattva and extensively perform the work of a Buddha;
thus, he gives this unprecedented food. Regarding the phrase "to avoid contradicting the previous teaching," the previous [passage] rebuked him for thinking about food, yet...
Now, if one were suddenly to give them their usual food, it would indeed contradict the previous censure;
however, since one is now giving them unprecedented food, it does not contradict that censure. Why is this? That which you have been thinking of is impure food, arising from perversion;
this present food is pure, arising from non-reliance and non-attainment. Furthermore, while that thought of food nourishes the fleshly body, this present...
Because food sustains the long life of wisdom, the previous reproach was that he now gives it; this statement reveals the virtue of the Bodhisattva.
If he were given ordinary food, they would think, "I too have such food," and would not rejoice in the Bodhisattva’s inconceivability.
Now, by being given this unprecedented food, they immediately praise the inconceivable power of the Bodhisattva’s virtuous qualities.

At that time, Vimalakīrti entered into samādhi and, by means of his supernormal powers, manifested to the great assembly a world-system in the upward direction beyond Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of forty-two Ganges Rivers.
There was a land named Sarvagandhasugandhā and a Buddha there named Gandhottamakūṭa, who currently resides therein.
The fragrance in that land is the most supreme among all the fragrances of humans and devas in the worlds of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions.
In that land, there are no names for śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; there is only a pure assembly of great bodhisattvas for whom the Buddha preaches the Dharma.
The entire realm consists of pavilions made of incense, walking paths of fragrant earth, and gardens all of incense.
Its food is permeated with fragrance that flows throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions. At that time, that Buddha, together with those bodhisattvas...
While they were sitting together to eat, there appeared various devaputras, all named Gandhavimāna, who had all resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
they made offerings to that Buddha and the bodhisattvas, and this entire great assembly beheld it with their own eyes.
At that time, Vimalakīrti entered into samādhi. This second section demonstrates the place where the food is kept;
previously, it was promised that there would be food of unprecedented quality, but its location was unknown, and thus he reveals that place here.
Within this context, he asks the bodhisattvas about the food and not the śrāvakas to clarify that even those seated nearby cannot ascend [to the seat], let alone others.
"Can one take that Buddha’s food? Furthermore, previously it was rebuked that the śrāvakas could not ascend the seat; now it is rebuked that the bodhisattvas cannot take the food. Question:
Now, since the food is shown and the assembly is told to take it, should he not have previously shown the place for the seats so that the assembly might take them?
Answer: The preceding and succeeding cases are analogous. Here, the intention is to clarify that while the chapters are distinct, each section possesses its own unique characteristics.
The shifting of circumstances and the application of skillful means are not uniform.
At that time, Vimalakīrti asked the assembly of bodhisattvas, "O virtuous ones, who among you can bring back the food from that Buddha?
Due to the majestic spiritual power of Mañjuśrī, they all remained silent. Vimalakīrti said, "Virtuous ones, is it not the case that this great assembly..."
The Venerable Mañjuśrī said, "As the Buddha has said, do not disparage those who have not yet studied.

Then, Vimalakīrti asked the assembly of bodhisattvas. This third section clarifies that the great assembly was unable to reach this state, thereby manifesting two inconceivable qualities of the householder:
first, that the assembly had never before seen such food, yet they were now able to see it; second, [that the assembly]... the great assembly.
It is not that Mañjuśrī can grasp the pure name while the great assembly cannot; rather, it is because of Mañjuśrī’s power that the great assembly remains silent.

This clarifies that although the bodhisattvas of the assembly are capable of grasping [the teaching], at this moment the conditions are centered precisely upon Vimalakīrti. It is Vimalakīrti who, by grasping [the opportunity], is able to perform buddha-work for the benefit of both himself and others.
If it were anyone else, they would not be able to bring about such mutual benefit. Mañjuśrī feared that among the assembly there might be bodhisattvas...
Because it would have been contrary to the proper principle for Vimalakīrti to depart so abruptly, he used his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) to cause the assembly to remain silent.
Furthermore, since Vimalakīrti was acting as the host while the bodhisattvas were guests, how could the guests take food and eat on their own? This being impossible, they remained silent.
When Vimalakīrti spoke [the following], this was the third point: he censured the great assembly by showing that the food was located there [with him] and was not [available to them].
Question: Does the one who takes up [the teaching] not feel shame? Question: Vimalakīrti is a bodhisattva; why does he slight the great assembly? Explanation:

It is intended to censure those at the beginning of their practice and urge them toward further study. When Mañjuśrī spoke these words, it was the fourth section where Mañjuśrī’s response clarifies that although they have not yet studied, because they desire to attain [realization], one should not slight them.
How do these two persons complement each other? Namely, Vimala... [text fragment ends].
The names "Ji" (Reviling) and "Shi Xing" (Beginning Practice) for Mañjuśrī, along with their initial resolve, each carry their own significance.
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti, without rising from his seat, manifested before the assembly a bodhisattva of exquisite physical marks, radiance, and majestic virtue that outshone the entire gathering.
He addressed him, saying: "Go to the world-systems of the zenith."

Beyond as many Buddha-lands as there are grains of sand in forty-two Ganges Rivers, there is a land named Saugandhika and a Buddha named Gandhottama, who is currently sitting together with various bodhisattvas to partake of a meal.
Go there and speak these words on my behalf: "Vimalakīrti bows his head at the feet of the World-Honored One;
he sends you boundless greetings and inquires after your well-being, asking whether you have little illness or affliction and whether your physical strength is secure."
"I pray that I may obtain the remains of the World-Honored One’s meal;

I shall perform the work of a Buddha in this Sahā world, causing those who delight in inferior teachings to attend to the propagation of the Great Way, and ensuring that the fame of the Tathāgata is heard everywhere."

Thereupon, Vimalakīrti did not rise from his seat; this is the fourth [section] concerning the dispatching of an emanation. Within this, there are several chapters and phrases, and now follows the first:
entering samādhi and truly dispatching the emanation, he addresses it as follows. This is the second [section]: the words of the emanation requesting food.
He inquires after that Buddha’s health, asking if he has little illness and little affliction. These words are difficult to understand in this land.
If that land is pure while this one is defiled, and if there is sickness here but none there, how can one inquire after their health with the words "Are you free from illness and affliction?
This is not yet understood; it should be explained as the words of a request for a meal addressed to those who perform the Buddha-work in the Sahā world.
Now, for the second explanation of the purpose of requesting the meal: the request for a meal is not for any other matter, but solely for the sake of the Buddha.
There are generally two kinds of serving the Buddha: first, propagating [the Dharma] upward; second, transforming [beings] downward.

Those who delight in the lesser Dharma are transformed downward; those who attain the great Way are propagated upward. That the Tathāgata’s fame is universally renowned refers to the excellence of the Dharma above, while now it praises the person.

Then the manifested bodhisattva immediately ascended to the upper regions before the assembly, and the entire multitude saw him depart for the World of Fragrant Offerings (*Gandhavatī*), where he prostrated at the feet of that Buddha.
They also heard his words: "Vimalakīrti bows his head at the feet of the World-Honored One;

he sends immeasurable greetings and inquires whether you are free from illness and affliction, and whether your strength and well-being are secure. He wishes to obtain [the teachings] from the World-Honored One."

With the remains of his meal, he desired to perform Buddha-work in the Sahā world, so that those who delight in inferior teachings might attain the Great Way, and so that the fame of the Tathāgata might be heard everywhere.
When those great beings saw this manifested Bodhisattva, they marveled at what they had never before seen, saying: "From where has this Superior Person come? Where is the Sahā world located?"
"What is meant by 'those who delight in inferior teachings'? he asked the Buddha. The Buddha told him:
"Below this world, past as many buddha-lands as the sands of forty-two Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Sahā, where the Buddha is titled Śākyamuni.

He currently dwells in this world of five turbidities and evil ages, expounding the Way and its teachings for the sake of sentient beings who delight in inferior teachings. Therein are bodhisattvas..."
The one named Vimalakīrti dwells in the inconceivable liberation;

because he is preaching the Dharma for the sake of the bodhisattvas, he has dispatched this transformation-body to extol my name and praise this land, so that those bodhisattvas may increase their merit and virtue.
Those bodhisattvas asked, "What kind of person is he, that he can produce such a transformation, possessing such power of virtue, fearlessness, and supernormal powers? The Buddha said:
Extremely great, they dispatch emanations throughout all the ten directions to perform Buddha-works and benefit sentient beings.
At that time, the emanated bodhisattvas descend; this refers to the third emanated bodhisattva proceeding [to the lower realms], the text below which is easy to understand.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata Gandhottamakūṭa filled a fragrant bowl with fragrant food and gave it to the transformed bodhisattva.

At that time, those nine million bodhisattvas all spoke in unison, saying, "We wish to go to the Sahā world to make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha and to see Vimalakīrti and the other assembly of bodhisattvas. The Buddha said, "You may go."
“Restrain the fragrance of your body so as not to cause those sentient beings to give rise to thoughts of delusion or attachment.
Furthermore, you should relinquish your original form so that those in that land who seek to become bodhisattvas do not feel self-contempt or shame.
Moreover, you must not harbor thoughts of disdain or create obstacles regarding them. Why is this? Because all lands in the ten directions are like empty space, and all Buddhas...”
It is because he wishes to transform those who delight in inferior dharmas that he does not fully manifest his pure land.
Thus, regarding the fourth section below [the description of] Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhavyūha), there are two instances of that Buddha giving food;
the first is the Buddha giving food, and the second is the Bodhisattvas wishing to come. Now, this is the first instance of that Buddha giving food, as in the text; at that time, those nine...

In the second section of the "One Million" [Chapter], there are two matters concerning the Bodhisattvas of that land who wish to come: first, the benefit of the fragrant food, which is the benefit of the *nirmāṇakāya* (dependent fruit);

second, the benefit of the Bodhisattvas' arrival, which is the benefit of the *dharmakāya* (primary fruit). These two benefits—the dependent and the primary—correspond to the two gates of teaching: the dependent and the primary. Question:

While the fragrant food may constitute a Buddha-activity (*buddhakārya*), how is it understood that the bodies of the Bodhisattvas perform Buddha-activities? Answer: There are two ways to explain this.
The first meaning is that it clarifies that even those from the Pure Land come to listen to the Dharma; since you are nearby, why do you not study?
The second meaning is that because the great bodhisattvas of the Pure Land all come to listen, one knows that Vimalakīrti is an inconceivable person and what he speaks is the inconceivable Dharma;
thus, one should increase the sense of its being difficult to encounter and give rise to deep reverence for him.
"This is a great benefit. The Buddha said, "If you may go, that Buddha permits your departure. There are two conditions: first, you must now restrain the fragrance of your body;
second, do not give rise to a sense of inferiority regarding this land. The former precept is for the sake of this land, and the latter precept is for the sake of that land.
Therefore, it is said that the former precept is for this land, in order to quell the delusions and attachments of the sentient beings here."

Therefore, the instruction to restrain the fragrance of one's body is followed by the precept regarding that land; this is because it is feared that Bodhisattvas from the Pure Land might develop a sense of inferiority upon seeing the impurity of this land.

Thus, the precept causes them to give rise to a heart of reverence. Question: Since one is already instructed to restrain the fragrance of the body, why not also instruct one to restrain the fragrance of the food?
Explanation: Each of these has its own specific reason. Why is this so? It clarifies that [the Buddha] is capable of becoming a Buddha.

The objection that it is not included because it is an "accident" (an external circumstance) is countered by the fact that even the body of a Bodhisattva can perform Buddha-works; thus, it too should not be excluded.

The explanation is that they are mutually illustrative, yet the body is included because it is appropriate for sentient beings. Furthermore, since food is the power of the Buddha, it is not included [in the category of the ordinary];
however, the Bodhisattva’s body is the power of the Bodhisattva, and because the Bodhisattva’s power is insufficient [to sustain itself independently], it necessitates inclusion.
When the manifested bodhisattva had accepted the bowl of food, he and those nine million bodhisattvas,
sustained by the spiritual power of the Buddha and the strength of Vimalakīrti, suddenly vanished from that world and,
in an instant, arrived at the house of Vimalakīrti. At that moment, Vimalakīrti immediately manifested nine million lion thrones, magnificent and exquisite.
When the previous bodhisattvas had all taken their seats upon them, the manifested bodhisattva offered a bowl filled with fragrant rice to Vimalakīrti.
The fragrance of that food permeated the city of Vaiśālī as well as the trichiliocosm.
At that time, the brahmins and householders of Vaiśālī, having smelled this fragrance, felt great joy in body and mind and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
The elder Candracchattra, accompanied by eighty-four thousand people, entered the house of Vimalakīrti.
Seeing that the bodhisattvas within his room were exceedingly numerous and that the lion thrones were all high, broad, and magnificently adorned, he was filled with great joy.
He prostrated before the assembly of bodhisattvas and great disciples, then withdrew to stand to one side. Thereupon, the earth deities, the space deities, and those of the desire and form realms...
When the devas smelled this fragrance, they all came into Vimalakīrti’s house.

At that time, Vimalakīrti said to Śāriputra and the other great śrāvakas, "Venerable ones, you may eat this food of the Tathāgata, which has the flavor of ambrosia and is permeated by great compassion.
Do not eat it with a limited mind, lest it cause indigestion. Then, a certain śrāvaka thought, "This food is little, yet these..."

The Great Assembly all wished to eat, but the Emanated Bodhisattva said, "Do not attempt to measure the Tathāgata’s immeasurable merit and wisdom with the minor virtues and limited knowledge of Śrāvakas.
The four oceans may run dry, but this food is inexhaustible.
Should all people take mouthfuls as large as Mount Sumeru, they would not be able to finish it even in an eon. Why is this? Because it is born of inexhaustible precepts, concentration, and wisdom."
The leftovers from the meal of one who is fully endowed with the merit of wisdom-liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation can never be exhausted;
thus, the rice in this bowl satisfied the entire assembly, yet it was still not depleted.
Those bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, devas, and humans who ate this food experienced physical peace and joy, just like the bodhisattvas in the Land of Universal Joyful Adornments.
Furthermore, from all his pores issued a wondrous fragrance, just like the fragrance of the trees in the land of *Sugandhavatī*.
At that time, the transformed Bodhisattva, having received the food from the fifth transformed Bodhisattva below, returned to the chamber of the Buddha to perform Buddha-works;
this constitutes two parts: first, the explicit clarification of the transformed Bodhisattva’s return; second, the clarification that the food serves as the Buddha-work.
As for the present matter, this is why Vimalakīrti manifested nine million lion thrones.
Previously, it was shown that the great enters the small, yet the ultimate limit of the inconceivable had not been fully exhausted. Why?

Because previously it was indicated that thirty-two thousand entered a square *zhang*, whereas now nine million billion enter a single square *zhang*; only now does it reach the ultimate limit of the inconceivable.
Furthermore, the seat borrowed previously was a real seat, whereas this present one is a transformed seat.
What was previously inconceivable through another’s borrowing is now inconceivable through one’s own provision. Question:

Since the seat is a borrowed seat and a transformed seat, the food should likewise be a transformed invitation and transformed food. Why do you not understand this? Why must everything follow this same analogy?
This demonstrates various kinds of inconceivability. As the text says: "When the devas of the desire and form realms hear the fragrance, they all come.

Regarding the meaning of the phrase "a number of people," what does it clarify? It clarifies that while the five faculties and five objects exist in the desire realm heavens, these do not exist in the form realm.
Why is this? Because in the first dhyāna, although the two consciousnesses of nose and tongue are absent, the two faculties of nose and tongue are present as ornaments.
If the body belongs to the second dhyāna or above, then the five consciousnesses do not exist. If this were the case, how could one come here upon smelling a fragrance?

If you say that one borrows the consciousness of a lower realm to come, then we must ask: did you borrow the consciousness for the sake of smelling the fragrance, or did you borrow it before you smelled it?
If you borrowed it after smelling it, there was no consciousness [at the time of smelling]; how then could you have known [the fragrance]? It is impossible to borrow [consciousness] retroactively.
Therefore, it was not possible. Now, it is clear that the knowledge of the Hīnayāna is limited while the wisdom of the Mahāyāna is vast;
thus, there is nothing it does not encompass. This is why they came from the desire realm upon hearing the fragrance. Next, Vimalakīrti commanded Śāriputra and the others to eat.
Although he now commands the great disciples, he is in fact commanding the entire assembly. As for why he now commands them all, it is because of [the previous incident].
Because he universally contemplates those above, he universally commands them. Regarding the phrase "the meal of ambrosial flavor," there are two meanings:
first, the flavor of this meal is like ambrosia; eating this meal can open the way to ambrosia, and that which opens the way to ambrosia is precisely the Right Path and Nirvana.
Second, this very meal is itself ambrosia. Why? Because this meal [is endowed with all... (The text fragment ends here).

The karma arising from the Buddha’s non-arising nature is itself the fruit of non-arising, which is Nirvana. Regarding the phrase "perfumed by great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā-paribhāvita*): this clarifies that these meals arise from the great compassion of all Buddhas; therefore, it is said they are "perfumed by great compassion. Question: Since the Tathāgata practices immeasurable virtues, for what reason is only "great compassion" mentioned? Answer: It is because there is no food that he does not eat [for the sake of others]. By means of this, he manifests his great compassion. Thus, although the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable virtues, he specifically mentions "great compassion" because it is the foremost among them. This is why it is called "perfumed by great compassion. Furthermore, the term "perfumed" (*paribhāvita*) signifies that the Buddha’s body is thoroughly saturated by the power of great compassion. Just as a cloth perfumed with sandalwood becomes permeated by its fragrance, so too the Buddha’s body is saturated by the power of great compassion. Therefore, it is said to be "perfumed by great compassion. As for the phrase "arisen from the karma of non-arising": this refers to the fact that the Buddha’s body arises through the power of non-arising karma. Because it arises from non-arising, it is called "non-arising. Because it is non-arising, it is called "Nirvana. Because it is Nirvana, it is called "the Dharma-body. Because it is the Dharma-body, it is called "the Tathāgata. Because it is the Tathāgata, it is called "the Buddha. Because it is the Buddha, it is called "the World-Honored One. Because it is the World-Honored One, it is called "the Great Compassionate One. Because it is the Great Compassionate One, it is called "the Perfumer. Because it is the Perfumer, it is called "the Perfumed. Because it is the Perfumed, it is called "the Arisen. Because it is the Arisen, it is called "the Manifested. Because it is the Manifested, it is called "the Food. Because it is the Food, it is called "the Meal. Because it is the Meal, it is called "the Offering. Because it is the Offering, it is called "the Merit. Because it is the Merit, it is called "the Fruit. Because it is the Fruit, it is called "Nirvana. Because it is Nirvana, it is called "the Ultimate. Because it is the Ultimate, it is called "the Unsurpassed. Because it is the Unsurpassed, it is called "the Peerless. Because it is the Peerless, it is called "the Incomparable. Because it is the Incomparable, it is called "the Supreme. Because it is the Supreme, it is called "the Perfectly Enlightened One. The seventh method is to constantly examine one's own faults: one should always reflect upon and scrutinize one's own transgressions, repenting for past offenses and not reciting the faults of others.

If one can examine one's own faults, then because of that self-examination there will be no further faults, and by not reciting the faults of others, one will likewise remain free from loss.
Constantly seeking all merits with a single mind—this is the eighth dharma; the remainder of the text follows.
