This is the fourth assembly, gathered again at the Ānanda Garden; this assembly consists of four chapters. The first three chapters belong to the main exposition (*samyag-deśanā*), while the final chapter is for circulation (*pravartana*).
This is not my own judgment; Master Sengzhao himself made this statement.

Within the main exposition, there are three chapters which constitute three parts: the first explains the practice of the bodhisattva, the second clarifies the vision of the Buddha, and [the third...]
The three dharma-offerings are now explained; the first is as follows: it speaks of the bodhisattva practice for the sake of the bodhisattvas of that land, and it is named from this.
However, the "Fragrant Accumulation" chapter teaches this [land] for the sake of that [land], while the current "Bodhisattva Practice" chapter teaches that [land] for the sake of this [land];
they are like a marketplace where goods are exchanged. Furthermore, a single meal from the Fragrant Accumulation serves as food for the Buddha.
The intent here is to clarify that all dharmas constitute the Buddha-work. This chapter is divided into two parts:

first, Vimalakīrti and the great assembly arrive at the Buddha’s abode; second, the Bodhisattvas from Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhavyūha) are about to depart, for which he explains the conduct of Bodhisattvas.
Thus, there is a pair consisting of coming and going, as well as a pair consisting of the Buddha-work and the Bodhisattva-conduct.
At that time, while the Buddha was preaching the Dharma in the Āmra Grove, the ground suddenly became vast and magnificent,
and the entire assembly turned the color of gold. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions has this occurred?"
As an auspicious sign, this place suddenly became vast and magnificent, and the entire assembly turned the color of gold.

The Buddha told Ānanda, "Because Vimalakīrti and Mañjuśrī, together with the great multitude, have respectfully surrounded themselves and intend to come, they have first manifested this auspicious response. Thereupon, Vimalakīrti spoke to Mañjuśrī.
We may go together to see the Buddha and the various bodhisattvas as they pay homage and make offerings to Mañjuśrī. Mañjuśrī said, "Excellent! Let us go;
now is precisely the right time.
This section is further divided into two parts: first, Vimalakīrti and the great assembly arrive; second, the Tathāgata offers praise.
The fixed outline of the first [section] is further divided into two parts: first, clarifying the intent for its arrival; second, clarifying the actual arrival.

This is now the first [part], which contains several phrases. First, the manifestation of auspicious signs: the reason for manifesting these signs is that, as he is about to expound a marvelous dharma, he manifests rare and extraordinary omens.
Second, the Bodhisattvas from Fragrant Accumulation are guests, and since they are preeminent guests, [the signs are manifested].

Therefore, he transformed the pure land. Thirdly, because Vimalakīrti was about to arrive, he first manifested these auspicious signs to manifest the reality of the layman’s sincere reverence and to reveal the inconceivable virtue of Vimalakīrti.
This involves two matters: first, the transformation of the land; second, the transformation of the assembly into golden color.

The transformation of the land refers to the transformation of the *āśraya* (the environment/support), while the transformation of the assembly refers to the transformation of the *sambhoga* (the sentient beings/subjects). Next, the question is asked.
The answer clarifies that this was composed by Vimalakīrti and not by the Buddha, thereby manifesting the power of Vimalakīrti’s virtue.
Regarding "the Buddha said," this is the third response from the Buddha as an auspicious sign. Now, concerning the fourth section below [the passage beginning with] "At that time, Vimalakīrti":

there are several reasons why Vimalakīrti specifically requested Mañjuśrī to come together with him. First, he wished to see the Buddha face-to-face to have his teachings confirmed and validated. If not...
First, there is no way for him to reach the Buddha’s presence and receive the seal of confirmation as a second [bodhisattva]. Second, Mañjuśrī was previously the one who inquired after his illness;
now that Vimalakīrti is able to go to the Buddha’s presence, he should go to the Buddha together with Mañjuśrī to repay his debt of gratitude.
Third, regarding the two intentions for the bodhisattvas from that land to come: first, they wish to meet with Vimalakīrti, and since that has already been accomplished...
"Because we wish to come before the Buddha to pay our respects, we have come together.
Vimalakīrti then, by means of his supernatural power, took the great assembly along with their lion-thrones and placed them upon his right palm;

he proceeded to the place where the Buddha was, and having arrived, he set them down on the ground, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and stood with palms joined in single-minded devotion.
As they stood to one side, those bodhisattvas all vacated their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and circumambulated him seven times before standing to one side.
The great disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Great Kings, and the others likewise vacated their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, having comforted the bodhisattvas in accordance with the Dharma, bade each of them return to their places.
As soon as they sat down, they all received the teaching.

Vimalakīrti, by his supernatural power, brought the great assembly forward; those who had previously appeared lying on their beds now suddenly became so vigorous that it was as if their former illness had been cured and their present illness had vanished.
He asked the assembly, "When the sickness of sentient beings is cured, the sickness of the bodhisattva is also cured."
If the Bodhisattva’s illness has not yet been cured while the illnesses of sentient beings today have not been cured, how can it be said that the Bodhisattva’s illness is already cured?

Let us explain this by way of a parable: when the Dharma was preached in a bright room, immeasurable people resolved their minds [on enlightenment] and immeasurable people attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).

Is this not, indeed, a cure? Furthermore, to challenge the previous point: if the Bodhisattva’s illness is equal to the future limit (*paścimakoṭi*) of sentient beings, then now that sentient beings...
Regarding the question of how that which was not yet exhausted has become exhausted, the explanation states that this meaning differs from what was said previously.

As for the phrase "equal to the future limit of sentient beings," it clarifies that because the sickness of great compassion is equal to the future limit of sentient beings, it is inexhaustible; thus, the great compassion of the Bodhisattva does not cease.
When the assembly had taken their seats, the Buddha said to Śāriputra, "Do you see the deeds performed by the sovereign spiritual power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva?
Śāriputra replied, "Yes, World-Honored One, I have seen them. What do you think? World-Honored One, I behold these deeds as inconceivable;
they are not within the scope of the mind's plotting, nor can they be measured by calculation. At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, now..."
"The fragrance we have smelled has never existed since time immemorial; what kind of incense is this? The Buddha told Ānanda, "This is the fragrance from the pores of those bodhisattvas.
Thereupon, Śāriputra said to Ānanda, "The fragrance from our own pores also issues forth like this.
Ānanda asked, "From where does this come? He replied, "It comes from the Elder Vimalakīrti, who took it from the Buddha of the Land of Universal Fragrance."
If those who eat the remaining food in their homes have all the pores of their skin fragrant in this way,
when the assembly has settled, this is the second section on the definitive teaching of the Tathāgata’s seal, consisting of several phrases. Now, first,
the Buddha confirms for Śāriputra that what was performed by Vimalakīrti is inconceivable and is indeed reality.

At that time, Ānanda descended. Regarding the second Buddha’s seal (*mudrā*) addressed to Ānanda, which authenticates what the Illustrious Name (Vimalakīrti) has done—how does this differ from the previous Buddha’s seal addressed to Śāriputra?
The explanation says: the former was a general seal for all matters, whereas the present one seals only the single chapter on the Fragrant Accumulation (*Gandhavyūha*).
Furthermore, it is because one now wishes to manifest that the Buddha-activities are not singular; for by means of the Buddha-mind...
All actions performed are entirely Buddha-activities. Regarding the question and answer in the text: it is stated that Ānanda smelled a fragrance and questioned the Buddha about it.
Previously, when the fragrance pervaded the ten directions, Ānanda was only a few *li* away from the Abbot’s quarters;

why did he not perceive it then? He only now raises the question. The explanation says: there is that which can be heard and that which cannot be heard; if one were to hear it [now], one would have had to hear it [before]. However, since he does not hear it now, it follows that he could not have heard it before.
To hear [this fragrance] is like thunder shaking the earth; those who are deaf do not hear it. One asks: "This is residual fragrance;
why then is it called the fragrance of the pores? The explanation says: Since there is no longer any food, and the food remains within the abdomen, it is called the fragrance of the pores.
While for other people the contents of the stomach are impure, within the food of a Bodhisattva there is a wondrous fragrance, as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Question: A bhikṣu who has been ordained for three years emits a wondrous fragrance when preaching the Dharma. If other people also eat this food, their pores likewise become fragrant;
why then do you speak only of that bodhisattva? Answer: It is said that because [the discourse] refers to the original [cause], it speaks only of that bodhisattva.
Previously, it was called "the fragrance that gathers the body"; why now is it again called "the fragrance of that bodhisattva"? Although...
Because it is included within existence, it is said that this is the fragrance of those bodhisattvas.
Ānanda asked Vimalakīrti, "How long will this fragrance remain? Vimalakīrti replied, "It will remain until this food is digested. [Ānanda asked,] "How long will this food take to be digested?
[Vimalakīrti replied,] "The power of this food will last for seven days, and only after that will it be digested."
Furthermore, Ānanda, if a śrāvaka who has not yet entered the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*) eats this food, it will be digested only after he enters that stage.
If one who has already entered the stage of certainty eats this food, it will be digested only after he attains liberation of mind (*ceto-vimukti*).
If one who has not yet resolved upon the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna-citta*) eats this food, it will be digested once he has resolved upon it; if one who has already resolved upon it eats this...
This rice is digested only after one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);

having attained the patience of non-arising, those who eat this rice find it digested only upon reaching the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood (*ekajāti-pratibaddha*). It is like a medicine named "Supreme Flavor" (*agrarasa*):
for whoever takes it, all poisons in the body are extinguished and only then is it digested. This rice is likewise the extinguisher of all poisons of affliction (*kleśa*).
Only then does it dissolve.
In the subsequent passage, Ānanda discusses with Vimalakīrti the duration of this dissolution; as for the mention of "seven days," this is based on the fact that conditions are not fixed.

The current statement of "seven days" refers to the potency of the rice substance reaching its limit at seven days. This is illustrated by the analogy of the "Seven-Step Snake" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which describes a snake that dies after taking seven steps.
When a person bitten by a venomous insect dies after only seven or eight steps, the same applies to the substance of food; its potency lasts for seven days.
Regarding *śrāvakas* who have not yet entered the state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*), there are two distinct categories depending on their conditions for proceeding toward the Noble Path:

first, those of the Hīnayāna, and second, those of the Mahāyāna. Within the Hīnayāna, there are further two types: first, those who have not yet entered the state of certainty, and second, those who have entered the state of certainty.

"Stage" refers to the beginning of the Hīnayāna, namely the attainment of liberation as an Arhat; "no-more-learning" (aśaikṣa) refers to the end of the Hīnayāna—this briefly summarizes the beginning and the end.

For the Śrāvaka, the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) constitutes the "correct stage" (*samyag-avasthā*); for the Bodhisattva, this is generally called the "Dharma-stage" (*dharmāvasthā*). Why is this so? Because for the Śrāvaka, it is "correct" in contrast to the heterodox;

whereas for the Bodhisattva, there are three stages: first, the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*); second, the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); and finally, [the stage of] fulfillment.

The dwelling is likewise so as to eliminate all afflictions. Question: Regarding the aforementioned single mouthful of food, how can it eliminate all afflictions and lead to the attainment of the Way?

Answer: It is explained that if a physician of the world can cure physical ailments with a single dose of medicine, how could the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas not be able to heal the mental maladies of sentient beings with the single medicine of the Dharma?
Furthermore, Master Kumārajīva said: "This food is the 'fruit of reliance' (niśraya-phala) of all Buddhas.
Having obtained this fruit of reliance, one must have deep faith in cause and effect. Once one has faith in cause and effect, upon eating this food, the mind immediately attains peace.

Because the mind is at peace, one recognizes cause and effect, thereby realizing the true nature (lakṣaṇa) and attaining awakening to non-arising (anutpāda). Question: If fragrant food can extinguish [afflictions]...
If all afflictions can lead sentient beings to realize the Way, for what reason does the Tathāgata not constantly perform Buddha-work through fragrant food?
Furthermore, since both [food and teaching] are equally effective in enabling one to extinguish afflictions and attain the Way, for what reason does the Tathāgata not constantly preach the teachings?
He replied: "The teachings can provide analytical discourse through which one may attain the Way; as for fragrance, if..."

[The Buddha] asked, "Is it able to distinguish [the teachings]? He explained: "There are the teaching of sound and the teaching of form; sound distinguishes sound, and form distinguishes form. The teaching of fragrance distinguishes fragrance, and the teaching of taste distinguishes taste.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "It is unprecedented, World-Honored One! Such fragrant food is able to perform the work of a Buddha."
It is said thus: "Ānanda, there are some buddha-fields where the work of a Buddha is performed by the Buddha’s radiance;
some where it is performed by bodhisattvas; some where it is performed by persons emanated by the Buddha;
some where it is performed by the Bodhi tree; and some where it is performed by the Buddha’s robes and bedding."
There are those who perform Buddha-work through food and drink; there are those who perform Buddha-work through gardens, groves, and palaces;
there are those who perform Buddha-work through the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics; there are those who perform Buddha-work through the Buddha-body;
there are those who perform Buddha-work through empty space; and there are those for whom sentient beings should enter into the practice of discipline by means of dreams.
Ānanda, there are those who perform the work of a Buddha through metaphors such as a magical illusion, a shadow, a reflection in a mirror, the moon in water, or a mirage;
some perform the work of a Buddha through sounds, speech, and written words;

and in some pure buddha-fields, the work of a Buddha is performed in silence—without speaking, without explaining, without indicating, without cognizing, without acting, and without conditioning. Thus it is, Ānanda.
In all the majestic deportment, movements, and activities of the Buddhas, there is nothing that is not the work of a Buddha.

Ānanda, although there are these four māras and eighty-four thousand gateways of affliction through which sentient beings become exhausted, the Buddhas perform the work of a Buddha by means of these very phenomena.
This is called entering the Dharma-gate of all Buddhas; when a bodhisattva enters this gate, [they enter the work of a Buddha].
If one sees all pure and beautiful buddha-fields, one does not feel joy, nor does one become greedy or conceited;

if one sees all impure buddha-fields, one does not feel sorrow, nor is one hindered or discouraged. Rather, toward all Buddhas one gives rise to a pure mind, with joy and reverence that has never before existed.
This is because the merits of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are equal, for the sake of teaching and transforming beings.
It is for the sake of sentient beings that the Buddha-lands appear to be different. Ānanda, you see that the lands of the various Buddha-fields have many variations, yet space has no such variations.
In this same way, you see that the physical bodies of the Buddhas have many variations, but their unimpeded wisdom has no variations.
Ānanda, the physical bodies, majestic marks, lineages, precepts, concentrations, and wisdoms of all Buddhas [are likewise without variation].
In terms of liberation through wisdom, the power of the knowledge and vision of liberation, the powers and fearlessnesses, the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma),

great loving-kindness and great compassion, majestic deportment, conduct, lifespan, preaching the Dharma, teaching and transforming beings, bringing sentient beings to maturity, purifying Buddha-lands,
and the fulfillment of all Buddha-dharmas, they are entirely equal. For this reason, he is named Samyaksaṃbuddha and named Tathāgata.
"Āgata" means "Buddha. Ānanda, if I were to explain the meaning of these three phrases in detail, you would not be able to receive them all even with a lifespan of an eon.

Even if all sentient beings filling the trichiliocosm were like Ānanda—foremost in learning, possessing mindfulness, and attaining dhāraṇī—even such people as these could not [master them] in a lifespan of an eon."
"Ānanda, such is the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas—its wisdom and eloquence are limitless and inconceivable.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "From this day forward, I shall not dare to call myself one of great learning.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Do not give rise to thoughts of retreat. Why is this? Because I have said..."
"Among the śrāvakas, you are the most learned, but this does not mean the same for bodhisattvas; let it be, Ānanda. One who possesses wisdom should not limit the bodhisattvas.

Even the depths of all the oceans may be measured, but the bodhisattvas' meditative concentrations, wisdom, dhāraṇīs, eloquence, and all their merits cannot be measured. Ānanda, you [and others] should abandon [such limitations]."
The spiritual power manifested by Vimalakīrti in a single moment regarding the conduct of bodhisattvas is such that all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
even if they exerted their full powers of transformation for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, could not accomplish.
Next, we clarify that all phenomena constitute Buddha-activities. Previously, this was briefly illustrated through the single instance of sealing incense and rice;

now, it is extensively illustrated by sealing all things as Buddha-activities. The reason for this extensive clarification is that what was previously explained in brief was not exhaustive, and it is now further elucidated in detail.
Although explained extensively, it does not go beyond four points or two pairs: namely, existence and non-existence, and good and evil, as Buddha-activities.
Question: Since it has already been stated that the Buddha’s thirty-two marks constitute the Buddha-work, why is it further said that the Buddha-body itself constitutes the Buddha-work?
Answer: It is explained that at times the Tathāgata manifests one mark or two marks, and at other times he manifests them all together.

Because these manifestations differ, the thirty-two marks were explained previously, while the Buddha-body is explained hereafter. Furthermore, there are those who [assert] that space [constitutes the Buddha-work].
To perform Buddha-work is precisely unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) Buddha-work; empty space performs Buddha-work, as when Mañjuśrī manifested a body of empty space to transform King Ajātaśatru.
Regarding the statement that the four Māras and the eighty-four thousand afflictions (kleśa) perform Buddha-work:
the preceding section clarified that good performs Buddha-work; now it clarifies that evil performs Buddha-work. Master Kumārajīva said: "In this context, [it is] clarified..."
The three natures are all Buddha-activities: previously, wholesome [dharmas] were Buddha-activities; emptiness and the indeterminate were Buddha-activities;

now, unwholesome [dharmas] are Buddha-activities. Using unwholesomeness through skillful means constitutes a Buddha-activity, whereas wholesome [dharmas] without skillful means result in demonic activities.
At that time, the bodhisattvas who had come from the World of Universal Fragrance joined their palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, when we first saw this land, we conceived an inferior notion of it; we now repent and reproach ourselves for abandoning such a mind. Why is this?
The skillful means of the Buddhas are inconceivable; for the sake of delivering sentient beings, they manifest buddha-lands according to what is appropriate for them."
"It is so, World-Honored One. We pray that you will grant us a small portion of the Dharma, so that upon our return to that land, we may keep the Tathāgata in mind.

At that time, the Bodhisattvas of the World of Various Fragrances—the second group of lower-grade Bodhisattvas—having requested the Dharma and being about to return to their own world, made this request. This chapter is named after it as "The Chapter on the Practice of Bodhisattvas."
The text has three parts; now, for the first, that bodhisattva’s repentance has two sections: first, self-reproach, and second, requesting the Dharma. Self-reproach is further divided into two:
first, the actual reproach, and second, the explanation of the intent behind the repentance. This is the first part, the actual reproach:
it clarifies that when I first came and saw this land’s impurity, I gave rise to thoughts of inferiority; now, through self-reproach, it clarifies that the fault lies with me.
Question: When he was coming here, that Buddha had already commanded him not to give rise to thoughts of inferiority; why then does he again give rise to such thoughts?

Does this not contravene the Buddha’s instruction? Explanation: Although he received the Buddha’s command, now that he has arrived and seen the impurity of the land, he unconsciously gives rise to thoughts of inferiority.
It is like people today who hear the scriptural teachings commanding them not to give rise to greed, yet when they encounter the actual objects of their perception, they unconsciously do so.
Furthermore, since the Buddha did not even command those born of greed to arise—let alone those who have received his direct command—how much less so for those who have not? Question:
The preceding text states that when those bodhisattvas sit beneath the fragrant trees and smell this wondrous fragrance, they immediately possess the Samādhi of the Treasury of All Virtues.
How can they then again give rise to thoughts of superiority and inferiority, or views of purity and impurity? Answer: This is shown [for a specific purpose].
This delusion arises because one takes this land to be what it appears to be; thus, in that land, one perceives it as being identical to this land.
Since one has now awakened to this land, one immediately awakens to that land as well. For this reason, I now repent. Why is this?

The second phrase below explains the intent of the repentance: because the manifestations produced by the various skillful means (*upāya*) of the Buddhas differ, one should not give rise to [deluded] views.
Because he teaches the Dharma to those of inferior minds, such is his skillful means. "So be it, World-Honored One;
we pray you grant us a minor teaching"—this is the second formal request, a matter intended for mutual benefit between them.

However, since the bodhisattvas of that land have already perfected their practice and have nothing further to doubt, they do not require these various practices; yet they requested that the various practices be taught.

This is also because the Bodhisattvas of this land requested [the teaching] by means of the four lines of verse; that [request] was for the sake of this [land], and this request was also for the sake of that [land].
Furthermore, that [request] was made for the sake of that [land]. Moreover, this is discussed from the perspective of the majority:
just as in this world sound serves as a Buddha-work, there are also other matters that serve as Buddha-works; whereas in that [land], the absence of speech serves as a Buddha-work.
Furthermore, there are indeed instances where verbal expression constitutes the Buddha’s work; this is simply the case in the majority of circumstances.

Moreover, a Bodhisattva must universally study the essence of a Bodhisattva, universally transform sentient beings, and universally travel to all lands. When transformation occurs through verbal expression, that is transformation by means of speech;
when transformation occurs without verbal expression, that is transformation by means of silence. For these reasons, it is necessary to request the Dharma.
The Buddha told the bodhisattvas: "There is a dharma-gate of liberation called 'the Exhaustible and the Inexhaustible,' which you should study.
What is meant by the exhaustible? It refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). What is meant by the inexhaustible? It refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

As for a bodhisattva, they do not exhaust the conditioned, nor do they dwell in the unconditioned. Why is it said that they do not exhaust the conditioned? Because they do not depart from great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) and do not abandon great [compassion]."
With profound compassion, they give rise to the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñā-citta*) without neglecting it; they teach and transform sentient beings without ever becoming weary;

they constantly practice the four methods of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*) in accordance with them; they protect and uphold the True Dharma without sparing their own bodies or lives; they plant all roots of goodness without weariness;

their resolve always dwells peacefully in skillful means and dedication (*pariṇāmanā*); they seek the Dharma without indolence; and they preach the Dharma without stinginess, exerting themselves diligently.
In order to make offerings to all Buddhas, they enter the cycle of birth and death without fear; amidst all honors and insults, their minds are free from sorrow or joy;
they do not slight those who have not yet studied, but revere those who study as if they were Buddhas; they cause those fallen into afflictions to give rise to right mindfulness;

they do not regard the pleasure of seclusion as supreme, nor do they cling to their own pleasure, but instead rejoice in the pleasure of others; regarding all meditative concentrations as if they were hellish states, [they apply themselves].
Within the cycle of birth and death, one should regard those who come seeking [help] as virtuous teachers; one should regard the relinquishing of all possessions as the attainment of omniscience;
one should regard those who violate the precepts with thoughts of rescue and protection; one should regard the *pāramitās* as one’s parents;

and one should regard the dharmas of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) as one’s kinsmen. One should cultivate roots of goodness without limit, using the various pure lands [as the field for their cultivation].
Adorning one's own buddha-field through the perfection of boundless giving, fulfilling the marks and signs of excellence, and eliminating all evils by purifying body, speech, and mind;
maintaining courage throughout countless kalpas of birth and death, remaining untiring in resolve upon hearing of the Buddha’s immeasurable virtues;
and using the sword of wisdom to slay the thieves of affliction, emerging from the aggregates and realms to bear the burden of sentient beings forever.

Causing them to attain liberation through great diligence, they subdue the armies of Māra; they constantly seek the wisdom of the true mark of non-conceptuality, practice few desires and contentment, and do not abandon worldly dharmas.
Without violating their dignified deportment, they are able to conform to worldly customs, giving rise to supernormal powers and wisdom to lead sentient beings on the Path.
Attaining mindfulness and *dhāraṇī*, they do not forget what they have heard; they skillfully discern the various faculties of beings and sever the afflictions of sentient beings.
Resolving doubts through the eloquence of joyful speech, they expound the Dharma without obstruction; they purify the ten paths of wholesome action to receive the blessings of humans and devas;

they cultivate the four immeasurables to open the path to the Brahma-world; they exhort [the Buddhas] to preach the Dharma, rejoice in others' merit, and praise their excellence, thereby attaining the voice of a Buddha;

through goodness of body, speech, and mind, they attain the majestic deportment of a Buddha; by deeply cultivating wholesome dharmas, their practice becomes ever more sublime, and through the teaching of the Mahāyāna, they become Bodhisattvas.
When the monastic mind is free from negligence and does not lose any wholesome conduct, such a dharma is called a bodhisattva’s non-exhaustion of existence.
What is meant by a bodhisattva not dwelling in the unconditioned? It means training in emptiness without taking emptiness as a realization;
training in signlessness and wishlessness without taking signlessness and wishlessness as realizations; and training in non-arising without taking non-arising as a realization.
To realize impermanence while never wearying of the roots of goodness; to contemplate the suffering of the world while not loathing birth and death;
to contemplate non-self while teaching others without weariness; to contemplate cessation while not remaining in eternal quiescence;

to contemplate detachment while cultivating goodness with body and mind; to contemplate the absence of a place of return while returning to and taking refuge in wholesome dharmas; and to contemplate non-arising.
One bears the burden of all beings through the nature of birth; one contemplates the outflow-free (anāsrava) yet does not sever the outflows;
one contemplates non-action yet teaches and transforms sentient beings through the dharma of action; one contemplates emptiness and non-existence yet does not abandon great compassion;

one contemplates the station of the True Dharma yet does not follow the Lesser Vehicle; one contemplates that all dharmas are illusory, lacking solidity, devoid of a person, devoid of a master, and without marks.

Because their original vows are not yet fulfilled, they do not remain in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); because their merit, meditative concentration, and wisdom are not in vain, they cultivate such dharmas as these—this is called the bodhisattva’s non-abiding in the unconditioned.
Furthermore, because they possess merit, they do not abide in the unconditioned; because they possess wisdom, they do not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Because of great compassion, they do not abide in the unconditioned; because they fulfill their original vows, they do not exhaust the conditioned. This is the accumulation of the Dharma.
Because they administer medicine, they do not abide in the unconditioned; because they bestow medicine according to the needs of others, they do not exhaust the conditioned.
Because they know the illnesses of sentient beings, they do not abide in the unconditioned; because they extinguish the illnesses of sentient beings, they do not exhaust the conditioned.

Sons of noble family, when Bodhisattvas have cultivated this dharma—neither exhausting the conditioned nor abiding in the unconditioned—it is called the Dharma-gate of Liberation through Exhaustion and Non-exhaustion. You...
"You should train thus.
In the second of the three sections following the Buddha’s address to the bodhisattvas, the Buddha provides a detailed exposition on the conduct of bodhisattvas, which consists of three parts:
first, the simultaneous presentation of the exhausted and the inexhaustible; second, the simultaneous explanation of the exhausted and the inexhaustible; and third, the simultaneous [conclusion].
The preceding section constitutes the first pair of headings, which provide the exhortation. What follows below is the second pair, which provides the explanation.

What is meant by "that which has an end"? It refers to conditioned birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); because it is conditioned, it is subject to wear and destruction, and thus has an end. What is meant by "that which has no end"? It refers to unconditioned *nirvāṇa*;
because it is unconditioned, it is not subject to wear and destruction, and thus has no end. As for the Bodhisattva, they do not exhaust that which has an end.
"To not abide in the unconditioned" correctly clarifies the Bodhisattva practice as a counter-demonstration against the Śrāvaka. Why?
Because while the Śrāvaka exhausts conditioned birth-and-death and abides in unconditioned Nirvāṇa, this Bodhisattva is different from that;
he constantly remains within birth-and-death without exhausting the conditioned, because he transforms sentient beings and therefore does not abide in the unconditioned. Thus it is said.

It is said that one who has severed the afflictions of the five stages of dwelling and attained eternal *nirvāṇa* exhausts all that is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and abides in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
If this were so, it would fall short of the causal practice; how could it be the merit of the fruit? Therefore, this is not tenable.
To say "not separated from great compassion" clarifies that because one possesses great compassion for sentient beings, one does not exhaust the conditioned.

"Furthermore, one who gives rise to the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*) and does not neglect it" refers to the fact that previously [the practitioner] was not separated from great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*), which is the downward transformation of beings;
now, giving rise to the mind of omniscience is the upward seeking of enlightenment. These two practices are the constant conduct of a Bodhisattva;

therefore, it says "and does not neglect it. Regarding the phrase "regarding all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*), one perceives them as if they were hell," this clarifies the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
The meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) that give rise to self-conceit (*māna*) and those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) destroy the bodhicitta;

since such concentrations thus destroy and extinguish the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), they are indeed nothing other than hell. Therefore, it is said that one should maintain the perception of being in hell while within meditative concentration.

Within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one should maintain the perception of a pleasure garden (*udyāna*); for the Bodhisattva practices within birth and death as if playing and enjoying oneself in a pleasure garden.
Is it not joyful that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) accomplish omniscience?
When the great garden trees grow, the Bodhisattva grows through correct contemplation within birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

To regard those who come seeking as one would a virtuous teacher—when a beggar comes to ask for alms, the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are immediately present; these six are indeed the Bodhisattva’s virtuous teachers. Thus they arise.

Though deaths have occurred countless billions of times, there are those who are courageous; as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the path of the Buddha is long and distant, yet sentient beings possess a nature that enables them to exert diligent effort to traverse it.
Next, the explanation of "not abiding in the unconditioned" follows the text:

those who abide in the unconditioned do so by forming a conceptual understanding (*vikalpa*) of the unconditioned, and such conceptualization constitutes "abiding. However, the Bodhisattva is not like this. [The passage] beginning with "O noble sons... [explains this further].
The third pair of verses:
At that time, when those bodhisattvas heard this Dharma being preached, they were all greatly rejoiced;
they scattered various kinds of exquisite flowers of diverse colors and diverse fragrances throughout the trichiliocosm as an offering to the Buddha and to this [Dharma].

The sutras and the bodhisattvas, having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, marveled at this unprecedented occurrence, saying, "Śākyamuni Buddha is truly able to employ such skillful means here! Having spoken, they suddenly vanished and returned to their own land.
At that time, those bodhisattvas, having heard this great exposition of the Dharma— the third instance of those bodhisattvas hearing the teaching—
rejoiced with great joy.
Chapter Twelve: Seeing the Buddha Akṣobhya.
Regarding why this chapter follows the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Practice," if we discuss it according to the text:
the preceding "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Practice" expounded the Dharma-gate for that land, whereas this chapter expounds the Dharma-gate for this land.

Now, in this "Chapter on Beholding the Buddha Akṣobhya," the Pure Land is manifested before this defiled land. Previously, for the sake of bodhisattvas in the Pure Land, the Dharma-gate of the defiled land was taught;

now, for the sake of bodhisattvas in the defiled land, the Buddha of the Pure Land is manifested before them. In the preceding chapter, the Dharma-gate of the defiled land was taught for the sake of the Pure Land;
likewise, here the Pure Land is manifested for the sake of this defiled land. Thus, it is attained for this land as well.
For this reason, even this land can be considered a Pure Land; however, the primary intent here is to manifest that purity within the context of what currently appears as defilement.
Furthermore, the reason this chapter has come forth is not merely for the immediate benefit of those present, but to provide a distant remedy for future generations. Why?

Because the people of the present age are all disciples of the Buddha, yet none of them recognize him. Now, if those who wish to see the Buddha were to ask how they might do so, [the answer would follow].
Regarding the Buddha: some worldly guests and their followers say that the Buddha image in the hall is the Buddha; others say that one *zhang* and six feet, or even ten thousand *chi*, is the Buddha.

Still others say there is a Buddha who possesses two bodies: the body of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which is with outflows (*sāsrava*), and the body of precepts, concentration, and so forth, which is without outflows (*anāsrava*).
That which is with outflows is the Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), and that which is without outflows is the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*). Although this is so...
All these are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). If they are conditioned, how can they be called seeing the Buddha? The Buddha is not conditioned;
what you now see as existing is still seeing existence—how could this be seeing the Buddha? Therefore, the *Śāstra* says: "Those with deep and heavy false views say that there is no Tathāgata;
yet even the conceptualization and discrimination of a 'Tathāgata in cessation' is not [the truth]. Furthermore, the masters of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* hold that [the Buddha] exists.

Second, the Kai-shan [school] explains that while the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) is impermanent, the *dharmakāya* (dharma body) is eternally abiding. They distinguish between the number of dharmas and the number of persons;
they hold that all human births and phenomena are impermanent, thereby clarifying that the response body is impermanent while the dharma body is eternally abiding. Zang-yang says:

"The birth-body (*janmakāya*) is existent, whereas the dharma body is neither existent nor non-existent. It transcends the two truths. The Di-lun [school] states: "The *dharmadhātu* is neither existent nor..."
In the absence of a teacher, one provisionally takes the Middle Way as the Buddha; now it is clarified that all such views fail to see the Buddha.
That you now see the Buddha as permanent is merely seeing permanence—what is meant by "seeing the Buddha"? If the Buddha were permanent, one would always see the Buddha;

yet the Buddha is not something seen through the permanence of a constant presence, so how could one see the Buddha? Since this statement regarding permanence is thus established, the same applies to the other three propositions.
All are thus. Now it is clarified that as one contemplates the true mark of the body according to the text, so too does one contemplate the Buddha;

for this reason, this chapter has come forth. Next, regarding the explanation of the chapter title: while the preceding chapter was named after its cause, this chapter receives its designation from its fruit.
The previous was called the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Practice," and thus it was named after the cause; this chapter, "Seeing the Buddha Akṣobhya," is named after the fruit.

Because it refers to a category, it is a name for a fruit. Furthermore, in the preceding chapter, "person" and "dharma" were mentioned together; in this chapter, both the "primary" (依) and the "auxiliary" (正) are presented as titles.

Regarding the statement that in the preceding chapter "person" and "dharma" were mentioned together: the Bodhisattva is the person, and the dharma is the practice. Now, regarding these two titles of the primary and auxiliary:
the Buddha is the primary fruit, and the land is the auxiliary fruit. Moreover, the title of the preceding chapter was...
To summarize: the title of this present chapter is an abbreviated version of what was explained at length in the preceding chapter.
"Abbreviated" refers to the fact that there are only two categories—person and dharma, subject and object. "Expanded" refers to the three characters [of the title] being condensed into two pairs:

"vision" (*darśana*) is the wisdom that is the perceiving subject, and "Buddha-land" (*buddhakṣetra*) is the realm that is the perceived object. Within this pair of object and wisdom, regarding the object itself, there are two: the Buddha is the primary [object].
The "Fruit Land" (Phala-kṣetra) refers to the support of the fruit; because it possesses both the pair of the environment and its inhabitants, it is said to be "vast.

Regarding Akṣobhya Buddha, this is the foreign term. Master Kumārajīva, Sengyuì, and others say it means "Immovable Buddha. The *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* by Dharma Master Huìyì of the Zōngdài school says it means "Angerless Buddha.
However, the character "chù" (閦) does not exist in this land [of China]; it was a transliteration provided by the translators according to the meaning.
These characters were composed for this purpose; because one now beholds that Buddha and takes him as the basis for this title, it is called the "Chapter on Beholding the Land of Akṣobhya Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked Vimalakīrti: "Do you wish to see the Tathāgata? By what means do you contemplate the Tathāgata?"
Vimalakīrti said: "Just as one contemplates the true reality of one's own body, so too does one contemplate the Buddha.

When I contemplate the Tathāgata, I see that he does not come from the past, nor does he go to the future, nor does he abide in the present. I do not contemplate form, nor the suchness of form, nor the nature of form;
I do not contemplate sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor the suchness of consciousness, nor the nature of consciousness. He does not arise from the four great elements."
Equal to empty space, the six sense bases are without accumulation; eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind have already transcended them and do not abide within the three realms.
Having already departed from the three defilements, one accords with the three gates of liberation and is endowed with the three types of supernormal knowledge.

Equal to ignorance, it is neither a single characteristic nor different characteristics; neither its own characteristic nor another’s characteristic; neither the absence of characteristics nor the grasping of characteristics; neither this shore nor the other shore.
Without dwelling in the middle stream, they transform sentient beings; they contemplate quiescent extinction, yet do not undergo eternal cessation.

They are neither here nor there, neither by this nor by that. They cannot be known by wisdom, nor can they be cognized by consciousness. They are without darkness and without light; without name and without mark;
without strength and without weakness; neither pure nor defiled; not abiding in any direction, yet not departing from any direction; and they are not conditioned.

It is not unconditioned, without demonstration, and without teaching; it is neither giving nor stinginess, neither precept-keeping nor transgression, neither patience nor anger, neither diligence nor indolence, neither concentration nor distraction, neither wisdom nor folly, neither sincerity nor deceit;

it neither comes nor goes, neither issues forth nor enters; all paths of speech are cut off; it is neither a field of merit nor not a field of merit, and it is not one to whom offerings should be made.

It is not that which should be worshipped; it is neither grasped nor abandoned; it is neither with marks nor without marks. It is equal to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and identical to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
it is ineffable and immeasurable, transcending all calculation and measurement. It is neither great nor small; it is neither seen nor heard, neither perceived nor known.
Free from all fetters and bonds, it is equal to the wisdom of all sentient beings, being non-discriminative toward all phenomena.

There is absolutely no gain and no loss, no turbidity and no affliction, no action and no arising, no birth and no cessation, no fear and no sorrow, no joy and no weariness, no past existence, no future existence, and no present existence;

it cannot be displayed through any verbal expression or conceptual discrimination. World-Honored One, one should contemplate the body of the Tathāgata as being thus, and observe it by means of this contemplation.
This is called right contemplation; if one contemplates otherwise, it is called false contemplation.
This chapter is divided into two parts for the sake of timing: first, the actual skillful means, and second, the skillful means based on reality. Now, these are further divided into two:
first, contemplating the body of the Buddha, and second, contemplating the land of Akṣobhya. Regarding the first [of these], it is again divided into two, the first of which is...

Regarding the second treatise on contemplating the Buddha, which concerns birth and death, this is now the first [section]: contemplating the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This has both general and specific aspects. To speak of the general:
it clarifies that while all sentient beings do not fail to desire to see the Buddha, they are simply unable to see him.
Why? Because some claim to see him by means of physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and vocal sounds. As the *Prajñāpāramitā* says: "If one sees me by means of form, or seeks me by means of sound..."
When [Vimalakīrti] sought [the Buddha] and could not see the Tathāgata, why was it that these five phrases all state he could not see him?

To speak of them separately clarifies that Vimalakīrti required the great assembly to come and see the Buddha. He said there is a Buddha who can be seen and that there is one’s own self that can see the Buddha;

this refers to the object of vision (*ālambana*) and the wisdom that sees (*jñāna*). He spoke thus because he perceived the Buddha’s body as superior and his own body as inferior—these are the two forms of seeing.
It is not that one sees the Buddha [therefore]; thus, Vimalakīrti breaks through [delusion] by contemplating the true mark of the body, and contemplating the Buddha is likewise so.
The *Nirvāṇa-śāstra* explains the "esoteric" [teaching]: "That there is Buddha-nature outside the bodies of sentient beings is not esoteric;
that there is Buddha-nature within the bodies of sentient beings is not esoteric; that sentient beings themselves are Buddha-nature is what is esoteric. Now...

To contemplate the body as real is to contemplate the Buddha; sentient beings are themselves the Buddha-nature—this is the secret. Why, then, does it say that contemplating the body is contemplating the Buddha?
In truth, they have never been two, nor have they ever been one. What is called "identity" (*iti*) here is said to be identity precisely because they are not identical.

To shatter the notion of non-identity is also to be unattached to identity; to shatter difference is to be unattached to unity. This is the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

When I contemplate the Tathāgata as one who does not come from the prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) nor go to the posterior limit (*aparakoṭi*), this is based on the contemplation of the three periods of time.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* clarifies that the past is the prior limit, the future is the posterior limit, and the present is the "present limit" (*pratyutpannakoṭi*).
If this is so, why is it now said that he does not come from the prior limit nor go to the posterior limit? The explanation is that there are two versions of the sūtra. In one...
In this version of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the passage corresponding to the "Great Chapter" (*Mahāprajñāpāramitā*) of other versions is as follows:
"Those who can understand [this] say that the Tathāgata comes from the future to the present; the present is the past, and the past is what has gone. The current text is not like this:

it states that he does not come from the prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) and does not go to the posterior limit (*aparākoṭi*). Regarding this, people say that the Tathāgata comes from the future to the present.

This existence re-enters the past from the past; because this existence returns to the present from the past, and the present again departs toward the future, to now demand that it be otherwise is incorrect.
Therefore, it is said that there is no coming from the prior limit (*pūrvānta*) and no going to the subsequent limit (*aparānta*).

This is the interpretation made by Dao-sheng. One does not contemplate form as before; having previously contemplated it according to the three periods of time, one now contemplates it according to the five [aggregates].

Regarding the examination of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) as not arising from the four great elements: previously, this was distinguished in terms of the result; now it is explained in terms of the cause.

"The six sense-bases have no accumulation" means that while the six sense-bases of sentient beings are accumulated, the Tathāgata does not accumulate them, and thus they are said to be without accumulation.

"Not being in the three realms" clarifies the absence of the three defilements (*kaṣāya*) which are the results of the three realms; "being free from [them]" clarifies the absence of the three causes of the three realms.

The "defilements" (*mala*) are the three poisons. The non-duality of the waters of the three gates of liberation (*trivimokṣamukha*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) is as explained in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*.
"Neither this shore, nor the other shore, nor the middle stream": birth and death are the "this shore," nirvāṇa is the "other shore," and the Eightfold Noble Path is the "middle stream.
Some say that the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) constitutes the middle stream. These [realities] cannot be known by the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*).
Because the six consciousnesses cannot cognize it, it is said that "it cannot be known by wisdom, nor can it be cognized by consciousness.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Vimalakīrti, "From where did you pass away to come and be born here?
Vimalakīrti replied, "Does the Dharma you have attained undergo passing away and birth? Śāriputra said, "There is no passing away or birth. [Vimalakīrti continued,] "If all dharmas..."
Regarding the absence of the marks of death and birth, how can you ask, "From where did you die to come and be born here"? What do you think?
For example, when a magician conjures an illusion of a man or a woman, do they truly die and are they truly born? Śāriputra replied, "There is no dying and no being born. [The interlocutor said:
"Have you not heard the Buddha teach that all phenomena have the characteristic of being like an illusion? He answered, "It is so. If all phenomena..."
Regarding those whose characteristics are like an illusion, why do you ask, "From where have you passed away to come to this birth?

Śāriputra, "passing away" refers to the characteristic of the deceptive dharma that is subject to disintegration; "birth" refers to the characteristic of the deceptive dharma that continues in succession.
Although a bodhisattva passes away, they do not exhaust their roots of goodness; although they are born, they do not increase in various evils. At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
There is a land named Abhirati where the Buddha is named Akṣobhya; it was from that land that Vimalakīrti passed away to be reborn here.
Śāriputra said, "It is unprecedented, World-Honored One! How can this man abandon a pure land to come to delight in this place of much anger and harm?
Vimalakīrti said to Śāriputra, "What do you think? Is the light of the sun..."
[The interlocutor] asked: "When it emerges, does it coincide with darkness? He replied: "No. When the sunlight emerges, there is no longer any darkness. Vimalakīrti said:
"For what reason does the sun travel over Jambudvīpa? He replied: "It is because it desires to illuminate and thereby eliminate the darkness. Vimalakīrti said:
"In this same way, although a bodhisattva is born in impure buddha-fields, they do not [associate with them] for the sake of transforming sentient beings."
It is merely that they conjoin with the darkness of ignorance; it simply extinguishes the darkness of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of sentient beings.
At that time, Śāriputra asked the second question regarding death and birth: "For what reason, O Noble One (*gṛhapati*), do you die and take birth?
The commentary explains that this intention is solely because [birth] arises from delusion. This was because Śāriputra asked, and the Tathāgata answered accordingly.
Since they have come from the world of *Sukhāvatī*, the great assembly now wishes to see the Tathāgata of that land;

therefore, he manifests him for them. Furthermore, as for those who have passed away and been reborn: since the preceding extensive praise of Vimalakīrti’s sublime virtue indicates that one born in such a place of high virtue must necessarily dwell in a pure realm, he now asks about the place of rebirth. This concludes the praise of Vimalakīrti’s virtues above.
This contemplation now praises the inconceivability of Vimalakīrti’s place of birth. Why? If one were born from impurity into impurity, it would not be inconceivable;
however, that he can now leave a pure land to come here to this realm of impurity, extensively propagate the transformation of the Way, and benefit sentient beings—this is indeed inconceivable.
Vimalakīrti said: "As for the Dharma you have attained, both this and its substance..."
Answer: To clarify, those who have realized the ultimate truth and attained the fruit of realization possess neither death nor birth;

yet for those who have not realized the ultimate truth and attained the fruit, there is not even the status of "fruit" or "non-fruit," so how could there be death or birth? By posing this counter-question, what do you intend to refute?
You followers of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) yourselves lack both death and birth; why then do you claim that we of the Great Practice (Mahāyāna) possess death and birth? What is your intention?
To explain this by way of analogy: it is said that in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), I have neither death nor birth;

in the ultimate truth, there is likewise neither death nor birth. However, in conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one ultimately perceives the existence of birth. Therefore, the analogy of an illusion is raised to clarify the absence of death and birth. Above, we addressed the absence of death and birth from the perspective of the ultimate truth;
now, we address the absence of death and birth from the perspective of conventional truth. Above, we spoke in terms of phenomena (*dharma*) to examine non-arising; now—
To provide an analogy for examining the absence of death and birth: at this time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra.
This clarifies that while Vimalakīrti above challenged the śrāvakas by declaring their questions invalid, the Tathāgata now answers Vimalakīrti.

The reason Vimalakīrti challenged [the notion of] death and birth was because they had come with a mind harboring such concepts; therefore, he had to challenge them. The great assembly should hear this.

Because there is benefit to be gained, the Buddha must provide an answer. Furthermore, having previously refuted the notion that there is no death or birth, one might fall into the pit of non-arising by claiming there is no death or birth;

therefore, it is now clarified that for a Bodhisattva, there is neither arising nor death, yet there is both arising and death, and likewise neither arising nor death, yet both arising and death—this is the "neither-arising-nor-death" arising-and-death.
Question: If a Bodhisattva has arising and death, how does this differ from that of an ordinary person?
What is the difference between these interpretations? Some say that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) have birth and death, whereas Bodhisattvas are without birth and death;

and that because there is no birth for those who are already born, they cause long-lasting joy, and because there is no extinction for those who are already extinguished, they cause long-lasting yearning—thus they differ.

Furthermore, the former was explained from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), while the latter answers from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) regarding the existence of birth and death, as clarified in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
When the light of Prabhūtaratna appeared as an auspicious omen, the Buddha asked about its cause and condition; Mañjuśrī replied that this light is wisdom, and wisdom is eternally abiding.
The Buddha said, "Do not enter into the profound samādhi of emptiness; you should explain this by means of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
It is the same here: Vimalakīrti spoke from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), whereas now [the Buddha] speaks from the perspective of conventional truth.
The first part concerning the Buddha’s explanation of the place of birth can be understood according to the text.

Next, Vimalakīrti, fearing that people might say that a bodhisattva abandons the pure for the defiled, cites the rising of the sun and moon as a metaphor. This is because the bodhisattva enters the defiled realm so that the defiled may become identical with the non-defiled.
At that time, the great assembly was filled with longing and desired to see the world of Sukhāvatī, the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, and his host of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
Knowing the thoughts of the entire assembly, the Buddha addressed Vimalakīrti, saying:
"Good son, for the sake of this assembly, manifest the land of Sukhāvatī, the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, and all the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas."
The assembly all desired to see them; thereupon, Vimalakīrti thought to himself:

"Without rising from my seat, I shall bring forth the world-system of Abhirati, along with its Iron Ring Mountains, mountains, rivers, valleys, streams, great oceans, springs, Mount Sumeru, the sun, moon, and stars, as well as the palaces of the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and brahmās, together with the multitude of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, cities, and towns."
The men and women, great and small, of the villages, as well as Tathāgata Acala and the various exquisite lotuses at the Bodhi tree that perform Buddha-work throughout the ten directions—
by means of three jeweled staircases leading from Jambudvīpa to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
the devas descend these jeweled stairs to pay homage to Tathāgata Acala and listen to and receive the Dharma.
The people of Jambudvīpa also ascended its steps and went up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where they beheld those gods.
Having accomplished such immeasurable merit in that World of Sublime Joy, [the Buddha] reached from the Akaniṣṭha Heaven above down to the water’s edge below;
with his right hand, he severed and took it up like a potter’s wheel and brought it into this world, showing it to all the multitudes as if it were a garland of flowers.
Having formed this thought, he entered into samādhi and manifested supernatural powers; with his right hand, he severed and took the world of Abhirati and placed it within this land.
The bodhisattvas and śrāvakas who had attained supernatural powers, as well as the other devas and humans, all cried out in unison:
"Indeed, World-Honored One! Who has taken us away? We pray that you will grant us protection! The Buddha Akṣobhya said:
"This was not done by me; it was produced by the supernatural power of Vimalakīrti.

Those others who have not yet attained supernormal powers were neither aware of nor perceived where they had gone. Although the world of *Sukhāvatī* entered this land, it neither increased nor decreased;
this world was not made cramped, remaining no different than before. At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed the assembly:
"Great assembly, you should all observe the world of Sukhāvatī and the Tathāgata Akṣobhya;
that land is magnificently adorned, the bodhisattvas' conduct is pure, and the disciples are stainless. They replied, "Yes, we have seen it.
The Buddha said, "If a bodhisattva wishes to attain such a pure buddha-field, they should study the path practiced by the Tathāgata Akṣobhya to manifest this world of Sukhāvatī."
At that time, fourteen *nayuta* of people in the Sahā world resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and all vowed to be born in the Buddha-land of Sukhāvatī.
Śākyamuni Buddha immediately bestowed upon them the prediction, saying:
"They shall be born in that land. At that time, the world of Sukhāvatī had already completed all the deeds necessary for the benefit of this world-system.
When [the world] returned to its original place, the entire assembly saw it. The Buddha asked Śāriputra, "Do you see this World of Wonderful Joy and the Buddha Akṣobhya?
He replied, "Yes, World-Honored One, I have already seen them.

The Buddha said, "I wish that all sentient beings may attain a pure land like that of Akṣobhya Buddha, and obtain supernatural powers like those of Vimalakīrti. World-Honored One, we have truly gained great benefit."
Those beings who now, in the present, or after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, hear this sutra shall likewise obtain excellent benefit;
how much more so those who, having heard it, believe, understand, accept, uphold, recite, explain, and practice according to the Dharma!
If anyone should obtain this sutra in their hands, they have already obtained the treasure of the Dharma.
If there are those in the land of Tibet who read and recite this, explain its meaning, and practice according to the teaching, they will be protected and remembered by all the Buddhas.
Those who make offerings to such persons should know that they are making offerings to the Buddha himself.

Those who copy and uphold this sutra scroll should know that the Tathāgata is present within their very home. Furthermore, if anyone hears this sutra and is able to rejoice in it with sympathetic joy—
Such a person shall proceed toward all-knowledge; if one can believe and understand even a single four-line verse of this sutra and explain it to others,
you should know that this person has received the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the great assembly descended from the high dais. This concludes the first contemplation on the Buddha’s body; now follows the second, the praise of the land of Akṣobhya Buddha.
The reason for this praise is that the great assembly, having heard [of it], will attain the Way; thus they are praised.
The reason the great assembly yearns with longing is that they have heard the Buddha say that Vimalakīrti has come from Abhirati, and that Vimalakīrti’s virtue is already inconceivable.
To deliberate upon a land must be with utmost subtlety; since there are already beautiful people, there must also be a subtle land.
Therefore, the desire to see it was fulfilled when the thirty-two thousand seats all entered the room; yet this was not yet inconceivable.
Now, to bring that great assembly here into this land without any obstruction, and to perform such deeds as creating the three paths and so forth—this is truly inconceivable. How could this be?
To claim that this [text] is for the purpose of circulation is a great error. Next, the attainment of the Way is explained according to the text.
Chapter Thirteen: Dharma-Service. Chapter Thirteen: Dharma-Service.
This is the third chapter within the "Third Collection of the Ānanda Garden" (Āmrapālī-vana-punaḥ-saṃgīti). Dharma.
Regarding the reason why this chapter on "Making Offerings" (Pūjā) appears here: as the preaching of the sutra was nearing its conclusion, [the Buddha] exhorted beings to propagate and proclaim it.
Thus, before entrusting the teaching for its wide dissemination, he first praised the offering of the Dharma; only after such praise could the entrustment for propagation take place.

As for what is called the "offering of the Dharma," there are many kinds of offerings: some are material offerings, such as kingdoms, cities, wives, children, and so forth; others are bodily offerings.
There are offerings such as those of Sadāprarudita, who sprinkled his face with blood; King Bhaiṣajyarāja, who burned his arm;

and others who offered praise, made reverent prostrations, and performed acts of veneration. Although there are such methods of offering, among all forms of offering, the offering of the Dharma is supreme.
This present instance is precisely the offering of the Dharma. As for what is called the "offering of the Dharma":
Furthermore, there are many types [of this]. To act as the Buddha did when he taught, and now to act according to what was taught—this is one kind of Dharma-offering.

Second, to act according to what was taught and furthermore to teach and transform sentient beings by acting accordingly so that they may awaken to the Way—this is also a Dharma-offering. Next, it clarifies the protection of both the speaker and the audience.

This is precisely what is meant by the "Dharma-offering. Next, it is clarified that not only the act of preaching and listening constitutes the Dharma-offering, but all five types of Dharma-preachers are also called Dharma-offerings. Question: To whom does the Dharma-offering make its offering?
If material offerings are made to a person before one, to what object does the Dharma-offering now make its offering? Answer: It makes an offering to the Buddha. Why is this so?
To act as one speaks and to speak as one acts accords with the Buddha’s mind; therefore, this is an offering to the Buddha.
Just as when one offers material wealth to another person and that person rejoices, it constitutes an offering, so too is it here:
to act as one speaks and to speak as one acts, thereby gladdening the Buddha’s mind, is to offer to the Buddha.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha in the midst of the great assembly, saying:

"World-Honored One, although I have heard hundreds of thousands of sūtras from the Buddha and Mañjuśrī, I have never before heard this sūtra of inconceivable, sovereign supernormal powers and the definitive true mark.
As I understand the meaning and intent of what the Buddha has taught, if there are sentient beings who hear this..."

Those who believe in, understand, accept, uphold, read, and recite this sutra-dharma will certainly attain this dharma without doubt; how much more so for those who practice according to the teaching—
such persons shall close off all evil destinies and open the gates to all virtues, being constantly protected and remembered by all Buddhas,
subduing heterodox scholars, destroying the enmity of Māras, cultivating and purifying bodhi, dwelling securely at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), and treading upon it.
"O World-Honored One, if there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice according to what the Tathāgata has taught, I shall, together with my retinue, provide offerings and service.

In whatever village, city, town, mountain forest, or wilderness this sutra may be found, I shall also go to that place together with my retinue for the sake of hearing and receiving the Dharma. As for those who have not yet developed faith..."
For those who have not yet given rise to faith, you should cause them to do so; for those who have already given rise to faith, you should provide protection for them.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, Devendra! It is as you have said. I rejoice in your words.
This sutra extensively explains the inconceivable *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present. Therefore, Devendra, if a good person..."

If a son or daughter of good family upholds, recites, and makes offerings to this sutra, they are thereby making offerings to the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, as well as to Śakra and Brahmā.
Suppose the Trichiliocosm were filled with Tathāgatas, like a thicket of sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, rice, or hemp;
if there were a son or daughter of good family who, for one kalpa or slightly less than a kalpa, [were to honor them...]
For one kalpa, they shall reverently honor, respect, praise, and make offerings to them, providing all that brings peace and comfort, until after the parinirvāṇa of those Buddhas;
for each and every relic of their entire body, they shall erect stupas made of the seven precious jewels, as vast as a four-continent world-system and reaching as high as the Brahma-heaven,
adorned with masts and banners, and provided with all kinds of flowers, incense, necklaces, victory banners, streamers, and exquisite, supreme music.
"Whether for one kalpa or for less than a kalpa, if one were to make offerings to them, what do you think, Śakra Devānām Indra?
Would the merit planted by that person not be great? Śakra Devendra replied, "It would be very much so, World-Honored One;

even if one were to spend hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas speaking of that merit, it could not be exhausted. The Buddha told Śakra Devendra, "You should know, O son of good family or daughter of good family..."
To hear this *Acintyavimokṣa* sūtra, to believe, understand, accept, uphold, recite, and practice it, brings forth merit far greater than that.
Why is this? Because the Bodhi of all Buddhas arises from this; the characteristics of Bodhi are immeasurable.
For these reasons, the merit is incalculable. The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas: "In the past, beyond measureless asaṃkhyeya kalpas..."

During a *kalpa* of the *kṣetra*, there was a Buddha named Bhaiṣajyarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. His world was named Mahāvyūha;
the kalpa was named Vyūha. The Buddha’s lifespan was twenty minor *kalpas*, and his assembly of śrāvakas numbered thirty [thousand].
There were sixty billion nayutas of bodhisattva monks and twelve billion Śakras.

At that time, there was a wheel-turning sage king named Ratnacchattra, who possessed the seven treasures and ruled over the four continents. He had a thousand sons, handsome, brave, and strong, capable of subduing all enemies.
Then, Ratnacchattra, together with his retinue, made offerings to the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja and bestowed gifts upon him.
Having remained in this state of peace for five full kalpas, and after those five kalpas had passed, he addressed his thousand sons:
"You, too, should follow my example and make offerings to the Buddha with a profound mind.

Thereupon, the thousand sons accepted their father king’s command and made offerings to the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja for another five full kalpas, providing all manner of comforts and security. Among them, one son named Candracchattra sat alone.

He reflected, "Is there perhaps a superior offering that surpasses this? By the Buddha's spiritual power, a deity in the sky said, "Good son, the offering of the Dharma excels all other offerings. He then asked, "What is meant by the offering of the Dharma?
The deity replied, "You should go and ask the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja; he shall extensively explain the offering of the Dharma for you. Immediately, the Moon...
Thus, the prince went to the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and standing to one side, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, among all forms of offering, the offering of Dharma is supreme. What is meant by the ‘offering of Dharma’? The Buddha said:
“Good son, the offering of Dharma refers to the profound sūtras spoken by all Buddhas, which are difficult for all the world to believe and difficult to accept.”
It is subtle, wondrous, difficult to see, pure, and unstained; it cannot be attained merely through conceptual discrimination or thought.
It is encompassed by the Dharma-treasury of the Bodhisattvas, sealed with the seal of *dhāraṇī*, and leads to non-retrogression.

It accomplishes the six perfections, skillfully discerns their meanings, accords with the Dharma of Bodhi, stands above all other sutras, enters into great compassion, and remains free from the works of Māra.
These various wrong views accord with the dharma of dependent origination—being without self, without person, without sentient beings, and without life-span;
being empty, signless, wishless, and unarisen—and are able to cause sentient beings to sit at the site of enlightenment and turn the wheel of Dharma.
They are praised by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others, and are able to cause sentient beings to enter the treasury of the Buddha-dharma and encompass all the worthy and holy ones.
The path practiced by all bodhisattvas, as taught by the All-Wise One, relies upon the meaning of the true nature of all phenomena;
it clearly proclaims the dharmas of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and cessation.

It can rescue all beings who violate the precepts, as well as māras, heterodox teachers, and those who are greedily attached; it inspires awe in them and is universally praised by all Buddhas and noble sages.
This teaching, which turns one’s back on the suffering of birth and death and reveals the bliss of nirvāṇa, has been expounded by all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Regarding the present text, at its beginning the Lord of Devas (Śakra) offers praise, saying: "Since I have heard many sūtras from the Buddha, I have never before heard this Sūtra of True Reality.
A question is raised: since the Lord of Devas had already previously heard the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras, why does he say he has not heard it?
"Have you ever heard of this true reality (*bhūtatathatā*)? The commentary explains: "The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin) is comprehensive, whereas this sutra is essential and concise. Why?

Because [the former] universally elucidates both the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and the two wisdoms of the Bodhisattva. To say that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* is comprehensive means that within it, the path is clarified from the initial resolve (*prathamacittotpāda*) up to the stage of the future Buddha (*abhiṣekasthāna*);
therefore, it is termed 'comprehensive. This sutra, however, universally elucidates the Dharma-body and the two wisdoms."
This is because [the Buddha] distinguishes between the two wisdoms of universal illumination and purity;
secondly, each has its own specific function and is called "foremost" as it is most appropriate for the particular occasion.
